cards.back: Hour 23 and hour 0 are one step apart but numerically 23 apart. Placing hours on a circle with $(\sin, \cos)$ makes neighbours close, and both are needed to tell positions apart.

cards.front: When prefer one-hot over ordinal encoding?
cards.back: When the categories have no order, particularly with linear models, which would otherwise treat the codes as magnitudes. Trees can cope with ordinal codes more easily.

cards.front: When should you use Feature Encoding (One-Hot, Target, Cyclical, Binning), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: One-hot for low-cardinality categories and linear models, target or frequency encoding for high-cardinality ones with tree or linear models, cyclical encoding for hour, weekday or angle, binning when a nonlinear step-like effect is expected, a log transform for skewed positive values.

Avoid it when: One-hot on very high-cardinality columns (huge sparse matrices), ordinal codes for unordered categories in linear models (they invent an order), and target encoding on tiny data where fold estimates are noisy. Tree ensembles often need no scaling or binning at all.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Feature Encoding (One-Hot, Target, Cyclical, Binning)?
cards.back:
• Fitting target encoding on all rows and then training on it leaks each label into its own feature; the model overfits and fails on new data
• Unseen categories at test time need a fallback, here the prior mean through $n=0$; one-hot needs an unknown-category rule
• Encoding statistics (categories, bin edges, prior) must come from training data only, never from validation or test
• A single raw number for a cyclical feature puts 23h and 0h far apart; $\sin$ alone is ambiguous, so use both $\sin$ and $\cos$

cards.front: Key formulas: Feature Encoding (One-Hot, Target, Cyclical, Binning)
cards.back:
One-hot: $e_k[j] = 1$ if $k = j$, else $0$
Target enc.: $\hat{c} = \frac{n\bar{y}_c + a\bar{y}}{n + a}$
Here $n$ counts rows in other folds, $a$ smooths
Cyclical: $(\sin\frac{2\pi x}{P}, \cos\frac{2\pi x}{P})$
Chord distance: $2\,|\sin(\pi\Delta/P)|$
Bin width $w = (x_{max}-x_{min})/k$
Bin id = floor of $(x - x_{min})/w$, max in last bin
Log transform: $z = \ln(1+x)$, $x \geq 0$

cards.front: What is Stratified Train/Test Split?
cards.back: Split data by shuffling and sampling each class separately so train and test keep (almost) the same class proportions as the full dataset.

cards.front: Stratified Train/Test Split: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A purely random split of an imbalanced dataset can, by bad luck, put too few or even zero minority samples in the test set, making the metric noisy or undefined. Sampling the same fraction from each class removes that source of variance: every class appears in test in proportion to its overall share, up to rounding.

cards.front: Why stratify?
cards.back: It keeps class proportions the same in train and test, so rare classes are represented in evaluation and metrics have lower variance.

cards.front: Does stratifying introduce bias?
cards.back: No for population-level estimates: each sample still has the same inclusion probability within its class, and the only change is removing class-count variance.

cards.front: When is stratifying the wrong tool?
cards.back: For temporal or grouped data, where you must split by time or by group to avoid leakage, and for continuous targets unless they are binned.

cards.front: How do you stratify on several columns?
cards.back: Combine them into one composite label (for example class and region) and stratify on that, making sure each combination has enough samples.

cards.front: When should you use Stratified Train/Test Split, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Classification with imbalanced or small classes, small datasets where one rare sample matters, and cross-validation folds (stratified k-fold).

Avoid it when: Time series or grouped data, where the split must respect time order or keep groups together instead (use a temporal or group split); also regression targets unless you bin them first.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Stratified Train/Test Split?
cards.back:
• Per-class rounding can make the total test size differ slightly from $f \cdot n$; sklearn allocates counts to hit it exactly, so splits are close but not identical
• A class with a single sample cannot appear in both parts; sklearn raises an error here, this code silently keeps it in train
• Stratifying does not fix leakage: duplicates or related rows can still straddle the split
• Split before preprocessing or feature selection, otherwise test statistics leak into training

cards.front: Key formulas: Stratified Train/Test Split
cards.back:
Class share: $\pi_c = \frac{n_c}{n}$
Test count per class: $k_c = \mathrm{round}(f\cdot n_c)$
Test $T = \bigcup_c$ ($k_c$ random of class $c$), train = rest
Gap: $\left|\frac{k_c}{|T|} - \pi_c\right|$ within rounding of $f\cdot n_c$
Unstratified: $k_c \sim \mathrm{Hypergeom.}$, var $> 0$ for small $n_c$

cards.front: What is K-Fold Cross-Validation?
cards.back: Estimate generalisation by splitting the data into k folds, training on k − 1 of them and scoring on the held-out one, rotating through all k.

cards.front: K-Fold Cross-Validation: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A single train/validation split wastes data and its score depends on which rows landed where. Rotating the held-out fold means every row is used for validation exactly once and for training k − 1 times, so the averaged score is steadier and the spread shows how fragile it is.

cards.front: Why k = 5 or 10 and not leave-one-out?
cards.back: Leave-one-out has low bias but the n models are highly correlated, so the estimate has high variance and costs n fits; 5 or 10 folds is a good compromise.

cards.front: Why use stratified k-fold for classification?
cards.back: It keeps the class proportions in every fold, so rare classes do not vanish from some validation folds.

cards.front: How do you tune hyperparameters without fooling yourself?
cards.back: Use nested cross-validation: an inner loop picks hyperparameters and an outer loop scores the whole selection procedure.

cards.front: When should you use K-Fold Cross-Validation, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Comparing models or hyperparameters on small to medium datasets when a single hold-out set would be too noisy or too costly in data.

Avoid it when: Skip plain shuffled k-fold for time series (use forward chaining) and grouped data (use group k-fold), and avoid it when one fit is so expensive that k fits are impractical.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of K-Fold Cross-Validation?
cards.back:
• Fitting preprocessing (scaler, imputer, feature selection) on all data before splitting leaks into the folds
• Using the CV score to tune many hyperparameters and then reporting it as final performance overfits to the folds
• Random folds on time-ordered or grouped data leak the future or the same entity

cards.front: Key formulas: K-Fold Cross-Validation
cards.back:
folds $F_1 \ldots F_k$ partition $\{1 \ldots n\}$, sizes differ $\leq 1$
$\hat{w}_{-i} = \mathrm{fit}(\mathrm{data\ outside\ } F_i)$
$\mathrm{CV} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_i \mathrm{score}(\hat{w}_{-i}, F_i)$
spread = std of the $k$ fold scores

cards.front: What is Bias-Variance Tradeoff?
cards.back: Split a model's expected squared error into bias (systematic miss), variance (sensitivity to the training sample) and irreducible noise.

cards.front: Bias-Variance Tradeoff: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Imagine retraining the same model on many fresh datasets. Bias is how far the average prediction sits from the truth; variance is how much single predictions scatter around that average. Flexible models shrink the first and inflate the second, so test error is U-shaped in complexity.

cards.front: How do you recognise high bias versus high variance from learning curves?
cards.back: High bias: train and validation error are both high and close. High variance: train error is low and validation error is much higher, with a large gap.

cards.front: How does regularisation move you along the tradeoff?
cards.back: Stronger regularisation constrains the model, which raises bias and lowers variance.

cards.front: Does more training data fix high bias?
cards.back: No. It reduces variance; a model that is too simple stays wrong however much data it sees.

cards.front: Why can test error never reach zero in this decomposition?
cards.back: The irreducible noise term $\sigma^2$ is part of every noisy target and no model can predict it.

cards.front: When should you use Bias-Variance Tradeoff, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Use it to diagnose whether a model underfits (high bias, both errors high) or overfits (high variance, big train-test gap), and to decide between more data, regularisation or a simpler or richer model.

Avoid it when: The clean decomposition is for squared loss. For 0-1 loss or very large over-parameterised networks the classical U-curve can break down (double descent), so treat it as intuition rather than a law.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Bias-Variance Tradeoff?
cards.back:
• Bias and variance cannot be computed on real data because the true $f$ is unknown; only simulation or proxies work
• Too few simulation runs give a noisy variance estimate
• Measured at one $x_0$ only; the trade-off differs across the input space

cards.front: Key formulas: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
cards.back:
$E[(y - \hat{y})^2] = \mathrm{bias}^2 + \mathrm{variance} + \sigma^2$
$\mathrm{bias}^2 = (E[\hat{y}] - f(x))^2$
$\mathrm{variance} = E[(\hat{y} - E[\hat{y}])^2]$
$\sigma^2$ = noise variance, a floor no model can beat
Expectation over training sets $D$ and noise in $y$

cards.front: What is Loss Functions for Regression and Classification?
cards.back: MSE, MAE, Huber, pinball, hinge, binary and categorical cross-entropy, each with its gradient, and why each one is a likelihood in disguise.

cards.front: Loss Functions for Regression and Classification: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A loss is a belief about the noise. Squared error is the negative log-likelihood of Gaussian noise, so it chases the mean and a single outlier drags it far. Absolute error is Laplace noise, so it chases the median and the pull of an outlier is capped. Huber is quadratic near zero and linear far away, taking the smooth gradient of MSE for small residuals and the robustness of MAE for large ones. Cross-entropy is the Bernoulli or categorical log-likelihood. The gradient tells the story: it is the residual (MSE), its sign (MAE), or the clipped residual (Huber), and for cross-entropy with logits it is simply prediction minus target. Flow: noise assumption → likelihood → loss → gradient on the prediction.

cards.front: Why does MSE correspond to Gaussian noise?
cards.back: The Gaussian negative log-likelihood is $\frac{(y-p)^2}{2\sigma^2}$ plus constants, so maximising the likelihood is minimising squared error.

cards.front: Why is MAE more robust than MSE?
cards.back: Its gradient has constant magnitude, so a large residual pulls no harder than a small one, whereas the MSE gradient grows with the residual. The MAE minimiser is the median, not the mean.

cards.front: What does Huber loss buy you?
cards.back: A smooth quadratic bowl near the optimum, which gives stable gradients, and linear tails that limit the influence of outliers. The threshold $\delta$ sets the switch.

cards.front: Why compute binary cross-entropy from logits?
cards.back: Forming $\sigma(z)$ and then $\log$ overflows or loses precision for large $|z|$. The combined form $\max(z,0) - zy + \ln(1+e^{-|z|})$ is exact and stable.

cards.front: When should you use Loss Functions for Regression and Classification, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: MSE for clean Gaussian-like targets, MAE or Huber when outliers exist, pinball for quantile forecasts, binary cross-entropy for binary labels, categorical cross-entropy for classes, hinge for margin classifiers such as SVMs.

Avoid it when: MSE on data with heavy-tailed outliers, MAE when you need a smooth gradient near zero, cross-entropy computed on probabilities that were already squashed (use the logits form), and accuracy as a training loss, since it has no useful gradient.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Loss Functions for Regression and Classification?
cards.back:
• Applying a sigmoid first and then log-loss on probabilities overflows or hits $\log 0$; use the logits form
• MAE and hinge have a kink, so the gradient there is a subgradient and is zero at the exact kink in this code
• These gradients average over the batch; summing instead multiplies the effective learning rate by $n$
• Hinge expects labels $-1$ and $+1$, whereas cross-entropy expects $0$ and $1$ (or class indices)

cards.front: Key formulas: Loss Functions for Regression and Classification
cards.back:
$\mathrm{MSE} = \mathrm{mean}((p-y)^2)$, gradient $2(p-y)/n$
$\mathrm{MAE} = \mathrm{mean}|p-y|$, gradient $\mathrm{sign}(p-y)/n$
Huber: $\frac{1}{2}r^2$ if $|r| \leq \delta$, else $\delta(|r|-\frac{1}{2}\delta)$
Huber gradient: $\mathrm{clip}(r,-\delta,\delta)/n$
Pinball: $\max(\tau r,\,(\tau-1)r)$, $r = y-p$
Hinge: $\max(0,\,1-ys)$ with $y$ = $-1$ or $1$
BCE on logit: $\max(z,0) - zy + \ln(1+e^{-|z|})$
BCE gradient: $\sigma(z) - y$
Categorical CE: $-\ln\mathrm{softmax}(z)_y = \ln\sum_j e^{z_j} - z_y$
CE gradient: $\mathrm{softmax}(z) - \mathrm{onehot}(y)$
Gaussian NLL: $\frac{(y-p)^2}{2\sigma^2} + \ln\sigma + \frac{1}{2}\ln 2\pi$
Laplace NLL: $\frac{|y-p|}{b} + \ln 2b$

cards.front: What is Precision, Recall and F1?
cards.back: Score a binary classifier by how clean its positive predictions are (precision), how many real positives it finds (recall), and their harmonic mean (F1).

cards.front: Precision, Recall and F1: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Accuracy hides the cost of rare positives, because predicting "negative" everywhere looks great. Precision asks "when I raise an alarm, how often am I right?" and recall asks "of the real events, how many did I catch?". The harmonic mean punishes a lopsided pair, so F1 is high only when both are.

cards.front: Why the harmonic mean rather than the arithmetic mean?
cards.back: The harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller value, so a model cannot hide a very low recall behind a high precision.

cards.front: How does raising the threshold move precision and recall?
cards.back: Fewer samples are called positive, so precision usually rises and recall falls.

cards.front: When prefer recall over precision?
cards.back: When misses are costlier than false alarms, such as screening for a serious disease.

cards.front: Why is accuracy misleading on imbalanced data?
cards.back: A classifier that always predicts the majority class scores high accuracy while finding no positives.

cards.front: When should you use Precision, Recall and F1, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Imbalanced problems such as fraud, defect or disease detection, and any time false positives and false negatives have different costs.

Avoid it when: Avoid F1 alone when the two error types have very different costs (use an F-beta or a cost-based metric), or when true negatives matter, or for threshold-free comparison (use ROC-AUC or PR-AUC).

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Precision, Recall and F1?
cards.back:
• Precision and recall are undefined with no predicted or no actual positives; pick an explicit convention
• Micro, macro and weighted averages tell different stories on imbalanced classes
• F1 depends on the threshold, so compare models at tuned thresholds
• Ignores true negatives, which can hide poor performance on the majority class

cards.front: Key formulas: Precision, Recall and F1
cards.back:
$\mathrm{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}$
$\mathrm{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$
$F_1 = \frac{2 \cdot P \cdot R}{P + R}$
$F_1 = \frac{2 \cdot TP}{2 \cdot TP + FP + FN}$
$F_\beta = \frac{(1 + \beta^2)\cdot P \cdot R}{\beta^2 \cdot P + R}$

cards.front: What is ROC Curve and AUC?
cards.back: Sweep the decision threshold, plot true-positive rate against false-positive rate, and summarise the curve by its area (AUC).

cards.front: ROC Curve and AUC: what is the key insight?
cards.back: AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative, so it measures ranking quality and ignores calibration and the chosen threshold. A curve hugging the top-left corner means positives are almost always ranked above negatives.

cards.front: What is the probabilistic meaning of AUC?
cards.back: The chance that a random positive scores higher than a random negative, with ties counting half.

cards.front: Does AUC depend on calibration?
cards.back: No. Any monotonic transform of the scores leaves the ranking, and so the AUC, unchanged.

cards.front: When is PR-AUC better than ROC-AUC?
cards.back: When positives are rare: FPR stays small even with many false positives, while precision exposes them.

cards.front: When should you use ROC Curve and AUC, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Comparing classifiers independent of threshold, or when the operating point is not yet known, and when classes are not extremely imbalanced.

Avoid it when: With heavy imbalance the false-positive rate hides many false alarms, so prefer a precision-recall curve. It also says nothing about calibration.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of ROC Curve and AUC?
cards.back:
• Needs both classes present, otherwise TPR or FPR is undefined
• Treating tied scores as ordered inflates or deflates AUC
• Optimistic on highly imbalanced data; check PR-AUC too
• Using hard 0/1 predictions instead of scores collapses the curve to one point

cards.front: Key formulas: ROC Curve and AUC
cards.back:
$\mathrm{TPR} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN},\;\; \mathrm{FPR} = \frac{FP}{FP + TN}$
$\mathrm{AUC} = \int \mathrm{TPR}\ d(\mathrm{FPR})$
$\mathrm{AUC} = P(s^+ > s^-) + \frac{1}{2}P(s^+ = s^-)$
$\mathrm{AUC} = \frac{U}{n_+ \cdot n_-}$
Trapezoid rule: $\sum \Delta\mathrm{fpr}\cdot\frac{\mathrm{tpr}_i + \mathrm{tpr}_{i-1}}{2}$

cards.front: What is Pipelines and ColumnTransformer (Leakage-Safe Preprocessing)?
cards.back: Every transformer learns its statistics in fit and applies them in transform. A Pipeline chains steps, a ColumnTransformer routes column subsets to different transformers, and fitting only on training rows keeps validation and test data out of the preprocessing.

cards.front: Pipelines and ColumnTransformer (Leakage-Safe Preprocessing): what is the key insight?
cards.back: Preprocessing is a learned function, not a fixed one: the mean, the scale and the category list are parameters estimated from data. If they are estimated on rows the model is later scored on, information leaks. Packing preprocessing and model into one object makes the right order automatic, because a single $\mathrm{fit}$ call sees only the rows it was handed, and a single $\mathrm{predict}$ reuses those frozen statistics. Flow: fit on train → transform train → transform val/test with train stats.

cards.front: Why put the scaler inside the pipeline instead of scaling first?
cards.back: Scaling first fits on all rows, including validation folds, which leaks. Inside the pipeline, cross-validation refits the scaler on each training fold only.

cards.front: What does a ColumnTransformer do with the outputs?
cards.back: It fits one transformer per column subset, transforms each subset, and concatenates the results side by side in the order given.

cards.front: What is the difference between fit_transform and fit then transform?
cards.back: Usually none in value; fit_transform is a shortcut and may be faster. It is applied to training data only, never to test data.

cards.front: Why clone a transformer before fitting it?
cards.back: A fitted object holds state from its rows. Fitting a copy lets one unfitted template be reused for every fold without leftover statistics.

cards.front: When should you use Pipelines and ColumnTransformer (Leakage-Safe Preprocessing), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any workflow with preprocessing before a model, especially mixed numeric and categorical tables, cross-validation and hyperparameter search, where preprocessing must be refit inside every fold.

Avoid it when: Stateless transforms such as a fixed $\log$ need no fitting, and a model that handles raw categories natively (some tree libraries) may not need an encoder. Do not use one global fit just because it is convenient.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Pipelines and ColumnTransformer (Leakage-Safe Preprocessing)?
cards.back:
• Calling fit or fit_transform on validation or test data silently recomputes the statistics and leaks
• An unseen category at test time breaks or silently shifts a naive encoder; real encoders need an ignore option
• Column order matters: the output block order follows the transformer list, not the input columns, so mappings of features to coefficients must use the output order
• Standardising a constant column divides by $\sigma = 0$; real scalers guard against it

cards.front: Key formulas: Pipelines and ColumnTransformer (Leakage-Safe Preprocessing)
cards.back:
$z = \frac{x - \mu_{\mathrm{train}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{train}}}$
Statistics from training rows only: $\mu_{\mathrm{train}}$
One-hot: $\mathrm{onehot}(x)_k = [x = c_k]$
Concat: $X^{\prime} = [\,T_1(X_{S_1}) \,|\, T_2(X_{S_2})\,]$
Chain: $X_{i+1} = T_i(X_i)$, then $\hat{y} = f(X_L)$
Centred fit: minimise $\|A\beta - t\|^2$

cards.front: What is Perceptron Learning Rule?
cards.back: Predict $\mathrm{sign}(w \cdot x + b)$ and, only on a mistake, nudge the weights towards the misclassified point. On linearly separable data it stops after a bounded number of mistakes; on XOR it never settles.

cards.front: Perceptron Learning Rule: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A mistake means the current hyperplane is on the wrong side of $x$, and adding $y\,x$ to $w$ rotates it towards the correct side of that point. Correct points cause no change at all, so the learner is purely mistake driven. Each update also increases the alignment with any true separator by at least the margin $\gamma$, while the weight norm grows only like $R\sqrt{k}$, which squeezes the number of mistakes $k$ below $(R/\gamma)^2$. Flow: predict → mistake? → add $y\,x$ → repeat until a clean pass.

cards.front: What is Novikoff's theorem?
cards.back: If the data is linearly separable with margin gamma and every point has norm at most R, the perceptron makes at most (R/gamma)^2 mistakes, regardless of the order and of the learning rate when starting from zero.

cards.front: What happens on XOR?
cards.back: No line separates XOR, so every pass contains a mistake and the weights cycle forever. A hidden layer or a feature such as the product of the inputs fixes it.

cards.front: How does the perceptron relate to logistic regression and the SVM?
cards.back: Logistic regression replaces the hard mistake test by a smooth loss and gives probabilities. The SVM also seeks a separator but picks the maximum-margin one, while the perceptron returns any separator.

cards.front: Does the learning rate matter?
cards.back: Starting from zero, scaling the rate only rescales $w$ and $b$, so the predictions and mistake count do not change.

cards.front: When should you use Perceptron Learning Rule, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Teaching the mistake-driven update, quick online baselines on data that is close to linearly separable, and as the unit that a neural network stacks: one neuron with a step activation.

Avoid it when: Non-separable problems (it oscillates forever), when calibrated probabilities are needed, or when a good margin matters; use logistic regression or a maximum-margin SVM instead.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Perceptron Learning Rule?
cards.back:
• Never converges when the data is not separable; always cap the epochs and track the training error
• The result depends on the example order and is not the maximum-margin separator, so it can generalise worse than an SVM
• Zero scores count as mistakes; using a strict test instead keeps the all-zero start from ever updating
• The bound uses the norm of the input including the constant bias feature

cards.front: Key formulas: Perceptron Learning Rule
cards.back:
Predict: $\hat{y} = \mathrm{sign}(w \cdot x + b)$
Mistake if $y\,(w \cdot x + b) \leq 0$
Update: $w \leftarrow w + \eta\,y\,x$, $b \leftarrow b + \eta\,y$
$\gamma = \min_i \frac{y_i\,(w^* \cdot x_i)}{\|w^*\|}$, $R = \max_i \|x_i\|$
After $k$ mistakes: $w \cdot w^* \geq k\eta\gamma$
and $\|w\|^2 \leq k\eta^2 R^2$, so $k \leq (R/\gamma)^2$

cards.front: What is Reverse-Mode Autograd Engine (Micrograd)?
cards.back: Each scalar Value remembers its parents and a tiny local backward rule. The forward pass builds the graph, and backward sorts it topologically and sweeps it in reverse, accumulating gradients with addition.

cards.front: Reverse-Mode Autograd Engine (Micrograd): what is the key insight?
cards.back: The chain rule needs no symbolic algebra: every operation only has to know its own local derivative, and the graph glues them together. A node that feeds two later operations receives two gradient contributions, one per use, so they must be added with $+=$, never assigned. Visiting nodes in reverse topological order guarantees that a node's gradient is complete before it passes anything to its parents. Flow: forward builds graph → sort → reverse sweep → accumulate grads.

cards.front: Why does backward use += and not =?
cards.back: A node used in several places receives a gradient from each use, and the total derivative is their sum. Assignment would keep only the last one.

cards.front: Why is a topological order needed?
cards.back: A node may only pass gradient to its parents after all its consumers have added theirs. Reverse topological order ensures that.

cards.front: Why do we zero gradients between steps?
cards.back: Gradients accumulate across backward calls. Without zeroing, stale values are added to the new ones, so leaf gradients come out wrong (exactly doubled for a single operation, more in deeper graphs). Training loops zero them before each step.

cards.front: Why is reverse mode used for neural networks and not forward mode?
cards.back: Training has one scalar loss and millions of parameters. Reverse mode gets all parameter gradients in one sweep, while forward mode needs one pass per input.

cards.front: When should you use Reverse-Mode Autograd Engine (Micrograd), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Understanding how a deep learning framework computes gradients, and checking hand-derived gradients on small graphs. The same mechanism, on tensors and with fused kernels, is what runs under every training loop.

Avoid it when: Anything real-sized: scalar Python objects are thousands of times slower than tensor kernels, and the engine has no broadcasting, no in-place checks and no memory-saving tricks.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Reverse-Mode Autograd Engine (Micrograd)?
cards.back:
• Using = instead of += in a local backward breaks any graph where a node is reused
• Not zeroing gradients between backward calls adds stale values to the new ones; leaves double for one operation and inflate further in deeper graphs
• Recursive graph traversal hits Python's recursion limit on very deep graphs; use an explicit stack
• The ReLU derivative at $0$ is a convention (here $0$); frameworks may differ in edge cases

cards.front: Key formulas: Reverse-Mode Autograd Engine (Micrograd)
cards.back:
Total: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_i} = \sum_j \frac{\partial L}{\partial z_j}\frac{\partial z_j}{\partial x_i}$
Add: $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 1$, $\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = 1$
Mul: $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = y$, $\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = x$
Power: $z = x^p$, $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = p\,x^{p-1}$
Tanh: $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 1 - z^2$
Exp: $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = z$
ReLU: $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = [x > 0]$
Rule: $g_{x_i} \leftarrow g_{x_i} + \frac{\partial z_j}{\partial x_i} g_{z_j}$

cards.front: What is AdamW Decoupled Weight Decay?
cards.back: Adam with L2 puts the decay term inside the gradient, where the adaptive denominator rescales it. AdamW subtracts the decay from the weights directly, so every weight shrinks at the same rate.

cards.front: AdamW Decoupled Weight Decay: what is the key insight?
cards.back: With L2 regularisation the penalty gradient $\lambda w$ is added to $g$ and then divided by $\sqrt{\hat{v}}$ like everything else, so a weight with a large gradient history is decayed less, and one with a small history is decayed more. That is not what weight decay means. AdamW takes the decay out of the gradient and applies it as a separate shrink $-\eta\lambda w$, so the regularisation strength no longer depends on the gradient scale and is easier to tune. Flow: gradient + history → adaptive step → separate decay → update.

cards.front: Why is L2 regularisation not the same as weight decay in Adam?
cards.back: The L2 term enters the gradient and is divided by the adaptive denominator, so weights with large gradient history are decayed less. Weight decay should shrink all weights by the same factor.

cards.front: What does AdamW change in the update?
cards.back: It adds $\lambda w$ to the final step, outside the ratio $\hat{m}/(\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon)$, instead of to the gradient.

cards.front: What happens to AdamW weights when the gradient is zero?
cards.back: The moments decay but the decay term still applies, so the weight keeps shrinking by about $\eta\lambda w$ each step.

cards.front: When should you use AdamW Decoupled Weight Decay, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Training transformers and most modern networks with Adam-style optimisers when weight decay is wanted; it is the standard choice.

Avoid it when: With plain SGD, where L2 regularisation and weight decay are equivalent and no change is needed. Decay is also usually skipped for biases and normalisation parameters.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of AdamW Decoupled Weight Decay?
cards.back:
• Passing the L2 coefficient to Adam and calling it weight decay; the behaviour differs from AdamW
• Applying the decay to biases and normalisation scales, which usually should not be decayed
• Assuming $\lambda$ is comparable across libraries; some scale the decay by the learning rate and some do not

cards.front: Key formulas: AdamW Decoupled Weight Decay
cards.back:
Adam+L2: $g^{\prime} = g + \lambda w$, then the Adam step
Effective L2 decay: $\frac{\eta\lambda w}{\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon}$
AdamW: $w \leftarrow w - \eta\left(\frac{\hat{m}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon} + \lambda w\right)$
Decay alone shrinks $w$ by $(1-\eta\lambda)$

cards.front: What is PyTorch Training Loop Anatomy?
cards.back: One training step is zero the gradients, forward, loss, backward, optionally clip, then step. Evaluation switches to eval mode and turns off gradient tracking.

cards.front: PyTorch Training Loop Anatomy: what is the key insight?
cards.back: PyTorch accumulates into .grad on every backward call instead of overwriting it, so the order of the steps carries the meaning. Clear first, or old gradients leak into the new step. Clip after backward (the gradient must exist) and before step (it must be used). The same accumulation lets $k$ microbatches imitate one large batch: scale each loss by $1/k$ and the summed gradient is the mean over all of the data. Dropout and batch norm act differently in train and eval mode, so evaluation also needs the mode switch. Flow: zero_grad → forward → loss → backward → clip → step.

cards.front: Why must zero_grad be called every step?
cards.back: Backward adds into the existing gradients rather than replacing them, so without clearing, the gradient is the sum over steps.

cards.front: How does gradient accumulation match a large batch?
cards.back: Scale each microbatch mean loss by $1/k$, call backward on each, and step once; the summed gradient equals the gradient of the mean over all samples.

cards.front: What do model.eval() and torch.no_grad() each do?
cards.back: eval switches layers such as dropout and batch norm to inference behaviour; no_grad stops graph construction. They are independent, so evaluation needs both.

cards.front: Where does gradient clipping go?
cards.back: After backward, so gradients exist, and before the optimiser step, so the step uses the clipped values.

cards.front: When should you use PyTorch Training Loop Anatomy, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Every PyTorch training job; gradient accumulation when the desired batch does not fit in memory, clipping when loss spikes appear.

Avoid it when: Accumulation does not reproduce batch statistics for batch norm, and with a sum-reduced or uneven microbatch loss the $1/k$ scaling must be adjusted. Clipping hides problems if gradients are constantly clipped.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of PyTorch Training Loop Anatomy?
cards.back:
• Forgetting zero_grad, so each step uses the sum of all past gradients
• Forgetting model.eval() or no_grad, which keeps dropout active and wastes memory in evaluation
• Not dividing each microbatch loss by $k$, which makes the update $k$ times too large
• Clipping before backward or after step, which has no effect on the update

cards.front: Key formulas: PyTorch Training Loop Anatomy
cards.back:
Large batch: $g = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\nabla \ell_i$
Microbatch $j$ loss $L_j$ (mean over its samples)
Accumulated: $\sum_{j}\nabla\frac{L_j}{k} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j}\nabla L_j = g$
Clip: $g \leftarrow g\cdot\min\left(1,\frac{\tau}{\|g\|}\right)$

cards.front: What is GPU Roofline Model?
cards.back: An operation is limited either by how fast the chip computes or by how fast it moves data. The roofline model predicts which one, from the FLOPs per byte the operation performs.

cards.front: GPU Roofline Model: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A GPU has a compute ceiling and a memory-bandwidth ceiling, and each operation hits whichever it reaches first. Arithmetic intensity, the FLOPs done per byte moved, decides it: a large matmul reuses every loaded number many times and saturates compute, while an elementwise add, softmax or layer norm touches each number once and waits on memory. LLM decoding is the extreme case, since each token streams all the weights to do about two FLOPs per weight, so batching (reusing the loaded weights for many tokens) and fused kernels such as FlashAttention (fewer bytes moved) are the main levers. Flow: FLOPs ÷ bytes → intensity → compare to ridge → memory or compute bound.

cards.front: What is arithmetic intensity?
cards.back: The number of FLOPs an operation performs per byte it moves to or from memory. It measures how much each loaded value is reused.

cards.front: Why is LLM decoding memory-bound at batch size 1?
cards.back: Each token reads every weight once but does only about two FLOPs per weight, so the intensity is far below the ridge point and speed is set by bandwidth divided by weight bytes.

cards.front: Why does batching raise decoding throughput?
cards.back: The weights are loaded once per step and reused for every sequence in the batch, so tokens per step grow while bytes per step stay the same, until compute becomes the limit.

cards.front: How does FlashAttention help in roofline terms?
cards.back: It does the same FLOPs but avoids writing and re-reading the large score matrix, so bytes moved fall and intensity rises.

cards.front: When should you use GPU Roofline Model, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Reasoning about why an operation or model is slow, estimating the best possible speed before profiling, and deciding whether to add compute, bandwidth, batching or kernel fusion.

Avoid it when: As an exact predictor. Real kernels also lose time to launch overhead, poor occupancy, caches and communication, so the roofline is an upper bound on speed rather than an estimate of it.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of GPU Roofline Model?
cards.back:
• Counting only the inputs; the output write is also traffic, and intermediate tensors that are written and re-read add more
• Treating a matmul as always compute-bound; with a small $m$ (small batch) its intensity falls below the ridge point
• Mixing units, such as FLOPs versus multiply-adds, or bits versus bytes, which shifts the ridge point by a factor of 2 or 8
• Reading the roofline as achieved speed; it is only the ceiling

cards.front: Key formulas: GPU Roofline Model
cards.back:
Matmul FLOPs: $2mkn$
Bytes moved: $b\,(mk + kn + mn)$
Intensity: $I = \frac{\mathrm{FLOPs}}{\mathrm{bytes}}$
Attainable: $\min(P,\; B \cdot I)$
Ridge point: $I^{*} = \frac{P}{B}$
Elementwise add: $I = \frac{n}{3bn} = \frac{1}{3b}$
Decode bound: $\frac{\mathrm{batch} \cdot B}{\mathrm{weight\ bytes}}$

cards.front: What is Text Preprocessing, Stemming and Lemmatisation?
cards.back: Turn raw text into clean tokens: lowercase, strip punctuation, split, drop stop words, then collapse word variants with a suffix-stripping stemmer or a dictionary lemmatiser.

cards.front: Text Preprocessing, Stemming and Lemmatisation: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A model that counts words sees "run", "runs" and "running" as three unrelated symbols, which splits the evidence for one idea. A stemmer merges them cheaply by chopping suffixes with rules, so its output may not be a real word ("ponies" becomes "poni"). A lemmatiser looks each word up in a dictionary and returns the true base form, so it maps "ran" to "run" and "mice" to "mouse", at the cost of needing a lexicon. Flow: raw text → lowercase → tokens → stop words out → stems.

cards.front: What is the difference between stemming and lemmatisation?
cards.back: A stemmer chops suffixes with rules and may output a non-word such as poni. A lemmatiser uses a dictionary and part of speech to return a real base form, so it handles ran to run and mice to mouse but is slower.

cards.front: Why remove stop words, and when is it harmful?
cards.back: They are very frequent and add little topic signal to counts. They matter for negation, phrases and language models, so removing them hurts sentiment and generation tasks.

cards.front: What is over-stemming and under-stemming?
cards.back: Over-stemming merges unrelated words into one stem; under-stemming leaves related words apart, such as ran and running. Aggressive rules trade one error for the other.

cards.front: When should you use Text Preprocessing, Stemming and Lemmatisation, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Bag-of-words, TF-IDF and search pipelines where vocabulary size and sparsity matter, and classical models that cannot share statistics between word forms on their own.

Avoid it when: Pretrained subword or transformer models, which expect raw text and its own tokenizer. Stripping stop words or suffixes also destroys negation and tense ("not good", "was") that some tasks need.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Text Preprocessing, Stemming and Lemmatisation?
cards.back:
• Apply the same preprocessing at training and inference time, or the vocabulary will not match
• This simplified stemmer covers only a few rules; words like branches or hoped need later Porter steps and come out differently
• Stemming ignores meaning, so unrelated words can collide and irregular forms such as ran stay apart

cards.front: Key formulas: Text Preprocessing, Stemming and Lemmatisation
cards.back:
Tokens: lowercase, keep letter and digit runs
Plurals: $\mathrm{ies}\rightarrow\mathrm{i}$, $\mathrm{sses}\rightarrow\mathrm{ss}$
Drop ing or ed if a vowel is left
Merging forms gives $|V_{stem}| \leq |V_{raw}|$

cards.front: What is Bag of Words and the N-gram Language Model?
cards.back: Bag of words counts each word per document and ignores order. A bigram language model counts adjacent word pairs and turns them into smoothed next-word probabilities.

cards.front: Bag of Words and the N-gram Language Model: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Bag of words keeps what words appear and throws away where, which is enough for topic-like tasks. A language model needs order, and the Markov trick makes it tractable: assume the next word depends only on the previous one, so a table of pair counts is the whole model. Unseen pairs would get probability zero and wreck any sentence that contains one, so add-$k$ smoothing moves a little mass to every pair. Flow: tokens → counts → smoothed probabilities → sentence log-prob.

cards.front: Why do n-gram models need smoothing?
cards.back: A pair never seen in training gets probability zero, which makes any sentence containing it impossible and perplexity infinite. Smoothing reserves some mass for unseen events.

cards.front: What is the downside of add-one smoothing?
cards.back: With a large vocabulary it takes too much mass from seen events. Using a small $k$, or better methods such as backoff and Kneser-Ney, works better in practice.

cards.front: Why use log probabilities for sentences?
cards.back: Multiplying many small probabilities underflows, while adding their logs is stable and gives the quantity used to compute perplexity.

cards.front: What does bag of words lose?
cards.back: Word order and context, so "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" get the same vector.

cards.front: When should you use Bag of Words and the N-gram Language Model, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Strong, cheap baselines: bag of words for classification and retrieval features, and n-gram models for quick language scoring, spelling correction and as a comparison for neural models.

Avoid it when: Tasks that depend on word order, long-range context or meaning, where one-hot counts treat "good" and "great" as unrelated. Large $n$ makes the count table huge and mostly empty.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Bag of Words and the N-gram Language Model?
cards.back:
• The row for the end marker has no observed successors, so smoothing makes it uniform; it is never used as a context when scoring
• Words not in the vocabulary raise a KeyError here; real systems map them to an unknown token
• Log-probabilities of sentences of different length are not comparable without normalising by length

cards.front: Key formulas: Bag of Words and the N-gram Language Model
cards.back:
BoW: $X_{d,w}$ = count of word $w$ in doc $d$
$P(w \mid \mathrm{prev}) = \frac{c(\mathrm{prev}, w) + k}{c(\mathrm{prev}) + kV}$
Rows sum to one: $\sum_{w} P(w \mid \mathrm{prev}) = 1$
$\log P(w_{1:T}) = \sum_{t} \log P(w_t \mid w_{t-1})$

cards.front: What is TF-IDF?
cards.back: Represent each document as a vector of word counts, rescaled so that words found in few documents count more than words found everywhere.

cards.front: TF-IDF: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A word that appears in nearly every document says little about any one of them, while a word concentrated in a few documents is a strong signature. Multiplying the term count by the log of inverse document frequency keeps the frequent-here, rare-elsewhere words and mutes filler such as "the".

cards.front: Why take the log in idf?
cards.back: It damps the ratio $N/\mathrm{df}$ so that a very rare word does not dominate, and it makes the weight behave like an information measure.

cards.front: Why normalise rows?
cards.back: Long documents have larger counts. L2 normalisation makes rows comparable and turns the dot product into cosine similarity.

cards.front: How does TF-IDF differ from word embeddings?
cards.back: TF-IDF vectors are sparse, one dimension per word, and carry no notion of meaning. Embeddings are dense and learned so similar words lie close together.

cards.front: When should you use TF-IDF, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Strong, fast baseline features for text classification, search ranking and document similarity, especially with linear models and small datasets.

Avoid it when: It ignores word order and meaning, so synonyms look unrelated. Prefer learned embeddings or transformers when semantics matter, and note that idf must be fitted on training data only.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of TF-IDF?
cards.back:
• Fitting idf on the full dataset leaks test statistics into training
• This sketch splits on spaces only; real tokenisation handles case and punctuation
• The dense matrix is huge for real vocabularies; use sparse storage
• Variants differ (log base, smoothing, norm), so scores are not portable between libraries

cards.front: Key formulas: TF-IDF
cards.back:
$\mathrm{tf}(t,d)$ = count of term $t$ in document $d$
$\mathrm{df}(t)$ = number of documents containing $t$
$\mathrm{idf}(t) = \ln\frac{1+N}{1+\mathrm{df}(t)} + 1$ (smooth form)
$x(t,d) = \mathrm{tf}(t,d)\cdot\mathrm{idf}(t)$
Row norm: $x(d) \leftarrow \frac{x(d)}{\|x(d)\|_2}$
Cosine of two rows = dot product after L2 norm

cards.front: What is Word2Vec Skip-gram?
cards.back: Learn a dense vector for every word by training it to predict the words that appear in a small window around it.

cards.front: Word2Vec Skip-gram: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Words used in similar contexts must give similar predictions about their neighbours, so the training signal forces them toward similar vectors. No labels are needed: the text supplies its own targets, and the vectors are the by-product of solving the prediction task.

cards.front: How does skip-gram differ from CBOW?
cards.back: Skip-gram predicts each context word from the centre word, while CBOW predicts the centre word from the averaged context. Skip-gram handles rare words better.

cards.front: Why is negative sampling used?
cards.back: The softmax normalises over the whole vocabulary on every pair. Negative sampling contrasts the true pair with a few random words, making each step cheap.

cards.front: Why are there two embedding matrices?
cards.back: A word plays two roles, centre and context. Separate tables keep the scores asymmetric, and the input table is usually kept as the final embedding.

cards.front: When should you use Word2Vec Skip-gram, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Cheap unsupervised word features from a large unlabelled corpus, or to understand how embeddings are trained before moving to contextual models.

Avoid it when: Each word has one vector regardless of context, so polysemy is lost. Use contextual encoders for that. The full softmax here is too slow for large vocabularies.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Word2Vec Skip-gram?
cards.back:
• The full softmax costs O(V) per pair; real implementations use negative sampling or hierarchical softmax
• The returned centre gradient applies to row c of W only; the rest of W has zero gradient
• Very frequent words dominate the pairs unless subsampled
• Two tables are learned; using only the input table is the usual convention

cards.front: Key formulas: Word2Vec Skip-gram
cards.back:
Pair $(c, o)$: predict context $o$ from centre $c$
$s = U v_c$ (one score per vocabulary word)
$p = \mathrm{softmax}(s)$
$L = -\log p_o$
$\frac{\partial L}{\partial s} = p - \mathrm{onehot}(o)$
$\frac{\partial L}{\partial U} = (p - \mathrm{onehot}(o))\,v_c^{\top}$
$\frac{\partial L}{\partial v_c} = U^{\top}(p - \mathrm{onehot}(o))$
Negative sampling: a few sigmoid terms, not softmax

cards.front: What is GloVe Embeddings?
cards.back: Learn word vectors by fitting the dot product of two vectors plus biases to the log of the word-word co-occurrence count, using weighted least squares.

cards.front: GloVe Embeddings: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Word2vec learns from one context window at a time; GloVe first sums the whole corpus into a co-occurrence matrix and then factorises it. The target is the log count, so that differences of vectors encode ratios of co-occurrence probabilities, which is what separates "ice" from "steam". The weight $f(x)$ caps the influence of very frequent pairs and shrinks noisy rare ones. Flow: corpus → co-occurrence matrix → log counts → weighted fit → vectors.

cards.front: How does GloVe differ from word2vec skip-gram?
cards.back: Skip-gram trains on local windows with a predictive loss, while GloVe fits global co-occurrence counts with a weighted least-squares loss. Both give similar quality when tuned well.

cards.front: Why fit the log of the counts?
cards.back: Ratios of co-occurrence probabilities carry meaning, and a log turns a ratio into a difference, which a linear dot-product model can represent.

cards.front: What does the weighting function do?
cards.back: It sets the weight to zero for unseen pairs, shrinks rare noisy counts, and caps frequent pairs at 1 so very common words do not dominate.

cards.front: When should you use GloVe Embeddings, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Static word vectors that use global corpus statistics, trained fast from a count matrix, as features for classical models or for initialising small neural NLP models.

Avoid it when: Tasks needing context-dependent meaning, where contextual models give a different vector for each occurrence. Polysemy and unseen words are not handled by a single static vector per word.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of GloVe Embeddings?
cards.back:
• The loss uses $\log X_{ij}$, so sum only over non-zero entries; a zero count gives minus infinity
• Initialise vectors with small random values; identical vectors never separate
• A fixed learning rate on raw counts can diverge; the paper uses AdaGrad

cards.front: Key formulas: GloVe Embeddings
cards.back:
$J = \sum_{i,j} f(X_{ij})\, r_{ij}^{2}$
Residual: $r_{ij} = w_i \cdot \tilde{w}_j + b_i + \tilde{b}_j - \log X_{ij}$
Weight: $f(x) = \min\left(1, (x / x_{max})^{\alpha}\right)$
$\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_i} = \sum_{j} 2 f(X_{ij})\, r_{ij}\, \tilde{w}_j$
Step: $w \leftarrow w - \eta \frac{\partial J}{\partial w}$

cards.front: What is Perplexity of a Language Model?
cards.back: The exponential of the average negative log-likelihood per token; how many equally likely choices the model is effectively hesitating between at each step.

cards.front: Perplexity of a Language Model: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Cross-entropy in nats is hard to feel, but its exponential has a concrete reading: a model that spreads probability uniformly over V tokens has perplexity V. A lower value therefore means the model is effectively choosing among fewer candidates, so it assigns higher probability to the text it actually sees.

cards.front: What does a perplexity of V mean?
cards.back: On average the model is as uncertain as if it picked uniformly among V tokens at each step.

cards.front: Why must the tokenizer be the same when comparing perplexities?
cards.back: Perplexity is per token. A tokenizer that splits text into more tokens spreads the same information over more steps, so per-token numbers are not comparable.

cards.front: How is perplexity related to bits per token?
cards.back: Bits per token is the cross-entropy in base 2, and perplexity equals 2 raised to that value, the same quantity as the natural-log version.

cards.front: When should you use Perplexity of a Language Model, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Comparing language models on the same text and tokenizer, tracking validation loss during pretraining, and detecting distribution shift.

Avoid it when: Comparing models with different tokenizers or vocabularies, where values are not comparable, or judging quality of generated text, since low perplexity does not guarantee helpful or factual output.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Perplexity of a Language Model?
cards.back:
• Average over all tokens, not per sequence, or short sequences are over-weighted
• Evaluate with enough context; truncated windows inflate perplexity
• Mask padding tokens in real code; this version assumes every target is a real token

cards.front: Key formulas: Perplexity of a Language Model
cards.back:
$\log p_i = z_i - \log \sum_j \exp(z_j)$
$\mathrm{CE} = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_n \log p(y_n\,|\,\mathrm{context}_n)$
$\mathrm{PPL} = \exp(\mathrm{CE})$
$\mathrm{PPL} = \left(\prod_n \frac{1}{p(y_n\,|\,\mathrm{context}_n)}\right)^{1/N}$
Uniform over $V$ tokens: $\mathrm{PPL} = V$

cards.front: What is Transformer Feed-Forward Network (GELU and SwiGLU)?
cards.back: The position-wise feed-forward network expands each token from $d$ to a wider hidden size, applies a nonlinearity and projects back; the gated SwiGLU variant multiplies a SiLU branch by a linear branch.

cards.front: Transformer Feed-Forward Network (GELU and SwiGLU): what is the key insight?
cards.back: Attention only mixes tokens linearly, so the feed-forward network is where each token gets its nonlinear processing, and most of a block's parameters live there. A gated unit lets one linear branch decide, per hidden unit, how much of the other branch passes, which is a richer nonlinearity for the same parameter budget once the hidden size is shrunk to about $\frac{8}{3}d$. Flow: token vector → expand → gate or activate → project back.

cards.front: Why is the gated hidden size about 8d/3 instead of 4d?
cards.back: The gated form has three weight matrices instead of two. Using $h = \frac{8}{3}d$ gives $3dh = 8d^2$, the same count as the $4d$ ungated FFN.

cards.front: What is the difference between exact GELU and the tanh approximation?
cards.back: Exact GELU uses the Gaussian CDF via erf; the tanh form is a cheap polynomial-inside-tanh fit that differs by about $10^{-3}$ at most.

cards.front: Why do gated FFNs help?
cards.back: The elementwise product of two projections gives each hidden unit a learned input-dependent gate, a multiplicative interaction that improves quality at matched parameters.

cards.front: When should you use Transformer Feed-Forward Network (GELU and SwiGLU), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Inside every transformer block. Use GELU for the classic BERT or GPT-2 style FFN, and SwiGLU when following modern LLM designs that report better quality at matched parameters.

Avoid it when: When the model has no token-wise MLP at all, or on tiny models where the extra weight matrix and the hidden-size bookkeeping buy little.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Transformer Feed-Forward Network (GELU and SwiGLU)?
cards.back:
• Comparing a gated and an ungated FFN at the same $h$ gives the gated one 50% more parameters
• The tanh and erf GELU variants differ slightly, so match the variant a checkpoint was trained with
• SwiGLU needs three matrices; loading weights with only $W_1$ and $W_2$ silently breaks the layer

cards.front: Key formulas: Transformer Feed-Forward Network (GELU and SwiGLU)
cards.back:
FFN: $\mathrm{FFN}(x) = \mathrm{GELU}(xW_1 + b_1)\,W_2 + b_2$
GELU: $x\,\Phi(x) = \frac{1}{2}x\left(1 + \mathrm{erf}\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$
Tanh form: $\approx \frac{1}{2}x\left(1 + \tanh\left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}(x + 0.044715x^3)\right)\right)$
SiLU: $\mathrm{silu}(x) = x\,\sigma(x) = \frac{x}{1 + e^{-x}}$
SwiGLU: $(\mathrm{silu}(xW_1) \odot xW_3)\,W_2$
Params: $2 \cdot d \cdot 4d = 8d^2$ vs $3dh$, $h = \frac{8}{3}d$

cards.front: What is Causal Masking in Attention?
cards.back: Set the attention scores for future positions to minus infinity before the softmax, so each token mixes only itself and earlier tokens.

cards.front: Causal Masking in Attention: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A language model is trained to predict token $t+1$ from tokens up to $t$, so if position $t$ could see later tokens it would simply copy the answer. Masking the upper triangle of the score matrix makes every row a distribution over the past only, which lets one forward pass train all next-token predictions in parallel without leaking the future.

cards.front: Why mask before the softmax rather than zero the weights after?
cards.back: Zeroing after the softmax leaves rows that no longer sum to 1 and still lets the future affect the normaliser. Masking scores with $-\infty$ gives exact zeros and a correct normalisation.

cards.front: How does one forward pass train every position at once?
cards.back: With the mask, row $t$ only uses tokens up to $t$, so the loss on every next token can be computed together without the model seeing its own targets.

cards.front: How is a causal mask different from a padding mask?
cards.back: The causal mask hides future positions and is the same for every sequence; a padding mask hides pad tokens and depends on each sequence's length. They are usually combined.

cards.front: When should you use Causal Masking in Attention, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Decoder-only language models, the decoder of encoder-decoder models, and any autoregressive generator, during both training and prefill.

Avoid it when: Bidirectional encoders such as BERT, where each token should see the whole sequence. For padding, use a separate key-padding mask instead.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Causal Masking in Attention?
cards.back:
• A row that is fully masked gives NaN from the softmax; always keep the diagonal
• Using a large negative number in half precision can overflow; $-\infty$ or the dtype minimum is safer
• This code builds the full $T \times T$ matrix; efficient kernels skip the masked blocks entirely

cards.front: Key formulas: Causal Masking in Attention
cards.back:
$S = \frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\;\; (T \times T)$
$M_{ij} = 0$ if $j \leq i$,  $-\infty$ if $j > i$
$A = \mathrm{softmax}(S + M)$ row-wise
$A_{ij} = 0$ for $j > i$,  $\sum_j A_{ij} = 1$
$\mathrm{Output} = A\,V$

cards.front: What is Pre-Norm Transformer Block?
cards.back: One decoder layer: layer-normalise, apply causal multi-head attention, add the result back, then layer-normalise and apply a feed-forward network with a second residual connection.

cards.front: Pre-Norm Transformer Block: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Attention moves information between tokens, and the feed-forward network transforms each token on its own; stacking the two gives a layer that both gathers context and processes it. Keeping a clean residual path $x + f(\mathrm{norm}(x))$ lets each layer make a small correction to the stream, so gradients reach early layers and deep stacks train.

cards.front: What is the difference between pre-norm and post-norm?
cards.back: Pre-norm normalises the input of each sublayer and keeps the residual path clean, which trains stably in deep stacks. Post-norm normalises after the addition, as in the original Transformer, and usually needs warmup.

cards.front: Why does the block have a feed-forward network after attention?
cards.back: Attention only takes weighted averages of values, which is linear in $V$. The MLP adds a non-linearity and most of the capacity, applied to each position independently.

cards.front: Where are most of the parameters in a block?
cards.back: In the MLP, whose hidden width is usually a few times $d$, so its two matrices outweigh the four attention projections.

cards.front: When should you use Pre-Norm Transformer Block, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: The building block of GPT-style decoder language models and of most modern transformer variants; stack it N times with embeddings in front and an output projection behind.

Avoid it when: Very long inputs where quadratic attention is too costly, or small tabular and low-data problems where a simpler network suffices.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Pre-Norm Transformer Block?
cards.back:
• This code has no dropout, attention biases or weight tying; real models add some of these
• It uses exact erf GELU; some libraries use the tanh approximation, which differs slightly
• A final LayerNorm after the last block is still needed in pre-norm models

cards.front: Key formulas: Pre-Norm Transformer Block
cards.back:
$y_1 = \mathrm{LN}(x) = \gamma\odot\frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} + \beta$
$x' = x + \mathrm{MHA}_{causal}(y_1)\,W_o$
$y_2 = \mathrm{LN}(x')$
$\mathrm{out} = x' + W_2\cdot\mathrm{GELU}(W_1 y_2 + c_1) + c_2$
$\mathrm{GELU}(u) = u\cdot\Phi(u) = \frac{1}{2}u\left(1 + \mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{u}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right)$

cards.front: What is Decoder-Only (GPT-Style) Transformer Block?
cards.back: A GPT-style layer with pre-LayerNorm: normalise, causal self-attention, add back, normalise, feed-forward, add back; stacked, it is the whole body of a decoder-only language model.

cards.front: Decoder-Only (GPT-Style) Transformer Block: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A decoder-only model has no encoder and no cross-attention; one stack of identical blocks reads the prefix and predicts the next token. Each block only adds corrections to a residual stream, and the causal mask guarantees that position $t$ never sees later tokens, so one parallel pass trains the prediction at every position at once. Flow: tokens → LayerNorm → causal attention → add → LayerNorm → FFN → add.

cards.front: What makes a block decoder-only?
cards.back: It uses causal self-attention only, with no cross-attention to an encoder, so each position sees just the tokens before it and itself.

cards.front: Why pre-LayerNorm instead of post-LayerNorm?
cards.back: Normalising inside the residual branch leaves the skip path as a pure identity, so deep stacks train stably and need less learning-rate warmup.

cards.front: How would you test that the mask works?
cards.back: Change a later token's input and check that all earlier output positions are unchanged.

cards.front: When should you use Decoder-Only (GPT-Style) Transformer Block, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Building or reading any GPT-style language model: embeddings, $N$ stacked blocks, a final LayerNorm and a projection to vocabulary logits.

Avoid it when: Tasks that need bidirectional context over a fixed input, where an encoder is a better fit, or very long contexts where quadratic attention cost dominates.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Decoder-Only (GPT-Style) Transformer Block?
cards.back:
• Applying the mask after softmax instead of before it leaks the future and breaks the row sums
• Forgetting the final LayerNorm after the last block when using pre-norm
• Adding the residual to the normalised tensor instead of the raw stream destroys the identity path

cards.front: Key formulas: Decoder-Only (GPT-Style) Transformer Block
cards.back:
Attention: $x^{\prime} = x + \mathrm{Attn}(\mathrm{LN}(x))$
FFN: $y = x^{\prime} + \mathrm{FFN}(\mathrm{LN}(x^{\prime}))$
Mask: $M_{ij} = -\infty$ for $j > i$
Attn: $\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_h}} + M\right)V$
LN: $\gamma\,\frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} + \beta$
Causal: $\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j} = 0$ for $j > i$

cards.front: What is Cross-Attention (Encoder-Decoder)?
cards.back: Let each decoder position look up information in the encoder output: queries come from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder.

cards.front: Cross-Attention (Encoder-Decoder): what is the key insight?
cards.back: Self-attention lets a sequence read itself; cross-attention lets one sequence read another. The decoder state asks "which source words do I need to produce the next word?", and the encoder outputs answer with keys to match and values to hand over. The source length and target length are independent, so the weight matrix is rectangular, one row per target position and one column per source position.

cards.front: Where do $Q$, $K$ and $V$ come from in cross-attention?
cards.back: Queries come from the decoder's current hidden states; keys and values come from the encoder's final outputs. The attention matrix is therefore target length by source length.

cards.front: Why can encoder keys and values be cached during generation?
cards.back: The source does not change while decoding, so its keys and values are computed once and reused at every step; only the new query is computed each step.

cards.front: Does cross-attention need a causal mask?
cards.back: No. The decoder may look at the whole source; causality applies only to the decoder's self-attention over its own previous outputs. A padding mask on the source is what it needs.

cards.front: When should you use Cross-Attention (Encoder-Decoder), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Translation, summarisation, speech recognition and any encoder-decoder model where the output must be conditioned on a separate input sequence, including image-to-text models whose encoder outputs are patches.

Avoid it when: Decoder-only language models have no separate source, so they use self-attention over a concatenated prompt instead. Very long sources make the target-by-source score matrix expensive.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Cross-Attention (Encoder-Decoder)?
cards.back:
• Forgetting the source padding mask lets the decoder attend to padding tokens
• A source that is entirely padding gives a fully masked row and NaN; real batches contain at least one real token
• Queries must come from the decoder; swapping the roles gives a source-by-target matrix instead
• This is one head with no output projection, residual or layer norm, which a real decoder layer adds

cards.front: Key formulas: Cross-Attention (Encoder-Decoder)
cards.back:
$Q = X_{dec}\,W_q \qquad (T_{dec} \times d_k)$
$K = X_{enc}\,W_k,\;\; V = X_{enc}\,W_v \qquad (T_{enc} \times d_k,\ T_{enc} \times d_v)$
$S = \frac{Q\,K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}} \qquad (T_{dec} \times T_{enc})$
Padding: $S[i, j] = -\infty$ if source $j$ is padding
$A = \mathrm{softmax}(S)$ row-wise, so each row sums to 1
$\mathrm{Output} = A\,V \qquad (T_{dec} \times d_v)$

cards.front: What is Next-Token Prediction Loss and Perplexity?
cards.back: Shift the sequence by one so position $t$ predicts token $t+1$, average the cross-entropy over all unmasked positions, and report perplexity as the exponential of that loss.

cards.front: Next-Token Prediction Loss and Perplexity: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A single sentence gives one training example per position: the input is the prefix and the label is simply the next token, so no human labels are needed. Perplexity turns the average loss into an effective branching factor, the number of equally likely tokens the model is choosing between, which is why uniform logits over $V$ tokens score exactly $V$. Flow: tokens → shift by one → log-probs → masked mean → exp.

cards.front: Why shift the targets by one?
cards.back: The model output at position $t$ is its prediction for the next token, so the label for position $t$ is token $t+1$; the last position has no label.

cards.front: Why mask prompt and padding tokens?
cards.back: Padding is not real text, and in fine-tuning the prompt is given rather than predicted. Masked positions are excluded from both the sum and the divisor.

cards.front: What does perplexity of 20 mean?
cards.back: The model is as uncertain as a uniform choice among 20 tokens at each step, on average in the geometric sense.

cards.front: Why is perplexity not comparable across tokenizers?
cards.back: A tokenizer with longer tokens makes each prediction harder and the sequence shorter, so per-token loss changes without a real quality difference.

cards.front: When should you use Next-Token Prediction Loss and Perplexity, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Pretraining and supervised fine-tuning of any autoregressive language model, and evaluating one on held-out text; use the ignore index to train only on response tokens.

Avoid it when: Comparing perplexity across models with different tokenizers, since the per-token loss is not on the same scale. Use bits per byte or character instead.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Next-Token Prediction Loss and Perplexity?
cards.back:
• Dividing by the total number of positions instead of the unmasked count biases the loss low
• Forgetting to shift makes the model copy its input, giving a near-zero loss that means nothing
• Masked targets must still be a valid index when gathering, or the lookup fails

cards.front: Key formulas: Next-Token Prediction Loss and Perplexity
cards.back:
Loss: $L = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t}\log p(x_{t+1} \mid x_{1:t})$
Chain rule: $p(x) = \prod_{t} p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$
Perplexity: $\exp(L)$
Bits per token: $\frac{L}{\ln 2}$
Uniform over $V$: $L = \ln V$, perplexity $= V$

cards.front: What is Autoregressive Decoding Loop?
cards.back: Generate text one token at a time. Read the next-token logits at the last position, pick a token, append it, and repeat until an end token or the length limit.

cards.front: Autoregressive Decoding Loop: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A language model only ever answers one question: given everything so far, what comes next? Generation is that question asked in a loop, with each answer fed back as input. Token $t+1$ needs token $t$, so the decode steps cannot run in parallel, unlike the prompt, which is processed in one pass (prefill). The loop is therefore latency-bound. Flow: prompt → logits → pick token → append → repeat until EOS.

cards.front: Why is generation sequential even though training is parallel?
cards.back: Training knows all the target tokens, so it can score every position at once with a causal mask. At inference the next token is not known until the previous one is chosen, so each step waits for the last.

cards.front: What are the prefill and decode phases?
cards.back: Prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass and is compute-bound. Decode generates one token per step, reads the model weights and cache each time, and is usually memory-bandwidth-bound.

cards.front: How does the loop know when to stop?
cards.back: It stops when the model emits an end-of-sequence token or when a maximum number of new tokens is reached, whichever comes first.

cards.front: Why does a KV cache not change the output?
cards.back: It only stores values that a causal model would recompute identically, so the logits match up to floating-point rounding.

cards.front: When should you use Autoregressive Decoding Loop, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any decoder-only language model producing text, from a chat reply to code completion. Swap the argmax for a sampling rule to get varied outputs.

Avoid it when: Greedy picking on long open-ended text, where it tends to repeat itself. Use sampling or beam search there. Training and scoring use teacher forcing with one parallel pass, not this loop.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Autoregressive Decoding Loop?
cards.back:
• Feeding the whole sequence again every step is correct but costs $O(T^2)$ forward work without a cache
• Using logits from any position other than the last gives the wrong next token
• Without a max length, a model that never emits EOS loops forever
• Greedy decoding can fall into repeating loops, as the repeated token in the example shows

cards.front: Key formulas: Autoregressive Decoding Loop
cards.back:
$p(x_{1:T}) = \prod_{t} p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$
Next token: $z_t = f(x_{1:t})_{\mathrm{last}}$
$x_{t+1} = \arg\max_{v}\, z_t[v]$
Stop at EOS or after $n_{\max}$ new tokens

cards.front: What is Temperature Sampling?
cards.back: Divide the logits by a temperature $T$ before the softmax. Low $T$ sharpens the distribution towards greedy, high $T$ flattens it towards uniform.

cards.front: Temperature Sampling: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Dividing logits by $T$ changes the gaps between them while keeping their order. Small $T$ stretches the gaps, so the top token takes almost all the probability. Large $T$ shrinks them, so every token becomes about equally likely. One scalar therefore slides between deterministic and random, and the entropy rises as it grows. Flow: logits → divide by T → softmax → sample a token.

cards.front: What does temperature do to the logits?
cards.back: It divides them by $T$ before the softmax. Their order stays the same, only the spread between them changes.

cards.front: What happens at $T \to 0$ and $T \to \infty$?
cards.back: At $T \to 0$ decoding becomes greedy argmax. At $T \to \infty$ the distribution becomes uniform over the vocabulary.

cards.front: Does temperature change which token is most likely?
cards.back: No. The ranking is unchanged, so the argmax is the same for any $T>0$. It only changes how much probability the others get.

cards.front: How does temperature combine with top-$k$ or top-$p$?
cards.back: They are usually applied together: scale the logits by $T$, then truncate the distribution, then renormalise and sample.

cards.front: When should you use Temperature Sampling, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Creative or varied text generation, where you want to control how adventurous the model is with a single knob. Use a low $T$ for factual or code answers and a higher one for brainstorming.

Avoid it when: When you need a deterministic answer: use greedy decoding, not a tiny $T$ with a random draw. $T=0$ is also undefined as a division, so implementations special-case it as argmax.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Temperature Sampling?
cards.back:
• $T=0$ divides by zero; handle it as argmax rather than passing it to the formula
• Skipping the max subtraction overflows $\exp$ for large logits at small $T$
• High $T$ gives the long tail of junk tokens real probability; truncate with top-$p$ if quality drops

cards.front: Key formulas: Temperature Sampling
cards.back:
$p_i(T) = \frac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_{j} \exp(z_j/T)}$
$T \to 0^{+}$: one-hot at argmax. $T=1$: softmax
As $T \to \infty$: $p_i \to 1/V$
$H(T) = -\sum_{i} p_i \log p_i \leq \log V$

cards.front: What is Top-k and Top-p (Nucleus) Sampling?
cards.back: Truncate the next-token distribution to the $k$ most likely tokens, or to the smallest set whose probability reaches $p$, then renormalise and sample from what is left.

cards.front: Top-k and Top-p (Nucleus) Sampling: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Sampling from the full distribution occasionally picks a token from the long, unreliable tail and derails the text, while greedy decoding is repetitive. Cutting the tail removes the junk and keeps real randomness among plausible tokens; top-p adapts the cut to the model's confidence, keeping few tokens when it is sure and many when it is not.

cards.front: How does top-p differ from top-k?
cards.back: Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens whatever the distribution looks like. Top-p keeps the smallest set reaching probability mass $p$, so its size adapts to how confident the model is.

cards.front: Why renormalise after truncating?
cards.back: The kept probabilities no longer sum to one. The softmax over the remaining logits rescales them so the sample is drawn from a valid distribution.

cards.front: What does temperature do and in what order is it applied?
cards.back: It divides the logits before the softmax; low values sharpen and high values flatten the distribution. It is normally applied first, then the truncation.

cards.front: When should you use Top-k and Top-p (Nucleus) Sampling, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Open-ended generation such as chat, stories and brainstorming, where diversity is wanted but low-probability tokens cause incoherence.

Avoid it when: Tasks with one right answer, such as translation or code, where greedy or beam search is better, and likelihood evaluation, where the full distribution must be used.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Top-k and Top-p (Nucleus) Sampling?
cards.back:
• Libraries differ on whether top-p uses the distribution before or after top-k; here top-p sees the renormalised top-k survivors
• top_p = 0 would drop every token; use a value above zero
• Ties at the cut are broken by sort order, so which tied token is kept is arbitrary

cards.front: Key formulas: Top-k and Top-p (Nucleus) Sampling
cards.back:
$p_i = \frac{\exp(z_i/\tau)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j/\tau)}$
Top-k: keep $i$ if $\mathrm{rank}(i) \leq k$
Sort $p_{(1)} \geq p_{(2)} \geq \ldots$; cumulative $C_j = \sum_{m \leq j} p_{(m)}$
Top-p: keep rank $j$ if $C_{j-1} < p$   ($C_0 = 0$)
$p'_i = \frac{p_i\,\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{kept}]}{\sum_j p_j\,\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{kept}]}$

cards.front: What is KV Cache for Autoregressive Decoding?
cards.back: Store the keys and values of all past tokens, so each new token only computes its own query, key and value and attends over the cache.

cards.front: KV Cache for Autoregressive Decoding: what is the key insight?
cards.back: With causal attention, the keys and values of an earlier token never change when later tokens arrive, so recomputing them at every generation step is pure waste. Caching them turns the work for a new token from reprocessing the whole prefix into one projection plus one attention over stored rows, trading memory for speed.

cards.front: Why can we cache keys and values but not queries?
cards.back: A query is only used once, at its own step. Later tokens need the earlier tokens' keys and values to attend to, not their queries.

cards.front: What is the cost of the KV cache?
cards.back: Memory grows linearly with context length, batch size, layers and heads, and often dominates GPU memory in long-context serving.

cards.front: How is the cache size reduced in practice?
cards.back: Multi-query or grouped-query attention shares keys and values across heads, and quantising or evicting cache entries also helps.

cards.front: When should you use KV Cache for Autoregressive Decoding, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any autoregressive generation with a transformer, which is almost every LLM serving stack, to make each step cost proportional to the context length instead of recomputing it.

Avoid it when: Training and prompt prefill, which already process all positions in one parallel pass. Bidirectional models have nothing to cache because earlier outputs change when later tokens arrive.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of KV Cache for Autoregressive Decoding?
cards.back:
• Growing the cache with vstack copies every step; real systems preallocate and write in place
• Position information such as RoPE must use the true absolute position of the new token
• This is one head and one layer; a real model keeps a separate cache for each layer

cards.front: Key formulas: KV Cache for Autoregressive Decoding
cards.back:
$q_t = x_t W_q,\;\; k_t = x_t W_k,\;\; v_t = x_t W_v$
$K_{1:t} = [K_{1:t-1} ;\, k_t],\;\; V_{1:t} = [V_{1:t-1} ;\, v_t]$
$o_t = \mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{K_{1:t}\,q_t}{\sqrt{d}}\right)^{\top} V_{1:t}$
Cache size $= 2 \cdot \mathrm{layers} \cdot \mathrm{kv\_heads} \cdot t \cdot d_{head} \cdot \mathrm{bytes}$

cards.front: What is Neural Scaling Laws (Chinchilla)?
cards.back: Model loss falls as a power law in parameters $N$ and tokens $D$ down to an irreducible floor. Given a fixed compute budget $C \approx 6ND$, there is a best split between model size and data.

cards.front: Neural Scaling Laws (Chinchilla): what is the key insight?
cards.back: Loss has three parts: an irreducible floor, a term that shrinks as the model grows, and a term that shrinks as it sees more data. Each term has diminishing returns, so spending the whole budget on a huge model with little data, or the reverse, wastes compute. At a fixed budget the best point balances the marginal gain of one more parameter against that of more tokens. Flow: budget C → constraint 6ND = C → minimise L(N,D) → N*, D*.

cards.front: What is the main message of the Chinchilla paper?
cards.back: For a fixed compute budget, many large models were undertrained. Model size and number of training tokens should be scaled up together, roughly in equal proportion.

cards.front: Where does $C \approx 6ND$ come from?
cards.back: A forward pass costs about $2N$ FLOPs per token and the backward pass about twice that, giving roughly $6N$ per token and $6ND$ for $D$ tokens.

cards.front: What is the roughly 20 tokens per parameter figure?
cards.back: A rule of thumb from the paper's compute-optimal results. Different fits give different ratios, and it ignores inference cost, so treat it as a guide, not a law.

cards.front: Why train beyond compute-optimal in practice?
