cards.back: A smaller model trained on more tokens costs less to serve, so total cost including inference can favour it even though training is less efficient.

cards.front: When should you use Neural Scaling Laws (Chinchilla), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Planning a pretraining run: choose model size and token count for a given FLOP budget, or predict the loss of a larger run from small ones before paying for it.

Avoid it when: As an exact law. The fitted constants depend on the data, the architecture and the fitting method, and the form ignores inference cost, data quality and repeated epochs. Training a smaller model on more data than compute-optimal can be right when it will be served a lot.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Neural Scaling Laws (Chinchilla)?
cards.back:
• Constants fitted on one setup do not transfer to another dataset or architecture
• Extrapolating far beyond the fitted range of $N$ and $D$ is unreliable
• $6ND$ is an approximation that ignores attention cost at long context
• Fitting $\alpha$ and $\beta$ jointly is ill-conditioned with noisy data; the optimum $N^*$ is sensitive to them

cards.front: Key formulas: Neural Scaling Laws (Chinchilla)
cards.back:
$L(N,D) = E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}}$
Compute: $C \approx 6ND$
Set $G = C/6$, so $D = G/N$
$N^{*} = \left(\frac{\alpha A}{\beta B}\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha+\beta}} G^{\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}}$
Then $D^{*} = G / N^{*}$

cards.front: What is Parameter Count, FLOPs and Memory of a Transformer?
cards.back: A decoder-only transformer has about $12 L d^2$ parameters plus $V d$ for embeddings, costs about $6 N D$ FLOPs to train and $2 N$ FLOPs per generated token, and needs bytes proportional to $N$.

cards.front: Parameter Count, FLOPs and Memory of a Transformer: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Almost all parameters live in a few square-ish matrices per layer, so the count is set by depth and width: $4 d^2$ for attention and $8 d^2$ for a $4\times$ FFN. Compute follows the same count, because each parameter is used in one multiply-add per token on the forward pass and about twice that on the backward pass. Memory is the count times bytes per value, plus gradients and optimizer state when training. Flow: layers and width → parameters → FLOPs per token → bytes.

cards.front: Why is training about $6ND$ FLOPs?
cards.back: The forward pass is about $2N$ per token (a multiply-add per weight) and the backward pass is about twice that, so $6N$ per token and $6ND$ for $D$ tokens.

cards.front: How much memory does training need beyond the weights?
cards.back: Gradients and optimizer state. With mixed precision and Adam a common estimate is 16 bytes per parameter: 2 for fp16 weights, 2 for gradients, 4 for fp32 master weights, 8 for the two Adam moments. Activations come on top.

cards.front: Where are most parameters in a transformer?
cards.back: In the per-layer matrices, about $12 d^2$ each layer, so they grow with depth and the square of width. The embedding adds $V d$, which matters for small models with large vocabularies.

cards.front: Does weight tying change the count?
cards.back: Yes. Sharing the input embedding with the output projection saves $V d$ parameters.

cards.front: When should you use Parameter Count, FLOPs and Memory of a Transformer, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Budgeting a training run, sizing a GPU for serving, or checking that a quoted model size matches its architecture before running anything.

Avoid it when: Precise accounting. The rules ignore attention over the context (matters for long sequences), activations, the KV cache, and sparse or mixture-of-experts models where only some parameters are active.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Parameter Count, FLOPs and Memory of a Transformer?
cards.back:
• The $6ND$ and $2N$ rules drop attention over the context, which adds real cost at long sequence lengths
• The 16 bytes per parameter figure assumes mixed-precision Adam with fp32 master weights; other setups differ, and activations are extra
• Biases are counted here; many modern models drop them, and gated FFNs use three matrices, so recount for the actual architecture

cards.front: Key formulas: Parameter Count, FLOPs and Memory of a Transformer
cards.back:
Attention per layer: $4 d^2$ (Q, K, V, O)
FFN per layer: $2 d\, d_{ff} = 8 d^2$
Total: $N \approx 12 L d^2 + V d$
Training: $\mathrm{FLOPs} \approx 6 N D$
Inference: $\approx 2 N$ FLOPs per token
Weight bytes $= N \cdot \mathrm{bytes}$
Training state $\approx 16 N$ bytes

cards.front: What is Why Context Length Is Limited?
cards.back: Attention builds a $T \times T$ score matrix, so compute and score memory grow as $T^2$ while the KV cache grows linearly in $T$; sliding windows and RoPE position interpolation stretch the limit.

cards.front: Why Context Length Is Limited: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Every token attends to every earlier token, so doubling the context quadruples the pairs to score. Separately, generation must keep keys and values for the whole context, which costs memory linearly. A model also only saw positions up to its training length, so longer inputs hit angles it never learned; squeezing positions back into the trained range is cheaper than retraining. Flow: longer context → more pairs → bigger scores and cache → limit.

cards.front: Why does doubling the context quadruple attention cost?
cards.back: Each of the $T$ queries scores all $T$ keys, so there are $T^2$ scores. Doubling $T$ gives four times as many.

cards.front: Does the KV cache also grow quadratically?
cards.back: No. It stores one key and one value per token per layer and head, so it grows linearly in $T$, but it can still dominate memory in long-context serving.

cards.front: What does RoPE position interpolation do?
cards.back: It multiplies positions by $L_{train}/L_{new}$ so a longer input maps into the position range seen in training, then usually fine-tunes briefly.

cards.front: How does a sliding window help?
cards.back: Each token attends only to the last $w$ tokens, so scores and compute are linear in $T$, though information beyond the window must flow through the layers.

cards.front: When should you use Why Context Length Is Limited, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Estimating whether a target context length fits in memory and time, and choosing between windowed attention, a bigger cache budget, or position interpolation to extend a pretrained model.

Avoid it when: Treating the quadratic score matrix as always materialised. Fused kernels avoid storing it, so the $T^2$ memory term then disappears even though the $T^2$ compute remains.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Why Context Length Is Limited?
cards.back:
• Fused attention kernels avoid storing the score matrix, so the quadratic memory figure is for the naive implementation; quadratic compute remains
• A model accepting a long input does not mean it uses it well; quality over long contexts must be measured, not assumed
• Interpolating positions without any fine-tuning degrades short-range resolution, since neighbouring tokens get closer angles

cards.front: Key formulas: Why Context Length Is Limited
cards.back:
Scores: $S = Q K^\top / \sqrt{d}$, size $T \times T$
Attention FLOPs $\approx 4 T^2 d_{head}$ per head
Score bytes $= T^2 \cdot \mathrm{bytes}$
KV bytes $= 2 L h_{kv} T d_{head} \cdot \mathrm{bytes}$
Window $w$: scores $= T \cdot \min(T, w)$
RoPE angle $= p' \theta_i$, $p' = p L_{train} / L_{new}$

cards.front: What is Hallucination Detection by Sampling Consistency?
cards.back: Sample several answers at temperature above zero and measure how much they agree: majority-vote confidence, answer entropy, and token overlap between a claim and the samples flag unreliable generations.

cards.front: Hallucination Detection by Sampling Consistency: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A model that actually knows a fact tends to produce it again and again, while an invented detail changes from sample to sample. So disagreement among samples is a signal of uncertainty that needs no ground truth, no labels and no access to the model's probabilities. Flow: question → several samples → agreement score → trust or check.

cards.front: Why sample at temperature above zero?
cards.back: At temperature zero the output is deterministic, so repeated runs agree trivially. Sampling exposes how much probability the model spreads over alternatives.

cards.front: Does high agreement mean the answer is correct?
cards.back: No. A model can be consistently wrong, for example from a common misconception in its training data. Agreement signals confidence, not truth.

cards.front: What is the entropy of $k$ answers that all differ?
cards.back: $\log k$, the maximum, since each has probability $1/k$. If all agree the entropy is 0.

cards.front: What is a grounding check?
cards.back: Verifying each claim against a trusted source, such as retrieved documents, and flagging claims that no source supports. It catches errors that consistent sampling misses.

cards.front: When should you use Hallucination Detection by Sampling Consistency, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Black-box models where you have no ground truth and no token probabilities, and a quick flag for answers that deserve a source check or a human look.

Avoid it when: As the only safeguard. Samples can agree on a wrong answer, and sampling multiplies inference cost by $k$. For factual claims, check against retrieved sources (grounding) instead of or as well.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Hallucination Detection by Sampling Consistency?
cards.back:
• Consistent answers can still be wrong; this method detects uncertainty, not falsehood, so confident hallucinations pass
• Free-text answers rarely match exactly; exact-match counting then gives low confidence for paraphrases, so cluster or use a semantic or overlap score
• Token overlap ignores meaning, so it rewards shared words even when a negation or number changes the claim
• With small $k$ the estimates are noisy; entropy of 5 samples is a rough signal

cards.front: Key formulas: Hallucination Detection by Sampling Consistency
cards.back:
Confidence $= \max_a n_a / k$
Entropy: $H = -\sum_a p_a \log p_a$
With $p_a = n_a / k$: $H \leq \log k$
Overlap: mean of $|C \cap S| / |C|$

cards.front: What is Byte-Pair Encoding Tokenization?
cards.back: Build a subword vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols in a corpus, starting from single characters.

cards.front: Byte-Pair Encoding Tokenization: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Frequent character sequences become single tokens, so common words are short in token count while rare words fall back to smaller pieces and never become unknown. The vocabulary size is simply the number of merges you choose to run, a direct knob between characters and words.

cards.front: How does BPE avoid unknown tokens?
cards.back: Its base alphabet is single characters, or bytes in byte-level BPE, so any word can be spelled out even if no merge applies.

cards.front: How do you encode a new word?
cards.back: Start from characters and apply the learned merges in the order they were learned, not by frequency in the new text.

cards.front: How is BPE different from WordPiece?
cards.back: BPE merges the most frequent pair. WordPiece picks the merge that most increases the likelihood of the training data under a language model.

cards.front: When should you use Byte-Pair Encoding Tokenization, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Tokenising text for language models and translation when you need a fixed-size vocabulary that handles rare and unseen words.

Avoid it when: Not ideal for languages without clear whitespace unless pre-tokenised appropriately, and merges chosen by frequency need not match morphology. Unigram or byte-level variants are alternatives.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Byte-Pair Encoding Tokenization?
cards.back:
• Recounting all pairs each merge is slow for big corpora; real code updates counts incrementally
• Without word-boundary markers a merge can cross word edges or lose where words end
• This sketch ignores word frequencies by taking a plain list of words, so repeats are counted by listing them
• Different tie-breaking gives different but equally valid vocabularies

cards.front: Key formulas: Byte-Pair Encoding Tokenization
cards.back:
Start: each word is a sequence of characters
$\mathrm{count}(a, b)$ = adjacent occurrences of $(a, b)$
Merge $(a^*, b^*) = \mathrm{argmax}\ \mathrm{count}(a, b)$
Replace each adjacent $a^*, b^*$ by $a^*b^*$
Repeat $k$ times; the merge list is the model
Encode a word: apply the merges in learned order

cards.front: What is WordPiece Subword Tokenisation?
cards.back: Split a word greedily into the longest vocabulary pieces, marking every non-initial piece with $\#\#$. Training merges the pair with the highest $\mathrm{freq}(ab)/(\mathrm{freq}(a)\,\mathrm{freq}(b))$, not the most frequent pair.

cards.front: WordPiece Subword Tokenisation: what is the key insight?
cards.back: BPE merges whatever pair is most common, which favours pairs made of very frequent pieces that would often appear together anyway. WordPiece divides by the frequencies of the two parts, so it prefers pairs that occur together far more often than chance, which is close to the likelihood gain of adding the merged token. At inference only the final vocabulary is kept and the word is cut by longest match, with $\#\#$ marking a piece that continues a word. Flow: characters → pair scores → best merge → vocabulary → longest match.

cards.front: How does WordPiece differ from BPE?
cards.back: BPE merges the most frequent pair. WordPiece merges the pair with the highest $\mathrm{freq}(ab)/(\mathrm{freq}(a)\,\mathrm{freq}(b))$, so pieces that are individually common are not merged just because they are common. At inference WordPiece uses longest match, not the learned merge order.

cards.front: What does the $\#\#$ prefix mean?
cards.back: It marks a piece that continues the previous one inside a word, so the original words can be rebuilt by joining pieces and stripping $\#\#$.

cards.front: What happens to a word that cannot be segmented?
cards.back: If at some position no prefix of the remainder is in the vocabulary, the whole word becomes [UNK], not just the unmatched part.

cards.front: Is greedy longest match always the best segmentation?
cards.back: No. It is fast and deterministic but can choose a worse split than a search over all segmentations, as a unigram model with Viterbi would.

cards.front: When should you use WordPiece Subword Tokenisation, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Building a subword vocabulary for BERT-style encoders, where an open vocabulary with a small table is needed and rare words should break into known pieces instead of one unknown token.

Avoid it when: When you need byte-level coverage with no unknown tokens at all, where byte-level BPE is the usual choice. WordPiece also replaces a whole word by [UNK] if any part cannot be matched.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of WordPiece Subword Tokenisation?
cards.back:
• Training needs the splits to start as characters with $\#\#$; plain characters give a different vocabulary
• The merged token drops the $\#\#$ of its second part, and keeps the $\#\#$ of its first part
• Inference ignores merge order, so it can differ from how the vocabulary was built

cards.front: Key formulas: WordPiece Subword Tokenisation
cards.back:
score $(a,b) = \frac{\mathrm{freq}(ab)}{\mathrm{freq}(a)\,\mathrm{freq}(b)}$
BPE picks the pair maximising $\mathrm{freq}(ab)$
Token = longest prefix in $V$; rest gets $\#\#$
No prefix of the rest in $V$: word $\rightarrow$ [UNK]

cards.front: What is SentencePiece Unigram Tokenisation?
cards.back: Give every token a probability and segment a word with the split that maximises the sum of token log-probabilities, found by Viterbi. Train by starting from a large vocabulary, fitting probabilities with EM and pruning the tokens whose removal costs the least likelihood.

cards.front: SentencePiece Unigram Tokenisation: what is the key insight?
cards.back: BPE and WordPiece build a vocabulary by adding merges. Unigram goes the other way: it keeps a probabilistic model of the text and deletes the tokens it does not need. Because every segmentation has a probability, tokenisation is a best-path search, and the ambiguity can even be sampled. SentencePiece also treats text as a raw character stream, with the space turned into a visible marker such as "▁", so no language-specific pre-tokeniser is needed. Flow: big vocabulary → EM probabilities → prune weakest → Viterbi segment.

cards.front: How does Unigram tokenisation differ from BPE?
cards.back: BPE greedily adds merges and applies them in order. Unigram holds a probabilistic model over a large vocabulary, prunes it down, and segments with the highest-probability path, so it can also sample alternative segmentations.

cards.front: How is the best segmentation found?
cards.back: By Viterbi dynamic programming over end positions: the best score ending at $j$ is the best over previous cut points $i$ of the score at $i$ plus $\log p$ of the piece.

cards.front: How are tokens pruned?
cards.back: For each token compute how much the corpus loss would rise if it were removed and refit; drop the lowest-impact fraction each round, always keeping single characters.

cards.front: What does SentencePiece do with spaces?
cards.back: It treats the text as a raw character sequence and replaces the space by a marker such as "▁", so detokenising is lossless and no pre-tokeniser is needed.

cards.front: When should you use SentencePiece Unigram Tokenisation, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Languages without spaces or with rich morphology, multilingual models, and settings where sampling several segmentations (subword regularisation) helps robustness.

Avoid it when: When a simple deterministic vocabulary is enough and training speed matters most, since Unigram training with EM and pruning is slower than counting merges in BPE.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of SentencePiece Unigram Tokenisation?
cards.back:
• Single characters must never be pruned, or some words become unsegmentable
• Viterbi favours fewer, longer tokens because every extra token multiplies in another probability below 1
• Probabilities must be renormalised after pruning so they sum to 1
• A hard Viterbi count is only an approximation of the EM expected counts

cards.front: Key formulas: SentencePiece Unigram Tokenisation
cards.back:
$P(x) = \sum_{s}\prod_{i} p(t_i)$ over segmentations
Viterbi: $b_j = \max_{i<j}\,(b_i + \log p(x_{i:j}))$
E-step: $c(t) = \sum_{w} f_w\, P(t \in w)$
M-step: $p(t) = c(t) / \sum_{t^\prime} c(t^\prime)$
Loss $= -\sum_{w} f_w \log P(w)$

cards.front: What is Cosine Similarity for Embeddings?
cards.back: Compare two embedding vectors by the cosine of the angle between them, ignoring their lengths, and use it to rank nearest neighbours.

cards.front: Cosine Similarity for Embeddings: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Embedding length often reflects things like word frequency or text length rather than meaning, while direction carries the semantics. Dividing the dot product by both norms keeps only direction, and after normalising rows, a whole similarity matrix is a single matrix product.

cards.front: Why use cosine similarity instead of the raw dot product?
cards.back: The dot product grows with vector length, so long vectors look similar to everything. Cosine removes length and compares direction only.

cards.front: Is cosine distance a true metric?
cards.back: No. 1 − cos can violate the triangle inequality. The angle itself is a metric, and the Euclidean distance between normalised vectors is too.

cards.front: How do you speed up cosine search over millions of vectors?
cards.back: Normalise once, then maximum inner product search with an approximate index works directly, since cosine becomes a dot product.

cards.front: When should you use Cosine Similarity for Embeddings, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Semantic search, retrieval for RAG, deduplication and clustering of text embeddings, and any model whose embeddings are trained with a cosine or contrastive objective.

Avoid it when: When vector magnitude carries information you want to keep, for example confidence or popularity, or with sparse count data where other measures fit better. Zero vectors have no direction.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Cosine Similarity for Embeddings?
cards.back:
• Zero vectors divide by zero without the epsilon floor, and then give similarity 0
• A cosine score is not calibrated; thresholds depend on the embedding model
• Full argsort is O(n log n); real systems use partial selection or an approximate index

cards.front: Key formulas: Cosine Similarity for Embeddings
cards.back:
$\cos(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\|a\|\,\|b\|}$
Normalise: $\hat{a} = \frac{a}{\max(\|a\|, \epsilon)}$
$S = \hat{A}\hat{B}^{\top}$ (all pairwise cosines)
For unit vectors: $\|\hat{a} - \hat{b}\|^2 = 2 - 2\cos(a, b)$
Cosine distance $= 1 - \cos(a, b)$

cards.front: What is Static vs Contextual Embeddings?
cards.back: A static table gives each word one vector whatever the sentence. A contextual model feeds the same table through attention, so each output vector is a mix of the word and its neighbours and changes with them.

cards.front: Static vs Contextual Embeddings: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A lookup table cannot tell "river bank" from "money bank" because the row for "bank" is fixed. Attention fixes this without changing the table: each token's output is a weighted average of value vectors over the whole sentence, with weights from query-key similarity, so the neighbours decide what the "bank" output contains. Stack such layers and the output becomes a representation of the word in its context, not of the word alone. Flow: tokens → static lookup → attention weights → mixed vectors.

cards.front: Why can a static embedding not handle polysemy?
cards.back: It stores one vector per word type, so every sense of "bank" shares the same vector, and the model downstream sees no difference between them.

cards.front: How do contextual embeddings get different vectors for the same word?
cards.back: The output at a position is a weighted mix of all tokens in the sentence, and the weights depend on those tokens, so a different sentence gives a different mix.

cards.front: Why is attention without positions permutation-equivariant?
cards.back: Every token is treated with the same weights and the output depends on the set of other tokens, not their order, so permuting the inputs permutes the outputs. Positional encodings are added to break this.

cards.front: What do ELMo and BERT do differently from word2vec?
cards.back: word2vec learns a fixed table. ELMo uses the states of a bidirectional language model and BERT uses a transformer encoder, so their vectors depend on the sentence.

cards.front: When should you use Static vs Contextual Embeddings, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Whenever meaning depends on context: word sense, coreference, any task where a word's role is set by its neighbours. Contextual outputs of a pretrained encoder are the standard input to downstream classifiers.

Avoid it when: When a cheap, fixed vector per word is enough, such as for fast retrieval baselines or low-resource devices, where a static table such as word2vec is smaller and faster.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Static vs Contextual Embeddings?
cards.back:
• With no positional encoding the layer ignores word order; "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" give the same set of outputs
• One attention layer on random weights only shows the mechanism; useful contextual vectors need trained weights and several layers
• A word's contextual vector is not a single "meaning"; compare vectors in the same context, not across layers blindly

cards.front: Key formulas: Static vs Contextual Embeddings
cards.back:
Static: $e_i = E[\mathrm{id}_i]$, same in every sentence
$Q = X W_q,\;\; K = X W_k,\;\; V = X W_v$
$A = \mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)$
Contextual output $H = A V$
$H_i = \sum_{j} A_{ij}\, v_j$, with $\sum_{j} A_{ij} = 1$

cards.front: What is BERT Masked Language Modelling?
cards.back: Pre-train a bidirectional encoder by hiding a random subset of input tokens and training it to predict the originals from the surrounding context on both sides.

cards.front: BERT Masked Language Modelling: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A left-to-right language model cannot see the future, but an encoder that sees the whole sentence would trivially copy its input. Masking breaks the copy: the model must reconstruct hidden words from context on both sides. Not every selected token becomes a mask symbol, though. Since the mask never appears at fine-tuning time, some selected tokens are swapped for random words or left unchanged, so the model cannot assume that only masked-looking positions need attention.

cards.front: Why not replace every selected token with [MASK]?
cards.back: The mask symbol never appears at fine-tuning time, creating a train-test mismatch. Leaving some selected tokens unchanged or random forces the model to produce good representations for all tokens.

cards.front: Why does the loss ignore unmasked positions?
cards.back: At unmasked positions the input equals the target, so predicting it is trivial and would dilute the signal. Labels of −100 are skipped by the cross-entropy so only hidden tokens train the model.

cards.front: What is the downside of masked language modelling compared with causal modelling?
cards.back: Only the selected fraction of tokens gives a training signal per sequence, and the model is not a natural generator, since it predicts tokens independently given the corrupted context.

cards.front: When should you use BERT Masked Language Modelling, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Pre-training encoder models for classification, tagging, retrieval and other tasks that need rich bidirectional context rather than text generation.

Avoid it when: Open-ended text generation, where a left-to-right decoder is the natural fit. Masked models also learn from only a fraction of positions per pass, so they are less sample-efficient per token than causal models.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of BERT Masked Language Modelling?
cards.back:
• This code treats every token as maskable; real pipelines never select special tokens such as [CLS], [SEP] and padding
• Random replacement here may draw any vocabulary id, including the mask id or the original token
• Averaging over masked positions means batches with few masks give noisy loss; an empty selection gives NaN here
• WordPiece pieces of one word are masked independently here; whole-word masking is a common variant

cards.front: Key formulas: BERT Masked Language Modelling
cards.back:
Select each token with probability $p = 0.15$
80% $\rightarrow$ [MASK], 10% $\rightarrow$ random, 10% $\rightarrow$ same
Labels: original id if selected, $-100$ elsewhere
$M$ = set of selected positions
$L = -\frac{1}{|M|}\sum_{i \in M} \log \mathrm{softmax}(z_i)[y_i]$
$z_i$: logits at position $i$;  $y_i$: original token id

cards.front: What is GPT Decoder-Only Language Model (Full Forward Pass)?
cards.back: The whole GPT model: token plus position embeddings, $N$ pre-norm causal blocks, a final LayerNorm, and a vocabulary projection that reuses the embedding matrix, giving next-token logits at every position.

cards.front: GPT Decoder-Only Language Model (Full Forward Pass): what is the key insight?
cards.back: Where the block card shows one layer, this is the full model. Token ids become vectors, a learned position vector is added so the model knows order, and $N$ identical causal blocks refine a residual stream. A final LayerNorm and the transposed embedding matrix turn each position back into scores over the vocabulary. Training scores every position's next token in one pass; generation feeds the sampled token back in. GPT is decoder-only: no encoder and no cross-attention, unlike BERT (encoder-only, bidirectional) or T5 (encoder-decoder). Flow: token ids → embeddings + positions → N blocks → final norm → logits.

cards.front: What makes GPT decoder-only, and how does it differ from BERT and T5?
cards.back: GPT is a single stack with causal self-attention and no encoder or cross-attention. BERT is encoder-only with bidirectional attention, and T5 pairs an encoder with a decoder that cross-attends to it.

cards.front: What is weight tying and why use it?
cards.back: The output projection reuses the token embedding matrix, so logits are $z E^{\top}$. It saves $V d$ parameters and often helps small models.

cards.front: How is the same model trained and then used for generation?
cards.back: Training applies a causal mask and next-token cross-entropy at all positions in parallel. Generation runs the same forward pass, samples from the last row and appends it, usually with a KV cache.

cards.front: Why a final LayerNorm before the logits?
cards.back: With pre-norm the residual stream is never normalised inside the stack, so one last LayerNorm gives the output projection a stable scale.

cards.front: When should you use GPT Decoder-Only Language Model (Full Forward Pass), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Understanding or implementing any GPT-style language model, and for explaining how training (parallel next-token loss) and inference (autoregressive decoding) share one network.

Avoid it when: Tasks that need bidirectional encoding of a fixed input, such as classification or span filling, where an encoder fits better, or sequence-to-sequence tasks where an encoder-decoder is a natural fit.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of GPT Decoder-Only Language Model (Full Forward Pass)?
cards.back:
• Using $E$ instead of $E^{\top}$ for the output, or transposing GPT-2 Conv1D weights that are already stored as (in, out)
• Feeding more tokens than the position table holds; learned absolute positions cannot extrapolate
• Forgetting the final LayerNorm, which changes every logit
• Mixing up shifts: row $t$ predicts token $t+1$, so targets are the inputs shifted left by one

cards.front: Key formulas: GPT Decoder-Only Language Model (Full Forward Pass)
cards.back:
Embed: $h^0 = E[\mathrm{ids}] + P_{0:T}$
Blocks: $h^{l} = h^{l-1} + \mathrm{Attn}(\mathrm{LN}(h^{l-1}))$, then FFN
Final norm: $z = \mathrm{LN}_f(h^N)$
Tied: $\mathrm{logits} = z\,E^{\top}$, shape $(T, V)$
Next token: $p(x_{t+1} \mid x_{\leq t}) = \mathrm{softmax}(\mathrm{logits}_t)$
Loss: $-\frac{1}{T}\sum_t \log p(x_{t+1} \mid x_{\leq t})$

cards.front: What is T5 Span Corruption Pretraining Objective?
cards.back: Replace random spans of the input with numbered sentinel tokens and train an encoder-decoder to output the dropped spans, each preceded by its sentinel, followed by an end-of-sequence token.

cards.front: T5 Span Corruption Pretraining Objective: what is the key insight?
cards.back: BERT predicts masked tokens independently in place, and GPT predicts the next token left to right. Span corruption turns denoising into a text-to-text task: the encoder reads the corrupted text once and the decoder writes out only what is missing. The target is short (about the corrupted fraction of the input), so pretraining is cheap, and the decoder must model whole spans jointly, not token by token. Flow: text → drop spans → sentinels → encoder → decoder writes spans.

cards.front: How does span corruption differ from BERT masking?
cards.back: BERT replaces tokens in place and predicts each masked token independently from the encoder output. Span corruption drops whole spans, collapses each to one sentinel, and a decoder generates the spans autoregressively.

cards.front: Why are the sentinels numbered?
cards.back: The number lets the decoder tie each output span to its gap in the input and keeps the spans in order, so the original text can be rebuilt exactly.

cards.front: Why is the target shorter than the input?
cards.back: Only the dropped tokens are emitted, plus one sentinel per span and an end token, so the target length is $m + k + 1$ for $m$ dropped tokens in $k$ spans.

cards.front: When should you use T5 Span Corruption Pretraining Objective, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Pretraining a text-to-text encoder-decoder, or any model that should learn to fill in missing spans, where the output is far shorter than the input.

Avoid it when: Decoder-only language models, which use the plain next-token loss, or encoder-only models where per-token masked prediction in place is enough and no generation is needed.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of T5 Span Corruption Pretraining Objective?
cards.back:
• Overlapping or unsorted spans break the sentinel order and the inverse; sort and merge spans first
• Computing the loss on the corrupted input as well as the target wastes capacity on copying
• A real tokenizer uses reserved sentinel ids; a literal text token that looks like a sentinel would be ambiguous

cards.front: Key formulas: T5 Span Corruption Pretraining Objective
cards.back:
Input length: $n - m + k$
Target length: $m + k + 1$
Spans: $k \approx \frac{r\,n}{\bar{\ell}}$
T5: $L = -\sum_j \log p(y_j \mid x, y_{<j})$
BERT: $L = -\sum_{i \in \mathrm{masked}} \log p(x_i \mid \tilde{x})$
GPT: $L = -\sum_t \log p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$

cards.front: What is Llama Blocks - RMSNorm and Grouped-Query Attention?
cards.back: RMSNorm rescales a vector by its root mean square with no mean subtraction and no bias. Grouped-query attention lets several query heads share one key/value head, shrinking the KV cache.

cards.front: Llama Blocks - RMSNorm and Grouped-Query Attention: what is the key insight?
cards.back: LayerNorm does two jobs, centring and rescaling, and the rescaling is what stabilises training, so RMSNorm keeps only that and saves work. For attention, decoding is limited by reading the KV cache, and queries are cheap while keys and values are what get stored; so many query heads can share a few key/value heads at little quality cost. Multi-head is one extreme and multi-query the other. Flow: x → RMS scale → Q heads → shared KV heads → repeat → causal attention.

cards.front: How does RMSNorm differ from LayerNorm?
cards.back: It skips the mean subtraction and the bias and only divides by the root mean square, so it is cheaper and in practice trains about as well.

cards.front: What are MHA, GQA and MQA in terms of KV heads?
cards.back: All have $n_q$ query heads. MHA has $n_{kv} = n_q$, MQA has $n_{kv} = 1$, and GQA uses a value in between, so the cache shrinks by $n_q / n_{kv}$.

cards.front: Why does GQA help inference but not training FLOPs much?
cards.back: The saving is in cache size and memory bandwidth while decoding. The score and mixing matmuls still run for all query heads.

cards.front: When should you use Llama Blocks - RMSNorm and Grouped-Query Attention, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Decoder LLMs where serving memory and decode speed matter: a few KV heads cut the cache and its memory traffic, and RMSNorm replaces LayerNorm for a slightly cheaper, simpler normalisation.

Avoid it when: Small models or short contexts where the KV cache is not the bottleneck, or when you need the quality of full multi-head attention and can afford its cache.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Llama Blocks - RMSNorm and Grouped-Query Attention?
cards.back:
• Using $n_{kv}$ that does not divide $n_q$ leaves some query heads without a KV head
• Repeating heads with tile instead of repeat-interleave pairs query heads with the wrong KV head
• Adding a mean-subtraction or bias to RMSNorm turns it into LayerNorm and breaks weight compatibility

cards.front: Key formulas: Llama Blocks - RMSNorm and Grouped-Query Attention
cards.back:
RMS: $\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_i x_i^2 + \epsilon}$
Norm: $\frac{x}{\mathrm{RMS}(x)} \odot g$
Group size: $r = \frac{n_q}{n_{kv}}$
Head: $\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{Q_h K_g^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_h}} + M\right)V_g$
KV bytes: $2 \cdot L \cdot n_{kv} \cdot T \cdot d_h \cdot b$
Saving vs MHA: $\frac{n_q}{n_{kv}}$

cards.front: What is Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)?
cards.back: Rotate each pair of query and key coordinates by an angle proportional to the token position, so attention scores depend on relative offsets.

cards.front: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE): what is the key insight?
cards.back: If you rotate a query by $m\theta$ and a key by $n\theta$, their dot product depends only on the angle difference $(m-n)\theta$, because rotations are orthogonal and compose by adding angles. RoPE therefore injects relative position directly into the attention score with no learned position table, and each coordinate pair uses its own frequency so both short and long ranges are covered.

cards.front: Why does RoPE give relative position?
cards.back: Rotations compose by adding angles and preserve dot products, so the query-key score depends on the rotation by $m-n$ and not on $m$ and $n$ separately.

cards.front: Why rotate only queries and keys?
cards.back: Position needs to enter the attention score $q \cdot k$. Values are just averaged, so rotating them would corrupt the content being passed along.

cards.front: How does RoPE differ from sinusoidal positional encoding?
cards.back: Sinusoidal encoding is added to the embeddings once at the input. RoPE multiplies $q$ and $k$ by rotations inside every attention layer and adds no parameters.

cards.front: When should you use Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Decoder language models and long-context models that want relative position information without a learned table; used in many open LLMs.

Avoid it when: Cases where absolute position matters more than offsets, or when the head width is odd. Beyond the trained length it needs rescaling methods to extrapolate.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)?
cards.back:
• Pairing convention differs between libraries (adjacent pairs here, split halves in others); weights are not interchangeable
• Apply it per head, to $q$ and $k$ after the projection and before the dot product
• In float16 the angles for large positions lose precision; compute cos and sin in float32

cards.front: Key formulas: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
cards.back:
$\theta_i = \mathrm{base}^{-2i/d},\;\;\; i = 0 \ldots d/2 - 1$
Pair $i$ at position $m$: $z_i = x_{2i} + \mathrm{i}\,x_{2i+1}$
$\mathrm{RoPE}(x, m)_i = z_i\,e^{\mathrm{i}\,m\theta_i}$
$(x'_{2i}, x'_{2i+1}) = R(m\theta_i)\,(x_{2i}, x_{2i+1})$
$\langle\mathrm{RoPE}(q, m), \mathrm{RoPE}(k, n)\rangle = \mathrm{Re}\sum_i q_i\,\mathrm{conj}(k_i)\,e^{\mathrm{i}(m-n)\theta_i}$

cards.front: What is Sliding-Window (Local) Attention?
cards.back: Each token attends only to itself and the previous $W - 1$ tokens through a causal band mask, so cost grows as $T \cdot W$ instead of $T^2$, and the KV cache can be a rolling buffer of size $W$.

cards.front: Sliding-Window (Local) Attention: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Most useful context is nearby, so a token does not need to look at the whole prefix in every layer. Information still travels far, because layer $l$ reads outputs that already mixed the previous $W - 1$ positions of layer $l-1$; stacking $L$ layers gives a receptive field of about $L \cdot W$ tokens. The cache only ever needs the last $W$ keys and values, so memory is constant in length. Flow: tokens → band mask → local attention → stack layers → far reach.

cards.front: How can a window of $W$ see more than $W$ tokens?
cards.back: Each layer's output already summarises the previous $W - 1$ positions, so after $L$ layers information has travelled about $L(W-1)$ tokens.

cards.front: How does the rolling-buffer cache work?
cards.back: The key and value for position $p$ go to slot $p \mathrm{mod} W$, overwriting the entry from $W$ steps earlier, so the cache holds exactly the last $W$ tokens.

cards.front: Does a dense mask make attention cheaper?
cards.back: No. A masked dense matrix still costs $T^2$. The saving needs a banded or blocked kernel that skips masked entries.

cards.front: When should you use Sliding-Window (Local) Attention, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Long sequences where nearby context dominates and a fixed-size cache is needed, such as long-document generation on limited memory.

Avoid it when: Tasks that need exact retrieval of any earlier token in a single layer, such as copying a fact from far back; a window can lose it unless depth carries it forward.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Sliding-Window (Local) Attention?
cards.back:
• Computing the full score matrix and then masking gives the right output but not the speed-up
• Off-by-one in the band: a window of $W$ includes the current token, so it reaches $W-1$ tokens back
• With a ring buffer, the slots are no longer in time order; positional encoding must use true positions

cards.front: Key formulas: Sliding-Window (Local) Attention
cards.back:
Mask: $M_{ij} = 0$ if $i - W < j \leq i$ else $-\infty$
Out: $\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{Q_i K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}} + M_i\right)V$
Cost: $T \cdot W$ entries vs $\frac{T^2}{2}$
Reach after $L$ layers: $L\,(W - 1)$
Ring slot: $\mathrm{pos} \mathrm{mod} W$

cards.front: What is Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Routing?
cards.back: A router scores $E$ expert networks per token, keeps the top $k$, softmax-normalises their gates and sums the chosen experts' outputs, so parameters scale with $E$ while compute scales with $k$.

cards.front: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Routing: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Capacity and per-token cost need not grow together. Store many feed-forward experts, but let each token wake up only the few the router likes: the model has the parameters of $E$ experts and the compute of about $k$. The catch is that a greedy router collapses onto a few favourites, so an auxiliary loss pushes the load flat. Flow: token → router scores → top-$k$ → softmax gates → weighted expert sum.

cards.front: Why does a mixture-of-experts layer add parameters without adding much compute?
cards.back: Each token runs only $k$ of the $E$ experts, so FLOPs scale with $k$ while the parameter count scales with $E$.

cards.front: What is expert collapse and how is it prevented?
cards.back: The router sends most tokens to a few experts, which then train more and win more. An auxiliary loss $E\sum_i f_i P_i$ penalises uneven load, and capacity limits cap each expert.

cards.front: What happens to tokens that exceed an expert's capacity?
cards.back: They are dropped from that expert and typically pass through the residual connection unchanged, so a too-small capacity factor hurts quality.

cards.front: Why is the balance loss differentiable although $f_i$ is not?
cards.back: $f_i$ comes from a hard top-$k$ count and carries no gradient, but $P_i$ is the mean softmax probability, so gradients flow through $P_i$.

cards.front: When should you use Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Routing, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Scaling model capacity under a fixed per-token compute budget, where memory for all experts is available and the batch is large enough to keep every expert busy.

Avoid it when: Memory-bound or on-device deployment, where holding $E$ experts costs more than the saved compute, and small-batch serving where few tokens reach each expert and hardware sits idle.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Routing?
cards.back:
• Too small a balance weight lets experts collapse; too large forces uniform routing that ignores token content
• All $E$ experts must sit in memory even though only $k$ run, so serving cost is memory-bound
• The Python loop here is for clarity; real layers group tokens by expert and run batched matrix products
• Taking the softmax over all $E$ logits and then keeping $k$ gives gates that do not sum to $1$

cards.front: Key formulas: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Routing
cards.back:
Router logits: $z = x W_r$
Gates on kept set: $g_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j \in S} e^{z_j}}$
Output: $y = \sum_{i \in S} g_i\, e_i(x)$
Load: $f_i = \frac{n_i}{T k}$, $P_i = \bar{p}_i$
Balance loss: $E \sum_i f_i P_i \geq 1$
Capacity: $c \cdot \frac{T k}{E}$ tokens per expert

cards.front: What is Choosing Among LLM Families (Decision Rule)?
cards.back: Pick a model by constraints, not by name: filter out candidates that break a must-have, rank the survivors by a weighted utility, and price the workload as cost per request.

cards.front: Choosing Among LLM Families (Decision Rule): what is the key insight?
cards.back: Model names and leaderboards go stale within months, but the trade-offs between hosted-large, open-medium, open-small, mixture and reasoning-tuned families stay put. Requirements such as privacy or on-device execution are not preferences you can trade away, so they are hard filters; only the soft goals (quality, cost, speed) enter a weighted score. This card teaches that method, with made-up profiles. Flow: requirements → hard filter → normalise scores → weighted utility → rank.

cards.front: Why treat privacy or on-device execution as a filter instead of a weight?
cards.back: A model that violates it is unusable however good it scores. A weighted sum could let high quality compensate, which is wrong for a hard requirement.

cards.front: Why price input and output tokens separately?
cards.back: Providers usually charge different rates for each, and output tokens are typically more expensive, so cost depends on the prompt-to-completion ratio of your workload.

cards.front: Why not just rank models by a public leaderboard?
cards.back: Leaderboards go stale, may not match your task or data, and ignore cost, privacy and latency. Evaluate the shortlist on your own examples.

cards.front: When does a larger weight on quality change the winner?
cards.back: When the quality gap between candidates outweighs their cost and speed ratios, as the weight on quality grows the best model moves toward the highest-quality family.

cards.front: When should you use Choosing Among LLM Families (Decision Rule), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Choosing between model families for a product, or justifying a choice to a team, when requirements such as privacy, latency, budget and context length are known and written down.

Avoid it when: As a replacement for evaluating candidates on your own task data. The utility only orders profiles you filled in; it does not measure quality, which you must test.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Choosing Among LLM Families (Decision Rule)?
cards.back:
• Model names, versions, prices and scores go stale quickly; use this as a method and refill the profiles from current data
• The quality field in a profile is a placeholder; replace it with scores from your own evaluation set
• Ratio-to-best normalisation depends on which candidates survive the filter, so adding a model can reorder the rest
• Self-hosting cost is hardware and operations, not a clean price per million tokens; the profile values are an estimate

cards.front: Key formulas: Choosing Among LLM Families (Decision Rule)
cards.back:
Cost: $\frac{n_{in}\, p_{in} + n_{out}\, p_{out}}{10^6}$
Feasible: all must-haves hold, ctx $\geq$ need
Cost score: $s_{cost}(m) = \frac{\min_j c_j}{c_m}$
Speed score: $s_{speed}(m) = \frac{\min_j \ell_j}{\ell_m}$
Utility: $U(m) = \frac{\sum_c w_c\, s_c(m)}{\sum_c w_c}$
Scaling: $w_c \rightarrow \lambda w_c$ leaves $U$ unchanged

cards.front: What is Few-Shot Prompting and Example Selection?
cards.back: Put $k$ worked input-output examples in the prompt before the real query so the model infers the task from context, with no weight updates; choose the examples by embedding similarity to the query.

cards.front: Few-Shot Prompting and Example Selection: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A language model continues text, so a prompt that already contains several solved instances makes "the next instance, solved" the most likely continuation. The examples specify format, label set and style better than an instruction can, and examples that resemble the query show the model a nearby solved case instead of a random one. Flow: query → embed → top-$k$ similar examples → prompt → completion.

cards.front: How is few-shot prompting different from fine-tuning?
cards.back: It changes only the input, not the weights, so it is instant and reversible, but the examples use context on every call and the gain is bounded by what fits.

cards.front: Why select examples by similarity instead of at random?
cards.back: Examples close to the query show the model a nearby solved case, which usually helps more than random ones, though it can overfit to surface similarity.

cards.front: Does the order of the examples matter?
cards.back: Yes. Models are often sensitive to order, with recent examples weighing more, so teams fix an order such as most similar last and test it.

cards.front: What goes wrong with an unbalanced example set?
cards.back: The model leans towards the majority label, so a set that is mostly one class inflates that prediction.

cards.front: When should you use Few-Shot Prompting and Example Selection, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: A new task with a handful of labelled cases and no budget for fine-tuning, when output format matters, or when a large labelled pool exists and similar cases can be retrieved per query.

Avoid it when: When examples would not fit in the context window, when the task is well served by an instruction alone, or when thousands of labelled cases justify fine-tuning a smaller, cheaper model.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Few-Shot Prompting and Example Selection?
cards.back:
• Choosing examples that all share one label biases the model towards that label
• Retrieving near-duplicates of the query can leak the answer in evaluation, so exclude the query itself from the pool
• A format that differs between examples and the query confuses the completion; use one template for all blocks

cards.front: Key formulas: Few-Shot Prompting and Example Selection
cards.back:
Cosine: $\frac{q \cdot e_i}{\|q\|\,\|e_i\|}$
Pick $S$ = top-$k$ of $\cos(q, e_i)$
Length: $L = L_{instr} + \sum_{S}(L_x + L_y) + L_q$
Limit: $L \leq$ context length
Balance: $p_c = \frac{n_c}{k}$, imbalance $= \max_c p_c$

cards.front: What is Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency?
cards.back: Ask the model to write its reasoning steps before the answer, then sample $n$ such reasoning paths at temperature above zero, parse each final answer and return the most common one.

cards.front: Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Intermediate steps give the model room to compute, because each generated token adds work before the answer is committed. A single path can go wrong anywhere, but wrong paths tend to disagree with each other while correct paths converge on the same result, so a vote over several paths filters out much of the random error. Flow: question → $n$ sampled reasoning paths → parse answers → vote.

cards.front: Why does self-consistency need temperature above zero?
cards.back: At temperature zero every sample is the same greedy path, so voting adds nothing. Sampling makes the paths differ and the vote averages their errors.

cards.front: Why is majority-vote accuracy higher than single-sample accuracy?
cards.back: For $p > 0.5$ the binomial tail above $n/2$ exceeds $p$ and grows with $n$, because independent errors rarely line up on the same wrong answer.

cards.front: When does self-consistency fail?
cards.back: When samples are correlated or the model is systematically wrong, since the same wrong answer repeats and wins the vote, and when $p < 0.5$ the vote makes things worse.

cards.front: How is it different from chain-of-thought alone?
cards.back: Chain-of-thought is one reasoning path, usually greedy. Self-consistency samples many paths and votes only on the final answers.

cards.front: When should you use Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Multi-step problems with a short checkable final answer, such as arithmetic, logic or multiple choice, when accuracy matters more than cost and latency.

Avoid it when: Open-ended generation with no single answer to vote on, latency or cost sensitive paths, and easy questions where one direct answer is already reliable.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency?
cards.back:
• Samples from one model are not independent; shared blind spots make the same wrong answer repeat, so the binomial formula is optimistic
• Wrong answers can agree on a popular mistake and win the vote; more samples then make the wrong answer more certain
• Unnormalised answers split votes (such as 1,200 and 1200); normalise before counting
• Cost grows linearly with $n$ in tokens and calls, and a shown reasoning chain need not be the real cause of the answer

cards.front: Key formulas: Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency
cards.back:
Tail: $\sum_{k > n/2}\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$
Votes $K \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n, p)$, win if $K > n/2$
Vote: $a^{*} = \arg\max_a \sum_i 1[a_i = a]$
At $p = 0.7$: 0.700, 0.837, 0.974 for $n$ = 1, 5, 21
For $p < 0.5$ accuracy $\rightarrow 0$ as $n$ grows

cards.front: What is Roles, System Prompts and Chat Templates?
cards.back: A chat is a list of role-tagged messages (system, user, assistant, tool); a chat template flattens it into the one token string the model actually reads, ending with a marker that starts the reply.

cards.front: Roles, System Prompts and Chat Templates: what is the key insight?
cards.back: The model never sees a structured conversation, only a single sequence of tokens in which role markers are ordinary text. The system message is simply the first block of that sequence, trained to be followed, so it sets standing behaviour but is not enforced by anything outside the model. Treat it as strong advice, never as a security boundary. Flow: messages → validate → template → one string → tokens → reply.

cards.front: Why must you use the model's own chat template?
cards.back: The model was fine-tuned on one exact format of control tokens, and a different format gives out-of-distribution input and usually worse behaviour.

cards.front: Is a system prompt a security boundary?
cards.back: No. It is text the model is trained to follow, so a crafted user message or retrieved document can override it. Enforce permissions outside the model.

cards.front: What does the generation prompt do?
cards.back: It adds the assistant start marker at the end, so the model writes a reply instead of continuing the user message.

cards.front: How do you trim a long conversation safely?
cards.back: Always keep the system message, drop the oldest turns first, and keep what remains well formed, starting on a user turn.

cards.front: When should you use Roles, System Prompts and Chat Templates, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any chat or agent application: set persistent behaviour and format rules in the system message, pass tool results back with the tool role, and render with the template the model was trained on.

Avoid it when: As the only defence against prompt injection or data leaks. Secrets and permissions belong in application code, because a user or a retrieved document can talk the model out of a system rule.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Roles, System Prompts and Chat Templates?
cards.back:
• User text containing role markers such as the system tag can forge a role unless markers are escaped or stripped
• Tokenizing a rendered string with extra special tokens can duplicate BOS or EOS; let the template add them
• Counting tokens of content only, not of markers, undercounts the budget
• Dropping the system message to save tokens silently removes the rules and persona

cards.front: Key formulas: Roles, System Prompts and Chat Templates
cards.back:
Input: $\mathrm{template}(m_1,\ldots,m_n)$ + marker
Budget: $T = \sum_i \mathrm{tokens}(m_i)$
Need $T \leq$ context length
Trim: keep $m_0$, newest turns while $T \leq B$
Reply: $\prod_t P(y_t \mid \mathrm{chat}, y_{<t})$

cards.front: What is Context Engineering and Token Budgeting?
cards.back: Treat the context window as a budget: reserve room for the output, spend the rest on the system prompt, recent history and the retrieved chunks with the best score per token, and place key facts at the ends.

cards.front: Context Engineering and Token Budgeting: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A context window is a fixed number of tokens shared by everything the model reads and writes, so every extra document displaces something else. Choosing what to include is a knapsack problem: take the chunks that give the most relevance per token, keep the most recent turns of history, and never spend the tokens reserved for the answer. Order matters too, since models use the start and end of a long prompt more reliably than the middle. Flow: window → reserve output → budget history → pack chunks by score per token → order.

cards.front: Why reserve tokens for the output?
cards.back: Input and output share the window, so a prompt that fills it leaves no room to generate, which truncates or fails the answer.

cards.front: Why is greedy by score per token not always optimal?
cards.back: Chunks are indivisible. A dense chunk can use space that would have fit two slightly less dense ones with more total value.

cards.front: How do you decide what to drop from long chat history?
cards.back: Drop the oldest turns first, or replace them with a summary, and keep the system prompt and recent turns that the next reply depends on.

cards.front: Where should the most important facts go in a long prompt?
cards.back: Near the start or end, since models tend to use information in the middle of a long context less reliably.

cards.front: When should you use Context Engineering and Token Budgeting, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any prompt assembled from several sources, such as RAG, chat with long history or tool outputs, where the total can exceed the window or where cost and latency grow with prompt length.

Avoid it when: Short prompts that fit comfortably, or tasks where every source is essential, so nothing can be dropped. When exact optimality matters on a small set, solve the knapsack exactly instead of greedily.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Context Engineering and Token Budgeting?
cards.back:
• Token counts must come from the model's own tokenizer; counting words or characters undercounts
• Greedy by density can be suboptimal for whole chunks, so compare against exact search on small cases
• Stopping at the first chunk that does not fit leaves budget unused; keep scanning smaller ones
• Dropping turns can remove the question a later turn refers to, so summarise or keep the pairs together

cards.front: Key formulas: Context Engineering and Token Budgeting
cards.back:
Budget: $\sum_{i \in S} t_i \leq W - R - t_{sys}$
Maximise $\sum_{i \in S} v_i$ s.t. $\sum t_i \leq B$
Density: $\rho_i = \frac{v_i}{t_i}$, take by decreasing $\rho_i$
Bound: $\max(V_{greedy}, \max_i v_i) \geq \frac{V_{opt}}{2}$
Docs: $B_{docs} = W - R - t_{sys} - t_{hist}$
Slack: $W - R - t_{in} \geq 0$

cards.front: What is Structured Outputs with JSON Schema?
cards.back: Ask the model for JSON in a fixed schema, extract it from the reply, validate it, and retry with the errors fed back; constrained decoding makes the output valid by construction instead.

cards.front: Structured Outputs with JSON Schema: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A program downstream cannot parse "Sure, here you go!". Prompting only makes valid JSON likely, so you wrap it in a check: extract, validate, and on failure retry with the error message. Constrained decoding goes further and removes the failure mode: at each step it zeroes the probability of tokens the grammar forbids, so every sampled sequence is valid and no retry is needed. Flow: prompt → reply → extract JSON → validate → retry or accept.

cards.front: Why is validating the output not enough on its own?
cards.back: Each retry costs a full generation and independence is optimistic, so with a low $p$ you pay roughly $1/p$ calls and still have no guarantee.

cards.front: How does constrained decoding guarantee valid JSON?
cards.back: A grammar or state machine tracks which tokens may come next; logits of all other tokens are set to $-\infty$ before softmax, so they can never be sampled.

cards.front: Does a schema-valid reply mean a correct reply?
cards.back: No. The schema checks shape, types and enums, not truth; the model can still fill valid fields with wrong values.

cards.front: Why feed the validation errors back on retry?
cards.back: The specific message, such as a missing key, lets the model fix that error instead of resampling blindly, which raises the success probability on later attempts.

cards.front: When should you use Structured Outputs with JSON Schema, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any pipeline where code consumes model output: tool calls, data extraction, classification labels, form filling. Validation plus retry works with any model; constrained decoding when you control the sampler and need a hard guarantee.

Avoid it when: Free-form prose where no downstream parser exists. Constrained decoding is unavailable on hosted models that expose no logits, and a schema valid in shape can still hold wrong values.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Structured Outputs with JSON Schema?
cards.back:
• Taking the first brace to the last brace breaks when prose contains braces; track depth and string state
• Retrying at the same temperature with the same prompt repeats the same mistake; add the error text
• Masking tokens can force a valid but wrong answer when the model wanted a forbidden token; the content may degrade
• Treating $1-(1-p)^n$ as exact: failures are often correlated across attempts, so real success is lower

cards.front: Key formulas: Structured Outputs with JSON Schema
cards.back:
Expected tries: $E[N] = \frac{1}{p}$
At least one valid: $1 - (1-p)^n$
Tries for target $q$: $n \geq \frac{\log(1-q)}{\log(1-p)}$
Masked: $p_i = \frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j \in A}\exp(z_j)}$, $i \in A$

cards.front: What is Prompt Templates and Safe Variable Filling?
cards.back: A prompt template has named placeholders filled from variables, with strict checks for missing or extra values, delimiters around untrusted text, a token budget, and a version label.

cards.front: Prompt Templates and Safe Variable Filling: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A template separates fixed instructions from variable data, and that boundary is a security boundary. If user text is pasted in raw, it can contain placeholders, braces or a closing tag and rewrite the prompt. Filling in a single pass, wrapping untrusted values in delimiters, and removing the delimiter from the value keeps data as data. Flow: template → check variables → wrap untrusted → fill → fit budget.

cards.front: How can a user value break a naive template?
cards.back: If values are substituted repeatedly or the delimiter is not stripped, user text can add placeholders or close the data block and inject its own instructions.

cards.front: Why raise on extra variables as well as missing ones?
cards.back: An extra variable usually means a renamed or misspelled placeholder, so the intended data silently never reaches the prompt.

cards.front: Why version templates?
cards.back: Prompt wording changes model behaviour, so pinning a version lets you reproduce results, compare changes and roll back.

cards.front: Do delimiters stop prompt injection?
cards.back: No. They help the model see where data starts and ends, but the model can still follow instructions inside the data, so other defences are needed.

cards.front: When should you use Prompt Templates and Safe Variable Filling, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any application that builds prompts from variables: chat apps, RAG prompts with retrieved passages, extraction jobs, evaluation harnesses where the same instructions run over many inputs.

Avoid it when: One-off exploratory prompts. Delimiters reduce but do not remove prompt injection, so they are not a substitute for permission checks on tools and outputs.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Prompt Templates and Safe Variable Filling?
cards.back:
• Using str.format on user-controlled templates lets values reach attributes; use a fixed regex filler
• Stripping the delimiter once can leave a rebuilt delimiter such as </da</data>ta>; strip until stable
• Whitespace tokens undercount for real tokenizers, so leave a safety margin below the true context limit
• Truncating the middle or end of a variable may drop the part that matters; choose what to cut deliberately

cards.front: Key formulas: Prompt Templates and Safe Variable Filling
cards.back:
Prompt: $\mathrm{fixed} + \sum_i \mathrm{value}_i$
Budget: $n_{fixed} + n_{var} \leq L$
Room: $r = L - n_{fixed}$
Kept: $\min(n_{var},\, \max(r, 0))$

cards.front: What is Systematic Prompt Optimisation?
cards.back: Improve a prompt by search instead of by feel: fix a metric and a dev set, propose candidate prompts, score each, keep the best, and report the uncertainty of every score.

cards.front: Systematic Prompt Optimisation: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A prompt is a discrete parameter and the dev-set accuracy is a noisy objective, so tuning it is hyperparameter search. With $n$ examples a score has a standard error near $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$, so a gain of two points on 100 examples is usually noise. Pair the candidates on the same examples, measure the gap with a bootstrap, and keep a final test set that the search never touched. Flow: metric → candidates → score on dev → keep best → confirm on test.

cards.front: Why report an interval and not just the accuracy?
cards.back: On a small dev set the standard error is several points, so two prompts that differ by one or two points are statistically indistinguishable.

cards.front: Why a paired bootstrap?
cards.back: Both prompts are scored on the same examples, so resampling examples and comparing the difference removes the shared example difficulty and gives a tighter estimate of the gap.

cards.front: How do you avoid overfitting the dev set?
cards.back: Every comparison made against the dev set leaks a little of it into the prompt, so keep a separate test set, score only the final prompt on it, and limit the number of candidates tried.

cards.front: When should you use Systematic Prompt Optimisation, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: A prompt is going into a product and you can write a metric and collect a few hundred labelled examples. Also for choosing between a handful of hand-written variants.

Avoid it when: No reliable metric exists, or the dev set is tiny, where the search mostly fits noise. A one-off prompt used once is not worth a search.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Systematic Prompt Optimisation?
cards.back:
• Selecting the best of many candidates on the dev set inflates its score, so the winner's dev accuracy overstates its real accuracy
• A model sampled at nonzero temperature makes scores noisy; fix the seed, or average several runs
• Greedy hill-climbing stops at the first local optimum; it does not explore edits that only help in combination

cards.front: Key formulas: Systematic Prompt Optimisation
cards.back:
Score: $\hat{p} = k/n$, $\mathrm{SE} \approx \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}$
Wilson centre: $\frac{\hat{p} + z^2/2n}{1 + z^2/n}$
Half-width: $\frac{z\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n + z^2/4n^2}}{1 + z^2/n}$
Paired gap: $\bar{d} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}(a_i - b_i)$
P(A beats B) = share of resamples, $\bar{d} > 0$

cards.front: What is Prompt Injection Defence in Depth?
cards.back: Untrusted text can carry instructions the model may follow. Defend with layers: delimit untrusted data, screen it, restrict tools, ask for confirmation on risky actions, and check outputs.

cards.front: Prompt Injection Defence in Depth: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A language model reads instructions and data as one stream of tokens, so nothing in the model itself marks a sentence in a web page as data rather than a command. Prompt wording can lower the risk but cannot enforce a boundary, so the strong controls live outside the model: what the tools are allowed to do and who confirms. Assume some injection succeeds and limit the damage. Flow: untrusted text → wrap → detect → gate tools → confirm → validate output.

cards.front: Why can't a system prompt alone prevent injection?
cards.back: The model processes instructions and data as one token stream, so a system prompt is only a strong hint. It is not an access control, and a crafted input can still override it.

cards.front: What is the single most effective control?
cards.back: Least privilege on tools: if the model cannot send email or read secrets, a successful injection has little to abuse. Confirmation by a human for risky actions adds a hard stop.

cards.front: Why use a random nonce in the delimiter?
cards.back: A fixed delimiter can be copied into the untrusted text to close the data block early. A random one is unknown to the attacker, and any copy that appears is removed anyway.

cards.front: When should you use Prompt Injection Defence in Depth, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any application that feeds web pages, emails, documents, tool results or user uploads into a model, especially when the model can call tools that read private data or change something.

Avoid it when: Do not rely on these steps alone: delimiters and regex screening do not stop a determined attacker. They are cheap layers to combine with tool restrictions, not a replacement for them.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Prompt Injection Defence in Depth?
cards.back:
• Regex detection is trivially bypassed by rephrasing, translation or encoding; treat a match as a signal, never as a guarantee
• The product formula assumes independent layers; layers that share a weakness, such as the same model, block less than it predicts
• Model output is untrusted too: rendering it as HTML or running it as a command reopens the hole
• No prompt-only defence is complete, so design the system to stay safe when an injection succeeds

cards.front: Key formulas: Prompt Injection Defence in Depth
cards.back:
Pass all: $P = \prod_{i}(1 - q_i)$
Blocked: $1 - \prod_{i}(1 - q_i)$
Example: $q = 0.5$ twice gives $0.5 \cdot 0.5 = 0.25$
Shared weakness: $P \geq \prod_{i}(1 - q_i)$

cards.front: What is Chat Completion Requests, Responses and Token Cost?
cards.back: A chat API takes messages, a model name and sampling parameters, and returns choices with a finish reason plus token usage. Validate both sides, price the usage, and check that the prompt and the reply budget fit the context window.

cards.front: Chat Completion Requests, Responses and Token Cost: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Almost every chat endpoint has the same contract: a list of role-tagged messages in, a list of choices out, and a usage record that is the basis of the bill. Two numbers matter most operationally. The finish reason says why generation stopped, and length means the reply was cut at the token limit, so the text may be incomplete. The token counts give the cost, and the prompt plus the reply budget must fit in the context window or the call is rejected or truncated. Flow: request → schema check → fits context? → response → usage → cost, truncated?

cards.front: Why are output tokens usually priced higher than input tokens?
cards.back: Prompt tokens are processed in one parallel pass, while output tokens are produced one at a time, each needing a full forward step, so they use more compute per token.

cards.front: What does a finish reason of length tell you?
cards.back: The reply hit the max_tokens limit or the context limit and was cut, so it may end mid-sentence or mid-JSON. Raise the budget, shorten the prompt, or ask the model to continue.

cards.front: Why validate the request locally?
cards.back: It fails fast with a clear message, avoids a billed or rate-limited round trip for an obviously bad call, and documents the contract in one place.

cards.front: How do you budget the context window?
cards.back: The prompt tokens plus the requested max_tokens must not exceed the window, so the reply budget is the window minus the prompt length.

cards.front: When should you use Chat Completion Requests, Responses and Token Cost, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any client or gateway that calls a chat endpoint: validate before sending to fail fast, and read usage and finish reason on every reply to track spend and detect cut-off answers.

Avoid it when: Do not rely on the schema alone for correctness of the model's text; it checks shape, not meaning. Providers differ in details, so use their own documented schema when you need strict compatibility.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Chat Completion Requests, Responses and Token Cost?
cards.back:
• Ignoring finish reason length and shipping a truncated answer or invalid JSON
• Reading prices as per token when they are quoted per million tokens, which is off by a factor of $10^6$
• Forgetting that $max\_tokens$ counts against the context window, so a long prompt leaves little room
• Hard-coding one provider's field names; keep the schema in one place so it can be swapped

cards.front: Key formulas: Chat Completion Requests, Responses and Token Cost
cards.back:
Cost: $\frac{p\,\pi_{in} + c\,\pi_{out}}{10^6}$
Total tokens: $p + c$
Fit: $p + \mathrm{max\_tokens} \leq L$
Reply budget: $\mathrm{max\_tokens} \leq L - p$
Mean price: $\frac{\mathrm{cost}}{p + c}$ per token

cards.front: What is LLM API Rate Limits, Token Buckets and Safe Retries?
cards.back: Provider limits are counted in requests and in tokens per minute. Estimate the token cost before sending, throttle yourself with a token bucket, honour 429 with Retry-After, and retry with an idempotency key.

cards.front: LLM API Rate Limits, Token Buckets and Safe Retries: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A generic retry loop reacts after the server says no, and every rejected call still burns time and may count against your quota. LLM APIs charge and limit by tokens, and you know most of the cost up front: the prompt length plus the $max\_tokens$ you ask for. So spend a budget you track locally. A token bucket holds up to $C$ units and refills at $r$ per second, which allows a burst of at most $C$ and a long-run rate of at most $r$; a request that does not fit waits exactly $(c - \mathrm{tokens})/r$ seconds instead of guessing. Flow: estimate cost → bucket check → wait or send → 429 → Retry-After → resend same key.

cards.front: Why a token bucket instead of a fixed counter per minute?
cards.back: A fixed window lets a client send a full quota at the end of one window and another at the start of the next, doubling the burst. The bucket refills continuously and bounds both burst and average rate.

cards.front: Why count tokens and not only requests?
cards.back: Providers limit tokens per minute and bill per token, so one long prompt can use more quota than many short ones. A request-only limiter would still trigger 429s.

cards.front: Why an idempotency key on retries?
cards.back: If a timeout hides whether the first call was processed, resending could run and bill the work twice. A stable key lets the server return the original result instead.

cards.front: How should concurrency interact with the limiter?
cards.back: Cap in-flight requests with a semaphore so a slow endpoint does not pile up work, and let the bucket gate the rate; the two limits protect different things.

cards.front: When should you use LLM API Rate Limits, Token Buckets and Safe Retries, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any client that calls a hosted LLM at volume: batch jobs, agents with parallel tool calls, evaluation runs. Combine the bucket with a concurrency cap (a semaphore) and with the general backoff in json-api-requests-retries.

Avoid it when: A single interactive caller far below the limits, where a plain retry on 429 is enough. The local estimate is also only an approximation, so it complements the server's own limit and never replaces it.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of LLM API Rate Limits, Token Buckets and Safe Retries?
cards.back:
• Estimating only the prompt and ignoring $max\_tokens$ undercounts what the provider reserves and bills
• Sleeping with the real clock inside the limiter makes tests slow and flaky; inject the clock and the sleeper
• Retrying without a stable idempotency key can duplicate a non-idempotent side effect or its cost
• A $c > C$ request waits forever if not rejected up front

cards.front: Key formulas: LLM API Rate Limits, Token Buckets and Safe Retries
cards.back:
Refill: $\mathrm{tokens} = \min(C,\, \mathrm{tokens} + r\,\Delta t)$
Allow if $\mathrm{tokens} \geq c$, then subtract $c$
Wait: $\max\left(0, \frac{c - \mathrm{tokens}}{r}\right)$
Released in a window: $\leq C + rT$
N requests need: $T \geq \frac{N c - C}{r}$
Cost: $c \approx \lceil \mathrm{chars}/4 \rceil + \mathrm{max\_tokens}$

cards.front: What is Streaming Tokens with Server-Sent Events?
cards.back: A streamed completion is a text/event-stream: lines of data, event and comment fields, each event closed by a blank line. Buffer bytes, decode incrementally, and join the JSON deltas into the final text.

cards.front: Streaming Tokens with Server-Sent Events: what is the key insight?
cards.back: The network cuts the stream wherever it likes, so a read can end in the middle of a line, in the middle of a JSON object, or in the middle of a multi-byte character such as an emoji. The parser must therefore never treat one chunk as one event: it appends bytes to an incremental decoder, splits only on complete lines, and emits an event only at a blank line. A correct parser gives the same events for every possible way of cutting the same bytes. Flow: bytes → incremental decode → line buffer → complete events → delta text.

cards.front: Why must the parser decode incrementally instead of decoding each chunk?
cards.back: A chunk can end halfway through a multi-byte character, and decoding that fragment alone raises an error or produces garbage. An incremental decoder holds the partial bytes until the rest arrives.

cards.front: How do you know an event is finished?
cards.back: A blank line ends it. Until then the data lines seen so far are buffered, and several data lines are joined with a newline.

cards.front: Why not parse tool-call arguments as each fragment arrives?
cards.back: Fragments of a JSON string are generally not valid JSON on their own. Concatenate them and parse once the call is complete, for example at the end of the stream.

cards.front: What is a good test for the parser?
cards.back: Feed the same bytes cut at every boundary and check that the events are identical, including cuts inside a multi-byte character.

cards.front: When should you use Streaming Tokens with Server-Sent Events, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Reading any token stream from a chat endpoint, so the user sees text as it is generated and a long answer does not wait for the last token. The same parser works for any text/event-stream source.

Avoid it when: Short answers or batch jobs where one complete response is simpler, and bidirectional or binary protocols, where a WebSocket or a different framing fits better.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Streaming Tokens with Server-Sent Events?
cards.back:
• Calling bytes.decode on each chunk breaks on emoji and other multi-byte characters that straddle a boundary
• Treating each network chunk as one event fails as soon as an event spans two chunks or one chunk holds two events
