• Calling json.loads on a partial tool-argument string raises an error; parse only the full concatenation
• Treating [DONE] as JSON raises an error; check for the sentinel before parsing

cards.front: Key formulas: Streaming Tokens with Server-Sent Events
cards.back:
Event: lines up to a blank line
Text: $\sum_{i} \delta_i$ (concatenated deltas)
Chunkings of $n$ bytes: $2^{n-1}$
UTF-8: 1 to 4 bytes per character
Cuts inside a $k$-byte character: $k - 1$

cards.front: What is Provider Fallback Router for LLM Calls?
cards.back: Send each LLM request down an ordered chain of providers, classify every error, and hop to the next provider only when that can help; unhealthy providers sit out a cool-down.

cards.front: Provider Fallback Router for LLM Calls: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Not every failure deserves a fallback. A timeout or rate limit says this provider is struggling, so try another; an invalid request will fail everywhere, so hopping only burns money; an auth failure condemns one provider but not the request. The router is a small state machine: classify the error, then decide whether to retry elsewhere, stop, or bench the provider for a while. Flow: request → provider 1 → classify error → provider 2.

cards.front: Which errors should trigger a fallback?
cards.back: Timeouts, rate limits and server errors, because another provider may succeed. An invalid request or content-policy block would fail everywhere, so it should be raised at once; an auth error only removes that provider.

cards.front: Why a cool-down rather than trying every provider each time?
cards.back: A provider that just failed is likely still failing, and retrying it adds its full timeout to every request. Benching it for a while keeps latency low and lets it recover.

cards.front: How do you compute the expected cost of a fallback chain?
cards.back: Sum over providers of the probability of reaching it times its cost, where the probability of reaching provider i is the product of the failure probabilities before it.

cards.front: Priority versus weighted routing?
cards.back: Priority always prefers the first healthy provider and uses the rest as backup. Weighted random spreads traffic in proportion to the weights, which balances load and quota.

cards.front: When should you use Provider Fallback Router for LLM Calls, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Production LLM features that must stay up when one provider is slow, rate limited or down, or that should spread load or cost across several models behind one interface.

Avoid it when: Flows that need identical outputs every time, since fallback models differ in style and capability, or non-idempotent calls where a half-finished request on one provider may still take effect.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Provider Fallback Router for LLM Calls?
cards.back:
• Treating every exception as retryable multiplies the bill for requests that can never succeed
• Without a cool-down, a hard-down provider adds its whole timeout to each request
• Fallback models answer differently, so evaluate each chain member on your own task
• Failures are not fully independent: a shared network or quota problem can take several providers down together, so $\prod_i f_i$ is optimistic

cards.front: Key formulas: Provider Fallback Router for LLM Calls
cards.back:
Reach: $P(\mathrm{reach}\ i) = \prod_{j<i} f_j$
Cost: $\mathbb{E}[c] = \sum_i P(\mathrm{reach}\ i)\,c_i$
Chain down: $P = \prod_i f_i$
Chain up: $P = 1 - \prod_i f_i$
Weighted: $P(i) = \frac{w_i}{\sum_j w_j}$

cards.front: What is Hugging Face Style Text Generation Pipeline?
cards.back: A generation call is text → tokenizer → input ids and attention mask → generate → output ids → decode; batches need left padding with a mask so that decoder-only models continue from real tokens.

cards.front: Hugging Face Style Text Generation Pipeline: what is the key insight?
cards.back: The model only sees integers. Batching forces equal lengths, so short prompts get pad tokens, and where those pads sit decides everything: a decoder-only model predicts the next token from the last position, so right padding makes it continue from a pad, while left padding keeps the real last token at the end. The attention mask hides the pads from attention, and generate adds each new token to the end of the same ids. Flow: text → ids + mask → generate → new ids → decode.

cards.front: Why must decoder-only models be left-padded for generation?
cards.back: The next token is predicted from the last position. With right padding that position is a pad, so the model continues from padding instead of the prompt; left padding keeps the last real token at the end.

cards.front: What does the attention mask do?
cards.back: It marks real tokens with 1 and pads with 0 so pad positions are excluded from attention. It also lets position ids be computed so real tokens start at position 0.

cards.front: Why does generate return the prompt too?
cards.back: For decoder-only models the new tokens are appended to the input ids. Slice off the first prompt-length columns to keep only the generated part.

cards.front: How do greedy and sampling differ in the call?
cards.back: Greedy takes the argmax each step. Sampling arguments such as temperature, top-k and top-p reshape the distribution and draw from it, so outputs vary from run to run.

cards.front: When should you use Hugging Face Style Text Generation Pipeline, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Understanding or debugging what a generation call does: why batched outputs differ from single ones, why a pad token must be set, and why generated ids include the prompt unless you slice them off.

Avoid it when: Encoder-decoder models, where the decoder starts from its own start token and padding conventions differ, or serving stacks with their own continuous batching that hide padding entirely.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Hugging Face Style Text Generation Pipeline?
cards.back:
• Using the default right padding with a decoder-only model silently degrades batched outputs
• Forgetting the attention mask or the pad token id makes pads count as real context
• Decoding the full output returns the prompt plus the answer; slice the prompt off first
• The default length cap is small, so set max_new_tokens explicitly

cards.front: Key formulas: Hugging Face Style Text Generation Pipeline
cards.back:
Position: $p_i = \left(\sum_{j \leq i} m_j\right) - 1$
Mask: $s_{ij} = -\infty$ where $m_j = 0$
Greedy: $x_{t+1} = \arg\max_v\, z_{\mathrm{last},v}$
Pads: $L_{\max} - L_i$ for prompt $i$
Use: $\frac{\sum_i L_i}{B \cdot L_{\max}}$
Length: $L_{\max} + T_{\mathrm{new}}$

cards.front: What is Runnable Chains and Pipe Composition?
cards.back: A runnable has invoke, batch and stream; the pipe operator composes runnables left to right, so prompt | model | parser is one runnable and a RAG chain is just a longer pipe.

cards.front: Runnable Chains and Pipe Composition: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Every stage of an LLM app, whether retriever, prompt template, model or parser, is a function from one value to the next. Give them all one interface and a pipe, and a pipeline becomes plain function composition: associative, testable stage by stage, and able to batch, stream or fan out with no per-stage code. This is the common pattern behind orchestration frameworks, not any one library's API. Flow: input → retriever → prompt → model → parser → output.

cards.front: What is a runnable?
cards.back: Any component with a common interface of invoke for one input, batch for many and stream for incremental output, so retrievers, prompts, models and parsers can be composed freely.

cards.front: What does the pipe operator do?
cards.back: It composes two runnables into a sequence where the output of the left becomes the input of the right, which is ordinary function composition.

cards.front: How is a RAG chain built this way?
cards.back: A parallel step builds the context from a retriever and passes the question through, then a prompt template, a model and a parser follow in the pipe.

cards.front: How does streaming work through a chain?
cards.back: Earlier steps run to completion, and the last step yields chunks as it produces them. Fully streaming every stage needs steps that can transform an incoming stream.

cards.front: When should you use Runnable Chains and Pipe Composition, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Pipelines of retriever, prompt, model and parser where each stage should be swappable, testable alone, and runnable over a batch or as a stream without rewriting glue code.

Avoid it when: Pipelines with loops, branching on model output or shared state, where an explicit graph or plain code is clearer than a straight pipe, and tiny scripts where a few function calls suffice.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Runnable Chains and Pipe Composition?
cards.back:
• A pipe needs compatible shapes: a prompt expects a dict, a parser expects text, and mismatches fail only at run time
• Wrapped errors without the step name make long chains hard to debug
• Streaming through a non-streaming middle step still waits for that step to finish
• Branches of a parallel step must not share mutable state

cards.front: Key formulas: Runnable Chains and Pipe Composition
cards.back:
Pipe: $(f \mid g)(x) = g(f(x))$
Assoc: $(a \mid b) \mid c = a \mid (b \mid c)$
Parallel: $\{k: f_k(x)\}$ for each branch $k$
Batch: $[\,f(x) \ \mathrm{for}\ x \in X\,]$
Stream: $\mathrm{join}(\mathrm{stream}(x)) = f(x)$
Time: $\sum_i t_i$ in series, $\max_k t_k$ in parallel

cards.front: What is Model Context Protocol (JSON-RPC Tool Servers)?
cards.back: A standard wire protocol for an LLM application (the client) to discover and call tools, and read resources, offered by separate servers; every message is JSON-RPC 2.0, so any client can talk to any server.

cards.front: Model Context Protocol (JSON-RPC Tool Servers): what is the key insight?
cards.back: Without a standard, each of $M$ applications needs custom glue for each of $N$ tools. With one protocol, a server describes its tools once (name, description, JSON Schema) and any client can list and call them, so the glue shrinks from $M \cdot N$ adapters to $M + N$ implementations. JSON-RPC supplies the envelope: an id pairs each response with its request, and a message without an id is a notification that never gets a reply. Flow: list tools → model picks one → call with arguments → validate → result or error → back to model.

cards.front: What is the difference between a request and a notification?
cards.back: A request has an id and must get exactly one response carrying the same id. A notification has no id and the receiver must not reply.

cards.front: Why does a parse error response have a null id?
cards.back: If the text is not valid JSON the server cannot read the request id, so the response uses a null id.

cards.front: Protocol error or tool error: where does a failing tool go?
cards.back: A malformed call or unknown method is a JSON-RPC error. A tool that ran and failed is better returned as a normal result with an error flag, so the model can read it and retry.

cards.front: What does the protocol not give you?
cards.back: Trust. Tool descriptions and outputs come from a server and can carry injected instructions, so clients still need confirmation and filtering.

cards.front: When should you use Model Context Protocol (JSON-RPC Tool Servers), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Exposing the same tools or data to several LLM applications, or letting users plug third-party tool servers into an application without writing adapters. The same messages travel over a local process pipe or over HTTP, so one server fits both.

Avoid it when: A single application calling a handful of its own functions in process, where a direct function-calling registry is simpler. A protocol also does not remove the need to treat tool output as untrusted input to the model.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Model Context Protocol (JSON-RPC Tool Servers)?
cards.back:
• Replying to a notification breaks the protocol; the sender is not listening for it
• Running the tool before validating the arguments lets a malformed model call cause side effects
• Returning an id other than the request id, or numeric ids as strings, breaks request matching
• Trusting tool descriptions and outputs: they are untrusted text that goes into the model context

cards.front: Key formulas: Model Context Protocol (JSON-RPC Tool Servers)
cards.back:
No protocol: $M \cdot N$ adapters
With protocol: $M + N$ implementations
Messages: $2(1 + k) + n$
Tool prompt cost: $T \cdot \bar{a}$ tokens
Servers: $T = \sum_{i} t_i$ tools in total
Success: $P = \prod_{j=1}^{k} p_j$

cards.front: What is SFT Loss Masking, Normalisation and Packing?
cards.back: Supervised fine-tuning scores only the response tokens: prompt and padding labels are set to $-100$, labels are shifted by one, and the loss is normalised either per token or per sequence. Packed rows need a block-diagonal causal mask so examples cannot attend to each other.

cards.front: SFT Loss Masking, Normalisation and Packing: what is the key insight?
cards.back: The prompt is given, not predicted, so training on it wastes gradient and teaches the model to write user messages. Masking is therefore a choice of what the loss rewards. The normaliser is a second choice in disguise: dividing by all response tokens in the batch gives every token equal weight, so long answers dominate; averaging per-sequence means gives every answer equal weight, so each token of a short answer counts more. Packing saves padding but only stays correct if the attention mask also stops at example borders. Flow: prompt + answer → labels with -100 → shift → masked loss.

cards.front: Why set prompt labels to -100 instead of deleting them?
cards.back: The prompt tokens must stay in the input so attention can read them, but they should not contribute to the loss. The ignore index removes them from the sum and the divisor only.

cards.front: Token mean or sequence mean?
cards.back: Token mean weights each response token equally, so long answers dominate the gradient. Sequence mean weights each answer equally, so tokens of short answers count more. Equal lengths make them identical.

cards.front: What goes wrong when packing without a block mask?
cards.back: Tokens attend to earlier unrelated examples, so the model learns from context that never exists at inference, and the loss is no longer the per-example loss.

cards.front: Why does gradient accumulation interact with the normaliser?
cards.back: Averaging micro-batch means gives each micro-batch equal weight even when token counts differ. Divide by the total unmasked tokens across all accumulation steps to match one large batch.

cards.front: When should you use SFT Loss Masking, Normalisation and Packing, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Instruction and chat fine-tuning, where the prompt is fixed context and only the answer should be learned. Use token mean when every response token should count equally, and sequence mean when each example should count equally regardless of length. Pack short examples to remove padding waste.

Avoid it when: Continued pretraining on raw text, where every token is a target. Masking the prompt can also hurt when the data is tiny and the prompt itself is a style you want the model to absorb.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of SFT Loss Masking, Normalisation and Packing?
cards.back:
• Forgetting that the first response label sits at position $t+1$, so the shift must happen before masking is read
• A batch whose responses are all masked divides by zero in token mode; guard the count
• Pad id and EOS id are often the same; masking by token id would also remove the real EOS, so mask by position
• Cross-example attention in packed rows silently leaks context while the loss still looks normal

cards.front: Key formulas: SFT Loss Masking, Normalisation and Packing
cards.back:
Token mean: $L_{tok} = -\frac{\sum_i m_i \log p_i}{\sum_i m_i}$
Sequence mean: $L_{seq} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b} \ell_b$
Token weight: $\frac{1}{N}$ vs $\frac{1}{B\, n_b}$
Target: $y_t = x_{t+1}$ if response, else $-100$
Mask: $M_{ij} = 1$ if $s_i = s_j$ and $j \leq i$

cards.front: What is Building Instruction-Tuning Examples and Data Mixtures?
cards.back: Render each (instruction, input, output) record or multi-turn chat into training text with a fixed template, append EOS after every assistant turn, label only assistant spans, and blend datasets with sampling weights $p_i \propto n_i^{\alpha}$.

cards.front: Building Instruction-Tuning Examples and Data Mixtures: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Inference-time templating only has to start a reply; training-time templating also has to teach the reply to end. If EOS is missing from the labels the model never learns to stop, and if user text is in the labels it learns to write user turns. Mixing is a weighting problem: sampling in proportion to size lets one huge set drown the rest, while a power $\alpha < 1$ flattens the distribution so small sets are seen more often per example. Flow: record → template → text + EOS → role mask → sampled mixture.

cards.front: Why append EOS during training?
cards.back: Generation stops when the model emits EOS. If the label sequence never contains it, the model has no gradient to learn that a reply ends, and it rambles or invents the next user turn.

cards.front: How is this different from the inference-time chat template?
cards.back: Inference adds an assistant header and lets the model write. Training renders the full conversation including the answer and EOS, and also needs a label mask.

cards.front: What does $\alpha$ do in the mixture weights?
cards.back: It sets $p_i \propto n_i^{\alpha}$: $\alpha = 1$ samples in proportion to size, $\alpha = 0$ samples every dataset equally, and values between up-sample small sets.

cards.front: What is the risk of strong up-sampling of a small dataset?
cards.back: It is repeated many times, so the model can memorise it and overfit while larger sets are seen less.

cards.front: When should you use Building Instruction-Tuning Examples and Data Mixtures, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Preparing any instruction or chat fine-tuning set: converting instruction-style records and chat logs to one format, making sure responses terminate, and blending several sources of very different sizes.

Avoid it when: Continued pretraining on raw text, which needs no template or role mask. Do not re-template data for a model that ships its own template unless you are deliberately changing the format.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Building Instruction-Tuning Examples and Data Mixtures?
cards.back:
• Tokenising the rendered text adds BOS or EOS twice if the tokenizer also adds them automatically
• Content that contains template markers can forge a turn boundary; escape or strip them
• Masking by token id instead of position removes the real EOS when pad and EOS share an id
• Weights computed from raw record counts ignore very different average lengths; token counts may be fairer

cards.front: Key formulas: Building Instruction-Tuning Examples and Data Mixtures
cards.back:
Text: $x = [r(m_1);\ldots;r(m_n)]$, EOS after assistant
Mask: $a_t = 1$ on assistant and EOS tokens
Loss: $-\frac{\sum_t a_t \log p(x_t \mid x_{<t})}{\sum_t a_t}$
Weights: $p_i = \frac{n_i^{\alpha}}{\sum_j n_j^{\alpha}}$
$\alpha = 1$: $p_i \propto n_i$;  $\alpha = 0$: $p_i = \frac{1}{K}$
Expected draws from set $i$: $N p_i$

cards.front: What is Fine-Tuning Data Prep with MinHash Dedup and Group Splits?
cards.back: Clean fine-tuning data by removing exact duplicates through a normalised hash, near duplicates through MinHash signatures, splitting train and validation by group, and flagging eval text that overlaps the training set by n-grams.

cards.front: Fine-Tuning Data Prep with MinHash Dedup and Group Splits: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Duplicates make validation scores optimistic and bias what the model memorises. Exact hashing misses lightly edited copies, and comparing every pair of documents is quadratic. MinHash fixes both: apply a random hash to every shingle and keep the minimum, and two sets agree on that minimum with probability equal to their Jaccard similarity, so a short signature estimates similarity. Random row splits still leak, since near copies from one source land on both sides, so split by group. Flow: texts → normalise → shingles → signatures → groups → split.

cards.front: Why does a MinHash match estimate Jaccard similarity?
cards.back: Under a random hash the smallest element of the union is equally likely to be any union member, and the two sets share the minimum exactly when it lies in the intersection, which has probability $J(A,B)$.

cards.front: Why split by group rather than at random?
cards.back: Items from one source or conversation are near duplicates of each other, so a random split puts copies on both sides and the validation loss measures memorisation.

cards.front: How many hash functions are needed?
cards.back: The error shrinks as $1/\sqrt{k}$, so $k = 128$ gives a standard deviation of at most about $0.044$, which is enough for coarse thresholds.

cards.front: Why remove eval overlap from training data?
cards.back: If eval text appears in training, the benchmark score reflects memorisation. N-gram overlap detects verbatim copies, though not paraphrases.

cards.front: When should you use Fine-Tuning Data Prep with MinHash Dedup and Group Splits, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any instruction or domain fine-tuning corpus scraped or merged from several sources, before training and before trusting a validation score or a benchmark number.

Avoid it when: Tiny hand-curated sets where every example is deliberate, or tasks where repeated phrasing is the signal itself, such as templated classification. Aggressive thresholds can delete legitimate variants.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Fine-Tuning Data Prep with MinHash Dedup and Group Splits?
cards.back:
• Python's built-in hash for strings changes between runs; use a stable hash for signatures
• Group labels must follow the leak path: split by source or conversation, not by row, or copies still straddle the split
• A very short n-gram length flags common phrases as contamination, a very long one misses lightly edited copies
• Normalising too aggressively merges items that differ in numbers or code and are genuinely distinct

cards.front: Key formulas: Fine-Tuning Data Prep with MinHash Dedup and Group Splits
cards.back:
Jaccard: $J(A,B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}$
Match prob: $P[\min h(A) = \min h(B)] = J(A,B)$
Estimate: $\hat{J} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i} [s^A_i = s^B_i]$
Spread: $\sqrt{\frac{J(1-J)}{k}}$
Hash: $h_i(x) = (a_i x + b_i)\ \mathrm{mod}\ p$
Overlap: $\frac{|G_{eval} \cap G_{train}|}{|G_{eval}|}$

cards.front: What is QLoRA and 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4)?
cards.back: Store a frozen base model in 4 bits using 16 levels placed at normal quantiles, quantised in blocks, and train only 16-bit LoRA adapters on top.

cards.front: QLoRA and 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4): what is the key insight?
cards.back: Trained weights are roughly bell shaped, so evenly spaced 4-bit levels waste codes in the sparse tails while crowding too few near zero. Placing the 16 levels at quantiles of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ gives each level about equal probability mass, and splitting the weights into small blocks with their own scale keeps the normal assumption true locally and contains outliers to one block. Flow: weights → scale per block → round to levels → dequantise.

cards.front: Why 4-bit NormalFloat instead of uniform 4-bit integers?
cards.back: Weights are close to normal, so quantile-spaced levels give each code about equal probability and lower average error than evenly spaced levels, which waste codes in the tails.

cards.front: Why must zero be an exact level?
cards.back: Zeros and near-zero weights are common, and representing them exactly avoids adding noise. The construction uses 8 positive, 7 negative levels and an explicit zero for this reason.

cards.front: What does double quantisation save?
cards.back: The per-block scales cost $32/64 = 0.5$ bits per parameter in fp32. Quantising the scales to 8 bits shrinks that to about $0.127$ bits per parameter.

cards.front: What is trained in QLoRA?
cards.back: Only the 16-bit LoRA adapters. The 4-bit base is frozen, dequantised on the fly for forward and backward passes, and gradients reach the adapters through it.

cards.front: When should you use QLoRA and 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Fine-tuning a large model on a GPU too small to hold it in 16 bits: the frozen base sits in 4 bits and only small adapters and their optimiser state use higher precision.

Avoid it when: Weights that are far from normal, very small models where memory is not the constraint, or deployments needing the fastest possible matmul, since 4-bit weights must be dequantised before use.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of QLoRA and 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4)?
cards.back:
• The exact level values come from the paper's specific construction (the asymmetric split and the offset); this card reproduces that construction, so treat small differences from a library's table as construction details, not bugs
• Smaller blocks cut error but raise scale overhead; $B = 64$ is a trade-off
• This code stores indices as uint8 for clarity; real storage packs two 4-bit codes per byte
• Dequantisation happens on every forward pass, so 4-bit saves memory, not necessarily time

cards.front: Key formulas: QLoRA and 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4)
cards.back:
levels $=$ quantiles of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, divided by max
$\hat{w} = s_b\, L[\arg\min_k |w/s_b - L_k|],\;\; s_b = \max|w_{block}|$
Bits per param $= 4 + 32/B$, fp32 scale
Double quant: $4 + 8/B + 32/(256B)$
Bytes per param $=$ bits$/8 \approx 0.5$

cards.front: What is Bottleneck Adapter Layers?
cards.back: Insert a small bottleneck module with a residual connection after a frozen sublayer and train only the module, a few percent of the weights.

cards.front: Bottleneck Adapter Layers: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A pretrained network already computes useful features, so a task only needs a small correction on top of them. A narrow down-then-up projection with a skip connection is exactly that: it can pass features through unchanged, or add a learned low-dimensional edit. Initialising the up-projection at zero makes the module the identity, so training starts from the pretrained function. Unlike LoRA, the module is a new sequential layer and cannot be merged away. Flow: sublayer output → down-project → nonlinearity → up-project → add back.

cards.front: Why is the adapter initialised near the identity?
cards.back: So the model starts exactly as the pretrained one. A random adapter would perturb every layer and destroy the pretrained features before training could help.

cards.front: How many parameters does one adapter add?
cards.back: $2dr + r + d$ with hidden size $d$ and bottleneck $r$: two weight matrices plus two bias vectors. For $r \ll d$ this is far less than $d^2$.

cards.front: Adapters versus LoRA: what is the trade-off?
cards.back: LoRA's low-rank update is parallel and merges into $W$, so inference is unchanged. Adapters add sequential layers and extra latency, but they are simple, modular and can use a nonlinearity.

cards.front: Where are adapters placed in a transformer layer?
cards.back: In the original design, after the attention sublayer's output projection and after the feed-forward sublayer, before the residual addition and layer norm.

cards.front: When should you use Bottleneck Adapter Layers, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Serving many tasks from one frozen base, where each task stores only small adapter weights, and when adding a task must not disturb earlier ones.

Avoid it when: Latency-critical inference, since adapters add sequential layers that cannot be folded into the weights. LoRA is preferred when merging for zero extra latency matters.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Bottleneck Adapter Layers?
cards.back:
• Exactly zero initialisation of both $W_u$ and $W_d$ would give zero gradients; zero only the up-projection and keep $W_d$ random
• Adapters cannot be merged into the base weights, so inference latency grows with depth
• Remember to unfreeze layer norms or task heads if the recipe trains them; this code covers only the adapter

cards.front: Key formulas: Bottleneck Adapter Layers
cards.back:
$y = x + W_u\,\sigma(W_d x + b_d) + b_u$
$W_d: d \rightarrow r,\;\; W_u: r \rightarrow d,\;\; r \ll d$
Params per adapter $= 2dr + r + d$
$W_u = 0,\; b_u = 0 \Rightarrow y = x$
LoRA: $y = Wx + \frac{\alpha}{r}\,BAx$, mergeable

cards.front: What is Int8 Post-Training Quantization?
cards.back: Store weights and activations as 8-bit integers plus a float scale, multiply in integers with 32-bit accumulation, then rescale the result.

cards.front: Int8 Post-Training Quantization: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A float tensor only needs enough levels to land within rounding distance of its true values, and 255 evenly spaced levels between $-\max|x|$ and $\max|x|$ often suffice. The cost is that one scale serves a whole group of numbers, so a single outlier stretches the step size for everyone else; giving each output channel its own scale, or handling outliers separately, keeps the step small. Flow: float tensor → absmax scale → round to int8 → integer matmul → rescale.

cards.front: Why accumulate int8 products in int32?
cards.back: Each product of two 8-bit values needs up to 16 bits and a dot product sums many of them, so 8-bit accumulators would overflow. The int32 result is exact and is rescaled once at the end.

cards.front: Why is per-channel weight quantisation better than per-tensor?
cards.back: Each channel's step is set by its own maximum, so channels with small ranges are not coarsened by one large channel. The error bound $s_j/2$ is tighter for them.

cards.front: What problem do outliers cause and how does LLM.int8() address it?
cards.back: One large value inflates $s$ and wastes most levels on rare magnitudes, so ordinary values round coarsely. LLM.int8() splits outlier feature dimensions into a 16-bit matmul and quantises the rest per vector.

cards.front: When would you use asymmetric quantisation?
cards.back: When values are skewed, such as post-ReLU activations, a zero point shifts the range so no levels are wasted on the empty negative side.

cards.front: When should you use Int8 Post-Training Quantization, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Reducing memory and bandwidth for inference of trained models, where weights are fixed and activations can be scaled on the fly. Per-channel weight scales are the usual default for linear layers.

Avoid it when: Models with strong activation outliers when only a single per-tensor scale is available, or when you need training in low precision, which needs different techniques than post-training rounding.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Int8 Post-Training Quantization?
cards.back:
• A single outlier sets $s$ and degrades every other value in its group
• Clipping to $[-127, 127]$ keeps the grid symmetric; using $-128$ breaks the exact symmetry of the scale
• This code uses float64 for clarity; real kernels use float16 scales and fused integer ops
• Activation scales must come from calibration or be computed per batch, which costs extra

cards.front: Key formulas: Int8 Post-Training Quantization
cards.back:
$s = \max|x|/127,\;\; q = \mathrm{clip}(\mathrm{round}(x/s), -127, 127)$
$\hat{x} = s\,q,\;\; |x - \hat{x}| \leq s/2$ in range
$s = (x_{max} - x_{min})/255$, asymmetric
$z = -128 - \mathrm{round}(x_{min}/s),\;\; \hat{x} = s\,(q - z)$
$Y \approx (X_q W_q^{\top})_{int32}\; s_x\, s_w^{\top}$
Per channel: $s_j = \max_i |W_{ji}|/127$

cards.front: What is Reward Model (Bradley-Terry Loss)?
cards.back: Learn a scalar reward for text from human comparisons by training so that the preferred response scores higher than the rejected one, using a logistic loss on the score difference.

cards.front: Reward Model (Bradley-Terry Loss): what is the key insight?
cards.back: People find it easier to say which of two answers is better than to give an absolute score. The Bradley-Terry model turns that into probability: the chance that the chosen response wins is a sigmoid of the difference between the two rewards. Only the difference matters, so the learned rewards have no absolute scale or zero point, and the loss simply pushes the gap in the right direction with more force when the model currently has the pair the wrong way round.

cards.front: Why is the loss a function of the reward difference only?
cards.back: The Bradley-Terry probability that one item beats another is a sigmoid of the difference of their scores. Adding a constant to all scores cancels, so absolute reward values are unidentifiable.

cards.front: Why does the loss equal $\log(1 + e^{-d})$?
cards.back: $-\log \sigma(d) = \log(1 + e^{-d})$. Computing it with logaddexp avoids overflow and underflow for large positive or negative differences.

cards.front: How does the reward model connect to DPO?
cards.back: DPO uses the same Bradley-Terry likelihood but defines the reward as a scaled log-ratio of policy to reference, so the policy itself plays the role of the reward model.

cards.front: When should you use Reward Model (Bradley-Terry Loss), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Building the reward model in RLHF from pairwise human or AI preference labels, or for any ranking problem trained on pairs.

Avoid it when: When labels are absolute scores (use regression), when preferences are intransitive or inconsistent across annotators, or when the reward will be optimised so hard that the model exploits its errors.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Reward Model (Bradley-Terry Loss)?
cards.back:
• Only reward differences are meaningful; normalise or centre rewards before using them elsewhere
• This code uses a linear reward on fixed features; a real model scores text with a transformer and a scalar head on its final token
• Noisy or contradictory labels cap how well pairs can be ordered
• Policies optimised against the reward can exploit its mistakes (reward hacking)

cards.front: Key formulas: Reward Model (Bradley-Terry Loss)
cards.back:
$P(\mathrm{chosen} \succ \mathrm{rejected}) = \sigma(r_c - r_r) = \frac{e^{r_c}}{e^{r_c} + e^{r_r}}$
Linear reward: $r(x) = w \cdot x$
$d = r_c - r_r = w \cdot (x_c - x_r)$
$L = -\mathrm{mean}\ \log\sigma(d) = \mathrm{mean}\ \log(1 + e^{-d})$
$\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = -\mathrm{mean}\left[\sigma(-d)\,(x_c - x_r)\right]$
Adding a constant to both $r$ leaves $L$ fixed

cards.front: What is RLHF Objective and the KL Penalty?
cards.back: RLHF maximises the reward-model score while a KL penalty keeps the policy $\pi$ close to the reference (SFT) policy $\pi_{ref}$; per token, the penalty becomes a small negative reward on every step.

cards.front: RLHF Objective and the KL Penalty: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A reward model is only trusted near the data it was trained on, so an optimiser that follows it freely finds gibberish that scores high. The KL term prices every step away from the reference: drift is allowed only when the reward gain pays for it, and $\beta$ sets the exchange rate. Because sequences are sampled from $\pi$, the KL is estimated from samples, and the estimator choice matters for noise. Flow: sample → compare to reference → penalise drift → add score → update.

cards.front: Why is a KL penalty needed in RLHF?
cards.back: The reward model is a proxy that is only reliable near the data it was trained on. Without the penalty the policy exploits its errors and drifts to degenerate text that scores high.

cards.front: How does the sequence-level KL become per-token rewards?
cards.back: The sequence log-ratio is the sum of per-token log-ratios, so charging $-\beta$ times each token's log-ratio sums to $-\beta$ times the sequence log-ratio, and the reward-model score is added at the last token.

cards.front: Why prefer $k_3$ over $k_1$ for estimating KL?
cards.back: Both are unbiased under samples from $p$, but $k_1$ can be negative per sample and is noisy, while $k_3$ is always non-negative and has lower variance.

cards.front: What does $\beta$ control?
cards.back: The trade-off between reward and staying near the reference. Large $\beta$ keeps the policy close and the gain small; small $\beta$ lets it drift and risks reward hacking.

cards.front: When should you use RLHF Objective and the KL Penalty, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any RL-style fine-tuning against a learned reward (PPO-style RLHF), and as a monitor of how far a tuned policy has moved from its start.

Avoid it when: Preference methods that fold the reference into the loss, such as DPO, need no separate penalty term. With a verifiable reward and no reward hacking risk the penalty may be set very small.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of RLHF Objective and the KL Penalty?
cards.back:
• Samples must come from $\pi$ (the first argument); sampling from $\pi_{ref}$ flips the direction and biases the estimate
• $k_1$ per sample can be negative, so a negative running KL is noise, not a bug in the model
• Using the policy's log-probabilities under a different temperature or mask than at sampling time corrupts the ratio
• A reference that is not frozen turns the anchor into a moving target

cards.front: Key formulas: RLHF Objective and the KL Penalty
cards.back:
$J(\pi) = \mathbb{E}[r(x,y)] - \beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi \| \pi_{ref})$
KL: $\sum_{x} p(x)\,\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$
Optimum: $\pi^{*} \propto \pi_{ref}\,\exp(r/\beta)$
Per token: $r_t = -\beta(\log\pi - \log\pi_{ref})$
Last token adds $r_{RM}(x,y)$ to $r_T$
$k_1 = \log\frac{p}{q}$ and $k_2 = \frac{1}{2}(\log\frac{p}{q})^2$
$k_3 = (\frac{q}{p} - 1) - \log\frac{q}{p}$
Unbiased: $\mathbb{E}_p[k_1] = \mathbb{E}_p[k_3] = \mathrm{KL}(p \| q)$

cards.front: What is Direct Preference Optimisation Loss?
cards.back: Fine-tune a language model on pairs of preferred and rejected responses by pushing up the log-probability gap between them, measured relative to a frozen reference model, with no separate reward model or reinforcement learning loop.

cards.front: Direct Preference Optimisation Loss: what is the key insight?
cards.back: DPO treats $\beta\cdot\log(\pi/\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})$ as an implicit reward: how much more the tuned model likes a response than the reference does. The loss is a logistic loss on the difference of that implicit reward between the chosen and rejected response, so it raises the chosen response and lowers the rejected one relative to the reference. Anchoring to the reference is what keeps the model from drifting arbitrarily far.

cards.front: How does DPO avoid training a reward model?
cards.back: It reparameterises the reward as a log-ratio of policy to reference, so the preference likelihood can be written directly in terms of the policy. Training the policy on that likelihood implicitly fits the reward.

cards.front: What does $\beta$ control?
cards.back: It scales the log-ratio reward, so it sets how strongly the policy is tied to the reference. A larger $\beta$ penalises movement away from the reference more and gives smaller updates for a given log-ratio gap.

cards.front: How does DPO relate to RLHF with PPO?
cards.back: Both target the same KL-regularised reward objective. PPO learns an explicit reward and samples from the policy online; DPO optimises a closed-form loss on a fixed dataset of preference pairs.

cards.front: When should you use Direct Preference Optimisation Loss, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Aligning an instruction-tuned model with a static dataset of preference pairs when a simple, stable supervised-style training loop is preferred over PPO.

Avoid it when: When preferences must be gathered online from the current policy, when a reusable reward model is needed for ranking or filtering, or when the preference data is far from the reference model's distribution.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Direct Preference Optimisation Loss?
cards.back:
• Inputs must be sequence-level log-probs (summed over response tokens), computed with the same prompt formatting
• Reference log-probs are constants; backpropagating into the reference is a bug
• Both chosen and rejected log-probs can fall during training; DPO constrains only their gap
• This code returns gradients with respect to the log-probs; a real model backpropagates them into its parameters, and long sequences make the log-probs very negative

cards.front: Key formulas: Direct Preference Optimisation Loss
cards.back:
Implicit reward: $r(x, y) = \beta\,\log\frac{\pi(y|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y|x)}$
Margin: $m = \beta\,[(\log\pi(y_w) - \log\pi_{ref}(y_w))$
$-\ (\log\pi(y_l) - \log\pi_{ref}(y_l))]$
Loss: $L = -\mathrm{mean}\ \log\sigma(m)$ over pairs
$\sigma(m) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-m}},\;\; \log\sigma(m) = -\log(1 + e^{-m})$
$\frac{\partial L}{\partial\log\pi(y_w)} = -\frac{\beta\,\sigma(-m)}{N},\;\; \frac{\partial L}{\partial\log\pi(y_l)} = +\frac{\beta\,\sigma(-m)}{N}$
$y_w$: preferred, $y_l$: rejected, $N$: pairs

cards.front: What is Evaluating a Fine-Tune - Win Rate and Sign Test?
cards.back: Decide whether a fine-tune beat its baseline: compare held-out loss, count pairwise wins with ties handled explicitly, test the wins and losses with an exact sign test, size the eval, and report forgetting.

cards.front: Evaluating a Fine-Tune - Win Rate and Sign Test: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A better loss number does not mean better answers, and a win rate of 55% on 40 prompts is mostly noise. Each prompt gives a paired verdict (win, loss or tie), and under "no difference" the non-tied pairs are fair coin flips, so the exact binomial answers how surprising the count is. Ties carry no direction, so report how you treated them. Flow: held-out loss → paired win/loss/tie → sign test → size → forgetting check.

cards.front: How should ties be handled in a win rate?
cards.back: Either count a tie as half a win, or drop ties and report how many there were. Whichever you pick, state it, because the two give different rates when ties are common.

cards.front: Why a sign test instead of a t-test here?
cards.back: The data are paired win, loss or tie verdicts, not numeric scores. Among non-tied pairs the null is a fair coin, so the exact binomial applies with no distributional assumption.

cards.front: How many prompts do I need to detect a small improvement?
cards.back: Use $n \approx z^2 p(1-p)/m^2$. For $p = 0.5$ and a margin of 0.05 at 95% confidence this is about 385 pairs, and halving the margin quadruples it.

cards.front: What is a forgetting check?
cards.back: Evaluate a general-capability benchmark before and after fine-tuning and report the change separately, since a gain on the target task can hide a loss elsewhere.

cards.front: When should you use Evaluating a Fine-Tune - Win Rate and Sign Test, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Comparing a fine-tuned model with its base or a previous version on open-ended prompts judged pairwise, by humans or by an LLM judge.

Avoid it when: Tasks with a deterministic metric and many examples, where a paired bootstrap on the score is simpler. A sign test also ignores the size of each win, so it is conservative when margins vary.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Evaluating a Fine-Tune - Win Rate and Sign Test?
cards.back:
• Counting ties as losses, or silently dropping them, shifts the win rate; always report the tie count
• Running many comparisons and reporting the best one inflates false positives; correct for multiple tests
• A judge that prefers longer or first-listed answers biases wins; randomise order and check length
• A significant win rate on a narrow prompt set says nothing about prompts outside it, or about forgetting

cards.front: Key formulas: Evaluating a Fine-Tune - Win Rate and Sign Test
cards.back:
Win rate $= (\mathrm{wins} + \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{ties}) / n$
Under $H_0$: wins $\sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n_e, \frac{1}{2})$
where $n_e = \mathrm{wins} + \mathrm{losses}$
Two-sided: $p = \min(1,\; 2\,\Pr[X \leq \min(w, l)])$
Wilson centre: $\frac{\hat{p} + z^2/2n}{1 + z^2/n}$
Sample size: $n \approx \frac{z^2\,p(1-p)}{m^2}$
Forgetting: $\Delta = M_{after} - M_{before}$

cards.front: What is RAG Retrieval (Chunk, Embed, Top-k)?
cards.back: Split documents into overlapping chunks, embed each chunk and the query as vectors, and return the k chunks whose vectors are most similar to the query to put in the language model's prompt.

cards.front: RAG Retrieval (Chunk, Embed, Top-k): what is the key insight?
cards.back: A language model cannot read a whole corpus, so retrieval chooses the few passages worth reading. Chunking sets the unit of retrieval: too large and the relevant sentence is diluted, too small and it loses its context, and overlap keeps a sentence that straddles a boundary from being cut in half. Normalising embeddings turns cosine similarity into a plain dot product, so search is one matrix-vector product.

cards.front: Why use overlapping chunks?
cards.back: Information near a chunk boundary would be split across two chunks and could be missed by both. Overlap repeats boundary text so at least one chunk contains the whole passage, at the cost of a larger index.

cards.front: Why normalise embeddings before search?
cards.back: For unit vectors the dot product equals cosine similarity, so exact search is a single matrix product and magnitude differences cannot affect the ranking.

cards.front: What are the trade-offs of exact versus approximate nearest-neighbour search?
cards.back: Exact search is simple and gives the true top-k but scales linearly with corpus size. Approximate indexes such as graph or clustering based ones are much faster on large corpora but can miss true neighbours.

cards.front: When should you use RAG Retrieval (Chunk, Embed, Top-k), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Question answering over private or fresh documents, where the model needs facts that are not in its weights and answers should cite sources.

Avoid it when: When the whole corpus fits in the prompt, when queries need exact keyword or ID matching that embeddings blur, or when the answer requires reasoning across many scattered passages that top-k cannot gather.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of RAG Retrieval (Chunk, Embed, Top-k)?
cards.back:
• The embedding here is a signed hashing bag of words, so it only matches shared words; it has no semantic understanding, unlike a trained embedding model
• Embedding the chunks inside retrieve is for brevity; real systems embed once and store the matrix
• Chunk by words here for simplicity; production systems chunk by tokens or sentences and keep metadata
• Query and chunks must use the same embedding model and normalisation

cards.front: Key formulas: RAG Retrieval (Chunk, Embed, Top-k)
cards.back:
Chunks: words$[i : i + size]$ for $i = 0, step, 2\cdot step, \ldots$
$step = size - overlap$
Embedding: $e(x) = \frac{v(x)}{\|v(x)\|_2}$ (unit length)
$\cos(q,c) = e(q)\cdot e(c)$ for unit vectors
Top-$k$: indices of the $k$ largest $\cos(q, c_i)$

cards.front: What is Document Loading and Text Extraction?
cards.back: Turn raw documents into clean text plus metadata before chunking and embedding: strip HTML boilerplate, normalise Unicode and whitespace, drop header and footer lines that repeat across pages, and tag every chunk with its source and page.

cards.front: Document Loading and Text Extraction: what is the key insight?
cards.back: An embedding model sees only the text it is given, so navigation menus, scripts, page footers and broken hyphenation become part of the chunk vectors and pull unrelated chunks together. Boilerplate repeats on most pages while real content does not, so a line seen on a large fraction of pages is almost certainly not content. Cleaning is cheap next to bad retrieval, and metadata attached now is what later makes citations and filters possible. Flow: raw file → parse → clean text → chunks with metadata → embeddings.

cards.front: Why clean text before embedding?
cards.back: Boilerplate and broken text add shared noise to chunk vectors, which makes unrelated chunks look similar and lowers retrieval precision. Clean input also gives stable tokenisation.

cards.front: How do you detect repeated headers and footers without layout analysis?
cards.back: Count how many pages each distinct line appears on and drop lines whose page fraction passes a threshold, masking digits so page numbers still match.

cards.front: Why attach metadata to every chunk?
cards.back: After chunking, a chunk no longer knows where it came from. Source, page and section let the system cite answers and filter retrieval by document, date or access level.

cards.front: What is the hardest part of document loading in practice?
cards.back: Non-HTML formats. PDFs, scans and tables lose reading order and structure on extraction, so they need layout-aware parsers or OCR and careful checking.

cards.front: When should you use Document Loading and Text Extraction, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any ingestion pipeline for web pages, reports or exports, as the first stage before chunking, where text quality directly limits retrieval quality.

Avoid it when: Do not rely on these rules for PDFs, scans and tables. Layout-aware parsers or OCR are needed there, and extraction errors in those formats are the main source of failures in retrieval pipelines.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Document Loading and Text Extraction?
cards.back:
• Digits are masked when counting so that Page 1, Page 2 match, which also merges unique lines that differ only by a number
• A low min_frac on a short document deletes real content; a short repeated line is only boilerplate if it appears on most pages
• NFKC changes meaning for some text, for example it turns superscript digits into ordinary ones, so keep the raw text if exact quotes matter
• PDFs, scanned pages and tables need dedicated parsers or OCR; these rules do not fix reading order or merged columns

cards.front: Key formulas: Document Loading and Text Extraction
cards.back:
NFKC: compatibility decomposition, then composition
$\mathrm{pc}(\ell)$ = number of pages containing line $\ell$
Drop line $\ell$ if $\frac{\mathrm{pc}(\ell)}{\mathrm{pages}} \geq \mathrm{min\_frac}$
Threshold in pages $= \lceil \mathrm{min\_frac} \cdot \mathrm{pages} \rceil$

cards.front: What is Document Chunking Strategies?
cards.back: Cut documents into retrievable pieces: fixed windows with overlap (stride $\mathrm{size} - \mathrm{overlap}$), or recursive splitting that tries paragraph, line, sentence and word boundaries in turn until every piece fits the size limit.

cards.front: Document Chunking Strategies: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A chunk is the unit that gets embedded, retrieved and pasted into the prompt, so its size sets a trade-off. Small chunks match a query precisely but lose the context around the fact; large chunks keep the meaning but blur many topics into one vector and waste prompt space. A fact of length $L$ is guaranteed to sit whole inside some chunk only if $\mathrm{overlap} \geq L - 1$, which is why overlap exists. Cutting at natural boundaries (paragraphs before sentences before words) keeps each piece readable and self-contained. Flow: document → split at boundaries → overlapping chunks → embeddings.

cards.front: How do chunk size and retrieval quality relate?
cards.back: Small chunks give precise matches but lack context, and large chunks keep context but dilute the embedding and use more prompt tokens. The best size is found by measuring retrieval recall on a labelled set.

cards.front: Why use overlap, and what does it cost?
cards.back: A fact that straddles a boundary would be cut in two; overlap at least as long as the fact guarantees one chunk holds it whole. The cost is a larger index and duplicate-looking results.

cards.front: How many chunks does a document of n items produce?
cards.back: With window size s and overlap o the stride is $s - o$, so the count is $\lceil (n - o)/(s - o) \rceil$ for $n > s$, and one chunk otherwise.

cards.front: What does recursive splitting add over fixed windows?
cards.back: It prefers natural boundaries such as paragraphs and sentences and only cuts finer when a piece is too long, so chunks are more coherent.

cards.front: When should you use Document Chunking Strategies, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Preparing any corpus for embedding and retrieval, where documents are longer than the embedding model's input or than the useful retrieval unit. Use recursive splitting for prose and fixed windows when the text has no structure.

Avoid it when: Short documents that already fit one chunk, or structured data such as tables and code, where the natural unit (a row, a function) should be the chunk instead of a character count.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Document Chunking Strategies?
cards.back:
• Measuring size in characters while the embedding model limit is in tokens; chunks can silently be truncated
• Overlap multiplies index size by about $\frac{\mathrm{size}}{\mathrm{size}-\mathrm{overlap}}$ and returns near-duplicate hits
• Splitting on a separator that is absent (a long line with no spaces) falls back to hard character cuts
• Splitting tables, code or lists by length destroys their structure; chunk them by their own units

cards.front: Key formulas: Document Chunking Strategies
cards.back:
$\mathrm{chunks} = \lceil \frac{n - \mathrm{overlap}}{\mathrm{size} - \mathrm{overlap}} \rceil$
Start of chunk $j$ = $j \cdot (\mathrm{size} - \mathrm{overlap})$
Blow-up $\approx \frac{\mathrm{size}}{\mathrm{size} - \mathrm{overlap}}$
Fact of length $L$ whole if $\mathrm{overlap} \geq L - 1$
$P(\mathrm{cut}) = \frac{L - 1}{\mathrm{size}}$ with no overlap

cards.front: What is Approximate Nearest-Neighbour Vector Index (IVF)?
cards.back: Exact search scans every vector for each query. An IVF index clusters the vectors with k-means, stores each one in its nearest cell, and at query time scans only the $n_{probe}$ cells closest to the query, trading a little recall for a large speed-up.

cards.front: Approximate Nearest-Neighbour Vector Index (IVF): what is the key insight?
cards.back: Nearby vectors tend to fall in the same cluster, so most of the corpus is provably irrelevant to a query that lands far from it. The index pays once to learn the clusters, then each query compares against $n_{list}$ centroids and scans only a few cells instead of all $N$ vectors. The cost is that a true neighbour sitting just across a cell boundary is missed unless a neighbouring cell is probed as well, which is why $n_{probe}$ is the recall-versus-speed dial. Graph indexes such as HNSW take a different route: a layered proximity graph where search greedily walks to closer nodes, from a sparse top layer down to the dense bottom layer, keeping a candidate list of size $ef$. Product quantisation instead compresses each vector into a few small codes so more of the index fits in memory. Flow: query → nearest cells → scan candidates → top-k.

cards.front: Why does IVF raise recall when nprobe grows?
cards.back: More cells are scanned, so more of the corpus is searched exactly. At $n_{probe} = n_{list}$ every vector is scanned and the result equals brute force.

cards.front: How does HNSW differ from IVF?
cards.back: HNSW is a layered proximity graph. Search enters at the sparse top layer, greedily moves to closer neighbours, then descends, keeping $ef$ candidates at the bottom. It usually gives high recall at low latency but uses more memory and has no training step.

cards.front: What does product quantisation do?
cards.back: It splits each vector into sub-vectors and replaces each with the index of its nearest codebook entry, compressing a vector to a few bytes. Distances are approximated from the codes, trading accuracy for memory.

cards.front: How do you choose nlist and nprobe?
cards.back: Pick $n_{list}$ near $\sqrt{N}$, then raise $n_{probe}$ until recall@k on held-out queries meets the target, accepting the latency that results.

cards.front: When should you use Approximate Nearest-Neighbour Vector Index (IVF), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Corpora of millions of vectors where brute force per query is too slow or too costly, and a small recall loss is acceptable because the generator or a re-ranker tolerates it.

Avoid it when: Small corpora, where exact search is one matrix product and has no recall loss. Also data that changes constantly with no retraining, since stale centroids hurt recall, and cases that need guaranteed exact results.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Approximate Nearest-Neighbour Vector Index (IVF)?
cards.back:
• Recall is not guaranteed: a true neighbour in an unprobed cell is lost, so always measure recall@k against brute force on real queries
• Cells are rarely balanced, so the real cost depends on the sizes of the probed cells, not just the formula
• Centroids go stale when the data distribution drifts; re-train the quantiser periodically
• Euclidean cells assume the metric matches the one used to cluster; normalise vectors if you search by cosine

cards.front: Key formulas: Approximate Nearest-Neighbour Vector Index (IVF)
cards.back:
Exact search per query: cost $= N d$
IVF: rank $n_{list}$ centroids, scan $n_{probe}$ cells
cost $\approx n_{list} d + \frac{n_{probe}}{n_{list}} N d$
Best split: $n_{list} \approx \sqrt{N}$
Lloyd step: $c_j \leftarrow$ mean of cell $j$ vectors
$\mathrm{recall@}k = \frac{|\mathrm{approx} \cap \mathrm{exact}|}{k}$

cards.front: What is Metadata Filtering in Vector Search?
cards.back: Restrict nearest-neighbour search to rows whose metadata matches a condition (date, tenant, source, access level), either before the search (pre-filter) or after it (post-filter with oversampling).

cards.front: Metadata Filtering in Vector Search: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Pre-filtering searches only the allowed rows, so the answer is exact but the index cannot use its usual shortcuts. Post-filtering searches everything and then discards, which is fast but wasteful: if only a fraction $s$ of rows pass the filter, only about $s$ of the returned hits survive, so asking for $k$ results gives far fewer. The fix is to fetch about $k/s$ candidates first. Because oversampling is only probabilistic, a filter that enforces access control must be applied as a hard pre-filter, never as a best-effort clean-up. Flow: query + filter → candidate rows → top-k scores → allowed results.

cards.front: What is the difference between pre-filtering and post-filtering?
cards.back: Pre-filtering restricts the candidate rows and then searches them, which is exact but may be slow. Post-filtering searches all rows and then drops hits that fail the filter, which is fast but can return fewer than k.

cards.front: How many candidates does post-filtering need to return k results?
cards.back: About $k/s$ for selectivity $s$, since only a fraction $s$ of candidates survive. A safety factor above 1 is needed because survivors are random.

cards.front: How should access control be enforced in retrieval?
cards.back: As a hard pre-filter on every query, using the user's permissions, so documents the user cannot see are never scored or returned.

cards.front: Why can filtered approximate search lose recall?
cards.back: A graph or cluster index is built over all vectors. A selective filter removes most nodes, so the remaining ones may not be reachable from the entry point and true neighbours are missed.

cards.front: When should you use Metadata Filtering in Vector Search, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Pre-filter whenever correctness or security matters (tenant, access level) or the filter is very selective. Post-filter with oversampling when the filter is loose and the index is much faster without it.

Avoid it when: Do not post-filter for access control, since a shortfall or a bug leaks or loses documents. Do not oversample blindly when the filter is correlated with the query, because the formula assumes survivors are spread evenly among the candidates.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Metadata Filtering in Vector Search?
cards.back:
• With oversample $= 1$ and a selective filter, post-filtering can return zero results, not just a few fewer
• Setting $c = k/s$ only gives $k$ survivors on average; about half of queries still fall short, so use a safety factor such as 2
• Access control applied after the search is unsafe; enforce it as a pre-filter or inside the index
• Filtering inside an approximate graph index can disconnect the graph and lower recall, so a very selective filter may need brute force over the subset

cards.front: Key formulas: Metadata Filtering in Vector Search
cards.back:
Selectivity $s = \frac{\mathrm{rows\ passing}}{N}$
Survivors $\sim \mathrm{Binomial}(c, s)$, mean $c \cdot s$
Needed candidates $c = \lceil k / s \rceil$
$P(\mathrm{fewer\ than\ }k) = \sum_{j<k} \binom{c}{j} s^{j} (1-s)^{c-j}$

cards.front: What is Hybrid Search (BM25 + Dense, Reciprocal Rank Fusion)?
cards.back: Run a lexical retriever (BM25) and a dense vector retriever side by side, then merge their ranked lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which uses only ranks so the incompatible score scales never need to be calibrated.

cards.front: Hybrid Search (BM25 + Dense, Reciprocal Rank Fusion): what is the key insight?
cards.back: Lexical and dense search fail in opposite ways: BM25 nails exact terms, names and IDs but misses paraphrases, while embeddings catch meaning but blur rare tokens. A BM25 score and a cosine similarity live on unrelated scales, so adding them needs fragile tuning. Ranks are comparable across any scorer, and giving each list a vote of $\frac{1}{k + \mathrm{rank}}$ rewards documents that both systems like while the constant $k$ stops one list's top spot from dominating. Flow: query → BM25 list + dense list → rank votes → fused top-k.

cards.front: Why use rank fusion instead of adding the scores?
cards.back: BM25 scores are unbounded and corpus dependent while cosine similarity is in a fixed range. RRF uses only ranks, so no normalisation or weight tuning is needed and monotonic score changes cannot alter the result.

cards.front: What does the constant $k$ in RRF do?
cards.back: It flattens the vote curve. A small $k$ makes the top ranks dominate, while a large $k$ makes lower ranks count more. About 60 is a common default.

cards.front: Why does BM25 saturate term frequency?
cards.back: The factor $\frac{f(k_1+1)}{f+k_1(\ldots)}$ approaches $k_1+1$ as $f$ grows, so the tenth occurrence of a word adds far less than the first, unlike raw TF-IDF.

cards.front: When does hybrid retrieval beat dense-only?
cards.back: When queries contain rare terms, names, codes or exact phrases that embeddings blur. The lexical list restores exact matches and fusion keeps the semantic ones.

cards.front: When should you use Hybrid Search (BM25 + Dense, Reciprocal Rank Fusion), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Retrieval for RAG and search where queries mix exact keywords or identifiers with natural-language intent, and where you cannot calibrate scores across retrievers.

Avoid it when: When one retriever clearly dominates on your data, since fusion adds latency and a second index. Also when you have labelled data to train a learned ranker, which can use the actual scores.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Hybrid Search (BM25 + Dense, Reciprocal Rank Fusion)?
cards.back:
• RRF discards score margins, so a dominant lexical match and a barely better one count the same; keep lists long enough that good documents appear in both
• Tokenisation and casing must match between the index and the query, otherwise BM25 silently scores zero
• This BM25 scans every document; real engines use an inverted index and precomputed statistics
• Ties in the fused score need a stable rule, here the document id, or results vary between runs

cards.front: Key formulas: Hybrid Search (BM25 + Dense, Reciprocal Rank Fusion)
cards.back:
$\mathrm{IDF}(t) = \ln\left(1 + \frac{N - n + 0.5}{n + 0.5}\right)$
$\mathrm{BM25}(D) = \sum_{t} \mathrm{IDF}(t) \cdot \frac{f(k_1+1)}{f + k_1(1 - b + b|D|/\mathrm{avgdl})}$
Here $f$ = count of $t$ in $D$, $N$ docs, $n$ with $t$
Over lists: $\mathrm{RRF}(d) = \sum \frac{1}{k + \mathrm{rank}(d)}$, $k \approx 60$
Monotone score maps keep ranks, so RRF is unchanged

cards.front: What is Reranking and MMR Diversity?
cards.back: Retrieve many candidates with a fast first stage, reorder the best few with a slower, more accurate reranker, and pick results with Maximal Marginal Relevance so they are relevant and not redundant.

cards.front: Reranking and MMR Diversity: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A bi-encoder embeds the query and each document separately, so one vector search scans millions of items cheaply, but the query and document never see each other. A cross-encoder reads them together and judges far better, yet is too slow to run on the whole corpus. So use the cheap model for recall over about 100 candidates and the costly one for precision over the top few. MMR adds a second fix: the top-k by similarity are often near-duplicates, so each new pick is penalised for resembling what is already chosen. Flow: query → 100 candidates → cross-encoder rerank → MMR → top few.

cards.front: Why not use a cross-encoder for the whole corpus?
cards.back: It must run a forward pass per query-document pair, so cost scales with corpus size and nothing can be precomputed. A bi-encoder precomputes document vectors, so search is a fast nearest-neighbour lookup.

cards.front: What does $\lambda$ control in MMR?
cards.back: $\lambda=1$ ignores redundancy and returns plain top-$k$ by similarity to the query, while $\lambda=0$ ignores the query and keeps picking the item least similar to those chosen.

cards.front: Where does the first MMR pick come from?
cards.back: The redundancy term is empty for an empty selected set, so the first pick is the most relevant document whenever $\lambda>0$.

cards.front: How would you measure whether reranking helped?
cards.back: Compare ranking metrics such as recall@k or MRR on labelled queries with and without the reranker, and check the added latency.

cards.front: When should you use Reranking and MMR Diversity, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: RAG and search where the first stage has good recall but noisy order, and where the prompt budget is small enough that duplicated passages waste it.

Avoid it when: When latency is tight and the first stage is already precise, when the candidate list is tiny, or when the task wants every near-duplicate, for example exhaustive legal or audit retrieval.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Reranking and MMR Diversity?
cards.back:
• MMR scores here use vector similarity; mixing a cross-encoder score with a cosine in the same formula puts them on different scales
• If the first stage misses the right document, no reranker can recover it; check first-stage recall
• Reranker latency grows linearly with candidates; cap N and batch the pairs
• Lowering $\lambda$ too far drops relevant items just to be different

cards.front: Key formulas: Reranking and MMR Diversity
cards.back:
MMR: next $= \arg\max_{d \notin S}$
$\lambda\,\mathrm{sim}(d,q) - (1-\lambda)\max_{s \in S}\mathrm{sim}(d,s)$
$\lambda=1$ gives plain top-$k$; $\lambda=0$ pure diversity
Unit vectors: $\mathrm{sim}(a,b) = a \cdot b$
Diversity: $\frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i<j}\mathrm{sim}(s_i,s_j)$
Rerank: sort by $f(q,d)$, keep the top $n$

cards.front: What is Query Transformation and HyDE?
cards.back: Fix the mismatch between a short question and answer-like documents before searching: embed a hypothetical answer (HyDE), search with several paraphrases and fuse the ranks, or rewrite the query using the chat history.

cards.front: Query Transformation and HyDE: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A question and its answer rarely look alike, and an embedding of a short question can land far from the passage that answers it. HyDE has the language model write a plausible answer first and embeds that instead: it is document-shaped, so it lands in the right neighbourhood even if its facts are wrong, because only the neighbourhood is used and the results are real documents. Multi-query search hedges by asking several ways and fusing the rankings. Flow: question → hypothetical answer → embedding → nearest real documents.

cards.front: Why embed a fake answer instead of the question?
cards.back: Documents look like answers, not questions. The hypothetical text is document-shaped, so its embedding falls near real relevant documents even when its facts are wrong.

cards.front: Why use ranks instead of scores when fusing multi-query results?
cards.back: Scores from different queries are not on a common scale. Ranks are, and reciprocal rank fusion needs no tuning beyond the constant $k$.

cards.front: What does query rewriting from chat history fix?
cards.back: A follow-up such as 'how much does it cost?' has no standalone meaning. Rewriting resolves pronouns and context into a self-contained query before retrieval.

cards.front: When does HyDE hurt?
cards.back: When the generator is wrong about the topic, the hypothetical text points to the wrong neighbourhood. It also adds latency and cost.

cards.front: When should you use Query Transformation and HyDE, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Zero-shot retrieval over a new domain with no relevance labels, short or vague user questions, and chat settings where the latest message depends on earlier turns.

Avoid it when: Latency- or cost-sensitive paths, queries that are exact identifiers or keywords, and topics the generator knows nothing about, where its hypothetical text can point the wrong way.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Query Transformation and HyDE?
cards.back:
• A hallucinated hypothetical document can pull retrieval to the wrong place, so check it against the original query or fuse it with plain query results
• HyDE adds an LLM call of latency and cost before every search
• The generator here is a stub; a real one makes results vary run to run unless temperature is zero
• Rewriting from chat history must keep the user's intent; an over-eager rewrite can drop a constraint

cards.front: Key formulas: Query Transformation and HyDE
cards.back:
HyDE: $\hat{d} = \mathrm{LLM}(q)$, $v = \frac{e(\hat{d})}{\|e(\hat{d})\|}$
Retrieve top-$k$ of $\cos(v, e(d_i))$ over the corpus
Multi-query: rankings $R_1,\ldots,R_m$
$\mathrm{RRF}(d) = \sum_{j} \frac{1}{k + \mathrm{rank}_j(d)}$, rank starts at 1
Typical $k = 60$; a document missing from $R_j$ adds 0

cards.front: What is Retrieval Metrics (Recall@k, MRR, nDCG)?
cards.back: Judge a ranked list of documents against known relevance labels: did the relevant ones appear in the top $k$, how high was the first one, and how good is the whole ordering.

cards.front: Retrieval Metrics (Recall@k, MRR, nDCG): what is the key insight?
cards.back: A retriever returns an ordered list, so correctness depends on position as well as membership. Recall@k asks what fraction of the relevant items made the top $k$, MRR rewards putting the first relevant item high, and nDCG discounts each item's relevance by the log of its rank and divides by the best possible ordering, so a perfect ranking scores one and graded relevance is handled.

cards.front: When is Recall@k the right metric for retrieval?
cards.back: For a first-stage retriever feeding a reranker or an LLM, since anything missing from the top $k$ can never be recovered later. Order within the top $k$ matters less.

cards.front: Why does nDCG normalise by the ideal DCG?
cards.back: Raw DCG grows with the number of relevant items, so queries are not comparable. Dividing by the best achievable DCG puts every query on a zero-to-one scale.

cards.front: How do MRR and nDCG differ?
cards.back: MRR only looks at the first relevant item and treats relevance as binary. nDCG uses the whole ranked list and supports graded relevance with a smooth position discount.

cards.front: When should you use Retrieval Metrics (Recall@k, MRR, nDCG), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Evaluating search, recommender candidate generation and the retrieval step of RAG systems when relevance labels exist for each query.

Avoid it when: When no relevance judgements are available, or when answer quality rather than retrieval quality is the goal; a high Recall@k does not guarantee a good generated answer. MRR ignores everything after the first relevant hit.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Retrieval Metrics (Recall@k, MRR, nDCG)?
cards.back:
• Queries with no relevant document divide by zero here; drop them or define them as zero
• Gain choice matters: this code uses linear gain, which is what scikit-learn uses; other libraries use $2^{\mathrm{rel}} - 1$
• Ties in scores are broken arbitrarily here by sort order; scikit-learn averages over ties by default
• The nDCG code needs $k$ no larger than the number of documents per query

cards.front: Key formulas: Retrieval Metrics (Recall@k, MRR, nDCG)
cards.back:
$\mathrm{Recall@}k = \frac{|\mathrm{relevant} \cap \mathrm{top}\text{-}k|}{|\mathrm{relevant}|}$
$\mathrm{RR} = \frac{1}{\mathrm{rank\ of\ first\ relevant}}$;  $\mathrm{MRR}$ = mean RR
$\mathrm{DCG@}k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{\mathrm{rel}_i}{\log_2(i+1)}$ (linear gain)
$\mathrm{nDCG@}k = \frac{\mathrm{DCG@}k}{\mathrm{IDCG@}k}$
$\mathrm{IDCG@}k$: $\mathrm{DCG@}k$ of the ideal ordering
Each metric is averaged over queries

cards.front: What is RAG Evaluation - Retrieval, Faithfulness, Relevance?
cards.back: Score a retrieval-augmented system in parts: did retrieval rank the relevant chunks high and cover the needed facts, is the answer supported by the retrieved text, and does it address the question.

cards.front: RAG Evaluation - Retrieval, Faithfulness, Relevance: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A single end-to-end score cannot tell a retrieval failure from a generation failure. Splitting the pipeline localises the fault: poor context precision or recall means fix the retriever, while good context but unsupported claims means fix the generator. Faithfulness asks only whether the answer follows from the context, not whether the context is true. Flow: query → retrieve → score contexts → split answer into claims → check support.

cards.front: How do you tell a retrieval failure from a generation failure?
cards.back: Look at the parts separately. Low context recall or precision points at the retriever. Good context with unsupported claims points at the generator.

cards.front: Why is context precision computed like average precision?
cards.back: Order matters, since models attend more to early chunks and context is limited. Average precision rewards ranking relevant chunks first, and dividing by the number of relevant items makes a missed relevant chunk cost score.

cards.front: Does high faithfulness mean the answer is correct?
cards.back: No. It only means the claims follow from the retrieved text. If the context is wrong or incomplete, a faithful answer can still be wrong.

cards.front: How reliable are LLM judges for claim support?
cards.back: They are useful but imperfect, with their own biases and errors, so validate them against a human-labelled sample and track agreement.

cards.front: When should you use RAG Evaluation - Retrieval, Faithfulness, Relevance, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Diagnosing a RAG pipeline, comparing retrievers or chunking choices, and regression-testing a pipeline when prompts or indexes change.

Avoid it when: As a measure of factual truth: faithfulness only checks agreement with the retrieved text. Without relevance labels or reference facts the retrieval metrics cannot be computed.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of RAG Evaluation - Retrieval, Faithfulness, Relevance?
cards.back:
• Token overlap is a crude proxy: it passes paraphrased contradictions that share words and fails correct paraphrases that do not
• An LLM or NLI judge for support has its own errors and biases; treat its scores as estimates and spot-check them against humans
• Retrieval labels depend on the annotator, so precision and recall are only as good as those labels
• Faithfulness ignores truth of the context and whether the answer leaves out needed facts

cards.front: Key formulas: RAG Evaluation - Retrieval, Faithfulness, Relevance
cards.back:
$P@k = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i \leq k} \mathrm{rel}_i$
Precision: $\frac{\sum_k P@k \cdot \mathrm{rel}_k}{\sum_k \mathrm{rel}_k}$
Recall: $\frac{\mathrm{facts\ found}}{\mathrm{facts\ needed}}$
Faithfulness: $\frac{\mathrm{supported\ claims}}{\mathrm{all\ claims}}$
Support: $\frac{|c \cap C|}{|c|} \geq \theta$

cards.front: What is Function Calling and Tool Dispatch?
cards.back: Tools are declared with a name, a description and a JSON Schema; the model emits a call as a name plus JSON arguments, and the application validates, runs the function and feeds the result back as a tool message.

cards.front: Function Calling and Tool Dispatch: what is the key insight?
cards.back: The model never runs anything. It only writes text that names a tool and its arguments, and that text is untrusted input. All the safety lives in the dispatcher: parse, validate against the schema, and only then execute. Returning a structured error instead of raising turns a bad call into feedback the model can read and correct on its next turn. Flow: declare tools → model emits call → parse JSON → validate → run → tool message → model answers or calls again.

cards.front: Why validate arguments if the model was given the schema?
cards.back: The model is a text generator and can still emit wrong types, missing fields or invalid JSON. Validation at the boundary keeps those out of your functions.

cards.front: Why return errors as tool messages instead of raising?
cards.back: A raised exception ends the loop. A structured error lets the model read what went wrong and retry with corrected arguments.

cards.front: How do parallel calls work?
cards.back: The model returns several calls in one turn, each with an id. You run them and return one tool message per id, then the model continues with all results.

cards.front: How is the loop kept from running forever?
cards.back: A step limit, plus returning a clear stop reason so the caller knows the answer was not reached.

cards.front: When should you use Function Calling and Tool Dispatch, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Letting a model act on the world or fetch fresh data: look up a record, call an API, run a calculation. Any time the model's output must feed code, a schema check at the boundary keeps bad calls harmless.

Avoid it when: Fixed pipelines where the steps are known in advance, which are cheaper and more predictable as plain code. Also avoid exposing tools with side effects, such as deletes or payments, without confirmation or a permission layer.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Function Calling and Tool Dispatch?
cards.back:
• Executing the function before validating lets malformed model output cause side effects
• Letting an exception escape dispatch ends the loop instead of giving the model feedback
• Dropping the call id breaks the pairing of results with parallel calls
• Vague tool descriptions make the model pick the wrong tool, since the description is its only guide

cards.front: Key formulas: Function Calling and Tool Dispatch
cards.back:
Input tokens: $\sum_{s=1}^{S} (P + s\,c) = SP + c\,\frac{S(S+1)}{2}$
Sequential latency: $\sum_{i} \ell_i$
Parallel latency: $\max_{i} \ell_i$
Success: $P = \prod_{s=1}^{S} p_s$
