The result is identical to standard attention, not an approximation. The gain is fewer slow GPU memory reads and writes, not fewer FLOPs. Flow: load block → scores → update max → rescale → accumulate → divide.

cards.front: Is FlashAttention an approximation?
cards.back: No. It computes exactly the same $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d})V$ as standard attention, up to floating-point rounding.

cards.front: Where does the speed-up come from if FLOPs are the same?
cards.back: Attention is limited by memory traffic. Tiling keeps blocks in fast on-chip memory and avoids writing and reading the $T \times T$ matrix in slow GPU memory.

cards.front: Why is the rescaling factor needed?
cards.back: The softmax terms were computed relative to an older maximum. Multiplying by $\exp(m - m_{new})$ re-expresses them relative to the new maximum so the sums stay consistent.

cards.front: What does it do to memory?
cards.back: The extra memory per row is a few scalars and one output vector, so it grows linearly in $T$ rather than quadratically.

cards.front: When should you use FlashAttention and Online Softmax, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Long sequences in training or prefill, where the $T \times T$ score matrix is too large or its memory traffic dominates runtime, and an exact result is required.

Avoid it when: Very short sequences where the score matrix is tiny, or when you need the full attention weights (for visualisation), since they are never materialised. Plain NumPy gains no speed; the benefit needs a fused GPU kernel.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of FlashAttention and Online Softmax?
cards.back:
• Initialising $m$ to $0$ instead of $-\infty$ gives wrong results when all scores are very negative
• With a causal mask a block can be fully masked for a row, so $m_{new} = -\infty$ and $\exp(m - m_{new})$ is NaN unless handled
• Forgetting to rescale $o$ as well as $\ell$ silently corrupts the output
• This NumPy version shows the arithmetic only; it is not faster and still forms a $T \times$ block tile

cards.front: Key formulas: FlashAttention and Online Softmax
cards.back:
New max: $m^{\prime} = \max(m, \max_j s_j)$
Denominator: $\ell^{\prime} = \ell\, e^{m-m^{\prime}} + \sum_j e^{s_j-m^{\prime}}$
Output: $o^{\prime} = o\, e^{m-m^{\prime}} + \sum_j e^{s_j-m^{\prime}} v_j$
Result: $\frac{o}{\ell} = \sum_i \mathrm{softmax}(s)_i\, v_i$
Scores: $s_j = \frac{q \cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d}}$

cards.front: What is Tensor Parallelism (Megatron-Style Sharded MLP)?
cards.back: Split one layer's weight matrices across devices: the first linear by columns, the second by rows, so the whole MLP needs a single all-reduce (sum) of the partial outputs.

cards.front: Tensor Parallelism (Megatron-Style Sharded MLP): what is the key insight?
cards.back: A nonlinearity cannot be applied to partial sums, so the split must not cut the contraction of the first matrix. Splitting $W_1$ by columns gives each device complete hidden units, so the activation is local. Splitting $W_2$ by rows then turns the output into a sum of per-device terms, and one all-reduce adds them. Attention does the same with heads. Flow: split weights → local compute → all-reduce → next layer.

cards.front: Why split the first linear by columns and the second by rows?
cards.back: Column blocks give each device whole hidden units, so the nonlinearity needs no communication. Row blocks of the second matrix make the output a sum of partials, which one all-reduce combines.

cards.front: How is attention split?
cards.back: Heads are divided across devices; each device holds its heads' $Q$, $K$, $V$ slices and the matching rows of the output projection, then one all-reduce sums the partial outputs.

cards.front: What does tensor parallelism cost in communication?
cards.back: One all-reduce of a $B \times T \times d$ activation per sharded block in the forward pass, and another in the backward pass, so it needs a fast interconnect.

cards.front: When should you use Tensor Parallelism (Megatron-Style Sharded MLP), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: A layer or model too large for one accelerator, on devices joined by a fast interconnect, since the all-reduce sits on the critical path of every layer.

Avoid it when: Across slow links, where the per-layer all-reduce dominates, or when the model fits on one device and data parallelism is enough.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Tensor Parallelism (Megatron-Style Sharded MLP)?
cards.back:
• Row-splitting the first matrix puts the activation on partial sums, which is wrong
• The degree must divide the number of heads and the hidden width evenly
• Tensor parallelism beyond one fast node usually loses to the communication cost

cards.front: Key formulas: Tensor Parallelism (Megatron-Style Sharded MLP)
cards.back:
$xW_1 = [xW_1^{(1)}, \dots, xW_1^{(n)}]$
$Y = \sum_{i} \mathrm{gelu}(xW_1^{(i)})\, W_2^{(i)}$
$\sum_i \mathrm{gelu}(z_i) \neq \mathrm{gelu}(\sum_i z_i)$
Comm bytes $= B \cdot T \cdot d \cdot \mathrm{bytes}$

cards.front: What is Pipeline Parallelism (GPipe Bubble and 1F1B)?
cards.back: Cut the model into $p$ stages of consecutive layers and stream $m$ microbatches through them; the idle warm-up and cool-down form a bubble of fraction $(p-1)/(m+p-1)$, and 1F1B bounds activation memory.

cards.front: Pipeline Parallelism (GPipe Bubble and 1F1B): what is the key insight?
cards.back: With one batch, stage $s$ must wait for stage $s-1$, so only one stage works at a time. Splitting the batch into microbatches lets stage $s$ start microbatch 0 while stage $s-1$ moves to microbatch 1. The pipeline still fills and drains, which costs $p-1$ idle steps per stage. 1F1B starts backward passes early so activations are freed sooner. Flow: split layers → feed microbatches → fill, steady state, drain → flush.

cards.front: Why does a pipeline have a bubble?
cards.back: The first microbatch must traverse the earlier stages before later stages can start, and the last stages sit idle while the pipeline drains. That is $p-1$ idle steps per stage.

cards.front: How do you shrink the bubble?
cards.back: Use more microbatches, since the fraction is $(p-1)/(m+p-1)$, at the price of smaller microbatches and lower per-step efficiency.

cards.front: What does 1F1B improve over GPipe?
cards.back: The bubble is the same, but backward passes start early, so a stage holds activations for at most about $p$ microbatches instead of all $m$.

cards.front: When should you use Pipeline Parallelism (GPipe Bubble and 1F1B), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Models too deep for one device, where layers can be cut into balanced stages and the link between stages only carries activations, which is cheap compared with a per-layer all-reduce.

Avoid it when: When $m$ is small compared with $p$ (the bubble is large), when stages cannot be balanced, or when the model already fits in memory.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Pipeline Parallelism (GPipe Bubble and 1F1B)?
cards.back:
• Unbalanced stages make the slowest stage set the pace for the whole pipeline
• Batch normalisation statistics change when the batch is split into microbatches
• Gradients from all microbatches must be accumulated before one optimiser step

cards.front: Key formulas: Pipeline Parallelism (GPipe Bubble and 1F1B)
cards.back:
Steps $= m + p - 1$
Microbatch $j$ on stage $s$ at step $t = j + s$
Idle slots $= p\,(p - 1)$
Bubble $= \frac{p-1}{m+p-1}$
1F1B warm-up on stage $s$ $= p - s - 1$

cards.front: What is Jailbreaks and Red-Team Evaluation?
cards.back: A jailbreak is user input crafted to make a model break its own policy. Red teaming measures that risk with a taxonomy of attacks, a seed test set, benign mutations and an attack success rate with a confidence interval, repeated after every change.

cards.front: Jailbreaks and Red-Team Evaluation: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A jailbreak is aimed at the model's policy by the user, whereas prompt injection hides instructions in untrusted data. You cannot list every bad phrasing, so you measure instead: take a fixed set of seed tests per category, rewrite each in cheap ways, and count how often the target misbehaves. A keyword filter blocks the plain seed but a trivial rewrite slips past, which is why the rate, not any one example, is the signal. With few attempts the rate is noisy, so report an interval. Flow: test prompts → mutations → target → success rate with interval.

cards.front: How does a jailbreak differ from prompt injection?
cards.back: A jailbreak is the user's own input trying to push the model past its policy. Prompt injection smuggles instructions inside untrusted data such as a web page, and the user may be innocent.

cards.front: Why report an interval and not just the attack success rate?
cards.back: With few attempts the rate is noisy, so a drop from one run to the next may be chance. The Wilson interval shows the plausible range and behaves sensibly near zero.

cards.front: Why do keyword filters fail?
cards.back: They match surface strings, and a rewrite with different spacing, casing or language keeps the meaning but removes the match. The model understands the rewrite while the filter does not.

cards.front: When must you re-run the evaluation?
cards.back: After every change to the model, system prompt, filters or tools, since any of them can reopen a gap, and keep the seed set fixed so versions compare.

cards.front: When should you use Jailbreaks and Red-Team Evaluation, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Before shipping a model or system prompt, and after every change to the model, prompt, filter or tool set, to compare robustness across versions and to find categories with no coverage.

Avoid it when: Do not treat a low rate as proof of safety: the seeds and mutations only sample the space of attacks. It also says nothing about injection through retrieved data, which needs its own tests.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Jailbreaks and Red-Team Evaluation?
cards.back:
• A low attack success rate only bounds the tested attacks; it is not a proof of safety
• Mutations of the same seed are correlated, so $n$ overstates the independent evidence and the interval is too narrow
• A fixed public seed set can be overfitted by tuning the system to it, so refresh it and keep a held-out part
• Categories with zero attempts look safe in the average; always report coverage next to the rate

cards.front: Key formulas: Jailbreaks and Red-Team Evaluation
cards.back:
Rate: $\mathrm{ASR} = k / n$
Estimate: $\hat{p} = k / n$
Wilson centre: $\frac{\hat{p} + z^2/2n}{1 + z^2/n}$
Half-width: $\frac{z\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n + z^2/4n^2}}{1 + z^2/n}$
Interval: centre $\pm$ half-width
Zero successes: upper $\approx 3 / n$ (95%)

cards.front: What is PII Detection and Redaction?
cards.back: Find personal data with pattern detectors, validate card numbers with a checksum, replace each value with a typed, consistent placeholder, and measure the detector with precision and recall.

cards.front: PII Detection and Redaction: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Text sent to a model, a log or a training set can carry identifiers that should not travel with it. Fixed formats such as emails and card numbers are easy to match, and a checksum rejects most random digit runs. A typed placeholder keeps the sentence useful, and giving the same value the same placeholder keeps references intact. Names and context-dependent facts have no fixed format, so patterns miss them. Flow: raw text → detect spans → drop overlaps → placeholders → redacted text.

cards.front: Why use a Luhn check on card numbers?
cards.back: Any long digit run matches a card regex, but real card numbers satisfy a checksum. About nine in ten random runs fail it, so false positives drop sharply.

cards.front: Why map the same value to the same placeholder?
cards.back: It keeps references and counts intact, so a model can still tell that two mentions are one person or address, without seeing the value.

cards.front: Which metric matters more for a redactor, precision or recall?
cards.back: Usually recall, because a missed identifier is a leak, while a false positive only removes some context. Track both and choose the trade-off per data type.

cards.front: Is redacted text anonymous?
cards.back: No. Names, rare facts or combinations of details can still re-identify someone, and the placeholder map is itself sensitive. Redaction lowers risk but does not guarantee anonymity.

cards.front: When should you use PII Detection and Redaction, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Cleaning text before logging, analytics, fine-tuning data or calls to an external model, where structured identifiers such as emails, phone numbers, IP addresses and card numbers must not leave the system.

Avoid it when: Do not rely on patterns alone for names, addresses or identifiers that depend on context; those need a named-entity model and human review. Redaction is also not anonymisation, since remaining text can still identify a person.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of PII Detection and Redaction?
cards.back:
• Regexes miss names, street addresses and free-form identifiers, so recall on the unchecked classes is unknown
• A phone or ID number can pass the card regex, so run the checksum and resolve overlaps
• Keeping the value-to-placeholder map next to the redacted text defeats the purpose; store it separately or drop it
• Evaluate on labelled synthetic or consented text, never on real people's data, and re-check when formats change

cards.front: Key formulas: PII Detection and Redaction
cards.back:
Luhn: $S \,\mathrm{mod}\, 10 = 0$ for digit sum $S$
Precision: $P = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}$
Recall: $R = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$
F1: $\frac{2PR}{P + R}$
Random digits pass Luhn: $\approx 1/10$

cards.front: What is Output Validation and Guardrails?
cards.back: Run model output through layered checks before it reaches a user or a tool, report every failure, retry with feedback or fall back, and decide whether a broken check blocks or lets the output through.

cards.front: Output Validation and Guardrails: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Treat the model as an untrusted producer: whatever it writes will be rendered, executed or acted on, so each destination deserves its own checks. Cheap checks (length, patterns, PII) run first and catch different failures than slow ones (grounding), so stacking them in series trades more false rejections for fewer misses. Each check also needs a policy for when it crashes: fail closed blocks safely, fail open keeps the product up. Flow: model output → validators → pass, retry with feedback or fallback.

cards.front: When would you fail open instead of fail closed?
cards.back: Fail closed when a bad output is costly, such as a tool call or a regulated answer. Fail open when availability matters more and the check is advisory, but log every skipped check so the gap is visible.

cards.front: How is this different from schema validation or injection defence?
cards.back: Schema validation checks only shape, and injection defence protects the input side and the tools. Output guardrails add content policy, privacy and grounding checks on whatever the model produced, whatever the cause.

cards.front: Why does adding more validators not always help?
cards.back: Each one raises the false-reject rate and latency. If validators share blind spots they miss the same outputs, so the gain is smaller than the independent product suggests.

cards.front: When should you use Output Validation and Guardrails, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Whenever model text is shown to users, parsed by code, or turned into a tool call, especially in regulated or customer-facing settings where a bad output has a real cost.

Avoid it when: Do not treat validators as a replacement for least-privilege tools and human approval of dangerous actions. Regex rules are brittle against paraphrase, and extra layers also add latency and false rejections.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Output Validation and Guardrails?
cards.back:
• Rates multiply only under independence; measure the combined rates on labelled data instead of trusting the formula
• Retry feedback that quotes the offending text can leak it back into the prompt; give reasons, not content
• Word-overlap grounding passes fluent but unsupported claims; use entailment checks for high stakes
• Validate for the destination, for example escape text before putting it in HTML or SQL, not only for content

cards.front: Key formulas: Output Validation and Guardrails
cards.back:
False reject of good output $F = 1 - \prod_i (1 - f_i)$
Bad output slips through $M = \prod_i m_i$
Assumes checks err independently
$\mathrm{grounded} = \frac{\mathrm{content\ words\ in\ sources}}{\mathrm{content\ words}}$
Attempts $\leq \mathrm{retries} + 1$

cards.front: What is Content Safety Classifiers and Thresholds?
cards.back: Moderate inputs and outputs with per-category classifier scores. Pick the threshold from the precision-recall trade-off, run a cheap filter first, escalate only the uncertain slice, and send the grey zone to humans.

cards.front: Content Safety Classifiers and Thresholds: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A classifier gives a score, and the threshold turns it into an action by trading missed harm against false alarms. For a severe category you fix the recall you must reach and take the highest threshold that still meets it, which keeps precision as high as that recall allows. Most traffic is clearly fine, so an expensive model only needs to see the band of scores the cheap one is unsure about. Flow: text → cheap score → clear cases decided → uncertain band → big model or human.

cards.front: How do you choose a threshold for a severe category?
cards.back: Set the recall you must reach on a validation set and take the highest threshold that meets it. That keeps precision as high as the recall target permits.

cards.front: When does a two-stage cascade save money?
cards.back: When the expected cost $c_1 + p\,c_2$ is below $c_2$, which means the escalated fraction satisfies $p < 1 - c_1/c_2$. A very cheap first stage allows escalating a large share.

cards.front: Why are calibrated scores useful for moderation?
cards.back: A calibrated score of 0.8 means about 80 percent of such items are truly positive, so thresholds and review bands can be set from costs, and they stay stable when scores are compared across categories.

cards.front: What goes to human review?
cards.back: The grey zone around the threshold, plus a random sample of confident decisions to audit for drift and silent errors.

cards.front: When should you use Content Safety Classifiers and Thresholds, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Gating prompts and responses with moderation scores, especially for severe categories where a target recall must be guaranteed on a labelled validation set, and where a cheap model can pre-screen traffic for a costly one.

Avoid it when: Do not use a recall target alone when the positive class is tiny, since the threshold then rests on a handful of examples. Do not treat raw scores as probabilities before checking calibration.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Content Safety Classifiers and Thresholds?
cards.back:
• The threshold is tuned on one sample, so recall on new traffic can be lower; keep a margin and re-measure
• Scores shift when the data or classifier changes, so a stored threshold can silently stop meeting the target
• Ties in scores can push recall above the target or make the picked point jump; check the confusion counts
• A rare positive class makes precision at high recall very unstable; report it with an interval

cards.front: Key formulas: Content Safety Classifiers and Thresholds
cards.back:
Recall: $\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$
Precision: $\frac{TP}{TP + FP}$
Rank: $k = \lceil r \cdot P \rceil$, thr = $k$-th top positive
Cascade cost: $\mathbb{E}[C] = c_1 + p\,c_2$
Cheaper than $c_2$ iff $p < 1 - \frac{c_1}{c_2}$

cards.front: What is Group Fairness Metrics and Counterfactual Tests?
cards.back: Compare a model's decisions across groups: selection rates, true and false positive rates, calibration, and for language models the change in output when only a group term in the prompt is swapped.

cards.front: Group Fairness Metrics and Counterfactual Tests: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Each criterion fixes a different quantity to be equal across groups: selection rate (demographic parity), true-positive rate (equal opportunity), both error rates (equalised odds), or calibration. They are different questions, and when base rates differ they cannot all hold at once, so the choice is a decision about the application. Flow: predictions + group → per-group rates → gaps → compare to a threshold.

cards.front: How do demographic parity and equal opportunity differ?
cards.back: Demographic parity compares how often each group receives a positive prediction, ignoring the true label. Equal opportunity compares the true-positive rate, so it only looks at people who truly qualify.

cards.front: Why can't all fairness criteria hold together?
cards.back: When base rates differ between groups, a classifier that is not perfect cannot satisfy calibration and equal error rates at the same time. The result is known and is stated here without proof.

cards.front: How do you test an LLM for group differences?
cards.back: Build prompts that are identical except for a swapped group term, score each response with a fixed scorer, and report the spread. A scorer that ignores the term gives zero.

cards.front: What does the 80% rule measure?
cards.back: It is a rule of thumb on the ratio of the lowest to the highest selection rate; a ratio below 0.8 is treated as a flag for review, not a verdict.

cards.front: When should you use Group Fairness Metrics and Counterfactual Tests, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Auditing a classifier or a model-assisted decision for gaps between groups, before and after changes, with the group label held out of the model's inputs but available for evaluation.

Avoid it when: As a proof that a system is fair. These are descriptive statistics on one dataset; they depend on label quality, group definitions and sample size, and small groups give noisy rates.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Group Fairness Metrics and Counterfactual Tests?
cards.back:
• Rates from very small groups are noisy; report counts or intervals
• A group with no positive labels makes the true-positive rate undefined
• Optimising one criterion can worsen another, so report several
• A counterfactual swap can change more than the group, such as names that carry other signals

cards.front: Key formulas: Group Fairness Metrics and Counterfactual Tests
cards.back:
$|P(\hat{y}=1 \mid A=a) - P(\hat{y}=1 \mid A=b)|$
Equal opportunity is the same gap on $y=1$
Equalised odds $= \max(\Delta_{\mathrm{TPR}}, \Delta_{\mathrm{FPR}})$
$\mathrm{DI} = \frac{\min_a P(\hat{y}=1 \mid a)}{\max_a P(\hat{y}=1 \mid a)}$
The 80% rule of thumb flags $\mathrm{DI} < 0.8$
$\max_g s(x[g]) - \min_g s(x[g])$

cards.front: What is LLM Cost and Latency Optimisation?
cards.back: Treat an LLM request as arithmetic: cost is tokens times price, and latency is time to first token plus output length times inter-token time. Optimise by caching shared prefixes, cascading cheap models, and shortening outputs.

cards.front: LLM Cost and Latency Optimisation: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Both bills scale with tokens, but not equally: output tokens are priced higher and are generated one at a time, so $n_{out}$ dominates latency while a long shared prompt dominates input cost. That tells you where to push: reuse the part of the prompt that repeats, send easy requests to a small model and escalate only the hard ones, and cut output length first. Streaming does not shorten the total time, it only moves the first visible token earlier. Flow: request → cache or cheap model first → escalate if needed → stream tokens.

cards.front: Why does output length dominate latency?
cards.back: Tokens are generated one at a time, so total decode time is $n_{out}$ times the inter-token time, while the prompt is processed in one parallel pass that only sets the time to first token.

cards.front: When does a model cascade save money?
cards.back: When the cheap model's cost $c_1$ is below $(1-e)\,c_2$, where $e$ is the fraction escalated to the big model. A high escalation rate or an expensive first stage removes the saving.

cards.front: Does streaming make a response faster?
cards.back: Total latency is unchanged. Streaming only shows the first token after the time to first token, so the perceived wait shrinks.

cards.front: What does prefix caching help with?
cards.back: Prompts that start with the same long system text or documents. Only the repeated prefix is billed at the discount, so the gain scales with the prefix share and the hit rate.

cards.front: When should you use LLM Cost and Latency Optimisation, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Sizing and budgeting an LLM feature, or deciding which lever (prefix caching, a model cascade, shorter outputs, streaming, offline batching) is worth building before you build it.

Avoid it when: Do not optimise cost blindly when quality is the bottleneck: a cascade that escalates too rarely or a truncated answer can lose more value than the tokens saved. Prices and latencies here are illustrative parameters, so measure your own.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of LLM Cost and Latency Optimisation?
cards.back:
• Counting the cascade saving without including the cost of calling the router or judging the first answer
• Assuming a prefix cache hits on text that changes early; the cached part must be an identical leading prefix
• Optimising average cost while ignoring tail latency and the extra delay when a request escalates

cards.front: Key formulas: LLM Cost and Latency Optimisation
cards.back:
Cost: $C = n_{in}p_{in} + n_{out}p_{out}$
Latency: $L = t_{ttft} + n_{out}\,t_{itl}$
Prefix: $C = n_p p_{in}(hd + 1 - h)$
Saved: $h(1-d)\,n_p\,p_{in}$
Cascade: $\mathbb{E}[C] = c_1 + e\,c_2$
Cheaper iff $c_1 < (1-e)\,c_2$
Equivalently $e < 1 - \frac{c_1}{c_2}$

cards.front: What is Semantic Cache for LLM Answers?
cards.back: Cache LLM answers by meaning: embed the query, find the nearest cached query and reuse its answer when cosine similarity reaches a threshold $\tau$, with expiry and per-tenant isolation.

cards.front: Semantic Cache for LLM Answers: what is the key insight?
cards.back: An exact-match cache misses "reset my password" versus "how do I change my password", but their embeddings are close. The threshold $\tau$ is the whole trade: lower it and the hit rate rises, but more hits are wrong answers served confidently. Pick it from labelled pairs so the precision of hits meets a target, then check that the hit rate times the model cost still beats the price of the lookup. Flow: query → embed → nearest cached query → hit if above τ, else call model → store answer.

cards.front: How do you choose the similarity threshold?
cards.back: Score labelled pairs of same-meaning and different-meaning queries, then take the lowest threshold whose hit precision meets the target. A lower threshold gives more hits but more wrong answers.

cards.front: What is the risk of a semantic cache?
cards.back: A false hit returns a confident but wrong answer for a question that only looked similar, so thresholds, TTL and tenant isolation are correctness controls, not just tuning.

cards.front: When does the cache pay for itself?
cards.back: When the hit rate $h$ exceeds $c_{lookup}/c_{llm}$. Every request pays the lookup, and only hits avoid the model call.

cards.front: Why key the cache by tenant?
cards.back: Without it, one customer's question can match another customer's cached answer and leak private data.

cards.front: When should you use Semantic Cache for LLM Answers, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Workloads with many paraphrased repeats of the same questions, such as support bots or FAQ-style assistants, where an answer stays valid for a while and is safe to share.

Avoid it when: Personalised, time-sensitive or high-stakes answers, where a near-duplicate question can need a different answer. Also when the hit rate is too low to cover the lookup cost.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Semantic Cache for LLM Answers?
cards.back:
• Comparing non-normalised vectors with a dot product, so the score is no longer a cosine in $[-1, 1]$
• Tuning $\tau$ on pairs that do not look like production traffic, so real precision is lower than measured
• Caching answers that depend on user, time or tool output, which are wrong for the next asker

cards.front: Key formulas: Semantic Cache for LLM Answers
cards.back:
Cosine: $\cos(q,c) = \frac{q \cdot c}{\|q\|\,\|c\|}$
Hit iff $\max_i \cos(q, c_i) \geq \tau$
Precision: $\frac{TP(\tau)}{TP(\tau) + FP(\tau)}$
Pick $\tau^{*} = \min\{\tau : \mathrm{prec}(\tau) \geq \mathrm{target}\}$
Savings: $h\,c_{llm} - c_{lookup}$
Break-even: $h^{*} = \frac{c_{lookup}}{c_{llm}}$
Live iff $\mathrm{now} - t_{put} < \mathrm{TTL}$

cards.front: What is SLO Error Budgets, Circuit Breakers and Retry Load?
cards.back: An SLO such as 99.9% success over 30 days leaves an error budget of $0.001$ of requests; a circuit breaker fails fast on a broken dependency, and retries must be bounded because they multiply load.

cards.front: SLO Error Budgets, Circuit Breakers and Retry Load: what is the key insight?
cards.back: An SLO below 100% is a spendable allowance. The budget is $1-\mathrm{SLO}$, and the burn rate $\frac{e}{1-\mathrm{SLO}}$ for error rate $e$ says how fast you spend it: 1 empties it exactly at the end of the window, 5 empties it in a fifth of the window. A circuit breaker protects the budget and the caller by refusing calls to a dependency that is already failing, so threads are not tied up waiting and the dependency gets room to recover. Retries do the opposite: each failure triggers extra calls, which is exactly when the dependency can least afford them. Flow: failures counted → threshold crossed → fail fast → probe → recover.

cards.front: What is an error budget and what is burn rate?
cards.back: The budget is the fraction of requests allowed to fail, $1-\mathrm{SLO}$. Burn rate is the observed error rate divided by that budget; 1 spends it exactly over the window and higher values run out early.

cards.front: Describe the circuit breaker states.
cards.back: Closed passes calls and counts failures. After a threshold it opens and fails fast. After a cool-down it goes half-open and lets one probe through, closing on success and re-opening on failure.

cards.front: Why can retries make an outage worse?
cards.back: Each failed request triggers up to $r$ more calls, so load grows by $\sum_{k=0}^{r} p^k$ exactly when the dependency is failing. Use backoff with jitter and a retry budget.

cards.front: Why alert on burn rate instead of raw error rate?
cards.back: Burn rate is relative to the SLO, so one threshold means the same thing for any target and tells you how soon the budget will be gone.

cards.front: When should you use SLO Error Budgets, Circuit Breakers and Retry Load, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any model service with an availability target, and any call to a dependency (feature store, vector index, model backend) that can fail or slow down: set an SLO, track burn rate, and wrap the dependency in a breaker with a bounded retry policy.

Avoid it when: Do not add a breaker around a call that must succeed or block, such as a write that cannot be dropped, and do not set an SLO tighter than the dependencies underneath can support. With very low traffic a failure count over a few calls is noise.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of SLO Error Budgets, Circuit Breakers and Retry Load?
cards.back:
• Letting several callers probe in half-open; allow exactly one so a recovering dependency is not flooded
• Retrying at every layer of a call chain multiplies attempts, $(r+1)^{\mathrm{depth}}$ in the worst case
• Counting only hard errors; slow responses should count as failures too
• Treating the budget as a target to spend rather than a limit that gates risky releases

cards.front: Key formulas: SLO Error Budgets, Circuit Breakers and Retry Load
cards.back:
Budget $= 1 - \mathrm{SLO}$
Outage minutes $= (1 - \mathrm{SLO}) \cdot T$
Burn rate $= \frac{\mathrm{error\ rate}}{1 - \mathrm{SLO}}$
Time to empty $= \frac{T}{\mathrm{burn\ rate}}$
Attempts $= \sum_{k=0}^{r} p^{k}$
Closed form $= \frac{1 - p^{r+1}}{1 - p}$

cards.front: What is Little's Law, Erlang C and Capacity Planning?
cards.back: Concurrent requests equal arrival rate times time in system ($L = \lambda W$); the M/M/c queue and the Erlang C formula give the wait for $c$ servers, so you can size a fleet to a wait target.

cards.front: Little's Law, Erlang C and Capacity Planning: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Throughput and latency fix concurrency: $L = \lambda W$, so 50 requests per second at 2 seconds each keeps 100 requests in flight. Capacity is then about queues, not averages. Utilisation $\rho = \frac{\lambda}{c\mu}$ must stay below 1 or the queue grows without bound, and as $\rho$ approaches 1 the wait explodes, so the last servers you add buy the most. Autoscalers react with lag, so you size for the wait target plus headroom, not for $\rho$ near 1. Flow: arrival rate → offered load → Erlang C wait → add servers → meet target.

cards.front: State Little's law and use it for an LLM service.
cards.back: The average number in the system equals arrival rate times average time in the system, $L = \lambda W$. At 50 QPS and 2 s latency about 100 requests are concurrent, which bounds the batch or replica count you need.

cards.front: Why does the wait blow up near full utilisation?
cards.back: The mean wait scales like $\frac{1}{c\mu - \lambda}$, which diverges as $\lambda$ approaches $c\mu$. Small load increases then cause large queues, so run at moderate $\rho$.

cards.front: What does Erlang C give you?
cards.back: The probability that an arriving request must wait because all $c$ servers are busy, assuming Poisson arrivals and exponential service. Multiply by $\frac{1}{c\mu - \lambda}$ for the mean wait.

cards.front: Why keep headroom even if the formulas say the target is met?
cards.back: Autoscaling reacts with lag and real traffic is burstier than Poisson, so capacity sized exactly to the mean misses the target during spikes.

cards.front: When should you use Little's Law, Erlang C and Capacity Planning, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Sizing replica counts or GPU pools for a service with roughly Poisson arrivals and similar request sizes, and sanity-checking concurrency limits from QPS and latency with Little's law.

Avoid it when: Bursty or heavy-tailed traffic, and LLM requests whose service times vary by orders of magnitude with output length. Batched servers also break the one-request-per-server model. Use the formulas as a first estimate and confirm with load tests or simulation.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Little's Law, Erlang C and Capacity Planning?
cards.back:
• Planning on average load; size for the peak and the scale-up delay
• Mean wait hides the tail; the p99 wait can be several times larger
• Assuming exponential service times when output lengths vary widely
• Using $\mu$ measured at low load; per-server speed can drop under contention

cards.front: Key formulas: Little's Law, Erlang C and Capacity Planning
cards.back:
$L = \lambda \cdot W$
$a = \frac{\lambda}{\mu}, \;\; \rho = \frac{\lambda}{c\mu} < 1$
$N = \frac{a^{c}}{c!} \cdot \frac{c}{c - a}$
$C(c, a) = \frac{N}{\sum_{k=0}^{c-1} \frac{a^{k}}{k!} + N}$
$W_q = \frac{C(c, a)}{c\mu - \lambda}$
$W = W_q + \frac{1}{\mu}$

cards.front: What is Bin Packing and Cluster Scheduling?
cards.back: A scheduler places each container on a node whose remaining capacity covers every requested resource; this is bin packing, NP-hard, so heuristics such as first-fit-decreasing are used.

cards.front: Bin Packing and Cluster Scheduling: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Placement is packing items of several sizes into bins that cannot be stretched. Every dimension must fit separately, so a node with free CPU and no free memory is full for that pod, and indivisible GPUs strand leftovers: two nodes with 3 free GPUs each cannot host a pod that needs 4. Sorting big items first works because large items are the hard ones to fit; small ones fill the gaps later. Requests drive placement while limits only cap runtime use. Flow: pod requests → filter nodes that fit → pick one → update free capacity.

cards.front: Why is scheduling a bin-packing problem?
cards.back: Each pod requests a vector of resources and each node has a fixed capacity vector, so placing all pods on the fewest nodes is packing items into bins, which is NP-hard.

cards.front: Why sort items by decreasing size?
cards.back: Large items are hardest to fit, so placing them first leaves small items to fill gaps. In one dimension first-fit-decreasing uses at most $\frac{11}{9}\,\mathrm{OPT} + \frac{6}{9}$ bins.

cards.front: What is the difference between requests and limits?
cards.back: Requests are what the scheduler reserves and uses for placement. Limits cap runtime use: exceeding a memory limit gets the container killed, exceeding a CPU limit gets it throttled.

cards.front: Why can a pod stay pending with enough total free GPUs?
cards.back: GPUs are indivisible and a pod needs them on one node, so free GPUs spread across nodes are fragmented. Three free on each of two nodes cannot serve a pod needing four.

cards.front: When should you use Bin Packing and Cluster Scheduling, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Understanding why pods stay pending although total free capacity looks sufficient, and sizing requests and node shapes so the scheduler can pack tightly, especially for scarce GPU nodes.

Avoid it when: Do not search for the optimal packing at scale, since it is NP-hard and the heuristics are near optimal. These simple rules also ignore affinity, spreading, priorities and preemption, which real schedulers add on top.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Bin Packing and Cluster Scheduling?
cards.back:
• Over-requesting resources strands capacity because placement uses requests, not actual use
• Multi-dimensional packing is not solved by sorting on one dimension; a node can fill up on memory while CPU stays free
• Best-fit is not always better than first-fit; both can be worse than first-fit-decreasing
• Setting memory limits below real peaks gets containers killed; CPU limits only slow them down

cards.front: Key formulas: Bin Packing and Cluster Scheduling
cards.back:
Bins $\geq \lceil \frac{\sum_{i} s_i}{C} \rceil$
$\mathrm{FFD}(I) \leq \frac{11}{9}\,\mathrm{OPT}(I) + \frac{6}{9}$
Fits iff $r_{p,d} \leq f_{n,d}$ for all $d$
Update $f_{n,d} \leftarrow f_{n,d} - r_{p,d}$

cards.front: What is Experiment Tracking - Runs, Params and Metrics?
cards.back: Record every training attempt as a run with fixed parameters, metrics logged per step, tags and artifacts, then compare runs by a metric while checking that the gap is larger than seed noise.

cards.front: Experiment Tracking - Runs, Params and Metrics: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A result you cannot reproduce is an anecdote. A run is the unit of evidence: its parameters are write-once inputs, its metrics are a time series indexed by step, and together with the code version, data version and random seed they pin down how the number was produced. Picking the best run is then a query, but a gap between two runs is only meaningful if it exceeds the spread across seeds, $s/\sqrt{n}$. Flow: run → params fixed → metrics per step → compare → pick.

cards.front: What do you need to reproduce a training result?
cards.back: The code version, the data version, all parameters and the random seed, plus the environment. A tracked run records these so the same number can be regenerated.

cards.front: Why are parameters immutable but metrics are appended?
cards.back: Parameters define what the run is, so changing one would make the record lie. Metrics describe how training progressed, so they grow as a time series over steps.

cards.front: Run A beats run B by 0.3 points. Is A better?
cards.back: Not necessarily. Repeat each configuration over several seeds and compare the gap with its standard error; if the gap is within about two standard errors it may be seed noise.

cards.front: Should the best run be chosen by the best step or the final step?
cards.back: Decide before looking. Best-step on a validation metric is fine if that checkpoint is what you ship, but selecting on test data leaks; report the test metric once.

cards.front: When should you use Experiment Tracking - Runs, Params and Metrics, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any experiment you may want to compare, repeat or audit later: hyperparameter searches, ablations, fine-tuning attempts and evaluation reruns, especially when several people share results.

Avoid it when: A throwaway notebook cell with nothing to compare. Tracking also does not replace versioning: if code and data are not pinned by a commit and a data version, the recorded params alone cannot reproduce a run.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Experiment Tracking - Runs, Params and Metrics?
cards.back:
• Logging params after the fact or overwriting them silently, so the record no longer matches the run
• Choosing the best run from one seed per configuration and mistaking noise for a win
• Comparing runs trained on different data versions or code commits as if they were equal
• Selecting a run on the test metric, which leaks the test set into model selection

cards.front: Key formulas: Experiment Tracking - Runs, Params and Metrics
cards.back:
$\mathrm{SE} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$
$\mathrm{SE}_{\Delta} = \sqrt{\frac{s_A^2}{n_A} + \frac{s_B^2}{n_B}}$
Credible gap $\Delta = \bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B$ if $|\Delta| > 2\,\mathrm{SE}_{\Delta}$
Seeds per arm $n \geq 2\left(\frac{1.96\,s}{\delta}\right)^2$

cards.front: What is Model Serving API Contract and Dynamic Batching?
cards.back: A model behind an HTTP API needs typed schemas, validation errors with field paths, versioned routes, separate liveness and readiness probes, and a server-side batcher that trades a bounded wait for throughput.

cards.front: Model Serving API Contract and Dynamic Batching: what is the key insight?
cards.back: The API is a contract: callers depend on the shape of requests and responses, so schemas are enforced at the edge and breaking changes go under a new route prefix. Liveness asks whether the process is up, readiness asks whether it can serve, and they differ while the model is still loading. Batching is a deliberate delay: waiting at most $W$ for company lets one forward pass serve many requests, raising throughput at the price of up to $W$ extra latency. Flow: request → validate → batch (size or wait) → forward pass → response.

cards.front: What is the difference between liveness and readiness?
cards.back: Liveness says the process is running and should not be restarted. Readiness says the model is loaded and the service can take traffic, so it is false during warm-up or when a dependency is down.

cards.front: Why return 422 with the field path?
cards.back: The caller learns exactly which field broke the contract, for example body then features, without the request ever touching the model. The status says the request was well formed but semantically invalid.

cards.front: How does dynamic batching affect latency and throughput?
cards.back: It raises throughput because the fixed cost of a forward pass is shared, but a request can wait up to the max wait, so tail latency grows with both the wait and the batch size.

cards.front: How do timeouts and retries interact with a prediction API?
cards.back: Clients set a timeout and retry with backoff. To make retries safe the request carries an id so the server can return the earlier result instead of doing the work twice.

cards.front: When should you use Model Serving API Contract and Dynamic Batching, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any model exposed to other services: schemas and versioned routes keep callers stable, probes let an orchestrator manage the process, and dynamic batching suits accelerators where one batched pass costs far less than many single ones.

Avoid it when: Skip dynamic batching when traffic is so low that batches never fill (you only add latency) or when a strict latency target leaves no room for $W$. Offline scoring needs no HTTP contract; run it as a batch job.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Model Serving API Contract and Dynamic Batching?
cards.back:
• Reporting ready before the model is loaded, so the first real requests fail
• Using one health endpoint for both liveness and readiness, so a slow model load causes restart loops
• Setting the wait too high for the latency target; $W$ is added to every request that arrives to a quiet queue
• Retrying a non-idempotent call without a request id, which can run the work twice

cards.front: Key formulas: Model Serving API Contract and Dynamic Batching
cards.back:
Worst case $L_{\max} = W + S(B)$
$S(b) = a + c\,b$ (fixed + per item)
$\mathrm{thr}(b) = \frac{b}{a + c\,b} \rightarrow \frac{1}{c}$
Batch size $b \approx \min(B,\; 1 + \lambda W)$

cards.front: What is Managed API vs Self-Hosting Break-Even?
cards.back: A managed API costs linearly with tokens, while self-hosting costs a whole number of GPUs plus operations, a step function of volume. The break-even volume is where the two curves cross.

cards.front: Managed API vs Self-Hosting Break-Even: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Self-hosting is a fixed bill you pay whether the GPUs are busy or not, so it only wins when volume is high enough to keep them utilised. Because you buy GPUs in whole units, the cost jumps each time volume passes the capacity of the current fleet, so the curves can cross, separate and cross again. Utilisation is the lever that matters: the same fleet serves more tokens, so each costs less. Flow: monthly tokens → GPUs needed (ceiling) → self-host cost vs API cost → cheaper option.

cards.front: Why is the self-host cost a step function?
cards.back: GPUs are rented in whole units, so cost is flat until volume exceeds $u\,\mathrm{cap}$ per GPU and then jumps by one GPU's monthly price.

cards.front: How does utilisation change the decision?
cards.back: Higher utilisation lets each GPU serve more tokens, so fewer GPUs are needed and cost per token falls. Low utilisation can make self-hosting more expensive than the API at any volume.

cards.front: Roughly where is the break-even at low volume?
cards.back: Near $(G + O)/p$ tokens a month, when one GPU plus operations costs the same as the API bill, provided one GPU can serve that volume.

cards.front: What can outweigh the cost comparison?
cards.back: Data privacy and residency, control over model versions, latency needs, and whether the team has the skills to run and monitor the serving stack.

cards.front: When should you use Managed API vs Self-Hosting Break-Even, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Deciding whether a steady, high-volume workload justifies running your own models, or sizing the volume at which a pilot on a managed API should be re-evaluated.

Avoid it when: Spiky or uncertain traffic, where idle GPUs make utilisation low, or when non-cost factors decide it: data privacy, control over the model, latency, and whether the team can run the system. Numbers here are illustrative parameters, not real prices.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Managed API vs Self-Hosting Break-Even?
cards.back:
• Using peak throughput as capacity; sustained utilisation is lower, and traffic peaks need headroom
• Forgetting operations cost $O$ and on-call effort, which makes self-hosting look cheaper than it is
• Reading one crossing as final: after the next step up the API can be cheaper again

cards.front: Key formulas: Managed API vs Self-Hosting Break-Even
cards.back:
API: $C_{api} = t\,p$
Fleet: $k = \lceil \frac{t}{u\,\mathrm{cap}} \rceil$
Self-host: $C_{self} = kG + O$
Per token: $\frac{C(t)}{t}$
Break-even in segment: $t = \frac{kG + O}{p}$
Valid if $(k-1)u\,\mathrm{cap} < t \leq k\,u\,\mathrm{cap}$
Long run: $\frac{G}{u\,\mathrm{cap}}$ per token

cards.front: What is Project Blueprint: Chatbot with Memory?
cards.back: Build a chatbot that keeps its system prompt first, holds a short recent window under a token budget $B$, folds dropped turns into a running summary, and recalls stated facts later by similarity search. The outcome is a bot that still answers a question about turn 1 after the window has overflowed, with a prompt that never exceeds $B$.

cards.front: Project Blueprint: Chatbot with Memory: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Two stores solve two different problems. The recent window keeps the conversation coherent but is bounded, so old turns must leave it. A summary keeps the gist at a few tokens, but it is lossy and exact details vanish, so durable facts are written to a vector store when they are said and retrieved by similarity when a later question needs them. Each turn assembles the prompt in a fixed order: system prompt, retrieved facts, summary, then recent turns. The main trade-off is the split of $B$: more window gives fluent recent context, more facts and summary give longer reach. Flow: user turn → retrieve facts → trim window to budget → prompt → reply → store facts.

cards.front: How do you split the token budget between window, summary and facts?
cards.back: Reserve the system prompt and output first, give facts a small fixed share of $k$ short items, cap the summary, and give the remainder to recent turns. Tune the split on conversations where the answer lies far back, and watch both recall of old facts and coherence of recent replies.

cards.front: Why keep a fact store when there is already a summary?
cards.back: A summary is lossy and gets worse when it is re-summarised, so specific values such as names, numbers and preferences disappear. A store keeps the exact text, and retrieval spends tokens on it only when the question is related.

cards.front: How would you test that memory works and not just the window?
cards.back: State a fact, push enough filler turns that it leaves the window, assert it is absent from the recent turns, then ask. A correct answer can then only come from retrieval. Also assert the prompt size bound on every turn.

cards.front: What are the privacy implications of long-term memory?
cards.back: Stored facts persist and may be personal, so store only what the user stated, scope memory per user, show and delete it on request, and avoid saving secrets.

cards.front: When should you use Project Blueprint: Chatbot with Memory, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Assistants whose conversations outgrow the context window, or that must remember user preferences and stated facts across many turns or sessions, at a cost per turn bounded by $B$.

Avoid it when: Short chats that fit in context, where retrieval only adds latency and a chance of surfacing a wrong fact, or cases needing verbatim history such as legal transcripts, where lossy summaries are unacceptable.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Project Blueprint: Chatbot with Memory?
cards.back:
• Counting words undercounts model tokens, so the real prompt can exceed the budget; use the model's own tokenizer in production
• If the newest turn alone exceeds $B$ this code keeps it anyway, so the bound needs a hard truncation for that case
• Hashing embeddings match only shared words and know nothing of paraphrase, so a trained embedding model is needed for real recall
• Stored facts can go stale or conflict (a changed preference); keep timestamps and prefer or replace the newest

cards.front: Key formulas: Project Blueprint: Chatbot with Memory
cards.back:
$t_{sys} + t_{facts} + t_{sum} + \sum t_{recent} \leq B$
$t_{facts} \leq k \cdot t_{fact}$, $t_{sum} \leq S$
Full history: $\mathrm{cost} \approx u \cdot \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$
Capped: $\mathrm{cost} \leq n B$ (200k vs 60k tokens)
Recall: $e(q) \cdot e(f) > \theta$, keep top-$k$
Turns kept $\approx \frac{B - t_{sys} - t_{facts} - t_{sum}}{u}$

cards.front: What is Project Blueprint: Question Answering over a PDF?
cards.back: Build a question-answering system over a document: clean each page, chunk it with page metadata, embed and index the chunks, retrieve the top-$k$ for a question, and answer with citations such as [p3]. The outcome is an answerer that cites only chunks it retrieved and says that it cannot answer when nothing in the document is similar enough.

cards.front: Project Blueprint: Question Answering over a PDF: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Grounding is the point: the model should answer from retrieved text, and the reader should be able to check the page. That needs metadata carried from ingestion to the answer, so every chunk keeps its page and a stable id, and the prompt numbers its context with those ids. Citations are then verified mechanically against the retrieved set, so a made-up page is caught. Retrieval is also the gate: when even the best chunk scores below a threshold $\theta$ the system abstains, trading some missed answers for fewer confident wrong ones. The threshold must sit between the best score of in-scope questions and of out-of-scope ones. Real PDFs add a stage before all this, a parser for text PDFs or OCR for scanned ones, because the text layer may be missing or in the wrong reading order. Flow: pages → clean → chunk with metadata → embed → top-k → numbered prompt → cited answer.

cards.front: How do you stop the model citing something that was not retrieved?
cards.back: Number the context with chunk or page ids, then verify the cited ids against the retrieved set after generation and reject or regenerate on a mismatch. This checks the source exists, not that it supports the claim, so a faithfulness check is still needed.

cards.front: How do you choose the abstention threshold?
cards.back: Score a labelled set of in-scope and out-of-scope questions, plot the best-chunk similarity for each, and place $\theta$ in the gap, leaning toward the side whose error costs more. Re-tune it when the embedder or chunking changes, since similarity scales differ.

cards.front: What changes for real PDFs?
cards.back: Text must be extracted first: a parser for digital PDFs, OCR for scans. Layout matters, since columns, headers, footers, tables and hyphenation corrupt the text, so clean it and chunk tables by their own units.

cards.front: How do you evaluate the pipeline?
cards.back: Separate retrieval from generation: recall@$k$ on labelled question and page pairs for the retriever, then faithfulness and answer relevance for the generated answer, as in a RAG evaluation.

cards.front: When should you use Project Blueprint: Question Answering over a PDF, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Question answering over reports, manuals or papers that are too long for the prompt or change often, where answers must point to a page so a reader can check them.

Avoid it when: Short documents that fit in the prompt, scanned files without OCR, or questions that need aggregation across the whole document (totals, summaries), which top-$k$ retrieval of a few chunks cannot supply.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Project Blueprint: Question Answering over a PDF?
cards.back:
• Real PDFs need a parser or OCR first; this code starts from page strings, so extraction errors are not covered
• The hashing embedder matches shared words only (with crude plural stripping), so paraphrased questions can fall below the threshold and abstain wrongly
• A citation check proves the page was retrieved, not that the text supports the answer
• Chunks that cross a page break lose their page label; this code chunks per page, so facts spanning two pages can be cut

cards.front: Key formulas: Project Blueprint: Question Answering over a PDF
cards.back:
Chunks per page: $\lceil \frac{n - \mathrm{overlap}}{\mathrm{size} - \mathrm{overlap}} \rceil$
Blow-up $\approx \frac{\mathrm{size}}{\mathrm{size} - \mathrm{overlap}} = 1.33$
$\cos(q,c) = e(q) \cdot e(c)$; abstain if $\max < \theta$
Recall@$k$: $\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_q \mathbb{1}[\mathrm{gold} \in \mathrm{top}\,k]$
$\theta$ between $0.18$ (out-of-scope) and $0.37$ (in-scope)
Prompt: $k \cdot \mathrm{size} + t_q + t_{inst}$ tokens

cards.front: What is Project Blueprint: Semantic Search Engine?
cards.back: Build a search engine over a small document set. It embeds documents with a hashing embedder, answers queries by nearest neighbours with optional metadata filters, adds a lexical term-overlap signal fused by reciprocal rank fusion, supports adding and deleting documents, and reports $\mathrm{recall}@k$ and MRR on a labelled query set.

cards.front: Project Blueprint: Semantic Search Engine: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Dense vectors capture meaning but blur rare tokens such as error codes, while term overlap nails exact tokens but misses paraphrases. Running both and fusing by rank needs no score calibration, so the main design trade-off is cost against coverage: a second index and extra latency buy robustness on exact-match queries. Filters are applied before ranking, so a filter can never be violated by a lucky hit, and an evaluation set turns every design choice into a number. Flow: query → filter documents → dense list + lexical list → rank fusion → top-k → recall and MRR.

cards.front: How do you decide whether hybrid search is worth its cost?
cards.back: Build a labelled query set that reflects real traffic, including exact-identifier queries, and compare dense, lexical and hybrid on recall@k and MRR. If hybrid gains on a meaningful share of queries without hurting the rest, the extra index and latency are justified.

cards.front: Why filter before ranking instead of after?
cards.back: Post-filtering a top-k list can leave fewer than k results and, for access control, risks leaking documents when a bug or shortfall occurs. Pre-filtering searches only the permitted set, so the guarantee holds by construction at the price of a less efficient approximate search.

cards.front: How would this scale from thousands to millions of documents?
cards.back: Replace the exhaustive scan with an approximate nearest-neighbour index tuned to a recall target such as 0.95 against exact search, and the term loop with an inverted index. Memory is about $N \cdot d \cdot 4$ bytes for float vectors, so quantisation or sharding enters when that exceeds one machine.

cards.front: How do you handle updates and deletes?
cards.back: Treat the document store as the source of truth and apply each change to every index. Deletes need tombstones or removal in the vector index, and periodic rebuilds restore ANN quality. A test that a deleted document never appears in any mode guards the behaviour.

cards.front: When should you use Project Blueprint: Semantic Search Engine, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Product, document or help-centre search where queries mix natural language with exact identifiers, and where you want a measurable baseline before adding learned rerankers or approximate indexes.

Avoid it when: Corpora so small that a keyword grep suffices, or so large that the exhaustive scan used here must be replaced by an approximate index and an inverted index. Not a substitute for a relevance model when you have plenty of click or label data.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Project Blueprint: Semantic Search Engine?
cards.back:
• Evaluating on queries you tuned on; keep a held-out labelled set and grow it from real queries
• Filtering after ranking can return fewer than $k$ results or leak documents; filter first
• Letting the index drift from the source: deletes and edits must reach every structure, and an ANN index may need a rebuild
• Reading MRR over only the top $k$; a relevant document ranked below $k$ counts as a miss, so quote $k$ with every metric

cards.front: Key formulas: Project Blueprint: Semantic Search Engine
cards.back:
$\mathrm{recall}@k = \frac{|\mathrm{top}_k \cap \mathrm{rel}|}{|\mathrm{rel}|}$
$\mathrm{MRR} = \frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q} \frac{1}{\mathrm{rank}_q}$
$\mathrm{RRF}(d) = \sum \frac{1}{k + \mathrm{rank}(d)}$, $k = 60$
Both lists rank 1: $\frac{2}{61} \approx 0.0328$; one list: $\frac{1}{61}$
Bucket: $\mathrm{crc32}(t) \;\mathrm{mod}\; d$
Collision chance for two terms: $\frac{1}{d}$
Memory $\approx N \cdot d \cdot 4$ bytes, 1.5 GB for 1M x 384

cards.front: What is Project Blueprint: RAG Knowledge Assistant?
cards.back: Build a company-knowledge assistant. Documents are ingested with owner and permission metadata, retrieval is hybrid, access control is a hard pre-filter, answers are grounded and cited, the assistant abstains on weak evidence, and the index stays fresh when documents change or are deleted.

cards.front: Project Blueprint: RAG Knowledge Assistant: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A plain PDF question-answering pipeline has one reader and a frozen corpus. A company assistant has many readers with different rights and a corpus that keeps changing, and those two facts drive the design. Permissions must be enforced at retrieval, before ranking and before the prompt is built, because anything that reaches the model can leak into the answer. Freshness needs a stable document id so a re-ingest replaces old chunks instead of adding to them. The model is the least trusted part: it only quotes what it is given, cites it, and abstains when the evidence is weak. Flow: user + question → permitted chunks → hybrid retrieval → evidence check → grounded answer with citations.

cards.front: Why enforce permissions at retrieval and not in the model prompt?
cards.back: A model cannot be trusted to withhold text it has seen, and instructions can be bypassed. If a forbidden chunk is never retrieved it cannot appear in the prompt, the answer or the citations. The filter must be a hard pre-filter, because oversampling and post-filtering are only probabilistic.

cards.front: How does this differ from a PDF question-answering pipeline?
cards.back: It is multi-user, so every chunk carries an ACL and queries carry an identity. It is updatable, so documents have stable ids and re-ingest replaces chunks. It also abstains and cites, since users act on the answers and need to verify them.

cards.front: How do you decide when to abstain?
cards.back: Use an evidence signal such as coverage of the question terms by the best chunk, or a retriever or reranker score, and set the threshold on a labelled set to trade wrong answers against needless refusals. Abstaining on no permitted evidence also avoids hinting that a hidden document exists.

cards.front: How do you keep the index fresh at scale?
cards.back: Process change events: on an edit delete the chunks of that document id and insert the new ones, on a delete remove them, on a permission change update the ACL metadata. Run periodic reconciliation against the source of truth and rebuild approximate indexes as deletions accumulate.

cards.front: What would you monitor in production?
cards.back: Retrieval recall on a labelled set, faithfulness and citation validity of sampled answers, abstention rate, index lag after edits, and a canary test that restricted documents never appear for unauthorised test users.

cards.front: When should you use Project Blueprint: RAG Knowledge Assistant, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Internal assistants over wikis, policies and tickets where users have different rights, documents change, and each answer must show its source and admit when it does not know.

Avoid it when: Single-user or static corpora, where plain retrieval is simpler. Also when permissions cannot be expressed as metadata on chunks, or when you need reasoning across many documents that retrieval of a few chunks cannot supply.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Project Blueprint: RAG Knowledge Assistant?
cards.back:
• Post-filtering by permission, or filtering only the citations, lets forbidden text reach the prompt; restrict candidates before ranking
• Stale ACLs: a permission change must update chunk metadata, or revoked users keep access and new users are locked out
• Re-ingesting under a new id instead of the same id leaves old chunks answering with outdated facts
• A model that paraphrases can still add unsupported claims; the quoting stub gets faithfulness 1 only because it cannot generate, so real systems need a claim-level check

cards.front: Key formulas: Project Blueprint: RAG Knowledge Assistant
cards.back:
$\mathrm{Visible}(u,c) = 1$ if $\mathrm{groups}(u) \cap \mathrm{ACL}(c) \neq \emptyset$
Candidates $= \{c : \mathrm{Visible}(u,c) = 1\}$, before ranking
$\mathrm{RRF}(c) = \sum \frac{1}{60 + \mathrm{rank}(c)}$
Evidence $= \max \frac{|Q \cap \mathrm{chunk}|}{|Q|}$; abstain if $< \tau$
Faithfulness: $\frac{\mathrm{supported\ claims}}{\mathrm{claims}}$
Chunks per doc: $\lceil \frac{\mathrm{doc\ tokens}}{\mathrm{chunk\ tokens}} \rceil$
Prompt $\approx$ system $+ k \cdot$ chunk tokens $+$ question

cards.front: What is Project Blueprint: Code Question-Answering Assistant?
cards.back: Build an assistant that answers questions about a small Python repository and suggests code. It parses sources with the standard library, indexes whole functions and classes, packs the best chunks into a token budget, and checks every suggestion before showing it.

cards.front: Project Blueprint: Code Question-Answering Assistant: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Code has structure that fixed windows destroy: a window can cut a function in half and splits a signature from its docstring. Chunking at function and class boundaries keeps each unit self-contained and gives it a name, a path and a line span to cite. The main trade-off is precision against coverage: exact identifier matches find the right symbol cheaply, embeddings rescue vague questions, and the budget decides whether you show many signatures or a few full bodies. The model's output is untrusted, so it is parsed and scanned but never executed by the assistant. Flow: source files → function chunks → retrieve → packed context → checked suggestion.

cards.front: Why chunk by function rather than by fixed token windows?
cards.back: A fixed window cuts through functions, separating a signature from its body and mixing unrelated code. A function or class is the natural unit of meaning, carries its own name, docstring and line span for citation, and keeps embeddings coherent. The cost is uneven chunk sizes, so very long functions may still need to be split and short ones merged.

cards.front: Why combine identifier overlap with embeddings?
cards.back: Code questions often contain the exact symbol name, and lexical matching finds it precisely and cheaply, where embeddings of short names are noisy. Embeddings help when the question describes behaviour in other words. Weighting names above docstring words above similarity lets exact hits win while keeping a fuzzy fallback.

cards.front: The model suggests code. Why not just run it to test it?
cards.back: Generated code is untrusted input, and executing it inside the assistant would hand it your process, files and credentials. The assistant only parses it and scans for dangerous calls. Real execution belongs in a separate sandbox with no network, resource limits and a disposable filesystem.

cards.front: What are the limits of an allow-list or deny-list scan?
cards.back: It is a cheap first filter, not a security boundary. Code can reach the same functions through aliases, getattr, string building or imports the scan does not model. Treat it as a way to flag the obvious cases, and enforce real safety with sandboxing and review.

cards.front: How do you evaluate this assistant?
cards.back: Build questions with known answer symbols and measure recall at k for retrieval, then measure answer faithfulness to the packed context and the fraction of suggestions that pass the checks and the repository tests. Separating retrieval from generation shows which half to fix.

cards.front: When should you use Project Blueprint: Code Question-Answering Assistant, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Answering questions about a codebase small enough to index whole, such as one service or library, where answers should point at a file and line range and suggestions must be screened before use.

Avoid it when: Cross-file reasoning that needs a call graph or type information, or repositories in languages the parser does not handle. Static checks do not prove a suggestion is correct or safe; they only catch syntax errors and obvious dangerous calls.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Project Blueprint: Code Question-Answering Assistant?
cards.back:
• Chunking only top-level definitions hides methods and module-level constants, so questions about them find nothing
• Line spans go stale after edits; re-index changed files and store a content hash so citations stay correct
• Whitespace word counts stand in for tokens; use the real tokenizer or leave a safety margin under $B$
• A syntax and call scan passes code that is wrong or unsafe in subtler ways; never execute suggestions outside a sandbox

cards.front: Key formulas: Project Blueprint: Code Question-Answering Assistant
cards.back:
Budget: $B = W - s - q - r$ (window, system, question, reserve)
Score: $3\,|N \cap q| + |D \cap q| + \cos(e_c, e_q)$
Packing: $\sum_{i \in S} \mathrm{cost}(t_i) \leq B$
Chunks per file $=$ top-level defs and classes
Recall: $\frac{|\mathrm{relevant} \cap \mathrm{top}_k|}{|\mathrm{relevant}|}$
Collision chance per word pair $= \frac{1}{d}$

cards.front: What is Project Blueprint: Cited Research Assistant?
cards.back: Build a research assistant that turns a question into a cited report. It plans sub-questions, searches a local corpus for each, keeps notes with source ids, writes claims that all carry citations, then verifies each claim against its source and flags the rest.

cards.front: Project Blueprint: Cited Research Assistant: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A report is only as trustworthy as the link from each claim back to text the system actually retrieved. Making the citation part of the data (claim plus source id) rather than part of the prose lets code enforce it: uncited claims are dropped and cited ones are checked against the source. The design trade-off is breadth against cost: every sub-question costs a search and tokens, so a step and token budget bound the run and the stop reason tells the user whether the report is complete or truncated. Flow: question → sub-questions → gather notes → cited claims → verify → report with flags.

cards.front: Why attach citations as data instead of asking the model to cite in prose?
cards.back: Prose citations can be invented or point at sources that were never retrieved, and code cannot reliably check free text. A claim record with a source id lets the system reject any claim whose id was not in the retrieved set and run a per-claim support check. It turns citation from a style request into an enforced invariant.

cards.front: What does the verification step add if the model already cited a source?
cards.back: A citation shows where the model claims the support is, not that the source says it. Verification compares each claim with its cited text and flags those that do not follow. Token overlap is a crude proxy, so production systems use an entailment model or a judge, and sample the results against human labels.

cards.front: Why deduplicate sources?
cards.back: Mirrors and copies make one source look like several, inflating apparent agreement and wasting the context budget and citations. Merging by normalised text or a hash is cheap; near-duplicates need fuzzy matching such as shingling.

cards.front: How do you choose the step and token budgets?
cards.back: Work back from the latency and cost you can afford: each sub-question costs one search plus the tokens of its notes, and the writer pays for all notes in its context. Set the cap, report the stop reason so users know when a report is partial, and prioritise sub-questions so the most important run first.

cards.front: What are the main failure modes of this design?
cards.back: A bad plan misses part of the question, retrieval finds a related but wrong source, and a claim can overlap its source in words yet contradict it. Evaluate the planner, retrieval and verifier separately so you know which stage to fix.

cards.front: When should you use Project Blueprint: Cited Research Assistant, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Questions that need several facts from a known document set, where readers must be able to check each statement against its source and the cost of a run has to be bounded.

Avoid it when: Single-fact lookups, where one retrieval and answer is enough, or open-web research where sources conflict and need credibility judgement. Token overlap cannot detect paraphrased contradictions.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Project Blueprint: Cited Research Assistant?
cards.back:
• Token overlap passes a claim that reuses a source's words but reverses its meaning; use an entailment model for anything important
• Dropping uncited claims silently hides writer errors; log how many were dropped
• Stopping on a budget leaves some sub-questions unanswered, so always surface the stop reason in the report
• Near-duplicate sources survive exact-hash merging and still inflate agreement

cards.front: Key formulas: Project Blueprint: Cited Research Assistant
cards.back:
Support: $\frac{|T_c \cap T_s|}{|T_c|}$ over word sets
Supported when $\mathrm{Support}(c, s) \geq \theta$
Citation coverage: $\frac{\mathrm{cited}}{\mathrm{claims}} = 1$
Verified: $\frac{\mathrm{supported}}{\mathrm{cited}}$
Search calls $= \min(s, \mathrm{max\_steps})$
Cost: $\sum_t n_t \leq B$ note tokens

cards.front: What is Project Blueprint: Customer Support Agent?
cards.back: Build a support agent that classifies intent with a confidence score, answers FAQs from a knowledge base with a cited source, looks up orders, requests refunds only after explicit confirmation, escalates to a human when unsure or when the customer is upset, and writes logs with personal data redacted.

cards.front: Project Blueprint: Customer Support Agent: what is the key insight?
cards.back: The model is the cheap, fallible part, so the design puts hard rules around it. Retrieval grounds answers in the knowledge base, a permission gate makes the one risky tool (refund) a two-turn handshake, and an escalation path catches anything the classifier is unsure about. The main trade-off is the confidence threshold $\tau$: a high $\tau$ is safe but sends more tickets to humans, a low $\tau$ automates more but lets wrong answers through. Redaction sits at the logging boundary so no code path can forget it. Flow: message → intent → answer, tool or escalate.

cards.front: Why must a refund need confirmation if the classifier is confident?
cards.back: Confidence measures how well the message matches an intent, not whether the customer meant it or whether the action is safe. A refund is hard to undo, so the gate is a rule that does not depend on the model. A confirm turn also gives the customer a chance to catch a wrong order id.

cards.front: How do you pick the confidence threshold?
cards.back: Label a sample of tickets, then sweep the threshold and plot the share automated against the error rate of those automated answers. Pick the point where the error rate is acceptable for the cost of a wrong answer, and re-check it as traffic changes. Risky intents can use a higher threshold than FAQs.

cards.front: What should the human receive on escalation?
cards.back: The full transcript, the detected intent and confidence, the reason for escalating and any pending action, so the customer does not repeat themselves. Redaction still applies to stored copies.

cards.front: How do you test an agent whose model is non-deterministic?
cards.back: Replace the model with scripted stubs and test the surrounding logic with fixed dialogs: gate, state, escalation and logging. Then evaluate the real model separately on a labelled set for intent accuracy and task success.

cards.front: When should you use Project Blueprint: Customer Support Agent, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: High-volume support with repetitive questions and a few well-defined actions, where a wrong answer is cheap to fix but a wrong refund is not. The structure also fits any agent with one risky tool.

Avoid it when: Open-ended or legally sensitive cases (disputes, medical or financial advice) where a human should lead, and flows with many interacting tools that need real planning rather than three fixed intents.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Project Blueprint: Customer Support Agent?
cards.back:
• Treating any message after a refund request as confirmation; only an explicit yes should execute, and the pending action must expire
• Redacting only the final reply while raw text leaks into logs, traces or error messages
• A keyword classifier is crude: negations and typos produce confident wrong intents, so measure it on real tickets
• Executing a retried or duplicated confirmation twice; refunds need an idempotency key, not just a UI check

cards.front: Key formulas: Project Blueprint: Customer Support Agent
cards.back:
Confidence: $c = \frac{\mathrm{hits}_{best}}{\mathrm{hits}_{all}}$
Escalate if $c < \tau$, $\cos < 0.1$ or upset
Rate: $e = P(c < \tau) + P(\mathrm{upset}) + P(\mathrm{weak})$
Cost: $(1 - e)\, c_{bot} + e\, c_{human}$
Example: $0.75 \cdot 0.02 + 0.25 \cdot 4 = 1.015$
Human load $= e \cdot N_{tickets}$ per day
Refund runs once: $|\mathrm{refunds}| = 1$ per confirm

cards.front: What is Project Blueprint: Multimodal Assistant?
cards.back: Build an assistant that accepts text, an image or both. A router picks the path, a shared embedding space retrieves the matching image or note, and a prompt builder counts image tokens as well as text tokens so every request fits the context budget.

cards.front: Project Blueprint: Multimodal Assistant: what is the key insight?
cards.back: The system is easy to get wrong because two different spaces matter. Retrieval needs images and text in one embedding space, which is what contrastive image-text training provides, so a text query can find an image directly. Generation needs images as tokens, and an image costs $N = (H/P)(W/P)$ patches, so a large image can eat the whole budget. The main trade-off is spatial detail against context: pooling $k \times k$ patches divides the cost by $k^2$, and the router keeps text-only requests from paying for vision at all. Flow: request → route → embed → retrieve → budgeted prompt → answer with citations.

cards.front: Why must text and images share an embedding space for retrieval?
cards.back: A text query can only be compared to an image vector if both live in one space. Contrastive training pulls matching pairs together there. Without it you need captions for every image and fall back to text search.

cards.front: How do you stop images from blowing the context budget?
cards.back: Compute the token count before calling the model: $N/k^2$ for pooled patches. Pool harder, downscale or tile selectively, and if even the strongest pooling does not fit, reject with the numbers instead of truncating, since truncation can cut image tokens and break the request.

cards.front: When does routing save money, and what can go wrong?
cards.back: Text-only requests skip the image encoder and its tokens, so they cost what they always did. The risk is a router that misclassifies, for example ignoring an attached image the question depends on, so log the route and test each branch.

cards.front: How would you evaluate the system end to end?
