cards.back: Evaluate in parts. Measure retrieval with recall at $k$ on labelled text-to-image and image-to-note queries, answer faithfulness against the cited items, and the token and latency distribution. A single answer-quality score cannot tell a retrieval fault from a generation fault.

cards.front: When should you use Project Blueprint: Multimodal Assistant, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: A product that mixes text and images, such as asking about a photo, a screenshot or a diagram, with a fixed context window and a gallery or notes store to ground the answers.

Avoid it when: Text-only products, where a vision path adds cost and failure modes, and cases where one image embedding already solves the task, such as plain image search with no generated answer.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Project Blueprint: Multimodal Assistant?
cards.back:
• Counting only text tokens in the budget, so a single image overflows the context at serving time
• A hashing embedder collides: unrelated words can share a bucket, so retrieval tests need a margin, and real systems use a trained encoder
• Text and image embeddings from separately trained encoders do not share a space, so cross-modal scores are meaningless
• Pooling that does not divide the patch grid evenly silently drops edge patches, so check divisibility

cards.front: Key formulas: Project Blueprint: Multimodal Assistant
cards.back:
$N = \frac{H}{P}\cdot\frac{W}{P}$, 64 for 32 by 32, $P=4$
Pooled: $N^{\prime} = \frac{N}{k^2}$, so 256 gives 16 at $k=4$
Prompt: $L_{text} + N^{\prime} \leq B$
Reject if $L_{text} + \frac{N}{k_{max}^2} > B$: $1 + 64 > 64$
Score: $\langle q, v\rangle$, $q = e_{text} + e_{img}$
KV bytes per token: $2 \cdot \mathrm{layers} \cdot \mathrm{kv\_heads} \cdot d_{head} \cdot \mathrm{bytes}$
Example: $2\cdot 32\cdot 8\cdot 128\cdot 2 = 131072$ B
Recall: $\frac{\mathrm{queries\ hit\ in\ top\ k}}{\mathrm{queries}}$

cards.front: What is Project Blueprint: Domain Fine-Tune Plan and Release Gate?
cards.back: Plan a domain fine-tune as code before spending GPU time. Curate and split the data, format chat examples with a response-only loss mask, check the step count and memory fit, and end with a release gate that returns ship or hold together with the reasons.

cards.front: Project Blueprint: Domain Fine-Tune Plan and Release Gate: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Most fine-tuning failures are decided before training starts: leaked validation data, loss on the prompt, a run that does not fit in memory, or a win that is noise. Each of these is checkable with a few lines of arithmetic, so the blueprint turns them into functions that fail loudly. The design trade-off is gating strictness: a tight gate blocks bad releases but costs reruns, and the gate has three checks because a model can improve on the domain, win by chance or forget general skills independently. Flow: raw data → curated set → trained model → gate → release.

cards.front: Why split by source group instead of randomly?
cards.back: Records from one source share phrasing and facts, so a random split leaks near-copies into validation and flatters the model. Splitting by group measures how it handles a source it has not seen.

cards.front: Why does the sign test ignore ties?
cards.back: A tie carries no preference. Among decisive pairs, no real difference means each side wins with probability one half, so the one-sided binomial tail on wins gives the p-value. Report the tie count alongside it.

cards.front: How do you estimate whether a fine-tune fits a GPU?
cards.back: Add bytes per parameter for weights, gradients and optimizer state, plus activations. Full Adam is about 16 bytes per parameter in mixed precision, while adapters pay 2 bytes for a frozen base plus 16 for the small trainable fraction.

cards.front: Why gate on forgetting as well as the domain win?
cards.back: Fine-tuning can raise domain scores while degrading general skills, and win rates on domain prompts do not show it. A general held-out set with a tolerance catches that regression before release.

cards.front: When should you use Project Blueprint: Domain Fine-Tune Plan and Release Gate, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Before any domain or style fine-tune, to catch leakage, masking and memory mistakes cheaply, and as the standing definition of when a checkpoint is good enough to release.

Avoid it when: When prompting or retrieval already meets the target, since a fine-tune adds a model to maintain. The gate also needs a held-out set and a comparison baseline, so it does not apply without them.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Project Blueprint: Domain Fine-Tune Plan and Release Gate?
cards.back:
• Exact-hash dedup misses near-duplicates, so paraphrased copies still leak across the split
• Memory estimates omit activations, fragmentation and long sequences, so keep headroom beyond the byte arithmetic
• Counting ties as wins or dropping them silently inflates or hides the win rate; report wins, losses and ties
• A small evaluation set gives a weak sign test: with few decisive pairs even a real gain may not pass, so size it in advance

cards.front: Key formulas: Project Blueprint: Domain Fine-Tune Plan and Release Gate
cards.back:
Steps: $E\,\lceil N/B\rceil = 3 \cdot 32 = 96$
Warmup: $\lceil 0.03 \cdot 96\rceil = 3$
Full Adam: $2+2+4+4+4 = 16$ bytes per parameter
Full, $7\times 10^{9}$ params: $7\times 10^{9}\cdot 16 = 112$ GB
Adapter: $2p + 16\,f\,p = 14 + 1.12$ GB, $f=0.01$
Sign test: $p = \frac{1}{2^n}\sum_{i \geq w}\binom{n}{i}$
Example: $w=30$, $n=40$ gives $p \approx 0.0011$
Forgetting: $g_{base} - g_{ft} \leq \tau$

cards.front: What is Project Blueprint: Multi-Agent Research Report?
cards.back: Build a planner, researcher, critic and writer that produce a cited report on a topic from a small corpus. The planner splits the topic into sections, researchers draft them, the critic rejects uncited drafts once, the writer assembles the report, and a score measures how many sections carry a valid citation.

cards.front: Project Blueprint: Multi-Agent Research Report: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Roles pay off when each one has a narrow job that can be checked. The critic enforces one concrete rule (a section must cite a document that exists), so quality becomes a loop with a measurable exit rather than a hope. The roles do not talk to each other; they read and write a shared blackboard, which keeps hand-offs inspectable and makes cost easy to count. The trade-off is cost: every extra role call adds tokens, so a revision cap and a turn limit bound the spend, and the finished report is scored on its own instead of trusting the loop. Flow: topic → plan → research → critique → revise once → write → score.

cards.front: Why a blackboard instead of agents messaging each other?
cards.back: A shared store gives one place to inspect, replay and cost every hand-off, and roles stay decoupled so one can be swapped or limited without touching the rest. Direct messaging can be faster for tightly coupled work but is harder to audit.

cards.front: Why allow only one revision per section?
cards.back: Each revision costs a researcher call and a critic call, and an unbounded loop can chase a rule the corpus cannot satisfy. One revision catches the common fixable failure, and sections that still fail show up in the coverage score for a human to look at.

cards.front: How do you evaluate the finished report?
cards.back: Score it separately from the loop. Citation coverage is cheap and checks the critic's rule, but it does not show that claims are supported, so add a faithfulness check and a human-labelled sample for quality.

cards.front: When does adding agents hurt?
cards.back: When roles repeat context in every prompt, token cost grows with each added role and turn, and errors can compound across hand-offs. Add a role only when it has a checkable job that a single prompt does not do reliably.

cards.front: When should you use Project Blueprint: Multi-Agent Research Report, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Report-style tasks that split into independent parts with a checkable quality rule, such as cited summaries, comparison tables or audits, where a bounded review loop is cheaper than a human edit pass.

Avoid it when: Short or tightly coupled tasks where one prompt suffices, and tasks with no verifiable rule for the critic. Extra roles then add cost and failure modes without raising quality.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Project Blueprint: Multi-Agent Research Report?
cards.back:
• A critic that only checks that a citation exists accepts irrelevant or fabricated support; verify the cited text actually backs the claim
• Stopping at the turn limit and still publishing the partial draft hides the failure; return the reason and no report
• Counting tokens from outputs only undercounts: prompts, which repeat shared context, usually dominate cost
• Letting roles read the whole blackboard each turn grows prompts with every turn; pass only the fields a role needs

cards.front: Key formulas: Project Blueprint: Multi-Agent Research Report
cards.back:
$T = 2 + 2S + 2R$ for $S$ sections, $R$ revisions
$R \leq S$: one revision per section at most
Expected turns: $2 + 2S(1 + p)$
Example: $2 + 6 \cdot \frac{4}{3} = 10$ turns
Cost: $\sum_{calls} (\mathrm{in} + \mathrm{out})$ tokens
Coverage: $\frac{\mathrm{cited\ sections}}{S}$
Stop when $T = \mathrm{max\_turns}$ and report why

cards.front: What is Project Blueprint: Self-Hosted LLM Platform?
cards.back: Build a small self-hosted model platform: a registry of models with size, quantisation and quality tier, a memory fit check against a GPU budget, a router that picks the smallest model meeting the tier and fitting in memory, admission control with a bounded queue, and fallback to the next model when one is unhealthy.

cards.front: Project Blueprint: Self-Hosted LLM Platform: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A shared GPU is a fixed memory budget, so every decision reduces to bytes. Weights are $P b / 8$ and the KV cache is a per-token constant times context times concurrent sequences, so concurrency is the knob that trades memory for throughput. Little's law ($L = \lambda W$) turns the traffic you expect into the concurrency you must support, and the fit check says which models can hold that concurrency. The router then spends quality only where the request asks for it: the smallest model that satisfies the tier is cheapest and fastest. Admission control protects the GPU: a bounded queue converts overload into a fast, explicit rejection instead of unbounded latency, and fallback keeps requests flowing when a replica is down. Flow: request → tier filter → memory fit → smallest healthy model → admission → run.

cards.front: How do you decide which models can share one GPU?
cards.back: Sum the weights $P b / 8$ and the KV cache for the concurrency each model must hold, add the overhead fraction, and compare with the budget. If the total exceeds it, lower the concurrency, quantise more, or move the model to another device.

cards.front: Why route to the smallest model that meets the tier?
cards.back: Smaller models cost less memory and time per token, so the cheapest model that still meets the quality floor leaves the most capacity for other requests. The router spends quality only where a request asks for it.

cards.front: How do you set the concurrency limit?
cards.back: Little's law gives the typical number in flight, $L = \lambda W$, for example 5 requests per second at 2 seconds is 10. Add headroom for bursts, then check the result against the memory limit $C_{max}$ and take the smaller of the two.

cards.front: Why a bounded queue with rejection instead of queueing everything?
cards.back: Past capacity, extra requests only add waiting time, so latency grows with the backlog and clients retry. Rejecting with a reason when the queue is full keeps latency bounded and lets callers back off or try another endpoint.

cards.front: What happens when the chosen model is unhealthy?
cards.back: The router skips it and takes the next candidate that meets the tier and fits memory. A fallback that was never fit-checked is a risk, so candidates are filtered before health is considered.

cards.front: When should you use Project Blueprint: Self-Hosted LLM Platform, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: A team serving a few open-weight models from one or a few GPUs, who need predictable memory use, a quality-aware choice of model, and explicit overload behaviour before adding a full orchestration stack.

Avoid it when: A single model on a single GPU with light traffic, where a plain server with a request limit is enough, or a large multi-node fleet that needs a real scheduler, autoscaler and per-replica health probes.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Project Blueprint: Self-Hosted LLM Platform?
cards.back:
• Sizing the cache for average concurrency; the fit check must use the limit you will actually admit
• Treating the tier as exact; a tier label comes from an evaluation and goes stale when prompts change
• An unbounded queue hides overload as latency, and clients time out and retry, which adds load
• Failing over to a larger model without re-running the fit check, which can crash the server with out-of-memory

cards.front: Key formulas: Project Blueprint: Self-Hosted LLM Platform
cards.back:
Weights $= \frac{P b}{8}$ bytes
KV $= k \cdot T \cdot C$, with $k = 2 L h_{kv} d_{head} b_{kv}$
Fit $(W_m + KV)(1 + \epsilon) \leq G$
Concurrency $C = \lambda \cdot W$
Limit $= \lceil \lambda W \cdot h \rceil$
$C_{max} = \lfloor \frac{G/(1+\epsilon) - W_m}{k T} \rfloor$
Queue wait $\leq \frac{Q}{\mu}$

cards.front: What is Project Blueprint: Multi-Tenant LLM SaaS Backend?
cards.back: Build the backend of a multi-tenant LLM product: API keys that map to tenants and plans, a token bucket per tenant, usage metering that turns each request into an idempotent billing event, tenant-isolated caching, a margin report per tenant and a hard daily cap against abuse.

cards.front: Project Blueprint: Multi-Tenant LLM SaaS Backend: what is the key insight?
cards.back: The model call is the easy part; the product is the layer around it. Three properties matter. Fairness: one bucket per tenant means a tenant that exhausts its quota hurts only itself. Correctness of money: clients and gateways retry, so every billing event carries an id and the meter ignores an id it has already seen, which makes recording idempotent. Isolation: anything stored or cached is keyed by tenant, because a cache shared by prompt alone would hand one customer another's answer. Revenue per tenant is price times tokens and cost is unit cost times tokens, so margin shows which plan loses money, and the daily cap bounds the worst case. Flow: request → tenant → quota check → model → usage event → invoice.

cards.front: How do you make usage billing safe against retries?
cards.back: Each request carries a unique id, and the meter stores events by that id and ignores one it has seen. Recording is then idempotent, so a retry after a timeout leaves the invoice unchanged. The id must come from the client or be fixed before the first attempt.

cards.front: Why a token bucket per tenant instead of one global limit?
cards.back: A global limit lets one heavy tenant starve the rest. A bucket per tenant with capacity $C$ and refill rate $r$ allows bursts up to $C$ and a long-run rate of $r$, and an exhausted bucket only rejects that tenant's requests.

cards.front: How do you isolate tenants in a shared cache?
cards.back: Put the tenant id in every key, here by prefixing the hash of the prompt, so the key spaces never overlap. The same applies to stored data, logs and any vector index, where a missing filter is the usual leak.

cards.front: What does the margin per tenant tell you?
cards.back: It is revenue minus cost, tokens times the difference between price and unit cost per 1,000 tokens. A plan with a flat fee and unlimited use can go negative for heavy users, so the daily cap and per-plan quotas bound the loss.

cards.front: When should the daily cap trigger, and what should the client see?
cards.back: It triggers when the day's recorded tokens reach the plan cap, before any model call, so the cost stops at a known bound. The client gets 429 with a reason such as daily cap, which differs from a transient rate limit that clears in seconds.

cards.front: When should you use Project Blueprint: Multi-Tenant LLM SaaS Backend, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Putting a model behind an API for several paying customers, where each needs its own quota, bill and data boundary, and where retries are routine so billing must be safe to repeat.

Avoid it when: An internal tool with one trusted team, where a single shared limit is enough, or real billing, which needs a durable ledger, invoicing rules and tax handling beyond this skeleton.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Project Blueprint: Multi-Tenant LLM SaaS Backend?
cards.back:
• Deriving the event id from a timestamp or counter on the server, which makes every retry look new; the client or request must supply it
• A cache key built from the prompt alone, which leaks one tenant's answer to another
• Checking the quota and then updating usage in separate steps without a lock, so concurrent requests overspend
• Pricing from average usage; a few heavy tenants can make a plan negative, so look at margin per tenant

cards.front: Key formulas: Project Blueprint: Multi-Tenant LLM SaaS Backend
cards.back:
Bucket bound: tokens in window $t$ $\leq C + r t$
Invoice $= \frac{\sum n_{unique}}{1000} \cdot p$
Cost $= \frac{\sum n_{unique}}{1000} \cdot c$
Margin $= \frac{n}{1000} (p - c)$
Margin fraction $= \frac{p - c}{p}$
Daily cap: spend $\leq \frac{D}{1000} \cdot c$

cards.front: What is SQL Interview Patterns - Joins, Windows, Top-N, CTEs?
cards.back: The handful of SQL shapes that data and ML interviews repeat: group with HAVING, joins and the anti-join, the join fan-out trap, window functions, top-N per group, de-duplication and CTEs.

cards.front: SQL Interview Patterns - Joins, Windows, Top-N, CTEs: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Every query is a pipeline over rows, and most mistakes are row-count mistakes. A join can multiply rows: a left join onto a table where a key matches $m$ rows returns $m$ rows for that key, so a $\mathrm{SUM}$ taken after the join counts the parent value $m$ times. Aggregates collapse rows into one per group; window functions keep every row and add a value computed over its partition and order. Ranking with a window plus a filter in an outer query gives top-N per group and de-duplication. Flow: table → join → group or window → ranked result.

cards.front: Why did my SUM double after a join?
cards.back: The join key matched $m$ rows on the other side, so each parent row was repeated $m$ times and the sum counted it $m$ times. Aggregate the many-side to one row per key first, or sum before joining.

cards.front: How do you find rows with no match?
cards.back: LEFT JOIN and keep rows where a right-side key IS NULL, or use NOT EXISTS. Avoid NOT IN when the subquery can return NULL, since it then matches nothing.

cards.front: ROW_NUMBER versus RANK on ties?
cards.back: $\mathrm{ROW\_NUMBER}$ gives every row a distinct number, breaking ties arbitrarily unless ORDER BY decides. $\mathrm{RANK}$ gives tied rows the same rank and skips the next numbers, e.g. $1,1,3$.

cards.front: How do you get the top-N rows per group?
cards.back: Compute $\mathrm{ROW\_NUMBER}$ or $\mathrm{RANK}$ partitioned by the group and ordered by the score in a CTE or subquery, then filter on rank $\leq N$ in the outer query.

cards.front: WHERE or HAVING?
cards.back: WHERE filters input rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after aggregation and can.

cards.front: When should you use SQL Interview Patterns - Joins, Windows, Top-N, CTEs, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Interview questions on tables of events, users or orders, and real feature extraction: counts per group, rows with no match, the latest or top row per group, previous-row deltas and running totals.

Avoid it when: Logic that needs loops, models or heavy string work; pull the rows out and use Python instead. Window functions over huge partitions are also costly, so filter and aggregate early.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of SQL Interview Patterns - Joins, Windows, Top-N, CTEs?
cards.back:
• Summing after a join onto a table with duplicate keys, which silently inflates totals
• Using ROW_NUMBER with a non-unique ORDER BY, so the kept row can change between runs
• Putting a filter on the right table in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN, which turns it into an inner join; put it in ON
• Using NOT IN with a nullable column, which returns no rows if any value is NULL

cards.front: Key formulas: SQL Interview Patterns - Joins, Windows, Top-N, CTEs
cards.back:
Inner join rows $= \sum_k a_k b_k$
Left join rows $= \sum_k a_k \max(1, b_k)$
Fan-out: parent value counted $\max(1, b_k)$ times
$\mathrm{ROW\_NUMBER}$ $1,2,3,4$ vs $\mathrm{RANK}$ $1,1,3,4$ on a tie
$\mathrm{LAG}(x)_i = x_{i-1}$, NULL at the first row
Running sum $S_i = \sum_{j \leq i} x_j$

cards.front: What is AI System Design - Capacity and Cost Estimation?
cards.back: Size an LLM feature on paper: users and requests give peak QPS, tokens per request give tokens per second, that gives GPUs, memory per replica, monthly cost, a latency budget and availability.

cards.front: AI System Design - Capacity and Cost Estimation: what is the key insight?
cards.back: An AI system-design answer is a chain of multiplications with units that cancel. Daily users times requests per user, divided by 86400 seconds, is the average rate; a peak factor turns it into the rate you must survive. Multiply by tokens per request to get tokens per second, divide by what one GPU really delivers (throughput times utilisation, never 100 percent) and round up. Little''s law then ties rate and latency to concurrency, $L = \lambda W$, which sets how many KV caches sit in memory next to the weights. Every hardware number is an assumption you state aloud and can change. Flow: users → peak QPS → tokens per second → GPUs → memory, cost, latency, availability.

cards.front: Walk me through sizing an LLM chatbot.
cards.back: Daily users times requests per user over 86400 gives average QPS, times a peak factor gives peak QPS. Multiply by tokens per request for tokens per second, divide by per-GPU throughput times utilisation, and round up. Then check memory, latency and cost.

cards.front: How many requests are in flight?
cards.back: Little's law,$L = \lambda W$: peak QPS times mean latency. At 300 QPS and 5.3 s that is 1590 concurrent sequences, each holding a KV cache.

cards.front: Why divide by utilisation?
cards.back: A GPU cannot run at its peak throughput all the time: queues need slack, traffic is bursty and batches are uneven. Planning at $u = 0.5$ doubles the fleet relative to $u = 1$ but keeps latency stable.

cards.front: What does a second replica buy?
cards.back: With independent failures the chance both are down is $p^2$, so availability goes from $1 - p$ to $1 - p^2$. Real failures are correlated (same zone, same bad deploy), so the true figure is lower.

cards.front: Where do the weights and the KV cache fit in?
cards.back: Weights are a fixed cost per replica, $P b_w$ bytes. The cache grows with the sequences on that replica and their length, so memory limits concurrency per GPU.

cards.front: When should you use AI System Design - Capacity and Cost Estimation, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: System-design interviews and early planning for an LLM feature: to show how users, token counts and hardware turn into a GPU count, a memory check, a bill and a latency budget before any load test.

Avoid it when: As a final sizing. Real throughput depends on batching, sequence lengths, the serving stack and traffic burstiness, so treat the answer as an order of magnitude and confirm with a load test.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of AI System Design - Capacity and Cost Estimation?
cards.back:
• Sizing for average QPS; the peak, not the mean, decides the fleet
• Using a vendor's peak tokens per second as $\tau$ with no utilisation margin
• Counting only weights and forgetting that the KV cache for in-flight sequences can fill the rest of the GPU
• Treating replica failures as independent when they share a zone, a rollout or a dependency

cards.front: Key formulas: AI System Design - Capacity and Cost Estimation
cards.back:
$\lambda_{avg} = \frac{\mathrm{DAU} \cdot r}{86400}, \;\; \lambda = f \lambda_{avg}$
$T = \lambda (t_{in} + t_{out})$ tokens per second
$\mathrm{GPUs} = \lceil \frac{T}{\tau u} \rceil$
$W = W_q + \frac{t_{in}}{\tau_{pre}} + \frac{t_{out}}{\tau_{dec}}$
Little: $L = \lambda W$
Memory $= P b_w + \frac{L}{\mathrm{GPUs}}\, t\, c_{kv}$
Cost $= \mathrm{GPUs} \cdot \mathrm{price} \cdot \mathrm{hours}$
Availability $= 1 - p^N$

cards.front: What is Reproducibility - Seeds, Determinism and Fingerprints?
cards.back: Seed every random source, request deterministic kernels, and hash the config and data so a result is tied to its inputs; know why bitwise equality can still break and why robust is stronger than reproducible.

cards.front: Reproducibility - Seeds, Determinism and Fingerprints: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A run is a function of code, data, config and every random draw. Fix all four and the same machine gives the same numbers, which is reproducible. The traps are hidden random sources (Python, NumPy, torch, each DataLoader worker) and floating point: addition is not associative, so a different reduction order, a GPU atomic add or another library version changes the last bits, and training can amplify that into a visibly different loss. Reproducible only says you can re-get one number; robust says the conclusion holds across seeds, and that needs several runs. Flow: seed all sources → deterministic kernels → hash config and data → rerun and compare.

cards.front: I set the seed but my runs still differ. Why?
cards.back: Common causes: an unseeded source (NumPy, Python, DataLoader workers), nondeterministic GPU kernels that use atomic adds, a different reduction order from thread or hardware changes, and different library versions. Floating-point addition is not associative, so order changes the last bits.

cards.front: Reproducible versus robust?
cards.back: Reproducible means the same code, data and seed give the same result. Robust means the conclusion holds across seeds and small perturbations. Report the mean and spread over several seeds, not one lucky run.

cards.front: How do you tie a result to its inputs?
cards.back: Hash the config as canonical JSON (sorted keys, fixed separators) and hash the data bytes or file list, then store both with the metrics. Any change to a value changes the digest.

cards.front: Does torch.use_deterministic_algorithms guarantee identical results everywhere?
cards.back: No. It makes torch pick deterministic implementations or raise an error where none exists, which helps on one platform and release. The PyTorch notes say identical results are not guaranteed across releases, commits or platforms, and CPU and GPU can differ.

cards.front: How do you seed DataLoader workers?
cards.back: Pass a seeded torch.Generator as the generator argument so the shuffle order is fixed, and a worker_init_fn that seeds NumPy and Python from torch.initial_seed() so per-worker augmentation is fixed.

cards.front: When should you use Reproducibility - Seeds, Determinism and Fingerprints, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Any experiment you may compare, debug or publish: before a hyperparameter search, when a bug appears only sometimes, and when a reviewer must be able to regenerate a table.

Avoid it when: Do not treat one fixed seed as evidence. Deterministic mode can slow kernels, and chasing bitwise equality across different GPUs or library versions is usually futile; compare metrics within a tolerance and across several seeds instead.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Reproducibility - Seeds, Determinism and Fingerprints?
cards.back:
• Seeding only torch while NumPy augmentation or Python shuffling keeps drawing fresh randomness
• Expecting bitwise equality across different hardware, thread counts or library versions
• Hashing a Python dict with str() or an unsorted dump, so equal configs give different hashes
• Treating one seed as the result; a gap smaller than the seed spread is noise

cards.front: Key formulas: Reproducibility - Seeds, Determinism and Fingerprints
cards.back:
$(a + b) + c \neq a + (b + c)$ in floating point
$|\mathrm{fl}(\sum x_i) - \sum x_i| \leq (n-1)\, u \sum |x_i|$
Unit roundoff $u = 2^{-53}$ for float64
Seed spread $\mathrm{SE} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ over $n$ seeds
Credible gap if $|\Delta| > 2\,\mathrm{SE}_{\Delta}$

cards.front: What is Metropolis-Hastings Sampling?
cards.back: Draw samples from a distribution known only up to a constant by running a Markov chain that proposes random moves and accepts them with a probability that favours higher density.

cards.front: Metropolis-Hastings Sampling: what is the key insight?
cards.back: You can evaluate how probable a point is relative to another, but you cannot sample from the distribution directly. Wander randomly: propose a nearby point, always move uphill in density, and move downhill only with probability equal to the density ratio. Time spent at each place then ends up proportional to its probability, and the unknown normalising constant cancels because only ratios appear.

cards.front: Why does the normalising constant not matter?
cards.back: The acceptance probability depends only on the ratio $p(y)/p(x)$, in which the unknown constant cancels.

cards.front: What is detailed balance and why does it matter?
cards.back: It says stationary probability flow $x$ to $y$ equals $y$ to $x$; any chain satisfying it with respect to $\pi$ has $\pi$ as a stationary distribution, which is the correctness condition.

cards.front: How do you choose the proposal step size?
cards.back: Tune it so the acceptance rate is moderate, neither near zero nor near one; both extremes give highly autocorrelated samples.

cards.front: How does Metropolis-Hastings differ from Gibbs sampling?
cards.back: Gibbs draws each variable from its exact conditional and always accepts; Metropolis-Hastings proposes from any distribution and corrects with an accept-reject step, so it needs no conditionals.

cards.front: When should you use Metropolis-Hastings Sampling, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Bayesian posteriors with unnormalised densities, low-dimensional problems with no conjugate form, and as the base for HMC and Gibbs-style samplers.

Avoid it when: High dimensions or strongly correlated, multimodal targets, where random walks mix very slowly (use HMC/NUTS or variational inference), or when a direct sampler or a deterministic integrator is available.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Metropolis-Hastings Sampling?
cards.back:
• This is a 1-D random walk with a symmetric proposal; asymmetric proposals need the Hastings correction
• Tiny steps accept almost everything but explore slowly; huge steps are mostly rejected
• Samples are autocorrelated, so naive standard errors are too small
• A single chain can look converged while stuck in one mode; run several and compare

cards.front: Key formulas: Metropolis-Hastings Sampling
cards.back:
Target: $\pi(x) \propto p(x)$, normaliser unknown
Proposal: $y \sim q(y|x)$, here $y = x + \sigma\varepsilon,\ \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$
Accept: $a(x \to y) = \min\left(1, \frac{p(y)\,q(x|y)}{p(x)\,q(y|x)}\right)$
Symmetric $q$: $a = \min\left(1, \frac{p(y)}{p(x)}\right)$
Log: accept if $\log u < \log p(y) - \log p(x),\ u \sim U(0,1)$
$\pi(x)\,q(y|x)\,a(x \to y) = \pi(y)\,q(x|y)\,a(y \to x)$

cards.front: What is Ridge and Lasso Regularization?
cards.back: Add a penalty on the size of the weights to least squares. L2 (ridge) shrinks all weights smoothly and has a closed form; L1 (lasso) also sets some weights exactly to zero and is solved by coordinate descent.

cards.front: Ridge and Lasso Regularization: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Penalising weight size trades a little bias for a lot less variance, so the fit stops chasing noise or collinear directions. The L1 penalty has a sharp corner at zero, so small coefficients are pushed all the way to zero, while the smooth L2 penalty only shrinks them.

cards.front: Why does L1 give sparse weights and L2 does not?
cards.back: The L1 penalty has a corner at zero so the optimum often lands exactly on an axis; L2 has a smooth bowl whose gradient vanishes at zero, so weights shrink but rarely hit zero.

cards.front: What is the Bayesian view?
cards.back: Ridge is MAP estimation with a Gaussian prior on the weights; lasso is MAP with a Laplace prior.

cards.front: How do you choose $\lambda$?
cards.back: Cross-validate over a log-spaced grid and pick the value with the best validation error, or the largest one within one standard error of it.

cards.front: When should you use Ridge and Lasso Regularization, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Many or correlated features, or fewer samples than features. Use ridge to stabilise and shrink, and lasso when you also want feature selection.

Avoid it when: Skip them when features are few, independent and data plentiful (plain least squares is fine), or when lasso faces groups of correlated features (it picks one arbitrarily; try elastic net).

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Ridge and Lasso Regularization?
cards.back:
• Unscaled features are penalised unevenly, so standardise first
• Do not penalise the intercept
• Lasso picks one of several correlated features arbitrarily
• sklearn's Ridge uses $\lambda\|w\|^2$ on the summed error but Lasso uses $1/(2n)$; the scales differ

cards.front: Key formulas: Ridge and Lasso Regularization
cards.back:
Ridge: $\min\; \|y - Xw\|^2 + \lambda\|w\|_2^2$
$w = (X^{\top}X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^{\top}y$ (centred, no bias penalty)
Lasso: $\min\; \frac{1}{2n}\|y - Xw\|^2 + \lambda\|w\|_1$
$\mathrm{Soft}(z, \lambda) = \mathrm{sign}(z)\cdot\max(|z| - \lambda,\, 0)$
$w_j \leftarrow \frac{\mathrm{Soft}(x_j^{\top}r/n,\; \lambda)}{x_j^{\top}x_j/n}$
$r = y - \sum_{k \neq j} x_k w_k$ (partial residual)
Intercept $b = \bar{y} - \bar{x}^{\top}w$

cards.front: What is Gaussian Process Regression?
cards.back: Place a Gaussian process prior over functions, condition it on noisy observations, and get a predictive mean and variance at any new input in closed form. The kernel decides what kind of functions are plausible.

cards.front: Gaussian Process Regression: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Instead of fitting parameters, keep every training point and let the kernel say how strongly nearby inputs share their outputs. Close to data the prediction is pinned down and the variance is small; far from data it falls back to the prior mean with the prior variance, so the model knows what it does not know.

cards.front: How is a GP different from kernel ridge regression?
cards.back: The posterior mean has the same form as kernel ridge with the noise variance as the ridge, but a GP also returns a predictive variance and tunes the kernel by marginal likelihood.

cards.front: What does the length scale control?
cards.back: How quickly the function varies: a short length scale gives wiggly fits that revert to the prior quickly, a long one gives smooth, slowly varying fits.

cards.front: Why use a Cholesky factor instead of a matrix inverse?
cards.back: It is faster and numerically stable for symmetric positive definite matrices and gives the log-determinant needed for the marginal likelihood for free.

cards.front: When should you use Gaussian Process Regression, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Small or medium datasets where calibrated uncertainty matters, Bayesian optimisation surrogates, smooth interpolation of expensive simulations, and regression where a kernel encodes domain knowledge.

Avoid it when: Skip it for large $n$, since training cubes and memory squares with the number of points, for high dimensional inputs with weak structure, or when a fast approximate model is enough.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Gaussian Process Regression?
cards.back:
• Training cost grows as $n$ cubed, so thousands of points need sparse or inducing-point approximations
• Tiny noise makes the kernel matrix near singular and the Cholesky fail; add jitter
• The variance returned here is for the latent function; add the noise variance for a new observation
• A zero prior mean pulls predictions to zero away from data; centre or normalise the targets

cards.front: Key formulas: Gaussian Process Regression
cards.back:
Prior: $f \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k),\;\; k(x, x') = s^2 \exp\left(-\frac{\|x - x'\|^2}{2\ell^2}\right)$
Noisy targets: $y = f(x) + \epsilon,\;\; \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_n^2)$
$K = k(X, X) + \sigma_n^2 I,\;\; K = L L^{\top}$ (Cholesky)
$\alpha = K^{-1} y = L^{\top} \backslash (L \backslash y)$
Mean: $\mu_* = k(X_*, X)\,\alpha$
Variance of $f$: $\sigma_*^2 = k(x_*, x_*) - \|L^{-1} k(X, x_*)\|^2$
$\log p(y) = -\frac{1}{2} y^{\top}\alpha - \sum_i \log L_{ii} - \frac{n}{2}\log 2\pi$

cards.front: What is Elastic Net via Coordinate Descent?
cards.back: Linear regression with a mix of L1 and L2 penalties, solved by cycling through coordinates and updating one weight at a time with a soft-threshold. The L1 part zeroes weights; the L2 part stabilises groups of correlated features.

cards.front: Elastic Net via Coordinate Descent: what is the key insight?
cards.back: With all other weights held fixed, the objective in one weight is a one-dimensional problem whose answer is closed form: take the plain least-squares fit to the current residual, shrink it toward zero by the L1 amount (stopping at exactly zero) and divide by a factor that includes the L2 penalty. Cycling over coordinates repeats this until nothing moves.

cards.front: Why use elastic net instead of lasso?
cards.back: Among correlated features lasso tends to pick one at random, while the L2 term makes elastic net share weight across the group and also lets it keep more than $n$ features when $p$ is larger than $n$.

cards.front: What does the soft-threshold do?
cards.back: It shrinks the least-squares coordinate estimate toward zero by the L1 amount and sets it exactly to zero when it is smaller than that amount, which is how sparsity arises.

cards.front: Why does coordinate descent converge here?
cards.back: The loss is smooth and convex and the penalty is convex and separable by coordinate, so exact one-dimensional minimisation steps decrease the objective and reach the global minimum.

cards.front: When should you use Elastic Net via Coordinate Descent, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Many correlated features where lasso picks one arbitrarily, $p$ larger than $n$, automatic feature selection with stable grouping, and large sparse problems where coordinate descent is fast.

Avoid it when: Skip it when you want unbiased estimates of the large coefficients (the penalty shrinks them), when features are unscaled, or when you need coefficient standard errors and p-values.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Elastic Net via Coordinate Descent?
cards.back:
• Unscaled features are penalised unequally; standardise first
• Intercept is not penalised, so centre $y$ and $X$ or fit it separately (this code has no intercept)
• Convergence is slow for highly correlated features and small $\alpha$
• Selected features can change across resamples; check stability, not just one fit

cards.front: Key formulas: Elastic Net via Coordinate Descent
cards.back:
$\min_w\ \frac{1}{2n}\|y - Xw\|^2 + \alpha\rho\|w\|_1 + \frac{1}{2}\alpha(1-\rho)\|w\|^2$
$r_j = y - \sum_{k \neq j} x_k w_k$ (partial residual)
$z_j = \|x_j\|^2/n,\;\; \rho_j = x_j^{\top} r_j/n$
$S(a, t) = \mathrm{sign}(a)\cdot\max(|a| - t,\, 0)$
$w_j \leftarrow \frac{S(\rho_j,\ \alpha\rho)}{z_j + \alpha(1-\rho)}$
$\rho = 1$ gives lasso, $\rho = 0$ gives ridge

cards.front: What is Gaussian Naive Bayes?
cards.back: Classify with Bayes' rule while assuming features are independent given the class. With Gaussian features, training is just a per-class mean, variance and prior.

cards.front: Gaussian Naive Bayes: what is the key insight?
cards.back: The independence assumption is wrong almost always, but it turns an impossible joint density into a product of one-dimensional densities, each estimated from a few numbers. Each feature then casts an independent vote, in log space, for every class, and the largest total wins.

cards.front: Why is it called naive?
cards.back: It assumes features are conditionally independent given the class, which lets the likelihood factorise into per-feature terms.

cards.front: Why does it work despite the false assumption?
cards.back: Classification needs only the argmax over classes; correlated evidence distorts the probabilities more than it changes which class is largest.

cards.front: Naive Bayes vs logistic regression?
cards.back: Naive Bayes is generative, fits fast and does well on little data; logistic regression is discriminative, handles correlated features better and wins with more data.

cards.front: When should you use Gaussian Naive Bayes, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: A fast baseline for small datasets, high-dimensional data and text (multinomial variant), and when you need training and prediction in a single cheap pass.

Avoid it when: Skip it when strongly correlated features carry the signal, when you need trustworthy probabilities, or when class-conditional features are far from Gaussian.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Gaussian Naive Bayes?
cards.back:
• Probabilities are over-confident when features are correlated
• A feature with zero variance in a class needs the smoothing floor
• Multiplying raw probabilities underflows; always sum logs
• Discrete variants need Laplace smoothing so unseen values do not zero a class

cards.front: Key formulas: Gaussian Naive Bayes
cards.back:
$P(c\,|\,x) \propto P(c)\cdot\prod_j P(x_j\,|\,c)$
$P(x_j\,|\,c) = \mathcal{N}(x_j;\ \mu_{cj}, \sigma^2_{cj})$
$\log P(x_j\,|\,c) = -\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{(x_j - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}$
$\mathrm{Score}(c) = \log P(c) + \sum_j \log P(x_j\,|\,c)$
$\hat{y} = \arg\max_c\ \mathrm{Score}(c)$
$P(c\,|\,x) = \mathrm{softmax}$ over $c$ of $\mathrm{Score}(c)$

cards.front: What is k-Nearest Neighbours?
cards.back: Predict a point's label by majority vote among the $k$ closest training points. There is no training step: the data itself is the model.

cards.front: k-Nearest Neighbours: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Nearby points tend to share labels, so instead of learning a boundary you look it up on demand. $k$ sets the smoothness: $k = 1$ follows every noisy point, while a large $k$ averages so widely that local structure is lost.

cards.front: How do you choose $k$?
cards.back: Cross-validate over odd values; small $k$ overfits noise, large $k$ underfits and blurs class boundaries.

cards.front: Why must features be scaled?
cards.back: Euclidean distance mixes units, so a feature with a large numeric range dominates which points count as near.

cards.front: Why does it struggle in high dimensions?
cards.back: Distances between random points concentrate, so the nearest neighbour is barely closer than the farthest and the vote becomes uninformative.

cards.front: When should you use k-Nearest Neighbours, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Small or medium datasets in a few meaningful, scaled dimensions, as a quick non-parametric baseline, or when the boundary is irregular.

Avoid it when: Skip it for large $n$ (each prediction scans all data), high-dimensional data (distances concentrate and lose meaning), or unscaled features.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of k-Nearest Neighbours?
cards.back:
• Unscaled features: the largest-range feature decides the neighbours
• Curse of dimensionality makes all points nearly equidistant
• Use an odd $k$ for two classes to avoid tied votes
• Irrelevant features add noise to every distance

cards.front: Key formulas: k-Nearest Neighbours
cards.back:
$d(a,b)^2 = \|a\|^2 + \|b\|^2 - 2\,a^{\top}b$
$N_k(x)$ = indices of the $k$ smallest $d(x, x_i)$
$\hat{y}(x) = \arg\max_c \sum_{i \in N_k(x)} \mathbb{1}[y_i = c]$
Weighted vote: $w_i = \frac{1}{d(x, x_i)}$

cards.front: What is Support Vector Machine?
cards.back: Find the separating hyperplane with the widest margin. The code is a simplified linear soft-margin SVM trained by full-batch sub-gradient descent on the hinge loss; kernels and the dual solver (SMO) are not implemented.

cards.front: Support Vector Machine: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Many hyperplanes separate two classes, but the one farthest from both is least likely to be thrown off by new points. Only the points on or inside the margin matter for the solution (the support vectors), so confidently classified points are simply ignored.

cards.front: What are support vectors?
cards.back: The training points on or inside the margin; they alone determine the hyperplane and removing any other point leaves it unchanged.

cards.front: What does $C$ control?
cards.back: The penalty on margin violations: large $C$ tolerates few violations (narrow margin, low bias), small $C$ allows more (wide margin, more regularisation).

cards.front: What is the kernel trick?
cards.back: The dual problem uses only dot products $x_i\cdot x_j$, so replacing them with a kernel $k(x_i, x_j)$ gives a linear margin in an implicit high-dimensional space without computing it.

cards.front: When should you use Support Vector Machine, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Medium-sized, high-dimensional problems (text, genomics) with a clear margin, and with a kernel when the boundary is curved.

Avoid it when: Skip kernel SVMs on very large datasets (training scales badly with $n$), when you need probabilities directly, or when classes overlap heavily and features are unscaled.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Support Vector Machine?
cards.back:
• Unscaled features let one large feature dominate the margin
• Scores are not probabilities; Platt scaling is needed
• RBF with a large gamma memorises the training set
• This card's code is linear only and uses sub-gradient descent instead of the dual solver

cards.front: Key formulas: Support Vector Machine
cards.back:
$f(x) = w^{\top}x + b,\;\; \hat{y} = \mathrm{sign}\,f(x),\;\; y \in \{-1, +1\}$
Margin width $= \frac{2}{\|w\|}$
$\min\ \frac{1}{2}\lambda\|w\|^2 + \frac{1}{n}\sum \max(0, 1 - y_i f(x_i))$
Violators $V = \{i : y_i f(x_i) < 1\}$
$\partial w = \lambda w - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in V} y_i x_i$
$\partial b = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in V} y_i$
Step size $\eta_t = \frac{1}{\lambda(t + 10)}$
Equivalent to sklearn $C = \frac{1}{\lambda n}$

cards.front: What is Decision Tree?
cards.back: Predict by asking a chain of yes/no questions on single features. The tree is grown greedily, choosing at each node the split that makes the two child groups as pure as possible.

cards.front: Decision Tree: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A tree carves feature space into axis-aligned boxes and predicts the majority class of each box. Growing it is just a repeated search: try every threshold on every feature and keep the one that most reduces impurity, then recurse on each side as if it were a new problem.

cards.front: Gini or entropy?
cards.back: Both measure impurity and usually pick near-identical splits; Gini avoids the logarithm so it is slightly faster.

cards.front: How do you stop a tree from overfitting?
cards.back: Limit depth, require a minimum leaf size, or grow fully and prune with cost-complexity; or average many trees in a forest.

cards.front: Do trees need feature scaling?
cards.back: No. Splits compare a feature to a threshold, so any monotonic rescaling gives the same tree.

cards.front: When should you use Decision Tree, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Interpretable models on tabular data with mixed scales and non-linear interactions, and as the base learner for forests and boosting.

Avoid it when: Skip a single deep tree when you need stable predictions or smooth boundaries: small data changes flip splits, and axis-aligned cuts approximate diagonal boundaries badly.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Decision Tree?
cards.back:
• Unlimited depth reaches 100% training accuracy and overfits
• Split search favours features with many distinct values
• Equal-gain splits are tied: sklearn breaks ties by a random feature order, so deep trees can differ from this code
• Predictions are piecewise constant, so a tree cannot extrapolate

cards.front: Key formulas: Decision Tree
cards.back:
$\mathrm{Gini}(S) = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2,\;\; p_k$ = share of class $k$ in $S$
$\mathrm{Entropy}(S) = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k$
Split cost $= \frac{|L|}{|S|}\mathrm{Gini}(L) + \frac{|R|}{|S|}\mathrm{Gini}(R)$
$L = \{x : x_j \leq t\},\;\; R = \{x : x_j > t\}$
$\mathrm{Gain} = \mathrm{Gini}(S) - \mathrm{Split\ cost}$
Leaf prediction $= \arg\max_k\, p_k$

cards.front: What is Linear Discriminant Analysis?
cards.back: Find the linear projections that push class means far apart while keeping each class tight. The same model doubles as a Gaussian classifier with a shared covariance.

cards.front: Linear Discriminant Analysis: what is the key insight?
cards.back: PCA looks for directions of large variance and ignores labels, so the top direction may mix the classes. LDA scores a direction by the ratio of between-class spread to within-class spread, so it picks the direction along which the classes are best separated relative to their own noise. Whitening by the within-class scatter is what makes distances in the projected space meaningful.

cards.front: How does LDA differ from PCA?
cards.back: PCA is unsupervised and maximises total variance; LDA uses labels and maximises between-class over within-class scatter, so it targets class separation instead.

cards.front: How many discriminant directions can you get?
cards.back: At most the number of classes minus one, because the between-class scatter is built from that many independent mean differences.

cards.front: LDA versus QDA?
cards.back: LDA assumes one shared covariance, giving linear boundaries and fewer parameters; QDA fits a covariance per class, giving quadratic boundaries but needing more data.

cards.front: What do you do when $S_w$ is singular?
cards.back: Shrink it toward a scaled identity, reduce dimension with PCA first, or use the SVD solver, which avoids forming the covariance explicitly.

cards.front: When should you use Linear Discriminant Analysis, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Multiclass problems with roughly Gaussian, similarly shaped classes, small datasets where a low-variance linear model helps, and supervised dimensionality reduction before another classifier.

Avoid it when: When class covariances differ a lot (try QDA), when classes are multimodal or non-linear, when features outnumber samples (the within-class scatter is singular, so shrink it), or when you need probabilities that are well calibrated under heavy tails.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Linear Discriminant Analysis?
cards.back:
• $S_w$ is singular when features outnumber samples or are collinear; this code would fail, so use shrinkage or PCA first
• Only $C-1$ meaningful directions exist; extra eigenvectors have zero eigenvalue
• Directions are defined up to sign, and scaling conventions differ between libraries; compare projections up to sign and scale
• The shared-covariance Gaussian assumption is strong; outliers and unequal covariances hurt

cards.front: Key formulas: Linear Discriminant Analysis
cards.back:
$\mu$: overall mean, $\mu_c$: class mean, $n_c$: class size
Within: $S_w = \sum_c \sum_{i \in c} (x_i - \mu_c)(x_i - \mu_c)^{\top}$
Between: $S_b = \sum_c n_c\,(\mu_c - \mu)(\mu_c - \mu)^{\top}$
Fisher: $J(w) = \frac{w^{\top} S_b w}{w^{\top} S_w w}$
Optimum: $S_w^{-1} S_b\,w = \lambda w$, top $\leq C-1$
Scale: $w^{\top} S_w w = 1$ (unit within-class variance)
$\delta_c(x) = x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_c - \frac{1}{2}\mu_c^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_c + \log\pi_c$

cards.front: What is Kernel Trick and RBF Kernel Ridge?
cards.back: Replace dot products by a kernel so a linear method works in a huge implicit feature space. With the RBF kernel and ridge regression this gives a smooth non-linear regressor using only an $n$ by $n$ Gram matrix.

cards.front: Kernel Trick and RBF Kernel Ridge: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Many linear algorithms touch the data only through dot products between points. If you swap each dot product for a kernel $k(x, z)$ that equals a dot product in some richer feature space, you get a non-linear model without ever building those features. The RBF kernel is a similarity that decays with distance, which corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature space.

cards.front: What is the kernel trick?
cards.back: If an algorithm uses data only through inner products, you can replace them with a kernel function that equals an inner product in a richer feature space, getting non-linearity without computing the features.

cards.front: What does the RBF bandwidth control?
cards.back: How fast similarity falls with distance: large $\gamma$ gives very local, wiggly fits that can overfit; small $\gamma$ gives smooth, nearly linear fits that can underfit.

cards.front: What makes a function a valid kernel?
cards.back: It must be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning every Gram matrix has non-negative eigenvalues (Mercer's condition).

cards.front: Kernel ridge versus SVM?
cards.back: Both use kernels; kernel ridge uses squared loss and has a closed form with all points contributing, while the SVM's hinge loss yields sparse support vectors via a quadratic program.

cards.front: When should you use Kernel Trick and RBF Kernel Ridge, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Small to medium datasets (up to a few thousand points) with smooth non-linear structure, kernel SVMs and kernel ridge baselines, and Gaussian-process-style regression.

Avoid it when: Large $n$, since the Gram matrix costs quadratic memory and the solve cubic time (use random features, Nyström or neural nets), or high-dimensional sparse data where a linear model already works.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Kernel Trick and RBF Kernel Ridge?
cards.back:
• Features must be scaled, otherwise $\gamma$ means different things per dimension
• Memory and time grow with $n^2$, so it does not scale to millions of rows
• This is kernel ridge (squared loss, dense $\alpha$), not an SVM: no sparse support vectors
• Far from the training data the prediction decays toward zero because the kernel does, so extrapolation is poor

cards.front: Key formulas: Kernel Trick and RBF Kernel Ridge
cards.back:
RBF: $k(x,z) = \exp(-\gamma\,\|x - z\|^2)$
Expand: $\|x - z\|^2 = \|x\|^2 + \|z\|^2 - 2\,x^{\top}z$
Gram matrix: $K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)$, symmetric and PSD
Kernel ridge: $\alpha = (K + \lambda I)^{-1}\,y$
Prediction: $f(x) = \sum_i \alpha_i\,k(x, x_i)$
Trick: $k(x,z) = \varphi(x)^{\top}\varphi(z)$ without computing $\varphi$

cards.front: What is Random Forest?
cards.back: Train many decision trees on bootstrap resamples, letting each split see only a random subset of features, then average their votes. The code is a simplified binary-class version, with no out-of-bag scoring or parallelism.

cards.front: Random Forest: what is the key insight?
cards.back: One deep tree has low bias but high variance, so its errors are largely random noise. Averaging many trees cancels that noise, but only if the trees disagree, which is why each gets a different bootstrap sample and a different random feature subset at every split.

cards.front: Why does bagging help but not hurt by adding more trees?
cards.back: Averaging reduces variance and leaves bias unchanged; extra trees only shrink the $(1-\rho)\sigma^2/B$ term, so the error plateaus rather than rises.

cards.front: What is the role of max_features?
cards.back: Fewer candidate features per split decorrelates trees, which lowers ensemble variance at the cost of weaker individual trees.

cards.front: What is out-of-bag error?
cards.back: Each tree misses about a third of the rows, so scoring each row only with trees that did not see it gives a free validation estimate.

cards.front: When should you use Random Forest, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: A strong default for tabular data: little tuning, handles non-linear interactions, mixed scales and noisy features, and gives feature importances.

Avoid it when: Skip it when you need a tiny fast model, extrapolation beyond the training range, or the last bit of accuracy (boosting usually wins), or with very sparse high-dimensional text.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Random Forest?
cards.back:
• Highly correlated trees give little gain, so keep $m$ below $d$
• Impurity-based feature importance favours high-cardinality features; use permutation importance
• Trees cannot extrapolate outside the training range
• This card's code simplifies sklearn: no out-of-bag scoring, binary labels only

cards.front: Key formulas: Random Forest
cards.back:
Tree $b$ on bootstrap sample $D_b$ ($n$ draws)
Each split: $m$ random features, $m \approx \sqrt{d}$
Classification: $\hat{y}$ = majority vote of the $B$ trees
Regression: $\hat{y} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_b f_b(x)$
$\mathrm{Var}(\hat{y}) = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{(1-\rho)\sigma^2}{B}$
Left out of bootstrap: $(1 - \frac{1}{n})^n \to \frac{1}{e}$ (OOB)

cards.front: What is Gradient Boosting?
cards.back: Build a model as a sum of many weak trees, each fitted to the errors the current sum still makes. The code is simplified to squared loss with depth-1 trees (stumps), which is exactly what sklearn does for that setting.

cards.front: Gradient Boosting: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Instead of one big model, keep a running prediction and repeatedly ask "what is still wrong?". For squared loss the answer is just the residuals, so each new small tree learns to correct the leftover error, and a small learning rate makes each correction cautious.

cards.front: Why is it called gradient boosting?
cards.back: Each tree fits the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current prediction, so adding it is a gradient descent step in function space.

cards.front: Bagging vs boosting?
cards.back: Bagging averages independent deep trees to cut variance; boosting adds shallow trees sequentially to cut bias.

cards.front: What is the trade-off between learning rate and number of trees?
cards.back: A smaller rate needs more trees but usually gives better generalisation; tune them together with early stopping.

cards.front: When should you use Gradient Boosting, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Usually the most accurate choice on tabular data, for both regression and classification, when you can afford some tuning.

Avoid it when: Skip it when training must be parallel or tiny, with very noisy labels (it keeps fitting noise without early stopping), or when you need extrapolation.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Gradient Boosting?
cards.back:
• Too many rounds with a large learning rate overfits; monitor a validation set
• Boosting is sequential, so it cannot be parallelised across trees
• Outliers dominate squared-loss residuals; use Huber or absolute loss
• This card's code is squared loss with stumps only; other losses fit pseudo-residuals instead

cards.front: Key formulas: Gradient Boosting
cards.back:
$F_0(x) = \bar{y}$   (best constant for squared loss)
$r_i = y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i) = -\frac{\partial L}{\partial F}$ for $L = \frac{1}{2}(y - F)^2$
$h_m$ = tree fitted to the residuals $r$
$F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + \eta\,h_m(x)$
Stump: $h(x) = a$ if $x_j \leq t$ else $b$
$a, b$ = mean residual on each side of the split
Best split maximises $\frac{(\sum_L r)^2}{|L|} + \frac{(\sum_R r)^2}{|R|}$

cards.front: What is AdaBoost (Discrete, Decision Stumps)?
cards.back: Build a strong classifier as a weighted vote of weak ones, training each new stump on the data re-weighted to emphasise earlier mistakes.

cards.front: AdaBoost (Discrete, Decision Stumps): what is the key insight?
cards.back: A stump alone is barely better than guessing, but different stumps can be wrong on different points. AdaBoost keeps a weight on every sample and, after each round, raises the weight of the points just misclassified so the next weak learner is forced to fix them. Stumps that do well get a larger say in the final vote.

cards.front: How does AdaBoost reweight samples?
cards.back: It multiplies the weight of each sample by $\exp(-\alpha\, y\, h(x))$: misclassified points are scaled up, correct ones scaled down, then all weights are renormalised.

cards.front: Why is a weak learner enough?
cards.back: The training error bound shrinks multiplicatively each round whenever the learner is even slightly better than chance on the current weights.

cards.front: Why is AdaBoost sensitive to noise?
cards.back: The exponential loss grows quickly for misclassified points, so mislabelled samples receive ever larger weights and the ensemble bends to fit them.

cards.front: How is AdaBoost related to gradient boosting?
cards.back: It is gradient boosting with the exponential loss; gradient boosting generalises the idea to arbitrary differentiable losses.

cards.front: When should you use AdaBoost (Discrete, Decision Stumps), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Tabular classification with clean labels where a simple weak learner is available, as a fast strong baseline, and to learn boosting before moving to gradient boosting.

Avoid it when: With noisy or mislabelled data, since the exponential loss keeps raising the weight of bad points and the ensemble chases them. Also when you need calibrated probabilities or very large datasets (gradient boosting libraries are faster and more flexible).

cards.front: Common pitfalls of AdaBoost (Discrete, Decision Stumps)?
cards.back:
• Labels must be $-1$ and $+1$ in this code; sklearn takes any labels
• Label noise and outliers get exponentially up-weighted and degrade the model
• An error of exactly zero would give an infinite vote weight, so the code clips the error
• The stump search here is the slow quadratic version; sort once per feature in practice

cards.front: Key formulas: AdaBoost (Discrete, Decision Stumps)
cards.back:
Weights: $w_i = 1/n$ initially, $\sum_i w_i = 1$
Weighted error: $\epsilon = \sum_i w_i\,[h(x_i) \neq y_i]$
Vote weight: $\alpha = \frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1-\epsilon}{\epsilon}$
Update: $w_i \leftarrow w_i \exp(-\alpha\,y_i\,h(x_i))$, then renormalise
Model: $F(x) = \sum_t \alpha_t h_t(x)$, prediction $\hat{y} = \mathrm{sign}\,F(x)$
Stump: $h(x) = s$ if $x_j \leq t$ else $-s$, $y_i \in \{-1,+1\}$

cards.front: What is Hidden Markov Model (Forward Algorithm)?
cards.back: Compute the likelihood of an observation sequence under a hidden Markov model by carrying a running belief over hidden states. Dynamic programming turns a sum over exponentially many state paths into one pass.

cards.front: Hidden Markov Model (Forward Algorithm): what is the key insight?
cards.back: The brute-force likelihood adds up the probability of every possible hidden path, which grows exponentially with sequence length. But the future depends on the past only through the current state, so all paths that end in the same state can be merged into one number. The forward vector stores exactly that merged mass per state, and each new observation costs one small matrix-vector product.

cards.front: Why is the forward algorithm polynomial when the path sum is exponential?
cards.back: Paths ending in the same state share an identical future, so their probabilities can be merged into one value per state; each step then costs $N^2$ work instead of multiplying the number of paths by $N$.

cards.front: How does Viterbi differ from the forward algorithm?
cards.back: Forward sums over predecessor states to get a likelihood; Viterbi takes a max and keeps back-pointers to recover the single most probable state path.

cards.front: How do you avoid underflow?
cards.back: Normalise the forward vector at every step and accumulate the log of the normalisers, or work fully in log-space with log-sum-exp.

cards.front: What is the forward pass used for in Baum-Welch?
cards.back: Together with the backward pass it gives the posterior probability of each state and transition at each time, which are the expected counts of the E-step.

cards.front: When should you use Hidden Markov Model (Forward Algorithm), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Scoring a sequence under a fitted HMM (speech, gesture, biological sequences, regime switching), model comparison between HMMs, and as the E-step ingredient of Baum-Welch training.

Avoid it when: When the state or observation dependence is long-range (use RNNs or transformers), when states are continuous and non-linear, or when you need the single best state path rather than a likelihood (that is the Viterbi algorithm, which replaces the sum by a max).

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Hidden Markov Model (Forward Algorithm)?
cards.back:
• Without rescaling or log-space, the raw forward probabilities underflow on long sequences
• This code handles discrete emissions with a fixed model; training the parameters needs the backward pass too (Baum-Welch)
• Zero entries in $A$ or $B$ make some sequences impossible, so smooth estimated parameters
• Forward gives the likelihood, not the best state sequence; use Viterbi for decoding

cards.front: Key formulas: Hidden Markov Model (Forward Algorithm)
cards.back:
$\lambda = (\pi, A, B),\; A_{ij} = P(z_{t+1}{=}j|z_t{=}i),\; B_j(o) = P(o|z{=}j)$
Likelihood: $P(o_{1:T}) = \sum_{z_{1:T}} \pi(z_1)\,B(z_1,o_1) \prod A\,B$
Init: $\alpha_1(j) = \pi_j\,B_j(o_1)$
Recursion: $\alpha_{t+1}(j) = \left[\sum_i \alpha_t(i)\,A_{ij}\right] B_j(o_{t+1})$
Result: $P(o_{1:T}) = \sum_j \alpha_T(j)$
Scaling: $c_t = \sum_j \tilde{\alpha}_t(j)$; $\log P = \sum_t \log c_t$
Cost: $O(T N^2)$ instead of $O(N^T)$ for the path sum

cards.front: What is Matrix Factorisation for Recommenders (ALS)?
cards.back: Approximate a sparse user-by-item rating matrix by a product of two low-rank factor matrices, fitted only on the observed entries by alternating least squares.

cards.front: Matrix Factorisation for Recommenders (ALS): what is the key insight?
cards.back: Tastes are not random: a few hidden factors (genre, mood, level) explain most ratings. Give each user and item a short vector and predict a rating as their dot product. With one side held fixed, finding the best vectors for the other side is an ordinary ridge regression for each user or item, so alternating the two solves a hard non-convex problem with easy convex steps.

cards.front: Why alternate instead of optimising $U$ and $V$ jointly?
cards.back: The joint problem is non-convex, but with one factor fixed it is a set of independent ridge regressions with exact closed-form solutions.

cards.front: How does ALS handle missing entries?
cards.back: It only sums over observed ratings, using the mask to select each user's rated items, so missing values are ignored rather than treated as zero.

cards.front: ALS versus SGD for matrix factorisation?
cards.back: ALS parallelises easily across users or items and each step is exact; SGD is cheaper per update and handles streaming or very large data.

cards.front: How do you evaluate a recommender factorisation?
cards.back: Hold out some observed ratings and compare RMSE against simple baselines like the global or per-item mean; also use ranking metrics when top-N matters.

cards.front: When should you use Matrix Factorisation for Recommenders (ALS), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Collaborative filtering with explicit ratings or implicit feedback, filling in missing entries of a low-rank matrix, and learning embeddings that feed other models.

Avoid it when: Cold start (new users or items with no ratings have no data to learn from), when side features matter more than interactions, or when a very large sparse matrix needs SGD or distributed ALS.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Matrix Factorisation for Recommenders (ALS)?
cards.back:
• $R$ is a dense array with a 0/1 mask $M$ here; real systems use sparse formats
• A user or item with no ratings gets a zero vector, so cold start needs other signals
• Plain $\lambda$ is not scaled by the number of ratings per user (the weighted-$\lambda$ variant does); a simplification
• No user or item bias terms, so subtract the global mean or add biases for better accuracy

cards.front: Key formulas: Matrix Factorisation for Recommenders (ALS)
cards.back:
Prediction: $\hat{r}_{ui} = u_u^{\top} v_i$
Loss: $L = \sum_{(u,i)\in\Omega} (r_{ui} - u_u^{\top} v_i)^2 + \lambda(\|U\|^2 + \|V\|^2)$
$\Omega$ = set of observed (user, item) pairs
User step: $(V_u^{\top} V_u + \lambda I)\,u_u = V_u^{\top} r_u$
$V_u$ = rows of $V$ for items rated by user $u$
Item step: $(U_i^{\top} U_i + \lambda I)\,v_i = U_i^{\top} r_i$
Each half-step is an exact ridge regression

cards.front: What is Gaussian Mixture Model (EM)?
cards.back: Model the data as a weighted sum of Gaussians and fit it by alternating soft cluster assignments (E-step) with weighted parameter updates (M-step). It is k-means with soft membership and per-cluster covariance.

cards.front: Gaussian Mixture Model (EM): what is the key insight?
cards.back: If you knew which Gaussian produced each point, fitting would be trivial weighted averaging; if you knew the Gaussians, assigning points would be trivial Bayes' rule. EM breaks the chicken-and-egg loop by using the current guess to assign fractional responsibilities, refitting with them, and repeating, and each round can never lower the likelihood.

cards.front: How is a GMM different from k-means?
cards.back: k-means is the hard-assignment, equal-spherical-covariance limit of EM; a GMM gives soft responsibilities and learns each cluster's weight and covariance.

cards.front: Why does EM never decrease the likelihood?
cards.back: The E-step builds a lower bound equal to the likelihood at the current parameters and the M-step maximises that bound, so the true likelihood can only go up.

cards.front: How do you pick the number of components?
cards.back: Fit several $K$ and compare BIC, which penalises parameters, or compare held-out log-likelihood; likelihood on training data always improves with $K$.

cards.front: What goes wrong when a covariance is singular?
cards.back: The density at that component's point blows up, so the fit chases a spike; a covariance floor or priors prevent it.

cards.front: When should you use Gaussian Mixture Model (EM), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Soft clustering with elliptical clusters of different size and shape, density estimation, anomaly scoring by low likelihood, and as a generative model per class.

Avoid it when: Skip it for non-convex shapes (use DBSCAN or spectral clustering), when clusters are tiny relative to the dimension (covariances become singular), or when you need a unique answer independent of initialisation.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Gaussian Mixture Model (EM)?
cards.back:
• Local optima: different starts give different fits, so run several restarts
• A component can collapse onto a single point, sending the likelihood to infinity without the $\epsilon$ floor
• Component labels are arbitrary, so compare fits after matching components
• Likelihood alone always favours more components; penalise with BIC or validate on held-out data

cards.front: Key formulas: Gaussian Mixture Model (EM)
cards.back:
$p(x) = \sum_k \pi_k\,\mathcal{N}(x;\ \mu_k, \Sigma_k)$
$\log\mathcal{N} = -\frac{1}{2}\left[d\log 2\pi + \log|\Sigma| + (x-\mu)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right]$
E-step: $r_{ik} = \frac{\pi_k\,\mathcal{N}(x_i;\ \mu_k, \Sigma_k)}{\sum_j \pi_j\,\mathcal{N}(x_i;\ \mu_j, \Sigma_j)}$
$N_k = \sum_i r_{ik}$
M-step: $\pi_k = \frac{N_k}{n},\;\; \mu_k = \frac{\sum_i r_{ik}\,x_i}{N_k}$
$\Sigma_k = \frac{\sum_i r_{ik}(x_i-\mu_k)(x_i-\mu_k)^{\top}}{N_k} + \epsilon I$
Objective: $\ell = \sum_i \log \sum_k \pi_k\,\mathcal{N}(x_i;\ \mu_k, \Sigma_k)$

cards.front: What is DBSCAN?
cards.back: Grow clusters from dense regions: a point with enough neighbours inside radius eps is a core point, clusters are chains of overlapping core neighbourhoods, and points reachable from no core are noise.

cards.front: DBSCAN: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A cluster is a region where you can keep walking from point to point without ever stepping across a gap bigger than eps in a crowd of at least min_pts. This defines clusters by connectivity of density rather than by distance to a centre, so it finds crescents and rings and needs no cluster count, and it can say that a point belongs nowhere.

cards.front: What are core, border and noise points?
cards.back: Core points have at least min_pts points within eps, border points are within eps of a core but not core themselves, and noise is everything else.

cards.front: How do you choose eps?
cards.back: Plot each point's distance to its $k$-th nearest neighbour sorted ascending and pick the knee, then sanity-check the clusters.

cards.front: Why can DBSCAN beat k-means?
cards.back: It needs no cluster count, finds arbitrary shapes, and marks outliers, whereas k-means assumes compact, similar-sized convex clusters and assigns every point.

cards.front: When should you use DBSCAN, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Non-convex clusters, unknown number of clusters, data with outliers you want flagged, and low-dimensional spatial or geographic data.

Avoid it when: Skip it when clusters have very different densities (one eps cannot fit both), in high dimensions where distances concentrate, or for big data without a spatial index (this code is quadratic).

cards.front: Common pitfalls of DBSCAN?
cards.back:
• Features must be scaled first, otherwise eps means nothing
• Border points touching two clusters go to whichever is reached first, so results depend on row order
• Mixed-density data: a single eps merges the dense clusters or drops the sparse ones as noise
• min_pts counts the point itself, so conventions differ between libraries

cards.front: Key formulas: DBSCAN
cards.back:
$N_{\epsilon}(i) = \{\, j : \|x_i - x_j\| \leq \epsilon \,\}$ (includes $i$ itself)
Core: $|N_{\epsilon}(i)| \geq \mathrm{minPts}$
$j$ reachable from $i$ if $i$ core and $j \in N_{\epsilon}(i)$
Cluster = linked core points plus their borders
Noise = not reachable from any core, label $-1$

cards.front: What is Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering?
cards.back: Start with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merge the two closest clusters, recording the merge distances. Cutting the resulting tree at any height gives a clustering, so k need not be fixed in advance.

cards.front: Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Merging order encodes the whole nested structure of the data: points that join early are tightly packed, and the heights at which groups join show how separated they are. The linkage rule defines what close means between groups, and that choice, not the algorithm, decides the shapes you find.

cards.front: How do single, average and ward linkage differ?
cards.back: Single uses the closest pair between clusters and can chain; average uses the mean pairwise distance and is a compromise; ward merges the pair that least increases within-cluster variance and favours compact, round clusters.

cards.front: How do you choose the number of clusters from a dendrogram?
cards.back: Cut where there is a large jump in merge height, meaning the next merge joins clusters that are far apart, or validate with a score such as the silhouette.

cards.front: Why is agglomerative clustering expensive?
cards.back: It stores all pairwise distances, which is quadratic in memory, and a naive search for the closest pair at each of n − 1 merges makes the time cubic.

cards.front: When should you use Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: A dendrogram for exploration, small to medium datasets, clusters of different scales, a cut chosen after seeing the merge heights, and non-Euclidean distances (except ward).

Avoid it when: Skip it for large n because the naive method is cubic and needs a distance matrix, for data with heavy noise (single linkage chains through it), or when you need to assign new points.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering?
cards.back:
• Single linkage chains points through bridges of noise into one long cluster
• Ward assumes Euclidean distance and favours compact, similarly sized clusters
• Merges are never undone, so an early mistake stays in the tree
• Ties in the minimum distance make the tree depend on the tie-breaking order

cards.front: Key formulas: Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering
cards.back:
Single: $d(A,B) = \min_{a \in A,\, b \in B}\|a - b\|$
Average: $d(A,B) = \frac{1}{|A||B|}\sum_a \sum_b \|a - b\|$
Ward: $\Delta(A,B) = \frac{|A||B|}{|A|+|B|}\,\|\mu_A - \mu_B\|^2$
$d(k, i \cup j) = \alpha_i d(k,i) + \alpha_j d(k,j) + \beta\, d(i,j)$
$+\ \gamma|d(k,i) - d(k,j)|$: $\gamma = -\frac{1}{2}$ single, 0 avg/ward
Average: $\alpha_i = \frac{n_i}{n_i + n_j},\ \beta = \gamma = 0$
Ward (squared d): $\alpha_i = \frac{n_k + n_i}{N},\ \beta = -\frac{n_k}{N}$
$\ \ $with $N = n_k + n_i + n_j$

cards.front: What is Local Outlier Factor?
cards.back: Score each point by comparing its local density with the density around its $k$ nearest neighbours. A score near one means a point is as dense as its surroundings; a much larger score marks a local outlier.

cards.front: Local Outlier Factor: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A point can be far from everything in absolute terms and still be normal if it sits in a naturally sparse region. What makes a point odd is being sparser than the neighbours it belongs to, so the score is a ratio of the neighbours' density to the point's own density rather than a raw distance.

cards.front: Why is LOF a local method?
cards.back: It compares a point's density with that of its own neighbours instead of the global average, so a point in a sparse cluster is not flagged just because the whole cluster is sparse.

cards.front: What does the reachability distance do?
cards.back: It replaces the true distance by the larger of the true distance and the neighbour's $k$-distance, which stops very close pairs from producing wildly large densities.

cards.front: How do you choose $k$?
cards.back: Use at least the size of the smallest group you would still call a cluster; larger $k$ smooths the scores, and ranking stability across a range of $k$ is a useful check.

cards.front: When should you use Local Outlier Factor, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Anomalies defined relative to local context, data with clusters of differing density, and unsupervised outlier ranking where no labels exist.

Avoid it when: Skip it when outliers are global extremes (simple distance or isolation forest is cheaper), in high dimensions where distances lose contrast, and for large n without a neighbour index.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Local Outlier Factor?
cards.back:
• Features on different scales make the distance, and so the score, meaningless
• Duplicate points give zero reachability distance, so a tiny constant avoids dividing by zero
• Ties at the $k$-th distance make the neighbour set depend on tie-breaking
• Scores are relative to $k$; there is no universal threshold above 1

cards.front: Key formulas: Local Outlier Factor
cards.back:
