$k$-$\mathrm{dist}(o)$ = distance from $o$ to its $k$-th neighbour
$\mathrm{reach}(p, o) = \max(\mathrm{kdist}(o),\ d(p, o))$
$\mathrm{lrd}(p) = \frac{1}{\mathrm{mean}_{o \in N_k(p)}\ \mathrm{reach}(p, o)}$
$\mathrm{LOF}(p) = \frac{\mathrm{mean}_{o \in N_k(p)}\ \mathrm{lrd}(o)}{\mathrm{lrd}(p)}$
$\mathrm{LOF} \approx 1$ inlier, $\mathrm{LOF} \gg 1$ outlier

cards.front: What is Non-negative Matrix Factorisation?
cards.back: Factor a non-negative matrix X into W H with both factors non-negative and a small inner rank. Multiplicative updates rescale each entry by a ratio of positive terms, so non-negativity is kept without any projection step.

cards.front: Non-negative Matrix Factorisation: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Forbidding negative entries means each row of X can only be built by adding parts, never subtracting them, so the learned factors tend to be parts such as topics, strokes or sources. The update multiplies each entry by how much the data wants it, over how much the model already uses it, which grows an entry when it is too small and shrinks it when too large.

cards.front: How is NMF different from PCA or SVD?
cards.back: NMF forces non-negative factors and gives additive, parts-based components that are not orthogonal and not unique; SVD allows signs, is orthogonal and gives the best rank-r approximation.

cards.front: Why do multiplicative updates preserve non-negativity?
cards.back: Each update multiplies an entry by a ratio of non-negative quantities, so entries stay non-negative if they start that way.

cards.front: Does NMF find the global optimum?
cards.back: No. The problem is non-convex in W and H jointly, so the updates reach a stationary point that depends on initialisation.

cards.front: When should you use Non-negative Matrix Factorisation, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Parts-based features from non-negative data such as word counts, images and spectra, topic modelling, and interpretable low-rank structure where signs would be confusing.

Avoid it when: Skip it when data has negative values, when you need a unique answer (the factorisation is not unique and depends on initialisation), or when plain SVD's optimality and speed are enough.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Non-negative Matrix Factorisation?
cards.back:
• Entries that reach exactly zero can never recover under multiplicative updates
• Different initialisations converge to different local solutions, so use restarts
• Convergence is slow compared with alternating least squares or coordinate descent
• Scale ambiguity: W and H can trade a scale factor, so normalise before comparing factors

cards.front: Key formulas: Non-negative Matrix Factorisation
cards.back:
$\min_{W, H \geq 0}\ \frac{1}{2}\|X - WH\|_F^2$
$W \leftarrow W \odot \frac{X H^{\top}}{W H H^{\top}}$
$H \leftarrow H \odot \frac{W^{\top} X}{W^{\top} W H}$
$\odot$ and the fraction are elementwise
$\nabla_W = W H H^{\top} - X H^{\top}$ (positive $-$ negative part)
Loss is non-increasing under the updates

cards.front: What is Feature Scaling?
cards.back: Rescale each feature to a comparable range so distance-based and gradient-based models are not dominated by whichever feature has the largest units. Standard, min-max and robust scalers differ in what they subtract and divide by.

cards.front: Feature Scaling: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Many models implicitly compare features with one shared yardstick: distances add squared differences, and a single learning rate steps every weight. A feature measured in thousands then drowns one measured in fractions. Scaling gives every feature the same units of spread, and the choice of centre and spread decides how outliers behave.

cards.front: Which models need feature scaling?
cards.back: Distance-based (k-NN, k-means, SVM), regularised and gradient-trained models; trees do not, since splits depend only on feature order.

cards.front: Standardisation or min-max?
cards.back: Standardise by default; use min-max when a bounded range is required and outliers are absent, and robust scaling when outliers are present.

cards.front: How does scaling relate to data leakage?
cards.back: The scaler's statistics are learned parameters, so fit them on training data only; fitting on everything lets test rows shape the transform.

cards.front: When should you use Feature Scaling, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: k-NN, k-means, SVM, PCA, regularised linear models and neural networks, and anything optimised with gradient descent.

Avoid it when: Tree-based models (splits are invariant to monotone rescaling) and features already on a meaningful common scale. Do not fit the scaler on test data.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Feature Scaling?
cards.back:
• Fitting on all data before splitting leaks test statistics
• Min-max is dominated by a single outlier, squeezing everything else
• Test values outside the train range land outside the target range
• Scaling a one-hot or sparse matrix by its mean destroys sparsity

cards.front: Key formulas: Feature Scaling
cards.back:
Standard: $z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$
Min-max: $z = \frac{x - \min}{\max - \min}$
Robust: $z = \frac{x - \mathrm{median}}{Q_3 - Q_1}$
Fit statistics on train only, then apply to val/test
Constant column: scale $0 \to 1$, so $z = 0$

cards.front: What is Class Imbalance?
cards.back: When one class is rare, plain training optimises mostly for the common class. Fix it by weighting the loss inversely to class frequency or by resampling the training set, and judge the result with metrics that ignore the base rate.

cards.front: Class Imbalance: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A loss that sums over examples is dominated by the majority class, so a model can look excellent by ignoring the minority. Reweighting says one rare example should count as much as many common ones, and resampling achieves the same by showing the rare ones more often. Neither adds information; they only change what the optimiser cares about.

cards.front: A fraud model has high accuracy but catches no fraud. Why?
cards.back: With a rare positive class, predicting all negatives scores high accuracy; use precision, recall, PR-AUC and a tuned threshold instead.

cards.front: Class weights or resampling?
cards.back: Weights are cheaper and add no duplicates; resampling works with any learner and can be paired with weights or ensembling. Compare them on validation data.

cards.front: How do you evaluate fairly after resampling?
cards.back: Keep validation and test sets at the natural class ratio and resample only the training fold, inside cross-validation.

cards.front: Does rebalancing fix probabilities?
cards.back: No, it distorts them; recalibrate or correct for the prior shift if you need real probabilities.

cards.front: When should you use Class Imbalance, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Fraud, defects, rare diseases and other skewed targets, when recall on the rare class matters and plain accuracy is misleading.

Avoid it when: Skip it when you need calibrated probabilities (reweighting distorts them unless you correct afterwards), or when a threshold change on an unweighted model already gives the trade-off you need.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Class Imbalance?
cards.back:
• Oversampling before the split puts duplicates of the same row in train and test, inflating scores
• Reweighting or resampling shifts predicted probabilities away from true rates
• Duplicated minority rows make flexible models memorise them and overfit
• Accuracy and ROC-AUC can both look fine while minority precision is poor

cards.front: Key formulas: Class Imbalance
cards.back:
Balanced weight: $w^c = \frac{n}{K\,n^c}$
Weighted loss: $L = \frac{\sum_i w_{y_i}\,\ell_i}{\sum_i w_{y_i}}$
Weighted log loss: $\ell_i = -[\,y \log p + (1-y)\log(1-p)\,]$
Oversample: draw $(n_{max} - n^c)$ extra rows of $c$
Do it on the training split only, never before splitting

cards.front: What is Probability Calibration?
cards.back: A model is calibrated when, among predictions of probability $p$, about a fraction $p$ are actually positive. Measure it with a reliability diagram, expected calibration error and the Brier score.

cards.front: Probability Calibration: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Ranking quality and honesty of probabilities are different things: a model can order examples perfectly yet say 99% for things that happen far less often. Bin the predictions, and in each bin compare the average predicted probability with the observed frequency of positives; the gap is the miscalibration, and decisions based on expected cost depend on it.

cards.front: What does it mean for a classifier to be calibrated?
cards.back: Among all cases given probability $p$, the observed positive rate is $p$; the reliability diagram then lies on the diagonal.

cards.front: How is the Brier score related to calibration?
cards.back: It is the squared error of the probabilities and a proper scoring rule, so it improves with better calibration and with sharper, more discriminative predictions.

cards.front: How do you fix a miscalibrated model?
cards.back: Fit a monotone post-hoc map such as Platt scaling, isotonic regression or temperature scaling on held-out data; ranking and AUC stay the same.

cards.front: When should you use Probability Calibration, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Whenever probabilities feed decisions (thresholds, costs, risk scores, ensembles), after training boosted trees, SVMs or networks that tend to be over- or under-confident.

Avoid it when: If only the ranking matters (AUC), calibration adds nothing. Binned ECE is noisy with few samples, so do not over-read a single number.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Probability Calibration?
cards.back:
• Calibrating on the training data, or on the same data used to evaluate it
• ECE depends on the bin count and is noisy in sparsely populated bins
• Isotonic regression can overfit when the calibration set is small
• A calibrated model can still be a poor classifier; check discrimination as well

cards.front: Key formulas: Probability Calibration
cards.back:
Calibrated: $P(y=1 \,|\, \hat{p}=p) = p$
Bin $b$: $\mathrm{acc}_b = \mathrm{mean}(y\ \mathrm{in}\ b),\;\; \mathrm{conf}_b = \mathrm{mean}(\hat{p}\ \mathrm{in}\ b)$
$\mathrm{ECE} = \sum_b \frac{n_b}{n}\,|\mathrm{acc}_b - \mathrm{conf}_b|$
$\mathrm{Brier} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (\hat{p}_i - y_i)^2$
Bins: equal-width on $[0, 1]$, empty skipped

cards.front: What is Grid vs Random Hyperparameter Search?
cards.back: Grid search tries every combination of listed values; random search samples configurations from distributions. Each configuration is scored with validation data and the best one is kept.

cards.front: Grid vs Random Hyperparameter Search: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Usually only a few hyperparameters matter much for a given problem. A grid spends its budget repeating the same few values of the important ones across every setting of the unimportant ones, whereas random sampling tries a fresh value of every parameter on every trial. At equal budget, random search explores the important axes more densely, and it can sample continuous ranges such as a log-uniform learning rate.

cards.front: Why does random search often beat grid search at equal budget?
cards.back: Most parameters barely matter, so a grid repeats the same few values of the important ones, while random trials test a new value of each every time.

cards.front: How should you sample a learning rate?
cards.back: Log-uniformly, because its effect is multiplicative; a linear scale puts nearly all trials at the large end.

cards.front: How do you avoid overfitting the search?
cards.back: Score with cross-validation inside the search, then evaluate the single chosen model once on untouched test data, or use nested cross-validation.

cards.front: When should you use Grid vs Random Hyperparameter Search, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Grid for a few parameters with small discrete choices; random search when there are many parameters, continuous ranges, or a fixed budget.

Avoid it when: Neither uses past results. For expensive models prefer successive halving or Bayesian optimisation, and never pick the model by the same data you report its final score on.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Grid vs Random Hyperparameter Search?
cards.back:
• Grids explode with the number of parameters
• Searching a learning rate on a linear scale wastes most trials
• Reporting the best validation score as the final estimate is optimistic; keep a test set
• This sampler draws with replacement, so repeats can occur; scikit-learn's ParameterSampler gives distinct combinations when every value is a list

cards.front: Key formulas: Grid vs Random Hyperparameter Search
cards.back:
Grid size $= \prod_j |V_j|$ (product over parameters)
Grid order: keys sorted, last key varies fastest
Random trial: $\theta_j \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(V_j)$ or a distribution
Best $\theta^* = \arg\max_\theta\ \mathrm{validation\ score}(\theta)$ over tried $\theta$
Log-uniform: $\log\theta \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(\log a, \log b)$

cards.front: What is Data Leakage?
cards.back: Information from the validation or test data leaks into training, so the measured score looks better than real-world performance.

cards.front: Data Leakage: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Anything computed with the test rows, such as scaling statistics, imputation values, selected features or even a duplicated row, lets the model peek at the answer sheet. The rule is simple: every data-dependent step is part of the model, so fit it on the training fold only and merely apply it to held-out data.

cards.front: Your model scores very well offline but poorly in production. What do you check first?
cards.back: Leakage: preprocessing or feature selection fit on all data, target-derived features, duplicates across splits, or a split that ignores time or groups.

cards.front: How do you prevent preprocessing leakage in cross-validation?
cards.back: Put the transforms and the model in one pipeline so each fold fits the transforms on its own training part only.

cards.front: Is scaling before the split really a problem?
cards.back: It is a mild leak since only means and variances cross over, but selection, imputation and target encoding can leak far more.

cards.front: When should you use Data Leakage, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Audit every pipeline before trusting a metric, especially when the score looks too good, or when preprocessing and feature selection precede the train-test split or cross-validation.

Avoid it when: Not a technique to apply but a failure to avoid. Statistics from the unlabelled target domain are legitimately used in transductive or domain-adaptation setups, if documented as such.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Data Leakage?
cards.back:
• Selecting features with the labels on all data before cross-validation inflates scores even on pure noise
• Random splits of time series let the model train on the future
• Duplicate or near-duplicate rows (or the same user) in both train and test
• Features computed after the outcome, such as a status flag set once the event happens

cards.front: Key formulas: Data Leakage
cards.back:
Correct: $\hat{\theta} = \mathrm{fit}(X_{train}),\;\; Z = \mathrm{transform}(X;\hat{\theta})$
Leaky: $\hat{\theta} = \mathrm{fit}(X_{train} \cup X_{test})$
Standardise: $z = \frac{x - \hat{\mu}}{\hat{\sigma}}$, using train $\hat{\mu}$ and $\hat{\sigma}$ only
Leaky stats shrink the train/test shift: test looks easier

cards.front: What is Multiclass Metrics (Macro, Micro, Weighted F1)?
cards.back: Reduce a $K$-class confusion matrix to per-class precision, recall and F1, then average them three ways. The choice of averaging decides whether rare classes count.

cards.front: Multiclass Metrics (Macro, Micro, Weighted F1): what is the key insight?
cards.back: A single accuracy number hides which classes fail. Per-class F1 exposes that, but you still need one headline score. Macro averaging gives every class equal say, so a failing rare class drags it down; micro averaging pools all decisions, so frequent classes dominate; weighted averaging sits between by weighting each class by its support.

cards.front: When use macro over micro F1?
cards.back: When all classes matter equally, especially with imbalance: macro exposes poor performance on rare classes that micro or accuracy would hide.

cards.front: Why does micro F1 equal accuracy in multiclass?
cards.back: Each misclassification is exactly one false positive for the predicted class and one false negative for the true class, so pooled precision and recall both equal the fraction correct.

cards.front: What does weighted F1 do?
cards.back: It averages per-class F1 with weights proportional to class support, so it tracks frequent classes but still reflects per-class balance of precision and recall.

cards.front: How do you handle a class that is never predicted?
cards.back: Its precision is undefined; set it to zero (zero_division) so its F1 is zero, and flag it explicitly in the report.

cards.front: When should you use Multiclass Metrics (Macro, Micro, Weighted F1), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Reporting multiclass classifiers, choosing the average to match the business goal (macro when every class matters, micro or accuracy when overall hit rate matters, weighted for a support-aware compromise), and diagnosing which class pairs get confused.

Avoid it when: When costs differ strongly between error types (use a cost matrix or per-class thresholds), for multilabel problems without adapting the counts, or when probability quality matters (use log loss or calibration instead of a hard-label metric).

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Multiclass Metrics (Macro, Micro, Weighted F1)?
cards.back:
• Labels must be integers 0 to $K-1$ here; map strings first
• Micro F1 equals accuracy for single-label problems, so it adds nothing beyond accuracy
• Macro F1 swings on tiny classes with few support samples, so report supports too
• A class missing from the true labels gives a zero F1 that still enters the macro mean in this code (sklearn behaves the same only if its labels are listed)

cards.front: Key formulas: Multiclass Metrics (Macro, Micro, Weighted F1)
cards.back:
Confusion: $C[i,j]$ = \# true class $i$ predicted as $j$
$TP_k = C[k,k],\ \mathrm{pred}_k = \sum_i C[i,k],\ \mathrm{supp}_k = \sum_j C[k,j]$
$\mathrm{Precision}_k = \frac{TP_k}{\mathrm{predicted}_k},\;\; \mathrm{Recall}_k = \frac{TP_k}{\mathrm{support}_k}$
$F1_k = \frac{2\,P_k R_k}{P_k + R_k}$
Macro: $F1_{macro} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_k F1_k$
Weighted: $\frac{\sum_k \mathrm{support}_k\,F1_k}{\sum_k \mathrm{support}_k}$
Micro: $F1_{micro} = \frac{\sum_k TP_k}{n} = \mathrm{accuracy}$

cards.front: What is A/B Test Significance (Two-Proportion z-Test)?
cards.back: Decide whether two conversion rates differ by more than chance with a pooled two-proportion z-test, and plan how many users each arm needs before the experiment starts.

cards.front: A/B Test Significance (Two-Proportion z-Test): what is the key insight?
cards.back: Under the null hypothesis both arms share one true rate, so the observed gap is just sampling noise whose size is known from the binomial variance. Dividing the gap by that noise gives a $z$-score that says how many standard errors apart the arms are. Sample size works the other way round: the smaller the effect you want to detect, the more users you need, growing with the inverse square of that effect.

cards.front: What does a $p$-value mean in an A/B test?
cards.back: It is the probability of seeing a difference at least this large if the two arms truly had the same rate; it is not the probability that the treatment is better.

cards.front: Why pool the rates for the test statistic?
cards.back: The null hypothesis says there is one common rate, so the pooled estimate is the best variance estimate under that null; the confidence interval uses unpooled variances because it describes the actual difference.

cards.front: What happens if you peek at the results every day?
cards.back: Each look is another chance for a spurious significant result, so the overall false-positive rate rises well above $\alpha$; use a fixed horizon or a sequential or alpha-spending design.

cards.front: How does sample size scale with effect size?
cards.back: Inversely with the square of the minimum detectable effect, so detecting half the effect needs about four times as many users.

cards.front: When should you use A/B Test Significance (Two-Proportion z-Test), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Comparing binary outcomes such as clicks or conversions between a control and a treatment with independent users, enough successes and failures in each arm, and a fixed analysis time decided in advance.

Avoid it when: Small counts (use Fisher's exact test), continuous metrics (use a t-test or bootstrap), repeated peeking at results without a sequential method, or users that are not independent (clustering, network effects).

cards.front: Common pitfalls of A/B Test Significance (Two-Proportion z-Test)?
cards.back:
• Peeking and stopping when $p$ dips below $\alpha$ inflates false positives; fix the sample size or use sequential tests
• The normal approximation needs enough successes and failures in each arm
• Testing many metrics or variants without correction raises the chance of a false win
• The constants 1.96 and 0.84 are rounded critical values for $\alpha=0.05$ two-sided and 80% power; pass other values for other settings, and check the interval for practical size, not just significance

cards.front: Key formulas: A/B Test Significance (Two-Proportion z-Test)
cards.back:
$\hat{p}_1 = \frac{x_1}{n_1},\;\; \hat{p}_2 = \frac{x_2}{n_2},\;\; \hat{p} = \frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2}$
Null SE: $\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}$
$z = \frac{\hat{p}_2 - \hat{p}_1}{\mathrm{SE}_{null}}$
Two-sided p-value: $p = 2(1 - \Phi(|z|)) = \mathrm{erfc}(|z|/\sqrt{2})$
CI: $(\hat{p}_2-\hat{p}_1) \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}$
$n = \frac{(z_{\alpha/2}+z_\beta)^2\,[p_1(1-p_1)+p_2(1-p_2)]}{\delta^2}$ per arm
$\delta = p_2 - p_1$ is the minimum detectable effect

cards.front: What is Silhouette, ARI and NMI?
cards.back: Three ways to score a clustering. The silhouette needs only the data and the labels and measures cohesion against separation; the adjusted Rand index and normalised mutual information compare two labelings, for example clusters against ground truth.

cards.front: Silhouette, ARI and NMI: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Cluster labels are arbitrary names, so a good score must not depend on which number is called which. The silhouette asks whether each point is closer to its own cluster than to the next one; ARI and NMI ask whether two labelings group the same pairs together, after subtracting what random labelings would score by chance (ARI) or normalising the shared information (NMI).

cards.front: How do you read a silhouette value?
cards.back: Near +1 the point is far from other clusters and close to its own, near 0 it sits between two clusters, and negative values suggest it was assigned to the wrong cluster.

cards.front: Why use ARI instead of the plain Rand index?
cards.back: The Rand index is high even for random labelings when there are many clusters; ARI subtracts the expected chance agreement so random labelings score near zero.

cards.front: How is NMI different from accuracy for clustering?
cards.back: NMI does not need cluster ids to match class ids; it measures shared information between the two partitions, so permuting cluster names leaves it unchanged.

cards.front: When should you use Silhouette, ARI and NMI, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Silhouette to compare values of k or algorithms without labels, ARI and NMI when reference classes exist, and benchmarking clustering methods on labelled datasets.

Avoid it when: Skip silhouette for non-convex clusters such as rings, where it favours convex shapes; NMI is biased toward many clusters unless adjusted, and none of these show whether clusters are useful for your task.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Silhouette, ARI and NMI?
cards.back:
• Silhouette is undefined for a single cluster and this code assumes at least two
• Silhouette prefers convex, evenly dense clusters and can rank a poor k-means above a correct density clustering
• NMI (unadjusted) tends to rise as the number of clusters grows
• ARI and NMI assume the ground-truth classes are the right notion of cluster

cards.front: Key formulas: Silhouette, ARI and NMI
cards.back:
$a_i$ = mean distance to other points in $i$'s cluster
$b_i$ = smallest mean distance from $i$ to a cluster
$s_i = \frac{b_i - a_i}{\max(a_i, b_i)},\;\; \mathrm{score} = \mathrm{mean}$ of $s_i$
$n_{ij}$ = #points in cluster $i$ of $U$, $j$ of $V$
$\mathrm{ARI} = \frac{\sum \binom{n_{ij}}{2} - E}{\frac{1}{2}\left[\sum \binom{a_i}{2} + \sum \binom{b_j}{2}\right] - E}$
$E = \frac{\sum \binom{a_i}{2} \cdot \sum \binom{b_j}{2}}{\binom{n}{2}}$
$\mathrm{MI} = \sum p_{ij}\log\frac{p_{ij}}{p_i\,p_j},\;\; \mathrm{NMI} = \frac{\mathrm{MI}}{(H(U) + H(V))/2}$

cards.front: What is Isotonic Regression (PAVA)?
cards.back: Fit the non-decreasing step function closest to the targets in least squares. The pool-adjacent-violators algorithm scans left to right and averages neighbouring blocks whenever the order is violated.

cards.front: Isotonic Regression (PAVA): what is the key insight?
cards.back: If two neighbouring values break the required order, the best you can do for both is to replace them with their weighted average, since any other common value is worse. Pooling can create a new violation with the block before it, so keep merging backwards until the sequence is ordered.

cards.front: What does the pool-adjacent-violators step do?
cards.back: When two adjacent fitted values are out of order it replaces them with their weighted average, and keeps merging backwards while order is violated.

cards.front: Why use isotonic regression for calibration?
cards.back: It learns any monotone map from scores to probabilities without a parametric form, correcting miscalibration while keeping the ranking of predictions.

cards.front: Is the PAVA solution optimal?
cards.back: Yes. Least squares isotonic regression is a convex projection with a unique minimiser, and PAVA finds it exactly in one pass.

cards.front: When should you use Isotonic Regression (PAVA), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Calibrating classifier probabilities with a monotone map, dose-response and other curves known to be monotone, and a nonparametric fit without choosing a smoothing parameter.

Avoid it when: Skip it with little data for calibration, where it overfits into steps (Platt scaling is smoother), when the relation is not monotone, or when you need a smooth curve with derivatives.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Isotonic Regression (PAVA)?
cards.back:
• Produces flat steps and can overfit when calibration data is small
• Predictions at new $x$ need interpolation between block values, usually linear
• Tied $x$ values must be pooled first, since the order among ties is arbitrary
• A single outlier at an end can drag a long block to a poor value

cards.front: Key formulas: Isotonic Regression (PAVA)
cards.back:
$\min_{f_1 \leq f_2 \leq \cdots \leq f_n} \sum_i w_i (y_i - f_i)^2$
Pool $B$ = block, value $m(B) = \frac{\sum_{i \in B} w_i y_i}{\sum_{i \in B} w_i}$
Violation: $m(B_{prev}) > m(B_{last})\;\Rightarrow$ merge
Merged weight $W = W_1 + W_2$
Merged value $m = \frac{W_1 m_1 + W_2 m_2}{W_1 + W_2}$
Fitted $f_i = m(\mathrm{block\ containing}\ i)$

cards.front: What is Exponential Smoothing (Simple and Holt)?
cards.back: Forecast a series with a running level (and optionally a trend) that is nudged toward each new observation by a smoothing weight. Simple smoothing gives a flat forecast; Holt's method adds a linear trend.

cards.front: Exponential Smoothing (Simple and Holt): what is the key insight?
cards.back: The newest observation is the best clue about where the series is now, but a single value is noisy. Blending it with the previous estimate gives weights on past values that decay geometrically, so recent data matters most and old data fades without being stored.

cards.front: Why is it called exponential smoothing?
cards.back: Unrolling the recursion gives each past observation a weight that shrinks by a constant factor $(1-\alpha)$ per step back, an exponential decay that sums to one.

cards.front: What do $\alpha$ near $0$ and $\alpha$ near $1$ mean?
cards.back: $\alpha$ near $1$ trusts the latest value and nearly copies it forward, a naive forecast; $\alpha$ near $0$ keeps the initial level almost unchanged, close to a long-run average.

cards.front: Why does simple smoothing fail on trending data?
cards.back: Its forecast is a weighted average of past values, so it always lags behind a rising or falling series; Holt's slope term removes that lag.

cards.front: When should you use Exponential Smoothing (Simple and Holt), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Short-horizon forecasts of many series, a cheap and strong baseline, demand or traffic with slowly drifting level, and online updating where only the last state is kept.

Avoid it when: Skip it when the series has seasonality you have not modelled (use Holt-Winters), when you need prediction intervals from a fitted likelihood, or when external regressors drive the series.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Exponential Smoothing (Simple and Holt)?
cards.back:
• Undamped Holt trends extrapolate forever and overshoot at long horizons
• A high $\alpha$ on a noisy series chases noise; the fitted values lag turning points when $\alpha$ is small
• The start state matters for short series, so conventions differ between libraries
• Pick $\alpha$ and $\beta$ by one-step error on held-out data, not by eye

cards.front: Key formulas: Exponential Smoothing (Simple and Holt)
cards.back:
Simple: $\ell_t = \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha)\ell_{t-1},\;\; \hat{y}_{t+1|t} = \ell_t$
Unrolled: $\ell_t = \sum_k \alpha(1-\alpha)^k y_{t-k} + (1-\alpha)^t \ell_0$
Holt level: $\ell_t = \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1})$
Holt trend: $b_t = \beta(\ell_t - \ell_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)b_{t-1}$
Forecast: $\hat{y}_{t+h|t} = \ell_t + h\,b_t$
Fit: minimise $\sum_t (y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1})^2$ over $\alpha, \beta$ (and $\ell_0, b_0$)

cards.front: What is Autocorrelation (ACF and PACF)?
cards.back: The ACF is the correlation of a series with a lagged copy of itself. The PACF is the correlation at each lag after removing the effect of the shorter lags, computed from the ACF with the Durbin-Levinson recursion.

cards.front: Autocorrelation (ACF and PACF): what is the key insight?
cards.back: If today resembles yesterday, the lag-1 correlation is high, but it also makes today resemble two days ago through yesterday. The ACF mixes direct and relayed dependence; the PACF strips the relayed part, so an AR($p$) process shows a PACF that cuts off after lag $p$ while its ACF decays.

cards.front: How do ACF and PACF identify an AR or MA model?
cards.back: An AR($p$) has a PACF that cuts off after lag $p$ and an ACF that decays; an MA($q$) has an ACF that cuts off after lag $q$ and a PACF that decays.

cards.front: What does the PACF at lag $k$ measure?
cards.back: The correlation between $y_t$ and $y_{t-k}$ after linearly removing the effect of the lags in between, equal to the last coefficient of an order-$k$ autoregression.

cards.front: Why divide by $n$ and not $n-k$ in the autocovariance?
cards.back: Dividing by $n$ guarantees the estimated autocovariance sequence is positive semi-definite, which the Yule-Walker system needs; $n-k$ is less biased but can give invalid values.

cards.front: When should you use Autocorrelation (ACF and PACF), and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Choosing AR and MA orders for ARIMA, spotting seasonality and trend from slowly decaying or periodic spikes, and checking that model residuals look like white noise.

Avoid it when: Skip it on non-stationary data without differencing first, for strongly nonlinear dependence that correlation misses, and for very short series where lag estimates are too noisy.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Autocorrelation (ACF and PACF)?
cards.back:
• Trending series give an ACF that decays very slowly and hides the real structure; difference first
• Many lags are tested at once, so a few spikes outside the band are expected by chance
• Seasonal data needs a lag at the season length, not just short lags
• Different libraries estimate the PACF differently (Yule-Walker, OLS, Burg), so small numeric differences are normal

cards.front: Key formulas: Autocorrelation (ACF and PACF)
cards.back:
Autocovariance: $c_k = \frac{1}{n}\sum_t (y_t - \bar{y})(y_{t+k} - \bar{y})$
ACF: $\rho_k = \frac{c_k}{c_0}$
Yule-Walker: $\rho_j = \sum_i \phi_{ki}\,\rho_{|j-i|}$ for $j = 1..k$
PACF: $\alpha_k = \phi_{kk}$ (last coefficient of the order-$k$ fit)
$\phi_{kk} = \frac{\rho_k - \sum_j \phi_{k-1,j}\,\rho_{k-j}}{1 - \sum_j \phi_{k-1,j}\,\rho_j}$
$\phi_{kj} = \phi_{k-1,j} - \phi_{kk}\,\phi_{k-1,k-j}$ for $j < k$
Approximate 95% band: $\pm\,\frac{1.96}{\sqrt{n}}$

cards.front: What is ARIMA Forecasting?
cards.back: Difference the series until it is roughly stationary, regress it on its own recent values, forecast the differenced series forward, and sum the forecasts back to the original scale. This card implements the AR part with d differences, ARIMA(p, d, 0).

cards.front: ARIMA Forecasting: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Many series wander, so their level is unpredictable, but the changes between steps are stable and depend on recent changes. Differencing turns the wandering series into a steadier one that a plain regression on lagged values can model, and summing the predicted changes brings the forecast back to the original level.

cards.front: What do p, d and q stand for?
cards.back: p is the number of lagged values in the autoregression, d the number of differences to make the series stationary, q the number of lagged forecast errors in the moving-average part.

cards.front: How do you choose d?
cards.back: Difference until a plot and the ACF look stationary, typically once or twice; stationarity tests such as ADF help, but over-differencing hurts.

cards.front: Why do ARIMA forecasts get flat at long horizons?
cards.back: Future values are fed back as inputs, so shocks average out and the forecast converges to the mean of the differenced series, which becomes a straight drift line once integrated.

cards.front: When should you use ARIMA Forecasting, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Univariate forecasting of autocorrelated series with trend that differencing removes, a transparent baseline to beat with machine learning models, and when ACF and PACF plots suggest low orders.

Avoid it when: Skip it for series with strong seasonality unless you add seasonal terms, for many exogenous drivers, for nonlinear dynamics, and for long horizons where forecasts collapse to a constant or a line.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of ARIMA Forecasting?
cards.back:
• Over-differencing adds negative autocorrelation and inflates forecast variance
• This is conditional least squares; libraries that fit exact likelihood or MA terms give slightly different estimates
• Point forecasts of a stationary part revert to the mean, so long horizons look flat
• Judge models on a rolling-origin hold-out, never on in-sample fit

cards.front: Key formulas: ARIMA Forecasting
cards.back:
Difference: $\nabla y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}$, apply $d$ times to get $z_t$
AR($p$): $z_t = c + \phi_1 z_{t-1} + \ldots + \phi_p z_{t-p} + \varepsilon_t$
LS: $\hat{\beta} = \arg\min \sum_t (z_t - X_t\beta)^2,\ \beta = (c, \phi_{1..p})$
Forecast: $\hat{z}_{t+1} = c + \sum_i \phi_i\,\hat{z}_{t+1-i}$ (reuse forecasts)
Integrate ($d=1$): $\hat{y}_{t+h} = y_t + \sum_j \hat{z}_{t+j}$
Add MA terms: $z_t = \ldots + \theta_1 \varepsilon_{t-1} + \ldots + \theta_q \varepsilon_{t-q}$

cards.front: What is Beam Search Decoding?
cards.back: Generate a sequence by keeping the $B$ highest-scoring partial sequences at every step instead of committing to a single best token.

cards.front: Beam Search Decoding: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Greedy decoding can take a locally best token that leads to a poor continuation, while checking every sequence is exponential. Beam search is the compromise: a small frontier of the best prefixes is extended and pruned each step, so a good path that starts with a second-best token can still survive.

cards.front: Is beam search optimal?
cards.back: No. It only keeps $B$ prefixes, so the best full sequence can be pruned early. It is exact only when $B$ covers all prefixes.

cards.front: What are greedy and exhaustive search as special cases?
cards.back: Beam width one is greedy. A width that never prunes is exhaustive search over all sequences.

cards.front: Why use log-probabilities?
cards.back: Products of many probabilities underflow, and sums of logs are numerically stable and additive over steps.

cards.front: When should you use Beam Search Decoding, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Machine translation, summarisation and speech recognition, where the single most probable output is wanted and the model is well calibrated.

Avoid it when: Open-ended generation, where beam search tends to give repetitive, generic text; sampling is preferred there. It also gives no guarantee of finding the true best sequence.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Beam Search Decoding?
cards.back:
• Raw summed log-probability prefers short sequences; normalise or add a length penalty
• This sketch decodes a fixed length and has no end-of-sequence token, which real decoders need
• Beams often collapse to near-identical outputs; diverse beam search addresses this
• A wider beam can lower quality in generation even though it raises model probability

cards.front: Key formulas: Beam Search Decoding
cards.back:
$\mathrm{Score}(y_1..y_T) = \sum_t \log p(y_t \,|\, y_1..y_{t-1})$
Beams at step $t$: top $B$ of $(y, y{+}w)$ pairs
Candidates per step: $B \cdot |V|$
$B = 1$ gives greedy decoding
$B \geq |V|^T$ keeps every prefix: exact search

cards.front: What is Additive (Bahdanau) Attention?
cards.back: Score each encoder state against the current decoder state with a small one-hidden-layer network, softmax the scores, and return the weighted sum of encoder states as the context vector.

cards.front: Additive (Bahdanau) Attention: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A sequence-to-sequence decoder that sees only one fixed summary of the source must squeeze a whole sentence into one vector. Additive attention lets the decoder look back at every encoder state at each step and decide which ones matter now. The relevance score comes from a learned tanh network over both vectors, so the two sides need not have the same size.

cards.front: Why is it called additive attention?
cards.back: The query and key projections are added before the tanh and scoring vector, unlike the multiplicative dot-product form.

cards.front: What problem does attention solve in seq2seq?
cards.back: It removes the fixed-size bottleneck by letting the decoder read all encoder states with a different weighting at each output step.

cards.front: How does it differ from scaled dot-product attention?
cards.back: It uses a learned one-hidden-layer scorer and works with different query and key sizes; dot-product is cheaper and parallelises but needs matching dimensions or a projection.

cards.front: What are the shapes of the attention weights and context?
cards.back: One weight per source position $(T,)$ and a context vector of the encoder width $d_h$.

cards.front: When should you use Additive (Bahdanau) Attention, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: RNN encoder-decoder models for translation, summarisation or speech, and whenever query and key have different dimensions or you need a small, parametrised scorer.

Avoid it when: Large transformer-style models where scaled dot-product attention is faster because it is a single matrix multiplication and parallelises well over positions.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Additive (Bahdanau) Attention?
cards.back:
• Padded source positions need masking before the softmax
• Original Bahdanau attention uses the previous decoder state; some variants use the current one
• Costs more than dot-product attention since scoring has its own hidden layer
• This sketch is one query and has no mask, bias or batching

cards.front: Key formulas: Additive (Bahdanau) Attention
cards.back:
$e_t = v^{\top}\tanh(W_s s + W_h h_t)\;\; (t = 1 \ldots T)$
$\alpha_t = \frac{\exp(e_t)}{\sum_j \exp(e_j)}$
$c = \sum_t \alpha_t h_t$
$s \in \mathbb{R}^{d_s},\ h_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h},\ W_s \in \mathbb{R}^{d_s \times d_a},\ W_h \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h \times d_a}$
Decoder update: $s' = \mathrm{RNN}(s, [y_{prev}\,;\,c])$

cards.front: What is IoU and Non-Maximum Suppression?
cards.back: Intersection-over-union measures how much two boxes overlap, and non-maximum suppression uses it to keep one box per object out of many overlapping detections.

cards.front: IoU and Non-Maximum Suppression: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A detector fires many boxes around the same object. Taking the most confident box and discarding every other box that overlaps it too much removes the duplicates, and repeating on the remainder leaves roughly one box per object. IoU is the yardstick for "overlaps too much" and is scale-free because it divides by the union.

cards.front: Why is IoU better than comparing coordinates?
cards.back: It is a single scale-free number that reflects overlap in area, whereas coordinate errors depend on box size.

cards.front: What problem does NMS solve and what is its weakness?
cards.back: It removes duplicate detections of one object, but it can also delete true detections of objects that overlap heavily.

cards.front: How does IoU relate to detection metrics?
cards.back: A predicted box counts as a true positive when its IoU with a ground-truth box exceeds a threshold, which then feeds precision, recall and mean average precision.

cards.front: When should you use IoU and Non-Maximum Suppression, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Post-processing the raw output of detectors such as YOLO and Faster R-CNN, and evaluating detections by matching boxes at an IoU threshold.

Avoid it when: Greedy NMS removes true objects that really overlap heavily, such as people in a crowd. Use Soft-NMS or learned set-based detectors in that case. IoU is also zero for any two disjoint boxes, so it gives no gradient there.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of IoU and Non-Maximum Suppression?
cards.back:
• Run NMS per class, otherwise a box can suppress a different class's box
• Degenerate boxes with zero area give 0/0 here; filter them first
• A low threshold removes real neighbouring objects, a high one keeps duplicates
• Greedy NMS depends on score order, so poorly calibrated scores hurt it

cards.front: Key formulas: IoU and Non-Maximum Suppression
cards.back:
Boxes as $(x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2)$, with $x_2 > x_1$ and $y_2 > y_1$
$\mathrm{inter} = \max(0, \min x_2 - \max x_1)\cdot\max(0, \min y_2 - \max y_1)$
$\mathrm{area}(A) = (x_2 - x_1)(y_2 - y_1)$
$\mathrm{union} = \mathrm{area}(A) + \mathrm{area}(B) - \mathrm{inter}$
$\mathrm{IoU}(A, B) = \frac{\mathrm{inter}}{\mathrm{union}}$
NMS: keep best box $i$, drop $j$ with $\mathrm{IoU}(i,j) > \mathrm{thr}$

cards.front: What is Receptive Field?
cards.back: The receptive field of a unit is the patch of the input that can influence its value. It grows layer by layer, and strides make it grow faster.

cards.front: Receptive Field: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Each layer looks at a $k$-wide window of the previous layer, but one step in a deeper layer already spans several input pixels. Every new kernel therefore adds $(k - 1)$ steps of the current spacing between neighbouring units, and strides multiply that spacing. This is why a stack of small kernels can see a large region, and why a unit can only reason about context inside its own receptive field.

cards.front: How does the receptive field grow with depth?
cards.back: Each layer adds $(k - 1)$ times the product of earlier strides, so it grows linearly with depth at stride 1 and much faster once strides or pooling are used.

cards.front: What is the effective receptive field?
cards.back: The region that actually carries significant gradient; it is roughly Gaussian and smaller than the theoretical field.

cards.front: How can you enlarge the field without more parameters?
cards.back: Use strides, pooling or dilated convolutions, which spread the same kernel weights over a wider window.

cards.front: When should you use Receptive Field, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Designing a conv backbone so the final features can see enough context for the task (segmentation, detection), or debugging why a model misses large objects.

Avoid it when: This theoretical field ignores how much each pixel actually matters. Actual influence is concentrated near the centre, so for what the network uses, measure gradients instead. It also does not describe attention layers, whose field is global.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Receptive Field?
cards.back:
• The theoretical field is much larger than the effective field that actually influences the output
• This code assumes no dilation and no padding offsets; dilation replaces $k$ by an effective kernel size
• Forgetting that strides multiply across layers underestimates growth
• Pooling layers count as layers with their own kernel and stride

cards.front: Key formulas: Receptive Field
cards.back:
$k_l$: kernel size, $s_l$: stride of layer $l$ (dilation 1)
Jump: $j_0 = 1,\;\; j_l = j_{l-1}\cdot s_l$
Field: $r_0 = 1,\;\; r_l = r_{l-1} + (k_l - 1)\cdot j_{l-1}$
Output $i$ maps to input $[lo, hi]$, $lo = i \cdot \mathrm{jump}$
Backwards: $lo \leftarrow lo\,s,\;\; hi \leftarrow hi\,s + k - 1$
Padding shifts the interval, not its width

cards.front: What is Depthwise Separable Convolution?
cards.back: Split a standard convolution into a per-channel spatial filter (depthwise) followed by a 1×1 convolution that mixes channels (pointwise).

cards.front: Depthwise Separable Convolution: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A standard convolution does two jobs at once: it looks at spatial neighbourhoods and it mixes channels, with a separate weight for every pair. Factoring these apart gives each channel its own small spatial filter, then mixes channels per pixel. The product of two cheap steps approximates the expensive joint one, and the saving grows with the number of channels and the kernel area.

cards.front: How does a depthwise separable convolution save parameters?
cards.back: It uses $C \cdot k^2$ spatial weights plus $F \cdot C$ mixing weights instead of $F \cdot C \cdot k^2$ for the full kernel.

cards.front: What does the depthwise step do?
cards.back: It filters each input channel independently with its own spatial kernel, so it mixes no information across channels.

cards.front: What does the pointwise step do?
cards.back: A 1×1 convolution that linearly combines channels at every position, producing the output channels.

cards.front: When should you use Depthwise Separable Convolution, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Mobile and edge models (MobileNet, Xception, EfficientNet) where parameters and compute are limited.

Avoid it when: When compute is plentiful and accuracy matters most; the factorised layer is less expressive and depthwise operations can run inefficiently on some hardware despite fewer operations.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Depthwise Separable Convolution?
cards.back:
• Fewer multiply-adds do not always mean faster inference; memory-bound depthwise kernels can be slow
• Normalisation and a nonlinearity between the two steps matter in real blocks; this sketch has none
• Biases are omitted in this sketch
• Compare parameter counts with equal accuracy, not with equal width

cards.front: Key formulas: Depthwise Separable Convolution
cards.back:
$m[n,c,i,j] = \sum_{u,v} d[c,u,v]\cdot x[n,c,si+u,sj+v]$
Pointwise: $\mathrm{out}[n,f,i,j] = \sum_c p[f,c]\cdot m[n,c,i,j]$
Params: standard $F C k^2$;  separable $C k^2 + F C$
Cost ratio (params): $\frac{1}{F} + \frac{1}{k^2}$

cards.front: What is Transposed Convolution?
cards.back: A learned upsampling layer: each input value paints a scaled copy of the kernel onto a larger output, and overlapping copies add up.

cards.front: Transposed Convolution: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A normal strided convolution shrinks a map by reading windows; the transposed one runs the same wiring backwards, so a small map grows. Instead of gathering a patch into one number, every input pixel scatters its value times the kernel into the output at stride spacing. Where those stamps overlap they sum, which is why mismatched kernel and stride produce a checkerboard pattern.

cards.front: What is the output size of a transposed convolution?
cards.back: $(H-1)\cdot s-2p+k$ along each spatial dimension, plus any output padding.

cards.front: Why is it called transposed?
cards.back: Its forward pass multiplies by the transpose of the matrix that represents the corresponding convolution.

cards.front: Why do checkerboard artefacts appear?
cards.back: Stamps from neighbouring inputs overlap unevenly when the kernel size is not a multiple of the stride.

cards.front: When should you use Transposed Convolution, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Decoders of segmentation networks, autoencoders and GAN generators that must produce a higher resolution map from a coarse one.

Avoid it when: When checkerboard artefacts matter, resize with fixed interpolation and then apply a normal convolution, or choose a kernel size divisible by the stride.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Transposed Convolution?
cards.back:
• Kernel size not divisible by stride gives uneven overlap and checkerboard artefacts
• Called deconvolution, but it does not invert a convolution's values, only its shape
• Dilation and output padding are not modelled in this sketch
• The same output size can come from several input sizes of a strided convolution

cards.front: Key formulas: Transposed Convolution
cards.back:
Input $x$: $(N, C, H, W)$; kernel $w$: $(C, F, kH, kW)$
$\mathrm{full}[n,f,si{+}u,sj{+}v]\ {+}{=}\ \sum_c w[c,f,u,v]\,x[n,c,i,j]$
Full size: $(H - 1)\cdot s + kH$ (same for width)
Output size: $(H - 1)\cdot s - 2p + kH$
Padding $p$ crops $p$ entries per border of full map

cards.front: What is Detection Mean Average Precision?
cards.back: Rank detections by confidence, mark each as a true or false positive by IoU matching, and take the area under the precision-recall curve per class, then average over classes.

cards.front: Detection Mean Average Precision: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A detector must both find objects and rank its confident boxes above its doubtful ones, so a single threshold hides too much. Sweeping the confidence threshold traces a precision-recall curve, and its area (AP) rewards detectors that keep precision high as recall grows. Matching uses IoU, so a box counts only if it overlaps a ground-truth box enough, and each ground-truth box can be claimed only once.

cards.front: What does a detection need to count as a true positive?
cards.back: Same class, IoU with an unmatched ground-truth box at or above the threshold; extra boxes on an already matched object are false positives.

cards.front: Why take the monotone envelope of precision?
cards.back: It replaces each precision with the best precision at that recall or higher, removing the zig-zag so AP is the area under a non-increasing curve.

cards.front: How does AP50 differ from COCO mAP?
cards.back: AP50 uses a single IoU threshold of $0.5$; COCO mAP averages over IoU thresholds $0.50$ to $0.95$ and also uses 101-point recall interpolation.

cards.front: Why must you sort detections by score first?
cards.back: The curve is built by lowering the confidence threshold, so confident detections must be matched first and claim ground truths before weaker ones.

cards.front: When should you use Detection Mean Average Precision, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Comparing object detectors and instance segmenters on a labelled benchmark (VOC, COCO), tuning NMS or score thresholds, and tracking detection quality across releases.

Avoid it when: Deployment decisions at one fixed operating point (use precision, recall or F1 at that threshold), or tasks without boxes, and when localisation quality at strict IoU matters more than one threshold shows.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Detection Mean Average Precision?
cards.back:
• Conventions differ: VOC07 uses 11 points, VOC10+ all points, COCO 101 points and averaged IoUs
• Detections must be matched within the same image and class only
• Unsorted detections, or unfiltered duplicates, change the result
• No crowd or ignore regions, area ranges or maximum-detection caps in this sketch

cards.front: Key formulas: Detection Mean Average Precision
cards.back:
$\mathrm{IoU}(a,b) = \frac{|a \cap b|}{|a \cup b|}$;  TP if $\mathrm{IoU} \geq t$ and GT unmatched
Sort by score; $TP_k, FP_k$ = cumulative counts at $k$
$\mathrm{Recall}_k = \frac{TP_k}{\#\mathrm{GT}},\;\; \mathrm{Precision}_k = \frac{TP_k}{TP_k + FP_k}$
$p_{interp}(r) = \max_{r' \geq r}\ \mathrm{precision}(r')$
$AP = \sum_k (R_k - R_{k-1})\cdot p_{interp}(R_k),\;\; R_0 = 0$
$\mathrm{mAP} = \frac{1}{C}\sum_c AP_c$; COCO: IoU 0.50 to 0.95

cards.front: What is Tabular Q-Learning?
cards.back: Learn the value of every state-action pair from experience by nudging each estimate toward the reward plus the discounted best value of the next state.

cards.front: Tabular Q-Learning: what is the key insight?
cards.back: $Q(s, a)$ should equal the reward you get now plus the value of playing optimally afterwards. Each step turns that definition into an update: compare the current estimate with reward plus discounted best next value, and move a little toward it. Because the target uses the max, the agent learns the optimal policy even while it explores randomly.

cards.front: Why is Q-learning off-policy?
cards.back: The target uses the max over next actions, the greedy policy, no matter which action the exploring behaviour policy actually took.

cards.front: How does Q-learning differ from SARSA?
cards.back: SARSA bootstraps from the action actually taken next, so it learns the value of the exploring policy. Q-learning bootstraps from the max, learning the optimal value.

cards.front: What is the exploration-exploitation trade-off?
cards.back: The agent must try uncertain actions to find better ones but also use what it knows. $\epsilon$-greedy mixes the two with a random-action probability.

cards.front: When should you use Tabular Q-Learning, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Small discrete state and action spaces, such as grids and toy control tasks, or as the conceptual base of DQN.

Avoid it when: Large or continuous state spaces, where a table is infeasible and function approximation can make updates unstable. Also not when transitions are costly to sample and a model is available.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Tabular Q-Learning?
cards.back:
• Terminal states must have value zero; here their rows stay zero because they are never updated
• The environment is deterministic here; stochastic transitions need decaying step sizes
• Starting each episode from a random state is a simplification that aids exploration of all pairs
• Max over noisy estimates is biased upward (overestimation); Double Q-learning corrects it

cards.front: Key formulas: Tabular Q-Learning
cards.back:
Bellman optimality: $Q^*(s,a) = r + \gamma\,\max_{a'} Q^*(s',a')$
TD target: $y = r + \gamma\,\max_{a'} Q(s',a')$
TD error: $\delta = y - Q(s,a)$
Update: $Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha\,\delta$
Behaviour: $\epsilon$-greedy, random action w.p. $\epsilon$
Policy: $\pi(s) = \arg\max_a Q(s,a)$

cards.front: What is REINFORCE Policy Gradient?
cards.back: Improve a stochastic policy directly by raising the log-probability of actions in proportion to the return that followed them.

cards.front: REINFORCE Policy Gradient: what is the key insight?
cards.back: You cannot differentiate through the environment, but you can differentiate the probability your policy gave to the actions it took. Scaling that gradient by the return makes good trajectories more likely and bad ones less likely. Subtracting a baseline leaves the expected direction unchanged but cuts the noise.

cards.front: What is the log-derivative trick?
cards.back: $\nabla p = p\,\nabla \log p$, which rewrites the gradient of an expectation as an expectation of a score-function term that can be sampled.

cards.front: Why does a baseline not bias the gradient?
cards.back: For a baseline independent of the action, the expectation of baseline times the score function is zero, so only the variance changes.

cards.front: How does REINFORCE relate to actor-critic?
cards.back: Actor-critic replaces the Monte Carlo return with a learned value-based estimate, lowering variance at the cost of some bias.

cards.front: When should you use REINFORCE Policy Gradient, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Problems with continuous or large action spaces and stochastic policies, as the foundation for actor-critic methods and PPO.

Avoid it when: When sample efficiency matters and episodes are costly: the estimates are high variance and need many episodes. Value-based methods are often better for small discrete problems.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of REINFORCE Policy Gradient?
cards.back:
• Gradient variance is high; without a baseline learning is slow and noisy
• This returns the ascent direction; frameworks minimise, so negate it for the loss
• A common implementation omits the $\gamma^t$ factor in the exact gradient, as here
• Updates must use trajectories from the current policy, so data cannot be reused freely

cards.front: Key formulas: REINFORCE Policy Gradient
cards.back:
$J(\theta) = E\left[\sum_t r_t\right]$ over trajectories from $\pi_\theta$
$\nabla J = E\left[\sum_t G_t\,\nabla \log \pi(a_t\,|\,s_t)\right]$
Return: $G_t = r_t + \gamma\,G_{t+1}$
Baseline: $(G_t - b)$ replaces $G_t$; $b \perp a_t$
Softmax policy $z = X\theta$: $\nabla_z \log \pi(a) = \mathrm{onehot}(a) - \pi$
Gradient ascent: $\theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha\,\nabla J$

cards.front: What is Value Iteration?
cards.back: Compute the optimal state values of a known MDP by repeatedly applying the Bellman optimality backup until the values stop changing, then read off the greedy policy.

cards.front: Value Iteration: what is the key insight?
cards.back: If you knew the best achievable future value of every state, the best action in a state would be the one maximising reward now plus discounted value of where it lands. Start with a guess of zero and apply that one-step lookahead everywhere over and over: information about rewards spreads outward one step per sweep until the guess is self-consistent.

cards.front: Why does value iteration converge?
cards.back: The Bellman optimality backup is a $\gamma$-contraction in the max norm, so repeated application converges geometrically to the unique optimal value function.

cards.front: Value iteration versus policy iteration?
cards.back: Policy iteration alternates full policy evaluation with greedy improvement and often needs few outer iterations; value iteration folds one evaluation step and improvement into a single max backup per sweep.

cards.front: How does value iteration relate to Q-learning?
cards.back: Both aim at the fixed point of the Bellman optimality equation; value iteration applies the exact backup with a known model, Q-learning applies it to sampled transitions.

cards.front: How do you get a policy from $V^*$?
cards.back: Pick in each state the action maximising reward plus discounted value of the next state, which is the greedy policy and is optimal.

cards.front: When should you use Value Iteration, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Small known MDPs (gridworlds, inventory, scheduling) where the transition model is available, as the exact reference to check model-free methods like Q-learning, and to teach dynamic programming in RL.

Avoid it when: When the model is unknown (use Q-learning or policy gradients), when the state space is huge or continuous (the sweep touches every state), or when $\gamma$ is close to one and convergence becomes slow.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Value Iteration?
cards.back:
• Needs the full model (next state and reward for every state-action pair); Q-learning does not
• Deterministic transitions only here; a stochastic MDP needs an expectation over next states
• Rows of $Q$ for terminal states are not meaningful; their value is fixed at zero
• The conventions (reward on the transition, terminal value zero) must match the environment, or comparisons with other methods will disagree

cards.front: Key formulas: Value Iteration
cards.back:
Bellman optimality: $V^*(s) = \max_a\,[\,r(s,a) + \gamma\,V^*(s')\,]$
$s'$ = next state; stochastic: $\sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a)[\ldots]$
$Q_k(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma V_k(s'),\; V_{k+1}(s) = \max_a Q_k(s,a)$
Terminal states: $V(s) = 0$
Contraction: $\|V_{k+1} - V^*\|_\infty \leq \gamma\,\|V_k - V^*\|_\infty$
Policy: $\pi(s) = \arg\max_a\,[\,r(s,a) + \gamma\,V^*(s')\,]$

cards.front: What is PPO Clipped Objective?
cards.back: Improve a policy with several gradient steps on one batch of experience, while clipping the probability ratio so a step cannot move the new policy too far from the one that collected the data.

cards.front: PPO Clipped Objective: what is the key insight?
cards.back: Reusing a batch of data is efficient but dangerous: the further the policy moves from the one that generated the data, the less the advantages mean. PPO measures movement by the ratio of new to old action probability and stops rewarding progress once that ratio leaves a small band around one, in the direction the advantage wants. Taking the minimum of the clipped and unclipped terms makes the objective a pessimistic bound, so there is no incentive to push further, but a harmful move is still fully penalised.

cards.front: Why take the minimum of the clipped and unclipped terms?
cards.back: It makes the objective a lower bound on the unclipped surrogate. Improvements beyond the clip band are not rewarded, while moves in the harmful direction keep their full gradient.

cards.front: When is the gradient zero?
cards.back: For a positive advantage when the ratio is above 1 plus $\epsilon$, and for a negative advantage when the ratio is below 1 minus $\epsilon$. In those regions the clipped term is a constant.

cards.front: How does PPO relate to TRPO?
cards.back: Both limit how far the policy moves per update. TRPO enforces a KL constraint with second-order optimisation, while PPO uses a first-order clipped objective that is simpler to implement.

cards.front: When should you use PPO Clipped Objective, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: On-policy deep RL and RLHF fine-tuning of language models, where stable updates with minimal tuning matter and rollouts are expensive to collect.

Avoid it when: When sample efficiency from off-policy replay is critical, or in settings with deterministic policies and continuous control tasks where off-policy methods such as SAC are preferred.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of PPO Clipped Objective?
cards.back:
• Clipping bounds the gradient incentive, not the actual policy change; large steps can still overshoot the band
• Advantages are usually normalised per batch; the sign of $\hat{A}$ decides which side of the band is clipped
• Log-probs must be from the policy that sampled the actions and be stored detached
• This is only the policy term; real PPO adds a value-function loss and an entropy bonus, and usually early-stops on KL

cards.front: Key formulas: PPO Clipped Objective
cards.back:
Ratio: $\rho = \frac{\pi_{new}(a|s)}{\pi_{old}(a|s)} = \exp(\mathrm{logp}_{new} - \mathrm{logp}_{old})$
Unclipped: $\rho\cdot\hat{A}$
Clipped: $\mathrm{clip}(\rho,\ 1-\epsilon,\ 1+\epsilon)\cdot\hat{A}$
$L_{CLIP} = \mathrm{mean}\left[\min\left(\rho\hat{A},\ \mathrm{clip}(\rho, 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon)\hat{A}\right)\right]$
Loss to minimise $= -L_{CLIP}$
$\frac{\partial L_{CLIP}}{\partial\,\mathrm{logp}_{new}} = \rho\hat{A}$ if unclipped is the min, else 0
$\hat{A} > 0$: gradient stops once $\rho > 1 + \epsilon$
$\hat{A} < 0$: gradient stops once $\rho < 1 - \epsilon$

cards.front: What is Generalised Advantage Estimation?
cards.back: Estimate how much better an action was than average by summing one-step temporal-difference errors with exponentially decaying weights, trading bias against variance with a single parameter $\lambda$.

cards.front: Generalised Advantage Estimation: what is the key insight?
cards.back: A one-step estimate of an action's advantage trusts the value function heavily: low variance but biased if the critic is wrong. A full Monte-Carlo return trusts only observed rewards: unbiased but noisy. GAE blends them: each TD error $\delta$ looks one step ahead, and the advantage is a decayed sum of future TD errors, with $\gamma\lambda$ controlling how far the sum reaches. Computing it is a simple backward recursion over the trajectory.

cards.front: What do $\lambda = 0$ and $\lambda = 1$ give?
cards.back: $\lambda = 0$ gives the one-step TD error, low variance but biased by the critic. $\lambda = 1$ gives the discounted Monte-Carlo return minus the value baseline, unbiased but high variance.

cards.front: Why is GAE computed backwards?
cards.back: Each advantage equals its own TD error plus $\gamma\lambda$ times the next advantage, so iterating from the end reuses the already-computed suffix and costs linear time.

cards.front: What does the done flag do in the recursion?
cards.back: It removes the bootstrap term at a terminal state and stops the running sum from carrying future advantages across an episode boundary.

cards.front: When should you use Generalised Advantage Estimation, and when not?
cards.back:
Use it when: Actor-critic methods such as PPO and A2C, where a value function is available and advantages should be less noisy than raw returns.

Avoid it when: When no value function is learned (pure REINFORCE with a baseline from returns), or when the critic is so poor that bootstrapping hurts. Off-policy replay needs importance-corrected estimators instead.

cards.front: Common pitfalls of Generalised Advantage Estimation?
cards.back:
• Bootstrap from last_value only if the rollout was cut off; a terminated episode must have done = 1 at its final step
• Time-limit truncation is not a true terminal and should still bootstrap from the value of the final state; this code treats done as terminal
• Values and last_value come from the critic at collection time and are not differentiated through
• This handles one environment; vectorised rollouts apply the same recursion per environment

cards.front: Key formulas: Generalised Advantage Estimation
cards.back:
TD error: $\delta_t = r_t + \gamma\,(1 - d_t)\,V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)$
GAE: $A_t = \sum_{l \geq 0} (\gamma\lambda)^l\,\delta_{t+l}$   (stops at episode end)
Recursion: $A_t = \delta_t + \gamma\lambda\,(1 - d_t)\,A_{t+1}$
$\lambda = 0$:  $A_t = \delta_t$   (one-step TD)
$\lambda = 1$:  $A_t = G_t - V(s_t)$   (Monte-Carlo advantage)
Value target: $A_t + V(s_t)$
$d_t = 1$ if the episode ends after step $t$, else 0

cards.front: Linear models: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: The model is one dot product, so the loss surface is a smooth bowl and the weights can be read as feature effects. Changing the loss (squared, log, hinge) changes the model but not the shape of the idea.

cards.front: Regularisation: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Every regulariser trades a little training fit for lower variance: penalties shrink weights, dropout and noise stop co-adaptation, early stopping limits how far optimisation goes. Pick the one whose bias you can live with.

cards.front: Gradient-based optimisation: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: The gradient says which way is downhill; the learning rate says how far to step. Momentum, adaptive scaling and schedules are all ways of choosing a better step from the same gradient history.

cards.front: Tree ensembles: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: One tree is high variance, so average many decorrelated trees (random forest) or add small trees that each correct the previous errors (boosting). Bagging cuts variance, boosting cuts bias.

cards.front: Probabilistic models: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Write down how the data could have been generated, then fit parameters by maximising likelihood or computing a posterior. Naive Bayes, Gaussian mixtures and logistic regression are all this idea with different assumptions.

cards.front: Distance and clustering: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Everything depends on the distance and the scale of the features. K-means uses centres, DBSCAN uses density, kNN uses the nearest labelled points; all fail if distances are meaningless.

cards.front: Classification metrics: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Accuracy counts all errors equally. Precision, recall and F1 expose the trade-off at one threshold, ROC-AUC summarises all thresholds, and calibration asks whether the probabilities mean what they say.

cards.front: Validation hygiene: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Anything that sees the test data, even through a scaler or feature selection, inflates the score. Fit every preprocessing step inside the training fold only, and keep one untouched final test set.

cards.front: Normalisation: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Subtract a mean and divide by a spread. Feature scaling does it once on the inputs; batch norm and layer norm do it on hidden activations, differing only in which axis the statistics are taken over.

cards.front: Attention and sequences: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Recurrent cells compress the past into one state, which is sequential and forgets. Attention scores every pair of positions directly, so it is parallel and long-range, at the price of quadratic cost and the need for positional information.

cards.front: Dimensionality reduction: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Find the directions that carry the most variance (PCA, via SVD) or learn a compressed code that reconstructs the input (autoencoder). A linear autoencoder spans the same subspace as PCA.

cards.front: Information-theoretic losses: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Cross-entropy equals entropy plus KL divergence, and the entropy of the data is fixed, so minimising cross-entropy minimises KL and maximises likelihood. Those three views are one idea.

cards.front: Network building blocks: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: A network is linear maps separated by non-linearities. Activations decide what gradients survive, and residual connections give the gradient a shortcut so depth stops hurting.

cards.front: Convolution and vision: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Sliding one small kernel over the image reuses its weights everywhere, which gives translation equivariance with few parameters. Pooling then shrinks the map, and IoU with non-maximum suppression cleans up detections.

cards.front: Text processing: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Models need numbers, so text is split into tokens. Tokens are then weighted by how informative they are (TF-IDF), mapped to vectors (word2vec), and generated by searching for the most likely sequence (beam search).

cards.front: Reinforcement learning: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Value methods such as Q-learning learn how good each action is and act greedily on it. Policy-gradient methods such as REINFORCE nudge the policy toward actions that led to high return. Both trade exploration against exploitation.

cards.front: Generative models: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Every generative model turns simple noise into data. VAEs do it with an encoder and a decoder trained on a likelihood bound, GANs with a generator trained against a critic, and diffusion models by learning to undo gradual noising.

cards.front: Transfer and adaptation: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Pretrained weights already encode useful features, so train only a small part (a head or low-rank update) or let a small student imitate the big teacher's outputs. You keep most of the accuracy for a fraction of the cost.

cards.front: Time series: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Time series break the independence assumption, so we model the memory directly. Exponential smoothing keeps a decaying average, autocorrelation measures how far back the memory reaches, and ARIMA turns that memory into a regression on past values after differencing away trends.

cards.front: Graph neural networks: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: One layer aggregates each node's neighbours (a normalised sum, or an attention-weighted sum) and then transforms the result with shared weights. Stacking k layers lets information travel k hops, but too many layers blur all nodes together.

cards.front: Preference alignment and policy gradients: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: A pairwise Bradley-Terry loss turns preferences into a reward score. DPO folds that reward into the policy's own log-ratios, so no separate reward model or sampling loop is needed. PPO and advantage estimation do the reinforcement-learning version, clipping how far each update can move the policy.

cards.front: Text evaluation and retrieval: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Overlap metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE count shared n-grams, so they are cheap but blind to meaning. Retrieval metrics judge the ranked list: recall at k asks whether the answer was found, MRR rewards finding it early, and nDCG also values graded relevance.

cards.front: Decoding and sampling: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Generation is a loop that converts logits into one token, appends it and repeats. Greedy takes the argmax, temperature rescales logits before the softmax, top-k and top-p drop the unlikely tail and renormalise before sampling, and beam search keeps the best few partial sequences by total log probability.

cards.front: LLM efficiency and parallelism: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Large-model serving and training are resource budgeting. Memory is weights plus the key-value cache, and both shrink when fewer bytes are stored per number. Speed is bounded by the lower of peak compute and bandwidth times arithmetic intensity, so decoding is usually bandwidth bound, and parallelism buys capacity by spending communication.

cards.front: Prompting and context: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: A prompt is an input you can engineer. Fill a fixed template with the task and examples, pack the most useful context into a token budget, then parse and validate the reply against a schema so that failures are caught. To choose between prompts, score both on the same cases and compare the paired results rather than overall averages.

cards.front: LLM safety and guardrails: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Language models cannot reliably tell instructions from data, so safety is built around them rather than inside them. Untrusted text is fenced and scanned on the way in, model output is validated against a contract on the way out, and each layer is an independent check with its own catch rate. If the layers fail independently, the chance that a bad item passes all of them is the product of one minus each catch rate.

cards.front: Agent building blocks: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: An agent is a loop of model decision, tool call and observation, and the surrounding code owns the control. A registry validates tool names and arguments, a step limit guarantees termination, and a state graph makes the allowed transitions explicit. Memory, planning, reflection and multi-agent designs are variations on what is stored in the context and who gets to act next.

cards.front: LLM production operations: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Production model serving is controlled by a few simple rules. Retries use exponential backoff with jitter so clients do not stampede, a token bucket caps the request rate, and a circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency until it recovers. Capacity follows Little's law, concurrency equals arrival rate times latency, which turns a traffic forecast into a number of workers.

cards.front: RAG pipeline stages: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Retrieval-augmented generation is a pipeline, and an error in an early stage cannot be repaired later. Chunking with overlap decides what can be found, embedding and cosine similarity find candidates, reciprocal rank fusion merges rankings from different retrievers without comparing their raw scores, and recall at k tells you whether the evidence even reached the generator.

cards.front: LLM evaluation methods: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Every evaluation method is a measuring instrument with its own bias, so pick one that matches the question and attach uncertainty to it. Perplexity summarises token log-probabilities, n-gram overlap compares text to a reference, and pairwise judging yields a win rate whose exact sign test says whether the gap beats chance, while Elo turns head-to-head results into a running rating.

cards.front: Multimodal and speech: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: A transformer only reads a sequence of vectors, so every modality is cut into pieces and projected. An image becomes non-overlapping patches, a video becomes a few sampled frames each turned into patches, and audio becomes overlapping windows whose count follows from window length and hop. Knowing the token count in advance is what makes the cost and the context budget predictable.

cards.front: Math foundations: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Almost every model reduces to a few primitives. Norms and dot products turn vectors into lengths and angles, repeated matrix-vector products expose the dominant eigenvector, the chain rule gives gradients that a central difference can verify, and the inverse cumulative distribution turns uniform noise into any distribution. Learning these once lets you read and debug everything built on top.

cards.front: Programming and tooling: what is the shared idea?
cards.back: Good data code pushes work out of the interpreter and into array operations, so broadcasting rules decide shapes instead of loops. It streams data lazily with generators so memory stays flat, and it fixes every source of randomness with a seed. Hashing a canonical form of the configuration then gives a stable fingerprint, so a run can be named, compared and reproduced.

cards.front: Compare: Ridge vs Lasso: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick ridge when most features carry some signal or are correlated.
• Pick lasso when you expect only a few features to matter and want a sparse model.
• Use elastic net when features are correlated and you still want sparsity.

cards.front: Compare: Random forest vs Gradient boosting: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick a random forest for a strong, low-tuning baseline that is hard to overfit.
• Pick gradient boosting when you can tune carefully and want the best accuracy on tabular data.
• Prefer the forest when training must parallelise easily, because boosting is sequential.

cards.front: Compare: Batch norm vs Layer norm: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick batch norm for convolutional networks with reasonably large batches.
