• Pick layer norm for transformers and recurrent models, or when batches are tiny or vary.
• Pick layer norm when training and evaluation behaviour must be identical.

cards.front: Compare: Precision-recall vs ROC: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick precision-recall when positives are rare and false alarms matter.
• Pick ROC-AUC when classes are fairly balanced or both error types matter equally.
• Report both when stakeholders care about different parts of the trade-off.

cards.front: Compare: SGD with momentum vs Adam: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick SGD with momentum for well-tuned vision training where the best final accuracy matters.
• Pick Adam for fast progress with little tuning, especially for transformers and sparse gradients.
• Pick Adam when parameters have very different gradient scales.

cards.front: Compare: PCA vs Autoencoder: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick PCA for a fast, deterministic, interpretable linear projection.
• Pick an autoencoder when the structure is curved and you have enough data to train one.
• Start with PCA as a baseline; an autoencoder must beat it to be worth the effort.

cards.front: Compare: k-means vs Gaussian mixture: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick k-means for fast, simple clustering of roughly round, equal-sized groups.
• Pick a Gaussian mixture when clusters differ in size or are elliptical.
• Pick the mixture when you need membership probabilities.

cards.front: Compare: k-means vs DBSCAN: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick k-means when you know roughly how many clusters there are and they are compact.
• Pick DBSCAN when clusters have odd shapes or the data has outliers.
• Avoid DBSCAN when the density varies a lot between clusters.

cards.front: Compare: LSTM vs Attention: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick attention for long-range dependencies and parallel training on modern hardware.
• Pick a recurrent cell for streaming input with small, constant memory per step.
• Pick attention-based models when you have enough data and compute.

cards.front: Compare: VAE vs GAN: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick a VAE when you need a smooth latent space and stable training.
• Pick a GAN when sharp, realistic samples matter more than stability.
• Pick a VAE when you also need to encode real data into latents.

cards.front: Compare: Naive Bayes vs Logistic regression: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick naive Bayes when data is tiny or very high-dimensional, such as text.
• Pick logistic regression when you have enough data and correlated features.
• Pick naive Bayes for a very fast baseline that trains in one pass.

cards.front: Compare: Squared error vs Cross-entropy: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick squared error for regression with roughly Gaussian noise.
• Pick cross-entropy for classification with softmax or sigmoid outputs.
• Avoid squared error on probabilities, because its gradient vanishes when the output saturates.

cards.front: Compare: Decoder vs Encoder vs Encoder-Decoder: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick a decoder-only model (causal mask, next-token loss) for open-ended generation, chat and in-context learning.
• Pick an encoder (bidirectional mask, masked-token loss) for classification, tagging, retrieval embeddings and other understanding tasks.
• Pick an encoder-decoder (bidirectional encoder, causal decoder, cross-attention) for input-to-output tasks such as translation and summarisation.
• If you must generate long free text, an encoder alone cannot do it, because it has no left-to-right factorisation.

cards.front: Compare: LoRA vs QLoRA vs Full Fine-Tuning: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick full fine-tuning when you have the memory budget and need the largest possible shift in behaviour.
• Pick LoRA when you want most of the quality with a tiny trainable footprint and small adapter files per task.
• Pick QLoRA when the frozen base model in 16 bits does not fit on your GPU but a 4-bit copy does.
• Prefer LoRA over QLoRA if memory is not the limit, since quantisation adds a little noise and some speed cost.

cards.front: Compare: RAG vs Fine-Tuning: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick RAG when facts change often, or when answers must cite a source or respect per-user access rules.
• Pick fine-tuning when you need a consistent style, output format, tone or a skill the base model lacks.
• Combine them when you need both: fine-tune for format and behaviour, retrieve for the facts.
• Try prompting first if neither updates nor format needs are strong, since it is cheapest.

cards.front: Compare: BPE vs WordPiece vs Unigram: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick BPE for a simple, fast, deterministic merge list; it is the common choice for byte-level generative models.
• Pick WordPiece when you want merges that favour pairs which belong together rather than pairs of merely common parts.
• Pick Unigram when you want a probabilistic vocabulary, several possible segmentations and subword sampling for regularisation.
• For any of them, train the vocabulary on text that matches your deployment language and domain.

cards.front: Compare: RLHF vs DPO: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick DPO when you have a fixed set of preference pairs and want a simple, stable supervised-style training loop.
• Pick RLHF when you need an explicit reusable reward model, or want the policy to learn from its own fresh samples.
• Pick RLHF when the reward can be queried online, for example from a verifier or a live preference source.
• Pick DPO first if compute or engineering time is limited, since it needs no sampler and no reward model.

cards.front: Compare: BM25 vs Dense Retrieval: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick BM25 when queries contain identifiers, error codes, names or rare jargon that must match literally.
• Pick dense retrieval when users paraphrase, ask in natural language or write in another language than the documents.
• Pick hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion when you cannot predict the query mix, which is the usual case.
• Start with BM25 as the baseline, since it needs no training and is hard to beat on in-domain keyword queries.

cards.front: Compare: Greedy vs Sampling vs Beam Search: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick greedy when you need the cheapest, fully repeatable output and the task has one clear answer.
• Pick beam search for translation, summarisation or speech, where the highest-probability whole sequence is the goal.
• Pick temperature plus top-p sampling for open-ended text, chat and creative writing, where varied output matters.
• Avoid beam search for open-ended generation; it favours bland, repetitive text.

cards.front: Compare: Tensor vs Pipeline Parallelism: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick tensor parallelism inside a node, where fast links such as NVLink make a per-layer all-reduce cheap.
• Pick pipeline parallelism across nodes, where only small activations cross the slow link between stages.
• Use both together for very large models, tensor inside a node and pipeline across nodes.
• Use many micro-batches with pipeline parallelism, otherwise the idle bubble wastes the devices.

cards.front: Compare: Int8 vs NF4 vs Pruning: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick int8 when you want a near-lossless 2x memory saving with simple, widely supported kernels.
• Pick NF4 to fit a model in 4 bits, especially for fine-tuning with LoRA adapters on a frozen base.
• Pick magnitude pruning when sparse kernels or hardware can turn zeros into real speed or size savings.
• Combine pruning with quantization when you need to shrink the model further.

cards.front: Compare: ReAct vs Plan-and-Execute: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick ReAct when the next step depends on what earlier tools return and the path cannot be known upfront.
• Pick plan-and-execute when the task has known sub-tasks, some of which are independent and can run in parallel.
• Pick plan-and-execute to cut cost and latency, since the planner is called once rather than at every step.
• Add a re-planning step to plan-and-execute when tool results can invalidate the plan.

cards.front: Compare: MHA vs GQA vs Sliding Window: when to pick which?
cards.back:
• Pick multi-head attention for the best quality when memory and long contexts are not a constraint.
• Pick grouped-query attention to shrink the KV cache and speed up decoding with little quality loss.
• Pick sliding-window attention when sequences are very long and local context is enough for most tokens.
• Combine grouped-query and sliding-window attention to cut both cache size and attended positions.
